title: How to train a quadruped robot to walk with reinforcement learning on one GPU
description:
Teaching a four-legged robot to walk is the "hello world" of robot reinforcement learning: thousands of copies of the robot try to follow velocity commands in parallel, and PPO turns their attempts into a walking policy. This walkthrough sets up a Unitree Go2 velocity task with Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning built on MuJoCo Warp and Newton, and shows the one command that trains it.

pip install alloy-engine gymnasium

1. Build the environment and step it 

import numpy as np
from alloy.envs.loco import go2_velocity

env = go2_velocity(num_envs=2, device="cpu")
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
print(env.obs_groups, {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in obs.items()})
for _ in range(10):
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(np.zeros((2, 12), np.float32))   # zeros hold the stand
print(tuple(reward.shape), env.xp.to_numpy(env.state["base.height"]).round(2))
env.close()

('policy', 'critic') {'policy': (2, 55), 'critic': (2, 79)}
(2,) [0.27 0.27]

The environment returns two observation groups: 55 numbers for the policy (what a real robot could measure) and 79 for the critic (the same plus values only a simulator knows, which helps training). The action is 12 joint targets; zeros hold the standing pose, with the base 0.27 m above the ground. The first build compiles kernels, so it takes a few minutes on a CPU.

2. Train on a GPU with one command 

pip install "alloy-engine[envs]" rsl-rl-lib
python -m alloy.envs.loco.train --num-envs 4096 --iterations 400 --out runs/go2

This trains PPO with rsl_rl across 4,096 parallel Go2 worlds on one NVIDIA GPU, prints a line every 25 iterations and saves the checkpoint as runs/go2/model_last.pt. Add --terrain rough to train on rough tiles instead of flat ground.

Alloy also ships wrappers for Stable-Baselines3 and skrl; the RL guide covers them.

Keep in mind

  • The policy walks blind: it has no height scan, and there are no stairs or gaps.
  • There is no actuator model, and no policy trained this way has been run on a real robot yet.
  • Training in practice needs a GPU. The docs keep the full list of limits.

Links

  • Docs page this is based on: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/how-to/quadruped-rl/
  • Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16312

title: Every despill formula bets on colours your subject isn't wearing
description:
A despill step is usually one line of maths, picked from whichever tutorial came first. To see what the three common lines cost, the comparison here uses a self-made 1280×720 test card with a green screen at RGB(20,175,65) and ten patches: hair strands, a white shirt, a light-blue shirt, light and dark skin, a yellow object and a grey veil at α=0.45. Clean foreground and alpha are known. The spill is not real light; it was added with a model that peaks at the outline, so the numbers describe this card only. Results are composited on grey (110,110,110) with the true alpha and compared to the clean version as ΔE76, hue as the HSV angle. One Apple-silicon Mac, Python and NumPy, FFmpeg for one cross-check, single run.

Spill sits on the outline more than inside

Uncorrected, the hair strands carried 30.7 of extra green, ΔE 24.0. The veil at α=0.45 came out with G about 41 above R and B, ΔE 28.8. The white shirt read ΔE 16.6 on its 6-pixel edge and 7.8 inside. Light skin was the worst case: its edge moved from hue 23° to 70°, ΔE 34.5, against 11.7 in the interior. Per pixel, a despill formula has to decide whether this green came from the screen or the object. It can't know, so it assumes.

Average-limit assumes nothing is greener than its neighbours

G = min(G, (R+B)/2) was the cleanest on almost everything: hair ΔE 6.2, veil 6.5, light-blue shirt 2.7. Its bet is that no real colour in the shot has green above the mean of red and blue, which yellow breaks by definition. The yellow patch, clean at (245,205,30), went from (248,228,39) with spill to (248,143,39) after the formula, hue 49° to 30°, ΔE 39.4. Untouched it was 12.1. Yellow-greens and pale cyans sit on the same side of the line. FFmpeg's despill filter at its defaults (mix 0.5, expand 0) matched this formula within 1 per pixel on this card. Its source wasn't read for this, so the claim stops at "almost the same on this card".

Max-limit assumes spill always pushes green to the top

G = min(G, max(R,B)) is the cautious one: yellow and skin interiors were not touched at all. That's its failure too. The light-blue shirt, clean at (196,214,236), picked up spill to (198,237,244). Green rose by 23, but it stayed under blue at 244, so the formula saw nothing to remove and left ΔE 12.3 exactly as it was. The light-skin edge stayed at (227,227,168), hue 60°, ΔE 27.6. The hidden bet is that spill only exists once green becomes the largest channel, and on pale blue or warm skin it can add a lot without winning.

Complement-fill assumes the lost energy belongs to magenta

The third family gives some of the removed green back to red and blue so the pixel doesn't darken. The variant used here takes s = max(0, G − (R+B)/2), subtracts s from green and adds s/2 to each of red and blue. Brightness held up, but the refill overshot. The light-skin edge came out (246,197,188), hue 23° to 9°, pink. The veil and the white shirt edge drifted toward purple, hues between 256° and 286°. Yellow was the worst result in the whole table, ΔE 50.8 inside and 54.3 on its edge. The refill ratio wasn't swept, so whether some split keeps skin warm without hurting yellow is still open.

One drift sits outside the formulas: after average-limit, half-transparent areas such as the hair strands landed on a blue-grey near hue 210°, because the screen has B=65 and R=20 and removing its green leaves the blue behind. That's a missing step, subtracting the screen colour first, not an assumption of any formula.

Choose the formula per shot as a policy

Formula What it assumes What broke on this card
Average-limit Nothing real is greener than (R+B)/2 Yellow 49° to 30°, ΔE 39.4
Max-limit Spill always makes green the top channel Light-blue shirt untouched, ΔE 12.3; skin edge ΔE 27.6
Complement-fill (s/2 to R and B) Removed green should return as magenta Skin edge 23° to 9°; yellow ΔE 50.8

Three years on codecs taught me to read every rounding rule as a choice of which error to ship, and this table reads the same way. Yellow props mean average-limit, and FFmpeg's default with it, will damage them, so max-limit or a mask is safer. Pale blue clothes or light skin under heavy spill mean max-limit leaves the green alone. Complement-fill trades skin tone for brightness. I'd record the choice per shot next to the key settings rather than bake one line into the pipeline.

The step belongs after alpha and before compositing; run before the key, it turned the screen dark blue-grey and the keyer stopped seeing it. AI matting doesn't remove the decision either. A real green-screen clip went through the video matting Beta of ImgIng https://imging.ai/ in a desktop Chromium-based browser, with the model running locally. Composited over grey at frame 45, its transparent WebM still had green-leaning pixels at the hair tips and on the hand, from 2.7% to 14.8% depending on region and on which of its two models produced the matte; average-limit took every one of those counts to zero. That module isn't mine. My reading is that the model returns transparency and the colour usually comes from the source frame, so the assumption is still yours to pick. Credit for the real clip goes to VOA Learning English via Wikimedia Commons (public domain; trimmed and re-encoded here). The test card is self-made, with spill added by a model.

title: Stacked sixes, safe stars and bonus rolls: how I coded Ludo's turn rules for a multiplayer browser game
description:
Ludo is the game everyone thinks they know. Roll a 6 to get out, race round the board, knock people home. Then you sit four people down and find out that everybody grew up with slightly different rules.

Ludo is one of the 60+ games on mympgames, my free multiplayer browser arcade, and it was harder to get right than chess. The board is easy. The turn flow is where it gets tricky: sixes that stack, a third six that cancels everything, bonus rolls that arrive in the middle of spending other dice, and a handful of house rules the host can switch on. This post walks through the server-side rules module, with real code (trimmed a little), and the decisions behind it.

One number per token

The first decision was how to store a token's position. Instead of storing board coordinates, every token is a single integer of progress relative to its own start square:

const TRACK = 52;  // squares on the shared loop
const ENTRY = 50;  // last shared square before the home column
const COL0  = 52;  // first home-column square
const HOME  = 57;
const START = { red: 0, green: 13, yellow: 26, blue: 39 };
const SAFE  = new Set([0, 8, 13, 21, 26, 34, 39, 47]);

// -1 = base, 0..51 = main track, 52..56 = home column, 57 = home
function absSquare(color, p) {
  return (START[color] + p) % TRACK;
}

That makes most questions trivial. "Is this token in base?" is p === -1. "Is it safe forever?" is p > 51. "How far along is it?" is just p, which the computer opponent uses directly. The only time I need the absolute square is when two colours might meet, so absSquare converts on demand, and captures and safe squares are checked in absolute terms.

The drawing code on the client does the reverse mapping to pixels. The rules never know what the board looks like.

Rule one: sixes stack, three sixes forfeit

In the turn flow I implemented (the style most people know from Ludo apps), a 6 doesn't move you straight away. You roll again, and the dice pile up. 6, 6, 4 means three dice to spend. Three 6s in a row and the whole turn is lost.

That rule is mostly a pending array and a counter:

function roll(st, seat) {
  if (seat !== st.turn) return { ok: false, error: 'Not your turn' };
  if (st.phase !== 'roll') return { ok: false, error: 'Use your dice first' };
  const d = rollDie(st);
  if (d === 6) st.sixes += 1;
  if (st.sixes === 3) {
    passTurn(st);            // all pending dice are thrown away
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.pending.push(d);
  if (d === 6) {
    st.phase = 'roll';       // keep rolling
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.sixes = 0;
  if (legalByDie(st).every((l) => !l.length)) {
    st.pending = [];         // nothing can move: drop the dice
    endOfDice(st);
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.phase = 'move';
  return { ok: true };
}

The phase field (roll, move, done) is the backbone. Every action checks it first, so a client that sends "move" while the server expects "roll" just gets an error back. There is no way to move twice or roll in the middle of spending dice.

Dice come from crypto.randomInt(1, 7) on the server. The rules factory also accepts an injected RNG, which is what the tests use to get repeatable games.

Rule two: moving is walking a path

Once the dice are rolled, the player spends them one at a time, in any order, on one token or split across several. The core function answers "where would this token end up with this die, and is that legal?" by literally walking the squares:

function step(st, seat, p) {
  if (p === ENTRY) return canEnterHome(st, seat) ? COL0 : 51;
  if (p === 51) return 0;
  return p + 1;
}

function pathFor(st, seat, token, d) {
  const p0 = st.tokens[seat][token];
  if (p0 === HOME) return null;
  if (p0 === -1) return leavesBase(st, d) ? [0] : null;
  const path = [];
  let p = p0;
  for (let k = 0; k < d; k++) {
    p = step(st, seat, p);
    if (p > HOME) return null;                 // overshot
    path.push(p);
    if (p === HOME && k < d - 1) return null;  // exact roll to finish
  }
  return path;
}

I could have done the arithmetic in one line, but walking square by square pays off three ways:

  1. Exact finish falls out of the loop. You can't overshoot home.
  2. The path is returned. The client animates the token hop by hop along it, and everyone sees the same route.
  3. Walls are easy. With the optional "blocks" rule, two tokens of one colour on a square form a wall that rivals can't land on or pass. That's one extra check inside the loop. A 6 is allowed to jump a wall, so a game can't deadlock with everyone stuck behind one.

step is also where the "kill before you go home" house rule lives. If a player hasn't captured anyone yet, square 50 leads to 51 and then back to 0 instead of into the home column, so the token keeps circling. Without that rule, 51 is never reached.

Legal moves are then just "every token whose pathFor isn't null". The server never keeps a separate rulebook for validation. A move is legal if and only if pathFor returns a path.

Rule three: captures, safe squares and partners

When a token lands on the main track, anything on that absolute square that isn't a friend goes back to base, unless the square is safe:

if (to <= 51) {
  const sq = absSquare(color, to);
  if (!isSafe(st, sq)) {
    for (const v of occupants(st, sq)) {
      if (friends(st, v.seat, seat)) continue;
      st.tokens[v.seat][v.token] = -1;
      (captured ||= []).push(v);
    }
  }
}
if (st.rules.bonusRoll && (captured || to === HOME)) st.bonusRolls += 1;

friends covers both "it's my own token" and team mode, where red and yellow play green and blue and partners can't capture each other. That one helper is reused by the wall check and the computer opponent, so teams only had to be taught once.

The tricky part: a bonus roll while dice are still pending

Here's the case that took me longest. You roll 6, then 3. You use the 3 first and it captures someone. You've earned a bonus roll, but you still owe the 6. What happens?

The answer I settled on: the bonus roll comes now, and its result joins the dice you still hold. So you roll again, get a 2, and now spend the 6 and the 2.

function endOfDice(st) {
  if (st.bonusRolls > 0) {
    st.bonusRolls -= 1;
    st.sixes = 0;
    st.phase = 'roll';      // pending dice are kept
    return;
  }
  if (st.pending.length && legalByDie(st).every((l) => !l.length)) {
    st.pending = [];        // leftover dice nobody can use
  }
  if (st.pending.length) { st.phase = 'move'; return; }
  passTurn(st);
}

Unless the move finishes that player's game, it ends in endOfDice, which decides in a fixed order: bonus roll first, then keep spending, then drop useless dice, then pass. Putting all of the "what happens next" logic in one function meant fixing this ordering once instead of in every branch.

Fewer pointless clicks

Ludo has lots of forced moves: one token out, one die, nothing else legal. Asking a player to tap their only option every time feels slow. The rules module works out the distinct choices, treating two tokens on the same square or two equal dice as the same move:

function choices(st, seat = st.turn) {
  const seen = new Map();
  st.pending.forEach((d, di) => {
    for (const t of legalMoves(st, seat, d)) {
      const k = `${st.tokens[seat][t]}:${d}`;
      if (!seen.has(k)) seen.set(k, { token: t, die: di, value: d });
    }
  });
  return [...seen.values()];
}

If there's exactly one, the view marks it as auto and the client plays it after a short beat. The server still validates it like any other move. The client just saves you a tap.

Keeping everyone in sync

In a multiplayer room, the risk is that a fast player or a bot moves while another screen is still animating the last move. So the server game wrapper puts an animation budget on each action and refuses the next one until it has played out:

if (st.animUntil && Date.now() < st.animUntil - GRACE)
  return { ok: false, error: 'Wait for the move to finish' };

The budget is computed from the move itself: a fixed time per square in the path, plus a pause and a "slide back to base" for any capture. Computer seats use the same number as their delay before acting. The tradeoff is a slightly slower game, but every player and spectator sees the same hop-by-hop move instead of tokens teleporting.

The computer opponent

The bot doesn't search ahead. Dice make deep search expensive and the benefit is small, so it scores each legal (token, die) pair and picks the best. Capturing is worth a lot, more if the victim was far along. Getting home, leaving base and reaching a safe square or the home column all add points. Landing within six squares in front of a rival subtracts points, and moving a token out of danger adds them. A little randomness keeps it from feeling robotic. Because it calls the same legalByDie, it can't make an illegal move, and house rules work for it automatically.

What I'd tell someone building Ludo

  • Store progress, not coordinates. One integer per token makes rules, bots and house rules much simpler.
  • Make the turn a small state machine. phase, pending, sixes and bonusRolls are enough to describe every point in a turn, and each action checks them first.
  • Return paths, not just destinations. Validation, walls, exact finishes and animation all reuse the same walk.
  • Put "what happens next" in one place. Most of my bugs were ordering bugs, and endOfDice is where they got fixed.

You can try all of this at mympgames.com/play/ludo. It's free and runs in the browser, with friends or computer players in empty seats. If Ludo isn't your thing, there are 60+ other games at mympgames.com.

title: GeoBIM for an Airport: Keeping BIM, GIS, and the Tunnel in One Coordinate System
description:
Most coordination failures I have seen on airport work were not geometry failures. They were unit failures. One team exports feet, another exports meters, and the tunnel arrives 3.28 times too long. The model still looks convincing, which is what makes it dangerous.
The project was HNTB's airport redevelopment: a terminal expansion, new boarding bridges, adjusted stand positions, and a deep tunnel beneath the apron. My work sat between the BIM team and the GIS team. I wrote the transforms, ran the checks, and kept the merge log. That space between the two teams is the GeoBIM gap.

Two origins, one model

BIM models usually start at a local origin near the building. GIS data arrives in a projected coordinate system, often a state plane zone or a UTM zone. Neither is wrong. They are just different answers to the question of where zero is. Before any merge, we picked one projected system, documented the EPSG code, and defined the vertical datum. Everything else converted into that frame. We called it the project frame. It had a name, a number, and a keeper.
The rule was simple: if a file did not state its coordinate system, it did not enter the merge. No exceptions for small layers. Small layers are how a fence ends up in the river. We also kept a short manifest for each layer: source, date, units, owner. It fit on one screen and answered most questions before they became meetings.

The transform in code

The conversion itself is short. The care is in the details around it.
Two things bite here. Axis order is one; some libraries expect latitude before longitude, and some expect the reverse, so we always use always_xy and test with a known point. Units are the other; a State Plane system may be in survey feet while the design is in meters. The vertical datum is a third. A model can be perfect in plan and eleven inches off in elevation.

Three checks before the first merge

We ran three checks in Python before anyone looked at the model. First, control points: eight survey monuments, each within two centimeters. Second, a bounding box sanity check: does the terminal sit inside the airport fence, and does the fence sit inside the county? Third, a vertical check against two known benchmarks. If any check failed, the merge stopped. We logged the results next to the file name, so the next person could see what had been verified. The control points were not evenly spread, which made the far taxiway the real test.
The checks caught more than bad data. They caught bad habits. A vendor once shipped a model that had been rotated ninety degrees to fit a drawing sheet. The bounding box did not notice. The control points did.

Where GeoBIM paid for itself

The tunnel was the reason. It carried the baggage system, a corridor for passengers, and a utility bank, and each had a clearance envelope. In a federated model, we could cut a section anywhere along its 900 feet and see all three at once. A clash detection pass found a duct bank intruding into the passenger envelope. Moving it in the model cost an afternoon. Moving it after the tunnel lining was poured would have cost a season.

Generated massing has a place

When we needed options, not answers, I used GenAnywhere. I selected the apron area on the map, generated a massing model, and dropped it into the same coordinate system. It gave us a believable mesh in minutes, at a level of detail that was honest about what it was. We used it to kill weak layouts before they earned a survey. It does not carry systems, and it should not. A massing study that pretends to be a design is worse than a sketch. The massing model inherits the coordinate system of the selection, not of the CAD file, which is one less thing to convert.

The rule I keep

Put the coordinate system in the file name and the document header. If two people on the same project cannot answer where the origin is, stop and fix that before modeling anything else. Interoperability starts with a number everyone agrees on. Everything after that is just geometry. A number everyone agrees on is cheaper than a meeting about a number.

title: How we read Korea's crypto licence register, and why the file fights back
description:
In Korea a crypto business may serve customers only on a report that the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (KoFIU) has accepted, renewed every three years. KoFIU publishes the list of those businesses, but not as an API: it is an Excel file attached to a notice on its board, and the link to that file changes on every page load.

We read it every day for X-RAY, and today we are publishing the reader as open source: github.com/xrayme1337/kofiu-vasp-register.

Three things make the file hard to read:

  1. The download works only inside the session that listed the notice. The file id is minted per request and tied to a cookie, so the reader lists the board, keeps the cookies and downloads in the same session.
  2. The header is not fixed. Some months it is one row, some months two, with group cells such as a renewal heading above its date. The reader maps a column only by its whole label and fails loudly on a label it does not know, instead of guessing.
  3. The file carries personal data next to company data: the representative's name and the office address. The reader never reads those columns, and masks phone numbers and e-mail addresses in anything it logs.

What it returns per provider: the service and legal name, the business registration number (with its check digit verified), the businesses it may run (buying and selling, exchange, transfer, custody, brokerage), and the dates of acceptance, renewal and any cancellation. A provider that leaves the file is reported as having left it, never as revoked: the file does not say why.

The data is public under Korea's Public Data Act; credit KoFIU (kofiu.go.kr) where you show it.

If you would rather not run a scraper, X-RAY serves the whole register, with each provider tied to its company, to AI agents over MCP: x-ray.me/registers/korea-vasps.

title: DSA
description:
Bubble Sort in Java

Introduction

Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm used to arrange elements in ascending or descending order.

It works by comparing two adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order.

Example

Let's take an array:

int[] arr = {11, 13, 10, 9};

Our goal is to sort it in ascending order.

Pass 1:

11 13 10 9
11 10 13 9
11 10 9 13

Pass 2:

10 11 9 13
10 9 11 13

Pass 3:

9 10 11 13

Now the array is sorted!

Java Code 

for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j < n - i; j++) {

        if (arr[j] < arr[j - 1]) {
            int temp = arr[j];
            arr[j] = arr[j - 1];
            arr[j - 1] = temp;
        }

    }
}

How It Works

  • Outer loop controls the number of passes.
  • Inner loop compares adjacent elements.
  • If the current element is smaller than the previous element, they are swapped.
  • After every pass, the largest unsorted element moves to the end.

Time Complexity

  • Best Case: O(n²)
  • Average Case: O(n²)
  • Worst Case: O(n²)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Conclusion

Bubble Sort is easy to understand and implement. It is a good starting point for learning sorting algorithms in Java.

title: Conversation-Level vs Trace-Level Online Evals: Which Failures Each Can See
description:
The unit you evaluate decides which failures you can see. A span-level evaluator judges one model call. A trace-level evaluator judges one request through the agent, including its tool calls. A conversation-level evaluator judges the whole multi-turn session after it ends. Most agent failures that cost customers only exist at the conversation level, but most eval tooling started at the span.

This is not a question of which is better. Each unit catches failures the others cannot, and each has a cost. For the broader picture of online evaluation, start with what are online evals.

The three units

Unit What the judge reads When it can run Typical cost per judgment
Span One LLM call: prompt, completion, maybe one tool call Immediately Low
Trace One request: the user turn, every step and tool call, the final answer When the request completes Medium
Conversation (session, thread) Every turn of the interaction, in order After the conversation ends or goes idle Higher

Vendors use different names. LangSmith calls conversations "threads", Arize and PostHog call them "sessions", Opik uses "threads". The idea is the same.

Failures only a conversation-level eval can see

Each of these passes every span and trace check:

  • Repetition and rephrasing. The user asks the same thing three ways. Each answer is plausible on its own. See repetition as a red flag.
  • Skipped prerequisite. The agent changes an account email in turn 6 but never verified identity in turns 1 to 5.
  • Contradiction across turns. The agent quotes one price in turn 2 and another in turn 7.
  • Unresolved goal. Every response is polite and accurate, and the user's actual request is never handled.
  • Silent abandonment. The user stops replying after a confusing answer. There is no error and no thumbs-down. See users who silently give up.
  • Late false completion. The agent says "done" in the last turn, and the action failed three turns earlier.

Failures a trace-level eval catches better

Conversation-level judging is not a replacement for trace and span checks:

  • Wrong tool or bad arguments. Visible inside one request. A trace check can point to the exact step.
  • Ungrounded answer. The answer contradicts the document retrieved for that same request.
  • Format and schema errors. Better handled by code at the span level.
  • Latency and cost outliers. Per-step metrics, not judgments.
  • Duplicate tool calls. See detecting duplicate tool calls.

A conversation judge reading 30 turns can miss a subtle argument error in step 4 of turn 12. Narrow checks are more precise for narrow failures.

The timing problem

A trace is complete when the request returns. A conversation has no clear end: users come back after lunch, or never reply.

Judging too early creates false failures. The identity check looks skipped because it happens next turn. The question looks unanswered because the answer is still coming. So conversation-level evaluators usually wait for inactivity, and the defaults vary widely. LangSmith's multi-turn evaluators wait until a thread has been idle for 10 minutes by default. Datadog treats a session as complete after 30 minutes of inactivity. Braintrust's trace and group scores wait 30 seconds by default, and Opik's thread rules use a configurable cooldown. Agnost waits for 15 minutes of inactivity before judging.

The trade-off is latency. A conversation-level eval cannot tell you about a failure while the conversation is still happening. If you need that, you need a guardrail in the request path, not an online eval. See online evals vs guardrails vs monitoring.

Choosing a unit for each evaluator

Question you are asking Unit
Is this output valid JSON? Span (code)
Did the agent pick the right tool with the right arguments? Trace
Does the answer match what was retrieved? Trace
Did the user get what they came for? Conversation
Was a required step done before the action? Conversation
Did the agent contradict itself or loop? Conversation
Did the agent claim success that didn't happen? Conversation plus outcome event

Running both without double-counting

When the same failure can be flagged at several levels, rates become confusing. Three rules help:

  1. Assign each failure to one unit. "Wrong refund amount" lives at the trace level; "refund never resolved" lives at the conversation level.
  2. Point conversation verdicts at a turn. A conversation-level judge should return which message failed, so the finding links to the trace that produced it.
  3. Report conversation rates per conversation, trace rates per trace. Mixing denominators makes a failure look ten times more or less common than it is.

Where Agnost fits

Agnost runs its online evals at the conversation level. After a conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, an LLM judge reads it from start to finish against your plain-English rules and flags the specific assistant messages that broke one. That keeps the advantage of whole-conversation context while making every finding point to a turn you can open. Tool calls nested under a turn are left out of the judge's transcript and tracked separately, with success rates and error distributions. If a rule depends on a tool outcome, record that outcome as its own event.

If your team already runs span or trace evals in a tracing tool, the conversation layer is the gap to fill. The online evaluation tools comparison shows which tools judge at which units, and evals, traces, and conversations covers how the layers fit together.

Frequently asked questions

What is a conversation-level online eval?

A conversation-level (also called session-level or thread-level) online eval judges an entire multi-turn interaction after it ends, rather than a single model call or request. It can see patterns across turns, such as a user repeating a question, a required step skipped several turns before an action, or a goal that was never resolved.

When should I use trace-level evals instead?

Use trace-level evals for failures contained within one request: a wrong tool choice, bad tool arguments, an answer that contradicts the document retrieved in the same request, or a slow step. They are cheaper per judgment and can run as soon as the trace arrives.

Why wait for a conversation to go idle before judging it?

Judging a conversation that is still in progress produces false failures: a step that looks skipped may happen two turns later, and a question that looks unanswered may be answered next. Most tools wait for a period of inactivity, often around 15 minutes, before running a conversation-level judge.

Are conversation-level evals more expensive?

Per judgment, yes, because the judge reads more tokens. Per useful finding, often not, because one conversation-level judgment can replace several trace-level ones and catches failures they cannot see. Filtering to relevant conversations controls cost better than sampling.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: Our Clean Up Merged Two Builders Who Shared a Yard and Put the Son on Stop for His Father's Debts
description:
Last year we ran a project to remove duplicate customer accounts. Over twenty years our branches had opened new accounts for customers they could not find quickly on the screen, and about six thousand accounts looked like the same customer twice. Duplicates do real harm, from split credit limits to statements showing half the balance.

A data quality tool scored pairs of accounts on name, address, phone number and email, and merged any pair that scored above a threshold. We checked a sample of a few hundred by hand, found the matches convincing, and let it merge four thousand two hundred accounts over a weekend.

Three weeks later a groundworker rang our credit controller, furious. His account was on stop, and the statement explaining why listed invoices he had never seen. His father runs a building firm from the same yard on the edge of a village. They share a surname, an address and an office phone, and the father's account was overdue. The tool had seen two accounts with nearly the same name at the same address and made them one, and our credit rules had done the rest.

When we looked properly, a hundred and thirty eight merges had joined different businesses: fathers and sons, brothers, and firms renting units on the same industrial estate whose addresses differed only by a unit number the tool treated as noise. Unpicking them was far harder than merging had been. Every invoice, payment and credit note had to be returned to the right customer by branch staff who knew them.

A duplicate is an inconvenience you can live with. A wrong merge is a mistake that spreads through every record attached to it. We had treated the threshold as a measure of how alike two accounts looked, when the question that mattered was whether they were the same business.

Merges are now proposals. Limited companies are merged only when their registration numbers match. Sole traders and partnerships are proposed to the branch that opened the accounts, and someone there confirms each one. Every merge keeps the original accounts so it can be reversed, and the tool is tested on samples drawn from shared addresses, which is where its mistakes live.

Two records that look alike are a question for someone who knows the customers, not an answer.

– Serguey Shinder

title: HTTP 100 Continue Expectation Header: When Clients Pause Before Sending Body
description:
Originally published on Code Beneath.

The HTTP 100 Continue Expect header is a mechanism that lets a client pause before sending a request body and wait for server permission. When a client sends Expect: 100-continue in the headers, it holds back the message body and waits for the server to respond with status code 100 (Continue) or reject the request outright. Many developers ignore this header entirely, leading to timeout hangs, wasted bandwidth on large uploads, or confused clients. Understanding the HTTP 100 continue expect header example implementation patterns is essential for building robust APIs that handle large payloads, file uploads, and resource-constrained scenarios efficiently.

Why Clients Send the Expect Header

Before uploading a 500 MB file or posting a large JSON body, a client may want to check: will the server accept this request at all? Perhaps the authentication token is invalid, the resource does not exist, or the content type is wrong. Without the Expect header, the client would waste time and bandwidth sending the entire body, only to receive a 401 or 400 response from the server.

With Expect: 100-continue, the flow is different. The client sends headers and waits. The server reads the headers, validates them, and either says "100 Continue, send the body" or "417 Expectation Failed" or rejects with another 4xx status. Only if the server says 100 do you transmit the body.

This is especially useful in handling HTTP requests where you need to validate early and avoid expensive resource allocation. A multi-part file upload endpoint can reject bad requests before the kernel buffers megabytes of data.

The Protocol Flow

The sequence goes like this:

  1. Client sends request line, all headers (including Expect: 100-continue), and waits without sending the body.
  2. Server reads the request headers, validates them (auth, content-type, size limits), and either sends 100 Continue or sends a final response like 417 Expectation Failed or 401 Unauthorized.
  3. If server sends 100, client sends the request body.
  4. Server reads the body, processes it, and sends the final response (200, 201, etc.).
  5. If server sends a final response (not 100), client stops and does not send the body.

Most clients set a timeout on the wait for 100 Continue, often 1 second or configurable. If the server does not respond within that window, the client may assume the server does not understand the header and send the body anyway.

Go Server: Accepting and Rejecting 100-Continue

Here is a complete, runnable Go server that demonstrates proper handling. The http.Server in Go does not automatically handle the Expect header, so you must do it manually. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
)

func uploadHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Check for Expect: 100-continue
    if r.Header.Get("Expect") == "100-continue" {
        // Validate headers before reading body
        contentLength := r.ContentLength
        maxSize := int64(10 * 1024 * 1024) // 10 MB limit

        if contentLength < 0 {
            // Content-Length not provided or chunked
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusLengthRequired)
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "Content-Length required\n")
            return
        }

        if contentLength > maxSize {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "File too large: %d > %d\n", contentLength, maxSize)
            return
        }

        // All checks passed, tell client to send the body
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue)
        // Important: flush the response to ensure client receives 100
        if f, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok {
            f.Flush()
        }
    }

    // Now read the body (after sending 100 or skipping this logic entirely if no Expect)
    body, err := io.ReadAll(r.Body)
    if err != nil {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest)
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "Failed to read body: %v\n", err)
        return
    }
    defer r.Body.Close()

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    fmt.Fprintf(w, `{"uploaded": %d, "status": "success"}`+"\n", len(body))
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/upload", uploadHandler)
    log.Println("Server listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Key points in this Go server:

  • We check the Expect header after the headers are parsed.
  • We validate Content-Length and other constraints before signaling 100.
  • We call w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue) to send 100.
  • We call Flush() to ensure the response is sent immediately, not buffered.
  • We then proceed to read the body with io.ReadAll(r.Body).
  • If validation fails, we send a final error status (417, 413, etc.) and do not send 100; the body is never read.

Python Server: Same Pattern with Flask

Here is the equivalent in Python with Flask. Flask does not automatically handle 100-continue either, but we can intercept the request before the WSGI server reads the body. 

from flask import Flask, request, Response
import sys

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def handle_expect_continue():
    """
    Intercept requests with Expect: 100-continue before WSGI reads the body.
    This runs before the route handler is called.
    """
    if request.headers.get("Expect") == "100-continue":
        # Validate headers
        content_length = request.content_length
        max_size = 10 * 1024 * 1024  # 10 MB

        if content_length is None:
            # No Content-Length header; reject
            return "Content-Length required\n", 411

        if content_length < 0:
            return "Invalid Content-Length\n", 400

        if content_length > max_size:
            return f"File too large: {content_length} > {max_size}\n", 413

        # All checks passed; send 100 Continue
        # We write directly to the WSGI input stream's underlying socket
        sys.stdout.flush()
        # In production, use the WSGI environ to access wsgi.input
        # and write to the client socket directly.
        # For now, we rely on the Flask test client or a proper WSGI server
        # to handle this. A real implementation requires gunicorn/uWSGI
        # middleware or a custom WSGI wrapper.

@app.route("/upload", methods=["POST"])
def upload():
    """
    Handle file upload. By the time this route is called,
    the client has already received 100 (or not).
    """
    if request.content_length is None:
        return "Content-Length required\n", 411

    data = request.get_data()
    return {
        "uploaded": len(data),
        "status": "success"
    }, 200

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # For testing with built-in server (not production-grade)
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8080, debug=False)

Flask's built-in development server does not handle Expect properly because it is single-threaded and does not separate header parsing from body reading. In production, use Gunicorn, uWSGI, or another WSGI server that lets you inject middleware to send 100 Continue at the socket level before the WSGI app reads the body. The pattern is to write the HTTP response "HTTP/1.1 100 Continue\r\n\r\n" directly to the client socket.

Python WSGI Middleware for 100-Continue

Here is a production-ready WSGI middleware that wraps any Flask or other WSGI app and handles 100-continue correctly by writing to the environ: 

import sys
import io

class Expect100ContinueMiddleware:
    """
    WSGI middleware that sends 100 Continue when appropriate.
    """
    def __init__(self, app, max_size=10*1024*1024):
        self.app = app
        self.max_size = max_size

    def __call__(self, environ, start_response):
        """
        Called by the WSGI server for each request.
        """
        expect = environ.get("HTTP_EXPECT", "").lower()

        if expect == "100-continue":
            content_length_str = environ.get("CONTENT_LENGTH", "")

            # Validate before reading body
            if not content_length_str:
                # Send 411 Length Required
                start_response("411 Length Required", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Content-Length required\n"]

            try:
                content_length = int(content_length_str)
            except ValueError:
                start_response("400 Bad Request", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Invalid Content-Length\n"]

            if content_length < 0:
                start_response("400 Bad Request", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Negative Content-Length\n"]

            if content_length > self.max_size:
                start_response("413 Payload Too Large", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [f"File too large: {content_length} > {self.max_size}\n".encode()]

            # Send 100 Continue to the client
            wsgi_input = environ["wsgi.input"]
            if hasattr(wsgi_input, "_sock"):
                # Direct socket access (not always available)
                try:
                    wsgi_input._sock.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 100 Continue\r\n\r\n")
                except Exception:
                    pass  # Ignore if socket not available

        # Call the wrapped WSGI app
        return self.app(environ, start_response)


# Example usage with Flask
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/upload", methods=["POST"])
def upload():
    return {"status": "success"}, 200

# Wrap the Flask app with the middleware
app.wsgi_app = Expect100ContinueMiddleware(app.wsgi_app)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Use a proper WSGI server: gunicorn -w 1 app:app
    app.run(port=8080)

This middleware validates headers before the WSGI app reads the body, and conditionally sends 100 Continue.

Go Client: Sending Expect: 100-Continue

Now let us write a client that actually sends the Expect header and handles the response properly: 

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

func uploadWithExpect(serverURL string, data []byte) error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
    }

    body := bytes.NewReader(data)
    req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", serverURL, body)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create request: %w", err)
    }

    // Set the Expect header to signal the server
    req.Header.Set("Expect", "100-continue")
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")

    // Important: explicitly set Content-Length so the server knows size before body arrives
    req.ContentLength = int64(len(data))

    log.Printf("Sending request with Expect: 100-continue, body size: %d bytes\n", len(data))

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("request failed: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    // Read the final response body
    respBody, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to read response: %w", err)
    }

    log.Printf("Server responded with status: %d\n", resp.StatusCode)
    log.Printf("Response body: %s\n", string(respBody))

    if resp.StatusCode >= 400 {
        return fmt.Errorf("server rejected request: %d", resp.StatusCode)
    }

    return nil
}

func main() {
    // Test data: 5 MB
    testData := bytes.Repeat([]byte("x"), 5*1024*1024)

    err := uploadWithExpect("http://localhost:8080/upload", testData)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Upload failed: %v\n", err)
    }

    log.Println("Upload succeeded")
}

Key points in the client:

  • We set Expect: 100-continue in the headers.
  • We set Content-Length explicitly so the server knows the body size.
  • We call client.Do(req), which handles the 100 Continue protocol automatically in Go: it waits for the 100 response before sending the body, or if it gets a final status, it stops.
  • The Go HTTP client has a default timeout of about 1 second for waiting on 100 Continue; if it does not arrive, it sends the body anyway.

Python Client: Sending Expect Header

In Python, the standard library urllib does not support 100 Continue well, but the requests library has better support: 

import requests
import io

def upload_with_expect(server_url, data):
    """
    Upload data using Expect: 100-continue.
    The requests library handles the protocol automatically.
    """
    headers = {
        "Expect": "100-continue",
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
    }

    # Create a BytesIO object to send as body
    body = io.BytesIO(data)

    print(f"Sending {len(data)} bytes with Expect: 100-continue")

    try:
        # requests automatically handles 100 Continue if present
        resp = requests.post(
            server_url,
            data=body,
            headers=headers,
            timeout=10,
        )

        print(f"Server responded: {resp.status_code}")
        print(f"Response: {resp.text}")

        if resp.status_code >= 400:
            raise Exception(f"Server error: {resp.status_code}")

        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Upload failed: {e}")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_data = b"x" * (5 * 1024 * 1024)  # 5 MB
    success = upload_with_expect("http://localhost:8080/upload", test_data)
    if success:
        print("Upload succeeded")

Comparison: When to Use Expect: 100-Continue

Scenario Use Expect: 100-continue? Reason
Large file uploads (100 MB+) Yes Avoid wasting bandwidth if server rejects early (auth, quota, format).
REST API with small JSON payloads (<100 KB) No Latency cost (extra round trip) outweighs benefit. Just send it.
WebRTC or streaming over UDP/QUIC N/A Not applicable; these protocols do not use HTTP semantics.
Resumable uploads with chunking Yes Server can reject at chunk boundaries or validate chunk signatures early.
gRPC or Protocol Buffers No gRPC has its own flow control and backpressure mechanisms; Expect not used.
Slow network, high payload latency Yes Server can reject before kilobytes arrive; saves time and data.

Common Mistakes

Not Flushing the 100 Response

If the server sends w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue) but does not call Flush(), the response may be buffered. The client waits forever (until timeout) for the 100 response, then sends the body anyway. Always flush after writing the 100 status.

Sending 100 After Reading Headers Incompletely

If you send 100 Continue and then discover a validation error, you cannot send another status code. The connection is locked into sending the body. Always validate all headers first (Content-Length, Content-Type, auth, etc.) before sending 100.

Client Not Setting Content-Length

If the client sends Expect: 100-continue without Content-Length, the server cannot validate the payload size upfront. Many servers will reject this or ignore the Expect header. Always pair Expect with an explicit Content-Length.

Ignoring the Header Entirely

Some servers read the entire request body without checking for Expect. This breaks the protocol: the client is waiting for 100, the server is reading the body, and they deadlock. Go and Python HTTP libraries handle this internally, but custom socket code must respect the header.

Timing Diagram

Client                                    Server
  |                                          |
  | POST /upload HTTP/1.1                   |
  | Expect: 100-continue                    |
  | Content-Length: 5000000                 |
  | (no body yet)                           |
  |---------------------------------------->|
  |                                    [parse headers]
  |                                    [validate size, auth, etc.]
  |                                    [all OK]
  |                                   
  | HTTP/1.1 100 Continue                   |
  |<----------------------------------------|
  |                                          |
  | [5MB body]                              |
  |---------------------------------------->|
  |                                   [read body]
  |                                   [process]
  |                                          |
  | HTTP/1.1 200 OK                         |
  | Content-Type: application/json          |
  | {"uploaded": 5000000, "status": ...}   |
  |<----------------------------------------|
  |                                          |

Measuring the Impact

To see real timing differences, use curl with the -w flag to measure handshake time vs. upload time: 

#!/bin/bash

# Generate a 10 MB test file
dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=10 of=testfile.bin 2>/dev/null

echo "=== Upload WITH Expect: 100-continue ==="
time curl -X POST \
  -H "Expect: 100-continue" \
  --data-binary @testfile.bin \
  -w "\nConnect: %{time_connect}s, Time-to-first: %{time_starttransfer}s, Total: %{time_total}s\n" \
  http://localhost:8080/upload

echo ""
echo "=== Upload WITHOUT Expect header ==="
time curl -X POST \
  --data-binary @testfile.bin \
  -w "\nConnect: %{time_connect}s, Time-to-first: %{time_starttransfer}s, Total: %{time_total}s\n" \
  http://localhost:8080/upload

On a good network with a responsive server, the difference is small. But if the server rejects the request (e.g., 401), the Expect version saves the time it would take to send the body.

FAQ

Does HTTP/2 support Expect: 100-continue?

HTTP/2 deprecates the Expect header in favor of its own flow control mechanisms. HTTP/2 uses SETTINGS frames and WINDOW_UPDATE to signal backpressure. However, if your HTTP/2 implementation maps it to HTTP/1.1 at the boundary, the header still works.

What if the server never sends 100 or a final status?

The client will wait for a configured timeout (usually 1-2 seconds) and then send the body anyway. This is a safety mechanism to handle servers that do not understand Expect. After the timeout, the client assumes it is safe to proceed.

Can I send 100-continue for GET requests?

Technically yes, but it makes no sense. GET requests do not have a body, so there is nothing to pause on. The server will likely ignore the header. Use Expect only with POST, PUT, or PATCH.

Should I always send Expect when uploading files?

Only for large files or when early validation is critical. For small uploads (under 1 MB), the latency of the extra round trip often outweighs the savings. Measure your use case.

How does Expect interact with Content-Encoding?

Expect is about request headers and size validation. Content-Encoding (gzip, deflate, etc.) happens after validation. The Content-Length in the Expect header validation should be the encoded size that actually goes on the wire.

What status codes reject Expect: 100-continue?

Common rejections: 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 413 Payload Too Large, 417 Expectation Failed. Any status code other than 100 or 1xx tells the client to stop sending the body.

Does nginx support Expect: 100-continue?

Yes. Nginx respects the Expect header by default. If you send Expect: 100-continue, nginx will read your headers, validate them against its proxy settings, and either send 100 or reject before the body is buffered. This is one reason nginx is efficient for file uploads.

title: In a Chat Message, the Formatting Is Part of the Data
description:
A lot of my work runs through one Slack channel. I post numbered requests, REQ-141, REQ-142 and so on, and a browser agent picks them up, does the work, and answers in the thread. A small script posts a weekly request of its own every Monday, and before posting it works out the next free number by reading the channel history.

On Monday the script posted REQ-143. There was already a REQ-143. I had posted it myself at one in the morning.

The underscore is a word character

The numbering code was one line:

nums = [int(n) for m in history for n in re.findall(r"\bREQ-(\d{3})\b", m["text"])]

That looks right. \b is a word boundary, so it stops XREQ-143 from matching, and the trailing \b stops it from reading the first three digits of REQ-1430.

But the requests I post go through a connector that writes my titles in italics, and Slack stores italics as underscores. My request's text began:

_REQ-143: Go ahead with part B now_

A word boundary is the point between a word character and a non-word character. In regex, word characters are letters, digits and the underscore. So between _ and R there is no boundary. Both sides count as "word". \bREQ never matched, my request was invisible to the counter, and the script happily took 143 again.

To the parser, the markup isn't around the message. It is the message.

I had been thinking of _..._ as "how it looks". The regex was reading what was actually stored, and what was stored was an underscore glued to the front of the thing I was searching for.

The fix keeps the guard I actually needed, digits after the number, and drops the one that assumed clean text before it:

re.findall(r"REQ-(\d{3})(?!\d)", text)

I tested it against the shapes that really occur in the channel, not the one I'd imagined:

>>> re.findall(r"REQ-(\d{3})(?!\d)", "_REQ-143: x *REQ-142* REQ-1234")
['143', '142']

Italic, bold and plain all match, and a four-digit number doesn't produce a false 123.

The language tag that ate a line

The same day, a request listed fifteen properties in a code block, so the agent would see a clean list:

```1. First property (city)
2. Second property
...
```

The agent answered items 2 to 15. I resent the missing one as part of the next request, formatted the same way. It went missing again.

Text on the same line as an opening triple backtick isn't content. It's the language tag, the thing that tells the renderer to highlight python or js. My first item had been sent as a language called 1. First property (city), which the renderer treated as metadata and quietly didn't show. Nothing errored. The list simply started at 2.

The fix is a newline after the opening fence, every time:

```
1. First property (city)
2. Second property
```

The same mistake twice

Both bugs came from writing for the renderer and forgetting that something else reads the source. I wrote italics so a title would look like a title. I put a list on the fence line so the message would look compact. In both cases the thing reading the text downstream, a regex in one, a markdown parser in the other, saw characters I'd stopped noticing.

What I do now:

  • Match against the stored form, not the displayed one. If a channel stores formatting as characters (_, *, ~, backticks), assume any line you parse may be wrapped in them. Don't lean on \b beside text that might start with an underscore.
  • Test parsers with real messages from the channel. My regex test strings were all clean, plain-text REQ-142. The channel has never contained a clean one.
  • Put a newline after every opening code fence in anything a machine will read. The first line belongs to the tag.

Neither bug was clever. Both sat in the gap between what a message looks like and what it contains.

title: The Software Development Bottleneck: Why Faster Coding Doesn't Mean Faster Delivery
description:
The Coding Revolution Has Created a New Engineering Problem

What if developers could write code twice as fast, but their organizations still couldn't release software any faster?

That is the paradox modern software engineering is facing.

AI coding assistants have changed how developers write, understand, and improve code. Tasks that once required hours of manual effort can now be completed much faster. Code generation, debugging assistance, documentation, and code suggestions are becoming increasingly automated.

But faster coding does not automatically translate into faster software delivery.

A software release involves much more than writing code. It requires architecture planning, requirement validation, dependency management, code reviews, testing, security checks, deployment approvals, and production monitoring. When these activities remain disconnected, improvements in coding speed simply move the bottleneck to another stage.

The real challenge is no longer how quickly developers can produce code. It is how efficiently an organization can move software from an initial requirement to a reliable production release.

Why Faster Coding Is Not Solving the Delivery Problem

Modern engineering teams work across multiple platforms, repositories, CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, monitoring systems, and project management tools.

Each system manages a different part of the development lifecycle. However, understanding how these systems influence one another often requires manual investigation and coordination.

Consider a simple enterprise software release. A developer completes a feature quickly, but the code review identifies a dependency risk. Testing then discovers an integration failure. The engineering team investigates logs, checks previous deployments, reviews configuration changes, and coordinates with other teams before the release can continue.

The coding task may have taken hours, but resolving everything around it can take considerably longer.

This creates a critical distinction:

Coding speed measures how quickly software is written. Delivery speed measures how efficiently the entire engineering ecosystem works together.

According to the challenges described in EzInsights AI SDLC Intelligence, fragmented engineering signals, slow root cause analysis, test coverage gaps, and manual compliance activities are important sources of enterprise engineering friction.

The Five Hidden Bottlenecks Slowing Software Delivery

The biggest delivery delays are often hidden between development activities rather than inside the coding process itself.

1. Fragmented Engineering Workflows

Engineering information is distributed across source code repositories, architecture documents, Jira tickets, CI/CD pipelines, logs, and monitoring platforms.

When these systems operate independently, engineers must manually connect information to understand the complete situation. This creates unnecessary coordination and investigation time.

2. Code Reviews and Dependency Management

Generating code faster can increase the volume of changes that need to be reviewed. Without sufficient architectural context, identifying breaking changes, dependency conflicts, and potential risks becomes difficult.

The result is a growing review workload that can slow down otherwise productive development teams.

3. Testing Cannot Keep Pace With Development

Software quality depends on testing more than just the newly written code. Teams must validate integration points, existing functionality, edge cases, APIs, and dependencies.

When testing remains heavily manual or disconnected from development context, faster coding can create larger testing backlogs.

4. Slow Root Cause Analysis

A failed deployment or production incident rarely has just one possible explanation. Engineers may need to investigate logs, recent commits, infrastructure changes, dependencies, and previous incidents.

Without connected engineering intelligence, identifying the actual cause becomes a time-consuming process.

5. Deployment and Compliance Delays

Security validation, governance requirements, approval workflows, and audit evidence are essential for enterprise software.

However, manually coordinating these activities across disconnected systems can delay releases even after development and testing are complete.

The Real Problem: Engineering Tools Understand Tasks, Not the Entire Lifecycle

Traditional DevOps transformed software delivery through automation, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure management, and monitoring.

These capabilities remain essential. However, modern enterprise environments require more than individual tools performing isolated activities.

A CI/CD platform understands pipeline execution. An observability platform understands metrics and logs. A project management system tracks tickets and tasks. An AI coding assistant helps developers generate and understand code.

But how do these systems collectively understand why a deployment failed, which services might be affected, which tests should be executed, and what needs to happen before a release becomes safe?

This is where engineering intelligence becomes important.

The future of software delivery requires connected information, contextual reasoning, and coordinated automation across the entire Software Development Lifecycle.

As explained in Why AI-Driven SDLC Platforms Are Replacing Traditional DevOps Tools, the next evolution is moving beyond execution automation toward intelligent systems that understand relationships across engineering workflows.

How AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence Changes the Equation

Instead of accelerating only code generation, AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence focuses on improving the complete software development lifecycle.

It connects design, development, testing, migration, documentation, deployment, and engineering knowledge into a unified intelligence ecosystem.

This approach helps engineering teams identify bottlenecks earlier, reduce repetitive work, and make better decisions using connected engineering context.

An important foundation of this approach is the Engineering Knowledge Graph (EKG).

An Engineering Knowledge Graph connects different engineering entities and their relationships, including:

Requirements and architecture documentation.

Source code and application dependencies.

APIs, services, and repositories.

Test cases and validation results.

CI/CD pipelines and deployment history.

Logs, incidents, and production changes.

Security policies and compliance requirements.

Instead of treating these as separate information sources, the knowledge graph creates connected engineering context.

For example, when a deployment fails, AI can use relationships between code changes, affected services, pipeline events, test results, and production logs to support a more informed investigation.

This moves engineering teams beyond searching through disconnected systems toward understanding how different engineering events are connected.

Multi-Agent AI: Moving Beyond Individual Coding Assistants

A single AI coding assistant can help generate code, explain functions, or suggest improvements. However, enterprise software delivery requires coordination across multiple specialized engineering responsibilities.

Multi-Agent AI introduces a different approach.

Instead of expecting one AI assistant to manage every engineering activity, specialized agents collaborate using shared engineering context.

An intelligent SDLC ecosystem can include:

Code Intelligence Agent: Reviews code, identifies risks, and analyzes dependencies.

QA Automation Agent: Generates unit, integration, and end-to-end test cases.

CI/CD Agent: Investigates pipeline failures and dependency mismatches.

SRE/RCA Agent: Connects logs, services, incidents, and code changes.

Compliance Agent: Identifies governance gaps and maps controls to evidence.

Architecture Agent: Analyzes system dependencies and architectural changes.

These agents can work together to create a more connected engineering workflow.

For example, when a developer introduces a significant code change, the system can help identify affected dependencies, highlight missing test coverage, support code review, and provide relevant deployment risk information.

The objective is not simply to automate individual tasks. It is to reduce the delays between engineering activities.

How EzInsights AI Is Addressing the Software Delivery Bottleneck

EzInsights AI introduces an AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence framework designed to connect engineering workflows through multi-agent automation and an Engineering Knowledge Graph.

Its approach focuses on bringing engineering signals together instead of allowing code, tests, pipelines, incidents, and architecture information to remain isolated.

Through its SDLC Intelligence Platform, organizations can explore capabilities such as:

Intelligent code review and dependency analysis.

Automated unit, integration, and end-to-end test generation.

CI/CD failure diagnosis.

AI-powered root cause analysis.

Architecture and dependency intelligence.

Security and compliance evidence automation.

Engineering knowledge and documentation intelligence.

The platform describes six specialized agents working through a shared Engineering Knowledge Graph to support engineering automation and contextual reasoning.

This creates a continuous intelligence flow:

Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Operations → Continuous Improvement

Every stage can provide useful information to the next, helping organizations reduce fragmented workflows and improve delivery visibility.

The Future of Software Delivery Is Not About Writing More Code

The next competitive advantage in software engineering will not come simply from organizations generating the largest amount of code.

It will come from organizations that can move from requirements to production with fewer delays, better quality, stronger engineering context, and more predictable releases.

AI coding tools are an important step forward, but they address only one part of a much larger engineering challenge.

Enterprises need connected intelligence that understands the relationships between development, testing, architecture, deployment, and operations.

Final Thought

The software development industry has spent years trying to make developers write code faster. AI is now making that possible.

But the next challenge is much bigger.

Can organizations eliminate the hidden delays between writing, reviewing, testing, deploying, and maintaining software?

Because the real measure of engineering productivity is not how much code a team produces.

It is how reliably and efficiently that code becomes valuable software in production.

The future of software development will not be defined by faster coding alone. It will be defined by intelligent software delivery.
