title: What Are Online Evals? Online vs Offline Evaluation for AI Agents
description:
Online evals are evaluations that run on an AI agent's real production traffic. Instead of feeding the agent a prepared test set, an evaluator (an LLM judge, a code check, or a user signal) scores the conversations, traces, or tool calls that real users already produced. Offline evals tell you whether a change is safe to ship. Online evals tell you whether the shipped agent is working.

The term comes from machine learning, where "offline" evaluation uses a held-out dataset and "online" evaluation measures a model while it serves traffic. For LLM agents, the split matters more than it did for classic models. An agent's inputs are open-ended, its tools change state in other systems, and its failures are often fluent and polite. A test set can only contain the failures someone already imagined.

Online vs offline evals at a glance

Offline evals Online evals
Input A fixed dataset of prepared cases Real production conversations, traces, or spans
When it runs Before release, usually in CI or an experiment After the interaction, continuously
Ground truth Expected answers, references, or a rubric Usually none; a judge, a rule, or an outcome signal
Main question Did this change make known cases worse? What is going wrong for real users right now?
Catches Regressions on known cases Unknown failure modes, drift, new user goals
Misses Anything not in the dataset Nothing until it happens at least once
Cost driver Dataset size times the number of runs Traffic volume times judge cost, reduced by sampling
Output A pass rate or score comparison between versions Rates over time, flagged examples, alerts

Neither column replaces the other. The useful pattern, covered below, is a loop in which online evals find failures and those failures become offline test cases.

What an online eval is made of

Every online eval has the same five parts, whatever tool runs it.

  1. A unit. What gets judged: a single LLM call (span), one request through the agent (trace), or a whole multi-turn conversation (session or thread). The unit decides which failures are even visible. A span-level judge cannot see that the user asked the same question four times. Read conversation-level vs trace-level online evals for how to choose.
  2. A trigger. When the judgment runs. Span and trace evals can run as soon as the data arrives. Conversation evals usually wait until the conversation has gone quiet, because judging a half-finished conversation produces false failures.
  3. An evaluator. The thing that decides. An LLM judge reading a rubric, deterministic code (schema validation, regex, a tool-result comparison), or a signal from the user or a downstream system, such as a thumbs-down, a refund request, or a support ticket.
  4. A population. Which traffic is judged: everything, a sample, or a filtered slice such as one agent, one customer tier, or conversations that used a refund tool.
  5. An action. What happens with the result: a dashboard rate, a review queue, an alert, a new regression test, or a code change.

Teams that skip part 5 end up with a dashboard of scores nobody acts on. The setup guide walks through each part with defaults.

What online evals catch that offline evals miss

Offline evals are strongest on known behavior: the canonical refund question, the formatting contract, the tool the agent must call. Production adds the cases nobody wrote down.

  • New user goals. People ask an onboarding agent about billing, or ask a coding agent to explain a stack trace it never saw. No test case exists because nobody predicted the request.
  • Silent wrong answers. The agent states a 30-day return window after retrieving a 14-day policy. Nothing errors. See how to catch wrong answers that don't show up as errors.
  • False success. The agent says the cancellation is done, but no cancellation call succeeded. See detecting when an agent claims success without acting.
  • Multi-turn friction. Each reply is reasonable in isolation, but the user rephrases four times and leaves. Only a conversation-level evaluator sees the pattern.
  • Drift. A model update, a prompt edit, or a changed upstream API slowly shifts behavior. Offline evals pass because the dataset did not change. See agent drift in production.

The 12 production failures your evals will never catch lists more. Read that title as "your offline evals": every item on it is a job for an online eval.

What online evals cannot do

Online evals have limits worth stating plainly.

  • They are retrospective. A failure has to happen before it can be scored. If a failure must never reach a user, it needs a guardrail or a code check in the request path, not an online eval. See online evals vs guardrails vs monitoring.
  • They inherit the evidence you send. A judge cannot verify a refund it cannot see. If the tool result or the system-of-record outcome is not captured, the evaluator can only judge what the agent said.
  • Judges make mistakes. An LLM judge needs a labeled sample before its rate is trustworthy. See how to calibrate an LLM judge.
  • They cost money at scale. Judging every conversation with a strong model adds up. See what LLM-as-a-judge costs in production.

The loop: online failures become offline tests

The two kinds of eval are most useful when connected.

  1. An online eval flags a pattern in production, for example the agent confirming refunds before the refund tool succeeds.
  2. Someone reviews the flagged examples and confirms the failure is real.
  3. A fix is proposed and reviewed: a prompt change, a tool contract, a code check.
  4. Representative failing examples, plus healthy controls, become offline regression cases. Turn production failures into regression tests covers how to do this without replaying real side effects.
  5. After the fix ships, the same online eval measures whether the failure rate actually fell.

Step 5 is the one most teams skip, and it is the one that tells you whether the fix worked. What to do when an online eval fails covers the whole path from flag to verified fix.

How Agnost AI runs online evals

Agnost is built around the online half of this loop, for conversational agents.

  • Rules in plain English. You write the behavior you expect, such as "state the cancellation policy before completing a cancellation". Each rule is an evaluator. How to define agent failures in natural language covers how to write rules a judge can apply consistently.
  • Whole-conversation judgment. Once a conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, an LLM judge reads it end to end against your active rules and flags the specific assistant messages that broke one. Conversations are processed in batches, so this is a review layer, not a real-time filter.
  • No sampling knob. Every analyzed conversation is judged, up to your plan's monthly event limit. When you add or edit a rule, Agnost also scores your most recent 1,000 conversations so the rule starts with a baseline.
  • Intents alongside rules. The same judge labels what users were trying to do, so a violation rate can be read per user goal.
  • Alerts and fixes. A rule's violation count can trigger a Slack or email alert. A fired alert can start Auto Improve, which opens a pull request for your team to review and re-checks the alert about an hour after the change merges.

What Agnost does not do is also worth knowing. Verdicts are pass/fail flags with the evidence message, not graded scores. There is no CI gate, and violations are a classified finding, not enforcement. Teams that need dataset experiments or a CI eval step often run Agnost alongside an offline eval tool; if Braintrust is on your shortlist for that job, Braintrust alternatives for AI agent evaluation compares it with the other options. The online evaluation tools comparison shows where each product fits, and the Violations guide covers setup.

Where to start

If you run no online evals today, start small:

  1. Pick one failure that would cost you a customer, such as a false completion, a skipped identity check, or a wrong policy answer.
  2. Write it as a single, narrow rule with clear evidence.
  3. Run it over a week of production conversations and read 20 flagged and 20 unflagged examples.
  4. Fix the rule wording until you agree with the judge, then set an alert threshold.

One trusted evaluator that someone acts on is worth more than twenty scores on a dashboard. For the difference between the evaluation layers in more depth, read evals, traces, and conversations: what each one catches.

Frequently asked questions

What are online evals?

Online evals are evaluations that run on an AI system's real production traffic instead of a prepared test set. An evaluator, usually an LLM judge, a code check, or a user signal, scores live conversations, traces, or spans after they happen, so the team can see how the agent behaves with real users and real tools.

What is the difference between online and offline evals?

Offline evals run a fixed dataset through the agent before a change ships and compare the results with expected answers or a rubric. Online evals score production traffic after it happens. Offline evals answer whether a change is safe to release; online evals answer whether the released agent is actually working for users.

Do online evals replace offline evals?

No. Offline evals catch regressions on known cases before release. Online evals find the failures nobody wrote a test for. The useful loop turns online-eval failures into new offline test cases, so the same failure is caught before the next release.

Are online evals the same as guardrails?

No. A guardrail runs inline and can block or rewrite a response before the user sees it, so it must be fast and cheap. An online eval runs after the interaction and only observes, so it can use a slower, more careful judge and look at the whole conversation.

Should online evals score every conversation or a sample?

Score everything for rare, high-severity failures and when volume is low enough to afford it. Sample when the judge is expensive and the failure is common enough that a sample still finds it. Whatever you choose, record the denominator so a rate can be interpreted.

How does Agnost AI run online evals?

You write rules in plain English, such as 'confirm identity before sharing account details'. Agnost's LLM judge checks every analyzed production conversation against those rules once the conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, flags the assistant messages that broke a rule, reports violation counts, and can alert Slack or email when a threshold is crossed. An alert can also open a pull request that is re-checked after merge.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: A Polite Reply Is Not Work Done: Five Jobs a Chatbot Leaves Undone
description:
A customer got a polite apology from the chatbot — and nothing else. The refund never moved, the booking never changed. The reply was fast, friendly, and correct in every word. It was also the end of the job, as far as the chatbot was concerned. The customer was still waiting, and the business did not know it, because a reply had been sent and the thread looked finished.

This article was drafted with AI assistance. It is written in plain English for people who run businesses, not for people who build software, and it makes no claim about any particular product. It is about the question this morning's post asked — when did a polite reply leave the real job undone? — and it works through five jobs a chatbot leaves undone, using the tools people already use, so you can check my working and tell me where I got it wrong.

The difference is one word: done

A chatbot's job ends when it has answered. An agent's job ends when the work is done — or when a human has said no. That sounds like a small difference. In a normal day it is the whole difference, because most of the work a small business does after a customer writes in is not answering. It is moving money, moving dates, moving orders, and chasing the people who went quiet.

Here are five jobs, numbered, each one with the tools people already use. Each one starts with a polite reply. Each one ends with the job still waiting.

1. The refund that never moved

A customer writes on WhatsApp: the order arrived damaged, can I have my money back? The chatbot apologises, explains the returns policy, and offers a form. The customer fills in the form. Nothing else happens. The refund is a job in the bank account or in Stripe — someone has to look at the order, check the amount, and press the button. The chatbot cannot press it, and nobody told a person that a form had been filled in.

The tools are ordinary: WhatsApp for the message, Gmail for the form, Stripe or the bank for the money, a spreadsheet for the record. Each one does its part. The gap is between them — the message arrived in one place, the money lives in another, and nobody owns the step in between.

2. The booking that never changed

A customer books for Thursday at 4pm, then writes to move it to Friday at 10am. The chatbot says "Of course, I have noted your request" — and nothing is noted anywhere that matters. Thursday 4pm stays booked in Google Calendar, Friday 10am stays free, and the slot that could have gone to the next person waiting sits empty twice over: once when the customer does not come on Thursday, once when nobody offers the freed time to anyone else.

The booking page, Calendly, does its part well — the customer picks a slot themselves. But a booking page cannot handle the customer who wants something the page does not offer, and it cannot hear a change that arrives as a message. The change lives in the message thread. The diary lives in the calendar. The owner is the only bridge between them, and the owner is busy.

3. The invoice nobody chased

An invoice is fourteen days overdue. The chatbot can write a beautiful reminder — "We hope you are well, a gentle reminder that invoice 1042 is now due" — and it can write it in seconds. But a reminder that is written and never sent chases nobody. The invoice sits in the spreadsheet, the customer's email sits in Gmail, and the polite draft sits in a chat window that closed when the owner got distracted.

This is the job with no deadline on it, so it never gets done. It is also the job that would tell the owner the most: which customers pay late every time, which ones pay when asked once, and which ones have quietly stopped paying at all. A reply is not a chase. A chase ends with money in the account or a decision to stop supplying — and a chatbot does neither.

4. The follow-up that never happened

A customer asked a question on Tuesday, got a polite answer, and never bought anything. Or a customer booked, did not show up, and nobody asked why. The follow-up is the job that has no owner and no deadline, so it waits forever — and it is the job that would tell the business the most about where it leaks.

The tools make it worse, not better. WhatsApp keeps the whole conversation in one thread, which is where the customer actually is — but a message thread is not a list, and a question buried under forty other messages is a question lost. The chatbot answered the question. Nobody answered the silence that followed it.

5. The wrong order that stayed wrong

The wrong item arrived. The customer writes in, the chatbot apologises, explains how returns work, and the customer is told someone will be in touch. Nobody is in touch, because "someone will be in touch" is not a job assigned to anyone. The replacement is never arranged, the courier is never booked, the wrong item sits in the customer's hallway, and the customer tells the next person they know that this business does not fix its mistakes.

The fix is four small jobs — check the order, arrange the replacement, book the collection, tell the customer when it is coming — and each one is a step in a different tool. The chatbot did the first step, the polite one, and the other four waited for a person who never got the message.

What a workforce does with the reply

This is the kind of work an AI workforce is for — not the clever part, the ordinary part. The reply is written, and then the work behind it is done too: the refund is drafted with the amount checked against the order, the booking change is drafted against the free slots, the reminder is drafted with the invoice number and the amount in it, the follow-up is drafted for the customer who went quiet, the replacement is drafted with the courier booked. And nothing is sent before you have seen it. You read the draft, you fix a line if it needs fixing, you say yes — and the customer hears from you the same day, not the next week.

The relief is not that a machine answered faster. It is that the answer stopped being the end of the job. You still decide what counts as a refund, what counts as a change, and what counts as a chase. You still approve every word that leaves. The difference is that the moving, the checking, and the chasing are done before you sit down, so the minutes you have are spent deciding — not digging through messages to find out what was never done.

Which job goes first

The refund goes first, because money is moving and a person is deciding right now. A customer who asked for their money back and heard nothing by the end of the day is a customer who is already telling someone else. The booking change goes next, because a freed slot has a value that drops to nothing the moment the hour passes. The invoice chase follows — it is the easiest of the five to get right, because it is the same message every time, with the facts changed. The replacement and the follow-up come after, because they need a judgement call: which item to send, what to say to the person who never showed.

That order is my answer. It is also a guess, and it is the part I most want corrected.

The short version

A polite reply is not work done. A chatbot's job ends when it has answered; the five jobs behind the answer — the refund, the booking change, the invoice chase, the follow-up, the replacement — still wait for a person. The tools most businesses use each do one part well; the gap is between them, and the owner is the glue. Let a workforce do the work behind the reply, draft it all, and keep the sending in your hands: you pick the order, you approve every word, and the polite apology stops being the last thing the customer ever hears.

So — when did a polite reply leave the real job undone in your business? Which of these five would you hand over first, and which would you never hand over? Tell me in the comments. I would rather be corrected than agreed with.

Ready-made AI agents for small businesses, built in public.

title: Oggi guidate per loro. Domani guideranno senza di voi.
description:
Come algoritmi, piattaforme digitali e robotaxi stanno cambiando il controllo economico del trasporto professionale.

C'è una domanda che dovrebbe interessare ogni tassista, conducente NCC, sviluppatore di piattaforme di mobilità e imprenditore del trasporto.

Che cosa succede quando il software che oggi vi procura lavoro diventa anche il sistema che può sostituirvi?

Non è più una domanda fantascientifica.

Per anni abbiamo raccontato le piattaforme di ride-hailing come un'innovazione capace di mettere in contatto passeggeri e autisti. Un'applicazione, un algoritmo di assegnazione, un sistema di pagamento e una commissione.

Un modello apparentemente semplice.

Ma dietro quell'interfaccia esiste un'architettura economica molto più importante: quella che determina chi controlla la domanda, i prezzi e la relazione con il cliente.

1. Il vero potere non è possedere le automobili

Una piattaforma può organizzare milioni di spostamenti senza possedere ogni automobile e senza assumere direttamente ogni conducente.

Il suo vantaggio competitivo è un altro: controlla il punto di accesso del passeggero al servizio.

Chi possiede l'interfaccia attraverso cui il cliente prenota può influenzare:

  • Quali offerte vengono visualizzate.
  • Come vengono calcolati e presentati i prezzi.
  • Quale conducente riceve una determinata richiesta.
  • Quali informazioni restano disponibili all'autista.
  • Se il cliente ritornerà direttamente dal professionista o dalla piattaforma.

Naturalmente, i modelli differiscono tra operatori e mercati. Non tutte le piattaforme determinano il prezzo nello stesso modo.

Ma il principio economico resta:

Chi controlla la domanda possiede un potere negoziale enorme su chi fornisce il servizio.

2. Dall'algoritmo di assegnazione all'automazione del conducente

Tecnicamente, una piattaforma di mobilità dispone già di alcuni componenti fondamentali per gestire un servizio automatizzato:

  • Un sistema per acquisire richieste di trasporto.
  • Un motore di pricing e assegnazione.
  • Un'infrastruttura per localizzazione e instradamento.
  • Un sistema di pagamento e gestione dell'esperienza del cliente.
  • Una base di utenti abituati a prenotare attraverso la stessa applicazione.

Nel ride-hailing tradizionale, il servizio fisico è fornito da un conducente.

In uno scenario robotaxi, parte di quel lavoro viene affidata a un veicolo autonomo, mentre restano necessari gestione della flotta, manutenzione, assistenza, supervisione e altre attività operative.

Il cambiamento più significativo è che l'interfaccia del passeggero può rimanere esattamente la stessa.

Il cliente apre l'applicazione, indica la destinazione, visualizza un prezzo e prenota.

Quello che cambia è chi, o che cosa, esegue la corsa.

3. I miliardi investiti non sono un'ipotesi

Il 19 marzo 2026 Uber e Rivian hanno annunciato una partnership che prevede investimenti potenziali fino a 1,25 miliardi di dollari entro il 2031, subordinati al raggiungimento di obiettivi tecnologici.

Il programma iniziale riguarda 10.000 robotaxi Rivian R2, con un'opzione per arrivare complessivamente a 50.000 veicoli.

I primi impieghi commerciali sono pianificati dal 2028.

Non significa che 50.000 veicoli siano già operativi.

Significa che esiste un progetto industriale formalizzato, accompagnato da impegni economici e obiettivi di distribuzione.

In Europa il processo è già cominciato.

Nell'agosto 2026 Uber, Pony.ai e Verne hanno avviato un servizio di corse autonome prenotabili tramite Uber a Zagabria. Nella fase iniziale è previsto un operatore di sicurezza a bordo.

La direzione degli investimenti è chiara, anche se la velocità della transizione resta incerta.

4. Il rischio più grande è perdere il cliente prima del lavoro

Immaginiamo un tassista con vent'anni di esperienza.

Conosce la città, ha una licenza, sostiene i costi del veicolo, paga assicurazioni e manutenzione.

Ma i passeggeri prenotano quasi esclusivamente attraverso una piattaforma.

Se domani cambia l'offerta disponibile sull'applicazione, quanti di quei passeggeri continueranno a cercare proprio lui?

Il problema è che il professionista può conservare la propria autorizzazione senza conservare il rapporto commerciale con il cliente.

Le leggi disciplinano il trasporto, le autorizzazioni, la sicurezza e le condizioni di esercizio.

Non garantiscono che un cliente rimanga fedele a un determinato conducente.

È questo il rischio strategico che il settore dovrebbe affrontare oggi.

5. Non tutte le piattaforme devono diventare operatori di robotaxi perché il rischio esista

Uber, Bolt, Lyft, FREE NOW e gli altri operatori non hanno strategie identiche.

Sarebbe scorretto sostenere che tutti abbiano gli stessi investimenti, gli stessi progetti o le stesse condizioni operative.

Il punto è più generale.

Un mercato nel quale il passeggero appartiene commercialmente alla piattaforma rende il fornitore fisico del servizio più facilmente sostituibile.

Oggi quel fornitore è un tassista, un conducente NCC o una flotta.

Domani, nei mercati dove tecnologia e normative lo permetteranno, potrà essere anche un veicolo autonomo.

6. Come dovrebbe essere progettata una piattaforma alternativa

La tecnologia non è necessariamente il nemico del professionista.

Un sistema moderno può gestire richieste, pagamenti, disponibilità, localizzazione, tariffe e dispatching senza sottrarre all'operatore ogni decisione economica.

Per realizzare un modello di questo tipo servono alcuni principi architetturali.

Autonomia tariffaria

Il conducente deve poter definire le condizioni economiche del proprio servizio nei limiti delle disposizioni applicabili.

Trasparenza degli algoritmi

Prima di accettare una corsa, il professionista dovrebbe conoscere il compenso previsto e le commissioni.

Continuità del rapporto commerciale

Le centrali e gli operatori devono poter mantenere e gestire i rapporti con i clienti che acquisiscono, nel rispetto della normativa sui dati personali.

Interoperabilità

Un professionista non dovrebbe dipendere tecnicamente da un unico intermediario per svolgere ogni attività.

Tecnologia al servizio dell'operatore

Il software dovrebbe ridurre i costi e aumentare l'efficienza, non necessariamente imporre le condizioni economiche.

7. La scelta che abbiamo fatto con UrbanGo

Abbiamo sviluppato UrbanGo partendo da un principio diverso.

Il professionista imposta le proprie tariffe, nel rispetto delle normative locali.

Quando opera attraverso una centrale, questa può applicare il proprio listino alle corse che gestisce, e l'autista conosce le condizioni prima di accettare.

Anche UrbanGo applica una commissione.

La differenza che vogliamo costruire non è l'assenza di costi, ma la trasparenza e la possibilità per gli operatori di governare le proprie condizioni economiche.

Non crediamo che il progresso tecnologico debba essere fermato.

Crediamo però che sia necessario distinguere tra digitalizzare un settore e trasferirne il controllo economico a pochi intermediari.

Conclusione: chi controllerà il prossimo mercato?

I robotaxi continueranno a evolversi.

Alcuni arriveranno sul mercato, altri progetti incontreranno ostacoli tecnologici, economici o normativi.

Ma per i professionisti del trasporto esiste una decisione che non può aspettare il 2030.

Continuare a utilizzare la tecnologia come strumento della propria impresa, oppure lasciare che sia la piattaforma a determinare il futuro della propria impresa.

Il vero tema non è soltanto chi guiderà l'automobile.
È chi controllerà la relazione commerciale quando il passeggero salirà a bordo.

UrbanGo, app per autisti

Fonti

  • Uber e Rivian, comunicato ufficiale del 19 marzo 2026.
  • Uber, Pony.ai e Verne, lancio del servizio a Zagabria, 19 agosto 2026.
  • Uber e Pony.ai, partnership europea del 13 agosto 2026.
  • UrbanGo, pagine App autisti, Prezzi e Termini del servizio.

Articolo di opinione e analisi industriale. Le strategie e gli investimenti citati non devono essere attribuiti indistintamente a tutte le piattaforme nominate.

title: Running Voice Agent Tests Fully Offline With Local Models
description:
Running voice agent tests against cloud APIs means sending your agent configs and test transcripts to a third-party provider. For some teams, such as healthcare, finance, and government, that's not allowed. For everyone else, the per-token cost adds up during development: every test run is a multi-turn conversation plus a judge pass, and you rerun the suite each time you touch a prompt.

Voicetest can run fully offline, with every LLM call going to a model on your own machine. No API keys, no network calls to model providers, and nothing leaves your machine. This post covers why that's now practical, the setup with llama.cpp, how to pick a model for each role, and when to use local versus cloud models.

Why this is practical now

Not long ago, a model that fit on one consumer GPU was a poor stand-in for the hosted models most voice agents run on. That has changed quickly.

Epoch AI's Capabilities Index combines dozens of benchmarks onto one scale. On it, the best open-weight model small enough for one consumer GPU went from 103 (Mistral 7B, September 2023) to 153 (Qwen 3.8 27B, August 2026). That's above GPT-5, which scored 150 when it was released in August 2025.

Local models aren't closing the gap. The frontier keeps moving, and the distance in points is about what it was in 2024. What they do is track the frontier roughly a year behind, and a year-old frontier model is plenty for playing a caller and iterating on prompts. Treat benchmark scores for small models with some care, though: Epoch notes they can be tuned toward benchmarks, so check results on your own test suite before trusting them.

Setup

llama.cpp is the open-source inference engine most local model tools are built on. It ships llama-server, a single binary that downloads a model from Hugging Face and serves it over an OpenAI-compatible API:

brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

Qwen3 models think before they answer by default. --reasoning-budget 0 turns that off. Thinking slows down every turn, and a long think can use up the response budget before any answer comes out, which shows up in voicetest as parse errors and retries.

Voicetest routes model calls through LiteLLM, and LiteLLM's llamafile/ provider talks to an OpenAI-compatible server at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1, which is where llama-server listens. Point all three roles at it:

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
judge = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"

The name after llamafile/ is only a label; the server answers with whatever model it loaded. If the server runs somewhere else, set LLAMAFILE_API_BASE. Then run tests as usual:

voicetest run --agent agents/receptionist.json --tests tests/receptionist.json --all

Picking a model for each role

The three roles don't need the same capability, and it helps to know which one is limiting you.

Simulator. The simulator plays the caller. It follows a persona prompt and moves toward the caller's goal. It's the easiest role, and an 8B model handles it well.

Agent. The agent plays your voice agent. It follows the graph's prompts, keeps track of where it is in the conversation, and chooses transitions. This is the hardest role. Bigger models follow complex graphs more consistently, and a small local model won't behave exactly like the model your production agent runs on. For graphs with real branching, use the strongest model that fits:

llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

Judge. The judge reads each finished transcript and scores it against every metric, explaining its reasoning. An inaccurate judge is worse than a slow one, because it gives you false passes or false alarms. Use the largest model you can run.

One llama-server serves one model, so the simplest setup gives every role the same one, sized for the hardest role you run locally.

To check that everything runs end to end, a tiny model is enough:

llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q8_0 --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0
voicetest smoke-test --model llamafile/qwen3-0.6b

That confirms the pipeline works. It says nothing about whether a prompt change is safe to ship: a model this small will fail plenty of metrics.

Hardware

Memory is the limit. An 8B model at Q4 fits comfortably on a laptop. A 27B model at Q4 needs around 17 GB for its weights, which means a 24 GB GPU or an Apple Silicon Mac with 32 GB or more. Anything much larger needs a workstation.

If you can't run a strong judge locally, there's a practical middle ground: keep the agent and simulator local, and point only the judge at a cloud model:

[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3.8-27b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3.8-27b"
judge = "openai/gpt-4o"

Only judge calls leave your machine, and they contain the simulated transcript and your metric criteria. They don't include your agent's graph or prompts.

The full voice stack, also local

voicetest up starts the services for live audio calls in Docker: a LiveKit server, faster-whisper for speech-to-text, and Kokoro for text-to-speech. With a local model configured, a live call test runs entirely on your machine, through the real audio pipeline, with nothing sent to an outside service.

What you give up

Local runs are slower than hosted inference. Every turn of every conversation waits on your hardware, and the judge pass adds a generation per metric. A suite that finishes in a few minutes against a hosted provider can take much longer locally. That's fine for a suite you run while you work on prompts, and less fine for a CI check on every pull request.

Results are also only as good as the model. A local judge that's much weaker than the model you'd normally use will pass things a stronger judge would fail. Check a sample of local results against a stronger judge before you rely on them.

When to use each

Scenario Recommendation
Iterating on prompts, rerunning tests often Local
Data can't leave your network Local, or local with a self-hosted judge
CI on every pull request Hosted provider, for speed
Final check before deploying Strongest judge you have access to
Limited hardware Hosted provider, or local agent and simulator with a hosted judge

Models can be swapped per role in settings without touching your tests. Iterate locally while you work, then let CI check the same suite against a hosted model before merging.

Chart data: Epoch AI, Epoch Capabilities Index, November 2026 snapshot, licensed CC-BY 4.0.

Voicetest is open source under Apache 2.0. GitHub: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest

title: Langfuse alternatives for understanding users, not just traces
description:
Stay on Langfuse for tracing, evals, and prompt management: it is MIT-licensed, free to self-host, and the better choice than every managed tool here if open-source tracing is your requirement. What it does not do out of the box is answer product questions such as "what are users trying to do" and "where do they give up", so most teams keep Langfuse and add one tool for that layer, reading the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace Langfuse only if you want a single vendor for both jobs. We make Agnost AI, so it is listed first; every tool gets the same structure and its limitations come from its own documentation.

Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026

If you found this page because of the Langfuse v4 cutover: Langfuse says trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4." On Langfuse Cloud they keep running until the cutover on November 16, 2026, then stop producing results. The recommended replacement is an observation-level evaluator, and Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date; trace-level evaluators stop there once you switch v4 to events_only mode. For most teams this is a migration, not a reason to leave. If you judged whole conversations with trace-level evaluators, note that Langfuse says its evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions." What to do about the Langfuse trace-level evaluator deprecation has the migration steps and the conversation-level options.

Langfuse vs the alternatives for understanding users

The columns are the three questions Langfuse leaves to you: what users wanted, whether they were frustrated, and whether they got what they came for.

Tool What users wanted Frustration or sentiment Outcome Open source Pricing
Langfuse Your own pipeline, written back as scores Custom LLM judge Custom score or reviewer label Yes (MIT core) Free self-host; Core $29/mo
Agnost AI Intents you define, plus suggested intents Patterns you track as intents or rules Rule or success field you define No Free; $49, $499/mo
Amplitude Agent Analytics Topic clustering, User Intent signal User Friction signal Task Completed signal No (SDKs only) Free; per agent session
PostHog Automatic trace clusters Message sentiment from a local model Task outcome judge template Yes (MIT core) 100k events/mo free
Braintrust Topics Task facet Topics Sentiment facet Issues facet; no completion rate documented No (SDK only) Free; Pro $249/mo
LangSmith Insights clusters (Plus and up) Custom attribute or evaluator Custom thread evaluator No (SDK only) Free seat; $39/seat/mo
Arize Phoenix On-demand error analysis via MCP User Friction evaluator Completeness evaluator Source-available (ELv2) Free
Opik Not documented UserFrustrationMetric judge SessionCompletenessQuality judge Yes (Apache-2.0) Free; Pro $19/mo

Where Langfuse is stronger

Langfuse is the reference open-source platform for LLM tracing, and none of the tools below replaces all of it.

  • Open source that is actually complete. The MIT version includes tracing, sessions, users, OpenTelemetry, prompts, datasets, LLM-as-judge, annotation queues, custom dashboards, enterprise SSO, and org-level RBAC. Enterprise-only features are mostly governance: server-side data masking, project-level RBAC, retention management, SCIM, and audit logs.
  • Free self-hosting. Docker Compose, a VM, or Kubernetes with Helm, plus Terraform for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
  • Prompt management, datasets, and experiments in the same product as tracing.
  • A per-user view. Langfuse lists users and segments them by token usage, trace count, and feedback, with all of a user's traces in one place. For "which users cost the most" or "which users left a thumbs-down", it is already enough.
  • Low entry price. Cloud Hobby is free and Core is $29 a month with unlimited users.

The gap this page is about. Conversation themes, intent labels, and outcomes are not built in. Langfuse's own guide for product teams says to "run an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores", treats resolution as a score filled in by reviewers or feedback, and mentions sentiment only as an example criterion for a custom judge. Live evaluators are recommended at the observation level, trace-level evaluators are deprecated, and session-level live evaluation is not described, which makes whole-conversation judgments harder to run continuously. You can build all of this on Langfuse; the tools below ship some or all of it.

Agnost AI

What it is. Conversation analytics for production AI agents. Agnost AI reads real chat and voice conversations to show what users wanted, where they got stuck, and where the agent broke its own rules, then turns recurring failures into pull requests your team reviews.

Best for. Teams that already trace with Langfuse and want the product layer on top without building an intent pipeline: what users ask for, where conversations go wrong, and what to fix first.

Key features.

  • Intents: plain-language definitions of what users want. Agnost classifies conversations against them, tracks volume over time, links to the evidence, and suggests new intents from your product description and observed traffic. This is the classification Langfuse's guide asks you to build.
  • Violations: rules written in natural language ("confirm identity before sharing account details") checked against every analyzed conversation, with the supporting messages attached. Frustration patterns such as rephrasing loops or requests for a human are tracked the same way, as intents or rules you define.
  • Conversation timelines that keep turns, tool calls, errors, and audio together, plus tool-call analytics for success rate, error distribution, and latency.
  • Alerts to Slack or email on an intent or violation threshold, a Daily Summary, and a summary when a new user intent appears.
  • Auto Improve: investigates a recurring finding, prepares a change, tests it against past runs, opens a pull request, and tracks the outcome after deploy.
  • A hosted OpenTelemetry endpoint that can run next to your Langfuse exporter, plus Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs, voice platforms (LiveKit, Vapi, Retell, Telnyx, Trellus), and the Agnost MCP server for Claude, Codex, and Cursor.

Limitations. Not open source; self-hosting is an Enterprise option, so it does not satisfy a strict open-source requirement. There is no built-in frustration score or conversation task-success metric: you define success with a rule or the success event field. No retention or cohort analytics. No built-in PII redaction before ingestion, so you redact in your app (data governance). It does not replace Langfuse's prompt management or experiments.

Pricing. Free (1,000 events a month, 7-day retention), Starter $49/month (10,000 events, 30-day retention), Pro $499/month (1,000,000 events, 90-day retention), Enterprise custom with self-hosted VPC.

Amplitude Agent Analytics

What it is. Amplitude's product analytics plus Agent Analytics, which observes what users ask an AI agent, evaluates where it fails, and ties traces and evals to conversion, retention, and revenue.

Best for. Teams that already standardize on Amplitude and want "what did users want and did they get it" inside the funnels, cohorts, and retention charts they use today.

Key features. Seven built-in session signals: Task Completed, Response Quality, Session Safety, User Intent, User Friction, Has Negative Feedback, and Data Quality Issues. Topic clustering across sessions on every plan. Custom LLM and code-based evaluators that run on all sessions (bring your own LLM key). OpenTelemetry GenAI spans flow in through a bridge, or use the Python and Node SDKs.

Limitations. Conversation text is kept 14 days on Free and Plus (30 days on Growth and Enterprise). Agent sessions are capped at 5,000 a month on Free and Plus. Sentiment isn't a named signal, and some sections are still labeled beta. Not open source (its SDKs are MIT-licensed), and it runs in Amplitude's AWS data centers in the US or EU rather than on your infrastructure. Pricing. Free (2M events and 5,000 agent sessions a month). Plus starts at $0 with the same agent-session allowance. Growth and Enterprise are custom. Agent Analytics is billed on agent sessions, not events.

PostHog

What it is. PostHog's AI Observability (formerly LLM analytics) captures every LLM call as a trace built on PostHog events, so each trace carries the user, their session replay, and any exceptions.

Best for. Teams that want user-level answers and an open-source core. It is the closest open-source option to a full user analytics stack: funnels, retention, and session replay sit on the same data as the AI traces.

Key features. Sessions via $ai_session_id; automatic clusters of similar traces with AI-generated titles; positive, neutral, and negative labels on user messages from a local model with no LLM cost; LLM-as-judge templates including Task outcome and User correction, run per generation, trace, or session; funnels and retention on the same data; OpenTelemetry support.

Limitations. Full prompt and response text is deleted after 30 days. Clustering needs at least 1,000 traces in the past week. LLM-judge evals need your own provider key, and trace-level user feedback is in beta. The core is MIT outside the ee/ directory, and self-hosting is free but officially unsupported. Prompt management and eval experiments are not its focus, so many teams keep Langfuse next to it.

Pricing. First 100,000 AI events a month free, then from $0.00035 per event, falling with volume. No per-seat charges. Each evaluation run counts as one event.

Braintrust

What it is. An evaluation-first platform where production traces become datasets and evals, with Topics for automatic classification of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that would replace Langfuse with a managed eval platform and want intent, sentiment, and issue clustering from the same vendor.

Key features. Topics classifies logs with built-in Task (user intent), Sentiment, and Issues facets plus custom facets, clusters similar requests into themes, and writes labels back to logs. Online scoring rules run scorers on production traces. Thumbs feedback attaches to spans. OpenTelemetry ingest.

Limitations. Topics needs at least 100 summaries before it clusters and regenerates daily, not in real time, and draws down monthly model credits. There is no dedicated per-user view (you filter or group logs by a metadata field such as metadata.user_id) and no built-in task-completion scorer; Braintrust's docs suggest writing a trace-level judge for workflow completion. The platform is not open source (the SDK is Apache-2.0), and self-hosting is Enterprise-only.

Pricing. Starter free (1 GB processed data, 10k scores, 14-day retention, unlimited users). Pro $249/month (5 GB, 50k scores, 30-day retention). Billed on processed data and scores, not seats.

LangSmith

What it is. LangChain's agent observability, evaluation, and deployment platform.

Best for. Teams building on LangChain or LangGraph who would consolidate tracing, evals, and conversation clustering in one vendor.

Key features. Threads group runs into conversations. Insights automatically clusters production traces, including full conversations, into usage patterns and failure modes. Thread-level online evaluators can judge intent, outcome, and trajectory. OpenTelemetry in both directions.

Limitations. Insights is on Plus and Enterprise, samples up to 1,000 traces per report, and runs as reports rather than continuously. Frustration and task outcome need custom attributes or evaluators. There is no dedicated user view; per-user analysis depends on storing user IDs as metadata. The platform is not open source, and self-hosting is an Enterprise add-on.

Pricing. Developer $0 (1 seat, 5,000 base traces a month). Plus $39 per seat per month (10,000 base traces), then $5 per 1,000 additional base traces (14-day retention), or $7.50 per 1,000 extended traces (180-day retention). ## Arize Phoenix

What it is. Arize's open-source AI observability platform for experimentation, evaluation, and troubleshooting, built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference.

Best for. Teams that must stay self-hosted, including air-gapped or regulated environments, and want ready-made conversation judges instead of writing their own.

Key features. Sessions track a whole conversation in one thread with a chat-style view. The pre-built User Friction evaluator detects corrections, retries after an unsuccessful response, frustration, and challenges to unexplained actions, at span, trace, or session level. A Completeness evaluator checks whether a conversation covered every request. An on-demand error-analysis skill run through MCP groups observed problems into labeled annotations with counts. Self-hosting is free with no feature gates.

Limitations. Licensed under the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved, though Arize calls Phoenix open source. Friction and completeness are evaluators you run and log, not an always-on classification layer; Phoenix docs describe exporting traces, running judges, and logging results back. Automatic grouping of recurring failures (Signal) and stakeholder dashboards are Arize AX features. Per-user analytics are not documented. Phoenix does not evaluate incoming production traces automatically: its server evals run on dataset experiments, and online evals are an Arize AX feature. Pricing. Phoenix is free to use and self-host. Arize AX Free is $0 (25k spans a month, 15-day retention), AX Pro is $50/month (50k spans, 30-day retention), and AX Enterprise is custom, with a self-hosted option. ## Opik

What it is. Comet's open-source observability and evals platform for agents, covering traces, threads, LLM-as-judge metrics, and online evaluation of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that want an Apache-2.0 platform with conversation-level judges they can switch on as rules, and a low-cost cloud option.

Key features. Threads group traces by thread_id. Conversation metrics include UserFrustrationMetric ("how frustrated the user became over the interaction") and SessionCompletenessQuality ("whether the user's top-level goals were met"). Online evaluation rules run at trace, thread, or span scope with sampling and filters; thread rules wait for a 15-minute cooldown by default. OpenTelemetry endpoint over HTTP.

Limitations. Topic or intent clustering of conversations is not documented, so "what users wanted" still needs your own classifier. Rules only apply to data logged after you create them. There is no per-user view: dashboards group trace metrics by tags, a metadata key, name, or error. The full platform, including online evaluation, is open source; Enterprise adds RBAC, SSO, and support SLAs. Pricing. Open source is free with unlimited spans and retention. Free Cloud covers 25k spans a month for up to 10 members. Pro Cloud is $19/month for 100k spans, then $5 per 100k spans.

How to choose

If your team… Start with
Keeps Langfuse for tracing and wants intents, rule violations, and fixes as PRs on top Agnost AI
Already runs Amplitude and wants intent, friction, and task-completion signals in its funnels Amplitude Agent Analytics
Wants user analytics plus an open-source core and session replay PostHog
Would move to a managed eval platform with topic clustering Braintrust
Builds on LangChain or LangGraph and wants one vendor for traces and clusters LangSmith
Must stay self-hosted and wants a ready-made friction evaluator Arize Phoenix
Must stay Apache-2.0 and wants frustration and session-completeness judges as rules Opik
Only needs per-user usage and feedback Stay on Langfuse; its user view covers it

If staying open source is non-negotiable, Phoenix, Opik, and PostHog are the closest options, but none of them gives you intent clustering and outcome tracking fully out of the box: you still configure judges or rules. If it is negotiable, the managed tools above ship more of that layer.

Using Langfuse with Agnost AI

Langfuse's Python and TypeScript SDKs are a thin layer on the official OpenTelemetry client, and Langfuse also accepts OTLP at /api/public/otel. Agnost AI runs a hosted OTLP collector, so if your spans pass through an OpenTelemetry tracer provider, you can append Agnost AI as an additional span processor and both tools receive the same spans (OpenTelemetry docs):

import os
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

trace.get_tracer_provider().add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(
        OTLPSpanExporter(
            endpoint="https://otel.agnost.ai/v1/traces",
            headers={"X-Agnost-Org-ID": os.environ["AGNOST_ORG_ID"]},
        )
    )
)

Set a stable conversation ID on your spans (agnost.session_id or session.id); without one, Agnost AI treats each trace as its own conversation. Langfuse keeps your traces, prompts, datasets, and evals; Agnost AI classifies the same conversations against your intents and rules, alerts when a rate moves, and opens pull requests for recurring failures. To start, follow the quickstart.

Related reading

  • Agnost AI vs Langfuse
  • Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026: what to do
  • Best conversation analytics tools for AI agents (2026), the full ten-tool comparison
  • LangSmith vs Langfuse vs Braintrust vs Phoenix vs Agnost, for tracing and eval workflows
  • Braintrust alternatives for conversation analytics
  • Intent analysis tools for AI conversations
  • Self-hosted agent observability checklist
  • LangSmith alternatives for agent evals and monitoring (2026)
  • Arize alternatives: options to Arize AX and Phoenix (2026)

Frequently asked questions

Does Langfuse have user analytics?

Partly. Langfuse has a user list and a per-user view that segments by token usage, number of traces, and feedback, plus sessions and custom dashboards. It does not ship built-in intent or topic grouping, sentiment or frustration detection, or conversation outcomes, so questions about what users wanted and where they gave up need extra work.

Can Langfuse detect user intent or frustration?

Not out of the box. Langfuse's own guide for product teams suggests running an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores, and sentiment appears only as an example criterion for a custom LLM judge. You can build both, but you write and maintain the classifiers yourself.

Should I replace Langfuse or add another tool?

Most teams should add one. Langfuse is strong at open-source tracing, evals, and prompt management, and a conversation analytics tool can read the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace it only if you want one vendor for both jobs, for example LangSmith, Braintrust, or PostHog.

What is the best open-source alternative to Langfuse for user analytics?

Arize Phoenix ships a User Friction evaluator and a Completeness evaluator, and Opik ships UserFrustrationMetric and SessionCompletenessQuality judges for threads. PostHog's MIT core adds message sentiment, trace clustering, and funnels. Note that Phoenix uses the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved.

Are there cheaper alternatives to Langfuse?

Rarely, for raw trace volume. Langfuse is free to self-host, Cloud Hobby includes 50,000 units a month, and Core is $29 a month for 100,000 units, then $8 per 100,000. Opik is the closest on price: free to self-host, 25,000 spans a month on Free Cloud, and $19 a month for 100,000 spans on Pro Cloud. Units and spans are counted differently, so compare on your own traffic.

Do I need a Langfuse alternative because trace-level evaluators are deprecated?

Usually not. Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at the v4 cutover on November 16, 2026, and the replacement, observation-level evaluators, covers most single-request checks. Look elsewhere only if you need live judging of whole multi-turn conversations, which Langfuse says its evaluators cannot apply to sessions directly.

Can I send the same traces to Langfuse and another tool?

Yes. Langfuse's SDKs are built on the OpenTelemetry client and it accepts OTLP, and most of the tools on this page accept OpenTelemetry too. Agnost AI can be added as an extra span processor next to your existing exporter, so both tools receive the same spans.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: Claude Code is third by stars and last by contributors, 8.5x behind Codex
description:
"I'll pick the top ten harnesses by stars, activity and contributors." Measured live: those four criteria disagree, and GetBB has no repository

Anton is going to deep-research the GetBB harness he already looked at. First study its GitHub. Then see what other harnesses exist and pick the ten strongest - by stars, activity, external contributors and overall quality. Then ten separate sessions, one per harness, each going through architecture, capabilities, issues, PRs and documentation: how strong and alive the project is, and what of his own work could be contributed there.

The four criteria are the interesting part, because measured today they produce four different top tens.

GetBB first. It exists - it is getbb.app - and there is no repository to study. getbb/bb and bb-ai/bb both return 404, and no repo named bb surfaces in search. What exists is a third-party layer on top: 8 repositories mentioning getbb.app, a community-curated index at MGrin/awesome-bb-plugins with 69 stars, and the plugins themselves at 1 to 6 stars - bb-plugin-boat (run bb threads on Boat sandboxes), bb-plugin-handoff (move a session between agents and machines), bb-plugin-noema (federated memory for bb agents), bb-plugin-harness (Explore, Plan, Worker, Critic). So step one of the plan has no object, and the contributable surface for GetBB is a plugin or an entry in that awesome list.

⚠️ And a search trap: bb-plugin in:name returns 1,484 repositories, but the top of that list by stars is an Xcode formatter at 1,182 stars, a BBC audio library, and the MyBB forum engine. The name collides with BBC, MyBB and BBEdit. Measuring "the bb ecosystem" with that query overstates it by two orders of magnitude.

Top ten by stars, measured today:

# repo stars open issues last push
1 anomalyco/opencode 227,681 4,060 18 Nov
2 Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT 188,084 690 18 Nov
3 anthropics/claude-code 156,083 17,134 18 Nov
4 openai/codex 135,720 27,730 18 Nov
5 google-gemini/gemini-cli 108,913 736 18 Nov

8 cline/cline 71,742 1,792 17 Nov
9 openinterpreter/openinterpreter 68,905 36 15 Nov
10 aaif-goose/goose 56,743 493 18 Nov

The activity criterion removes three candidates a star-sorted list would include. Aider-AI/aider - 50,162 stars, last push 22 May, nearly six months of silence. RooCodeInc/Roo-Code - 24,238 stars, last push 15 May. And a trap in the name: opencode-ai/opencode has 13,915 stars and has been dead since 18 September 2025, while the live 227k project is anomalyco/opencode, a different owner. Pick ten by stars off a cached list and the first sessions go into archives. The guard is one field: pushed_at.

And the external-contributors criterion inverts the ranking completely:

repo contributors stars rank
openai/codex ~478 4
OpenHands/OpenHands ~460 7
aaif-goose/goose ~451 10
anomalyco/opencode ~450 1
google-gemini/gemini-cli ~443 5
QwenLM/qwen-code ~414 13
cline/cline ~349 8
Aider-AI/aider ~172 11
charmbracelet/crush ~165 14
anthropics/claude-code ~56 3

Third by stars, last by contributors, 8.5x behind Codex. The harness he uses every day is the most closed of the ten to outside work. If the criterion is "where can I actually get something merged", Claude Code lands at the bottom of the list rather than the top.

And most of the doors are unmarked. Open issues with newcomer labels, today: opencode 0 good-first-issue, 0 help-wanted; codex 0 and 0; goose 0 and 0. Only two of the five biggest mark anything: gemini-cli (1 and 10) and cline (2 and 4). So in three of five, "find what to contribute" is not working a labelled queue - it is reading the codebase and proposing unprompted. Different task, different merge odds.

What we have already shipped into this world, and where. 377 PRs on the account. The merged external ones are small and specific: doobidoo/mcp-memory-service 4 of 5, eugeniughelbur/obsidian-second-brain 2 of 3, InftyAI/Awesome-LLMOps and gavischneider/awesome-llm-wiki 1 each. The bulk - 49 PRs - is into three of our own repositories, all merged. And into the ten harnesses: zero. Not one PR to claude-code, codex, opencode, cline, goose, OpenHands, zed, AutoGPT or open-interpreter. "Contribute to ten harnesses" starts from nothing in all ten.

Two different outcomes sit in that same table. Where there was an actual maintainer conversation, the merge rate is 4 of 5 and 2 of 3. Where it was a single cold PR into an awesome list, it is 2 merged out of 11. The shape of the plan - ten repos, one PR each, cold - matches the second pattern, not the first.

⚠️ There is one live thread on exactly this topic: PR #442 to ai-boost/awesome-harness-engineering, "Add sqlite-graph-memory (Memory & State)", opened today, still open.

And the strongest criterion is the one the post does not name. 210 reviews of other people's pull requests, and 246 comments in PRs we did not author. The canon rule of 1 October says it plainly: you become an insider in a repository by reviewing other people's work, not by arriving with your own PR. That ledger is healthy - roughly one review for every two PRs we have authored. It is the only number in this sweep that argues the ten sessions will end in merges rather than refusals.

⚠️ What I did not do. I did not read the architecture, capabilities or documentation of any of the ten - that is precisely the ten sessions the post commissions, and doing them in one pass would produce a worse version of them. I did not verify the GetBB plugin list beyond search results and did not look for GetBB outside GitHub, so "no public repository" means "none that search and two direct lookups find".

⚠️ Method caveat. Contributor counts are estimates from the API pagination header at one item per page - accurate to within a few, excluding anonymous contributors. Stars and push dates are direct API reads of 18 November and move daily.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261116.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261116.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

title: Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026: what to do
description:
Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at its v4 cutover on November 16, 2026. Existing trace-level evaluators keep producing scores until then and stop after it. The replacement is an observation-level evaluator, usually pointed at the root observation of each trace. If you rely on trace-level evaluators, upgrade your SDK, run the in-app upgrade, and compare old and new scores side by side before the 16th. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date.

We make Agnost AI, which judges whole conversations rather than single traces. For many teams the right answer is to stay on Langfuse and migrate, and this page says so. Every Langfuse claim below comes from Langfuse's own docs, checked on 2026-11-12. For background, see what online evals are.

What is changing

Langfuse v4 moves to an observations-first data model: "One denormalized observations table replaces read-time joins between traces and observations." Evaluators move with it.

  • What is deprecated. "Trace-level evaluators are built on the old trace-centric data model and are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4."
  • When. "Langfuse Cloud becomes v4-only on November 16, 2026." On that date, legacy v3 APIs, features, and ingestion are removed.
  • What happens to existing evaluators. On Cloud, they "keep running until the v4 cutover" and then "stop producing results." Historical results stay accessible.
  • What replaces them. "Observation-level evaluators are the recommended target for live production data." LLM-as-a-judge can now run on observations or on experiments.
  • Self-hosted. There is no forced cutover, and v3 gets security patches through January 2027. On self-hosted v4, trace-level evaluators stop once you run in events_only mode, so Langfuse says to migrate evaluators as the last step before switching.
  • Sessions. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions, as Langfuse does not inherently know when a session has concluded." Multi-span evaluation is planned on the new model but not described as available.

Option A: stay on Langfuse and move to observation-level evaluators

This is the right path if your trace-level evaluators judged one request: a single answer, a retrieval plus a response, one agent run. The steps from Langfuse's migration guide:

  1. Upgrade the SDK or ingestion path. Python SDK v4.7.0 or later, JS/TS SDK v5.4.0 or later, or direct OpenTelemetry ingestion with the header x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4.
  2. Keep trace input and output for now. After the upgrade, trace input and output are no longer written automatically. If your old evaluators read them, keep calling set_current_trace_io() (Python) or setActiveTraceIO() (JS/TS) until the new evaluators are validated. These methods are removed in Python SDK v5 and JS/TS SDK v6.
  3. Run the upgrade in Langfuse. Open Evaluation in the app. On Cloud, the Halo assistant handles minor changes. Self-hosted deployments use the coding-assistant path.
  4. Check the target and variable mapping. If every variable came from the trace, target the observation that holds the same values, often the root. If values are split across observations, write them to the root or to a dedicated evaluation observation, or pass trace fields down with propagate_attributes(). Remapped evaluators default to the filter isRootObservation = true.
  5. Check the score count. A trace-level evaluator wrote one score per trace. An observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, so a trace with three matches gets three scores. Narrow the filter to one observation if dashboards or alerts assume one score per trace.
  6. Run old and new side by side, then switch. Compare scores on the same traffic and deactivate the trace-level evaluator when they agree. To revert, deactivate the new evaluator and reactivate the old one.

Do this before November 16. After the cutover there is no old evaluator left to compare against, and any alert built on those scores goes quiet.

If your evaluator judged a conversation. Some teams used trace-level evaluators to judge multi-turn behavior, because the trace carried the chat history. Langfuse's guide to evaluating sessions suggests writing the complete history onto the root observation or the LLM call that receives it, then evaluating that. To avoid judging every turn, tag the final trace (for example conversation_end) and filter on the tag. This works, but your application has to decide when a conversation has ended. The alternative is to compute session scores in your own job and send them with only a sessionId.

Option B: evaluate whole conversations instead

Some failures only exist across turns: the user repeats a request three times, the agent skips an identity check two turns before a refund, or it claims a task is done when no tool call succeeded. One observation cannot show these. Conversation-level vs trace-level online evals lists which failures need which unit.

Agnost AI is built for this unit. You write rules in plain English, and an LLM judges each conversation against them after it has been idle for 15 minutes, in batches rather than in real time. What it does and does not do:

  • Verdicts are pass or fail per assistant message. There are no numeric scores, and the judge's reasoning is not stored.
  • Judging reads the conversation. Tool and sub-agent spans are excluded from the judge's input.
  • No sampling. Every conversation is judged, up to your plan's event limit (Free 1,000, Starter 10,000, Pro 1,000,000 events a month).
  • Backfill. Adding or editing a rule scores your last 1,000 conversations, so you see examples before trusting the rate.
  • Alerts go to Slack or email. There are no webhooks and no CI integration.
  • A fired alert can start Auto Improve, which opens a pull request for your team to review.

Agnost AI accepts OpenTelemetry, so it can read the same spans you send to Langfuse. Keep Langfuse for tracing, prompts, datasets, and observation-level evaluators, and add Agnost AI as a second span processor for conversation rules. Agnost AI vs Langfuse shows the setup, and Agnost AI vs Langfuse vs Arize compares how each catches quality failures.

Option C: other tools with conversation-level online evals

If you are moving off Langfuse anyway, these tools document live evaluation above a single span. Each summary comes from the vendor's docs, checked on 2026-11-12.

  • LangSmith. Multi-turn online evaluators run "once per completed thread, not once per trace." A thread counts as complete after an idle period: 10 minutes by default, 2 minutes minimum. The judge can see all messages or the full trajectory with tool calls. Sampling and filters are supported. Limits: traces must carry a messages list, only runs from the past 7 days count, at most 500 threads per execution, and 10 multi-turn evaluators per workspace.
  • Braintrust. Online scoring runs at span, trace, or group scope. Trace scope waits for an idle timeout (30 seconds by default), and its LLM judges can reference a {{thread}} variable. Group scope scores related traces together, up to 64 traces over a 24-hour interval by default.
  • Arize AX. Session-scoped evaluation tasks can run continuously, with a one-time backfill and sampling per session. Results are written to the root span of the session's first trace. Open-source Phoenix runs session evaluation as code: pull spans, group by session, run judges, and log session annotations yourself.
  • Opik. Online evaluation rules run at trace, thread, or span scope. Thread rules wait for a 15-minute cooldown by default and include templates for task completion, coherence, and user frustration. Rules only score data logged after you create them, unless you run them manually on older items. Opik is open source and its Pro Cloud plan is $19 a month.

Which to choose

If your situation is… Choose
Your evaluators judge one request or one agent run Stay on Langfuse; migrate to observation-level evaluators
You self-host Langfuse and are not on events_only yet Stay on Langfuse; migrate before switching modes
You need multi-turn judging and can mark the last turn yourself Stay on Langfuse; put the history on the root observation and filter on a tag
You want plain-language rules over every whole conversation, with alerts and PRs, next to Langfuse Agnost AI alongside Langfuse
You are on LangChain or LangGraph and want thread-level judges LangSmith
You want open-source thread rules with a frustration template Opik
You already use Arize and want session-scoped tasks Arize AX

For a broader comparison, see Langfuse alternatives for user and conversation analytics and the best online evaluation tools for AI agents.

Frequently asked questions

Are Langfuse trace-level evaluators deprecated?

Yes. Langfuse's docs say trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4. On Langfuse Cloud they keep running until the v4 cutover on November 16, 2026, and stop producing results after it. Self-hosted deployments have no forced date; there, trace-level evaluators stop once you switch Langfuse v4 to events_only mode.

What replaces trace-level evaluators in Langfuse?

Observation-level evaluators. You point the evaluator at one observation, usually the root observation that already holds the trace's input and output, and map its variables from that observation. Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps, and the Evaluation page in the app offers an upgrade path. Note that an observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, not one per trace.

Will my existing Langfuse evaluators keep running after November 16?

Not on Langfuse Cloud. Existing trace-level evaluators keep running until the cutover, then stop producing results. Historical scores stay accessible. You can run old and new evaluators side by side before the date and deactivate the trace-level one once the new one matches.

Can Langfuse evaluate a whole conversation or session?

Not with a built-in live evaluator. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators cannot be applied directly to sessions because it does not know when a session has ended. Its suggested workarounds are to write the full conversation history onto one observation and evaluate that, often only on a tagged final turn, or to add session scores yourself through the SDK, API, or annotation queues.

What is the best Langfuse alternative for evals?

For most teams, staying on Langfuse and moving to observation-level evaluators is the cheapest path. If you need live evaluation of whole multi-turn conversations, LangSmith has multi-turn online evaluators, Opik and Arize AX have thread- or session-scoped online rules, and Agnost AI judges every conversation against plain-language rules. Agnost AI can run next to Langfuse on the same OpenTelemetry data, so you do not have to replace it.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: How to Turn One Photo Into a 12-Second AI Birthday Video (Candles, Zodiac Props, and Audio)
description:
AI birthday video generator from a single photo: they pop champagne on a park bench, blow out a Scorpio cake, or light a crown cake at the car window. Most people only think of a birthday clip five hours before midnight, which leaves zero time for a group shoot or an editing timeline. Turning one photo into a full 12-second birthday scene in your browser—with no slideshow, no timeline, and no subscription—is the shortest way to get a real celebration clip ready before the clock hits twelve.

Putting someone inside a 12-second birthday scene from one camera-roll photo comes down to three details: what kind of photo keeps their face intact, which prompt lines control the cake number and star sign, and how to add the birthday song after downloading the vertical MP4.

1. Pick one unobstructed photo, not a collage

Single-photo video models keep identity steady when the input shows one face clearly in even lighting:

  • Front or slight three-quarter angle: Sunglasses, heavy bangs over one eye, or side profiles force the model to guess the hidden half of the face when the head turns toward the cake.
  • Keep hands and props away from the chin: A drink held in front of the mouth during the source shot often melts into the candle-blowing motion.
  • Cropping: Waist-up or chest-up shots give the scene room for a seated park bench, a table with a layered cake, or a car window frame without squeezing the subject into a corner.

For pets—especially dogs in party hats or gift boxes—the same rule applies: look for clear markings on the coat and ears in bright daylight rather than a dim indoor blur. That is the exact setup behind the happy birthday dog video templates.

2. Edit the three variables before pressing generate

Every preset scene on AI Birthday Video Generator lets you rewrite the prompt before generating a 12-second 720p vertical (9:16) clip on Seedance 2 Mini:

  1. Age or candle number: Swap the number on the candle (28, 30, 50) explicitly in the prompt so the closeup matches the year.
  2. Star sign & table props: Change Scorpio cake and the black scorpion prop to match their sign, or switch to a crown cake and warm car-window framing.
  3. On-screen birthday text: If you want their first name or a short line written right on a sign, frosting, or black-and-white freeze frame, use the happy birthday AI templates built around readable in-frame lettering.

Note on the reference frames above: those frames come from creator posts on Instagram (@prachikarkun) and TikTok (@kidsaroundtheworldmimo) showing the visual look—they were not generated on our site.

3. Export and drop the birthday song in your posting app

The generated 9:16 MP4 finishes with its own party sound effects (cork pop, ambient chatter, celebratory beat) and no watermark, without locking a copyrighted song into the video file. Once you save the clip:

  • Instagram Stories / Reels & TikTok: Upload the 9:16 MP4 directly and pick the birthday song from the app audio library before posting at midnight.
  • Family WhatsApp or iMessage: Send the clip as-is—vertical 720p fills the phone screen immediately on tap.

Pricing and guarantees
