If you were making a 12-second birthday clip tonight for a friend or family member, which detail matters most to lock down first—the exact age on the candles, their zodiac table props, or their name written across the cake?

title: Your Dependencies Have a Maintenance Cost. Here's Why It Matters.
description:
Every dependency you add to a project comes with a responsibility.

You have to install it, keep it updated, monitor vulnerabilities and deal with it when something breaks.

That doesn't mean dependencies are bad. Good packages save developers enormous amounts of time. The problem starts when we introduce packages without thinking about whether we actually need them.

The hidden cost of dependencies

Think about a typical backend project.

You start with a framework, add a database library, bring in a queue package, install a caching solution and before long, your application has accumulated quite a few dependencies.

Some are essential. Others might not even be used anymore.

The more packages you introduce, the more things your team potentially needs to keep track of.

A different approach with ZinTrust

This is one of the ideas behind ZinTrust.

Instead of building its core around Express or Fastify, ZinTrust provides its own backend framework architecture, with integrations available through adapter packages.

For example:

  • PostgreSQL: zin add db:postgres
  • Redis queues: zin add queue:redis
  • Other integrations can be added as your application requires them.

The idea is to avoid introducing integrations you don't currently need.

Three questions worth asking before installing another package

  1. Do I need this for the feature I'm building now?
  2. Is there already something in my existing stack that handles it?
  3. Who will be responsible for maintaining it?

These questions might seem simple, but they can save a lot of unnecessary complexity over time.

Final thought

You don't have to avoid dependencies to build good software.

You just need to be intentional about them.

That's the approach we're taking with ZinTrust.

Explore ZinTrust:

  • Website: https://zintrust.com
  • Documentation: https://zintrust.com/adapters
  • GitHub: https://github.com/ZinTrust/zintrust

Get started:

npm install -g @zintrust/core && zin new my-app

title: Our label service logged every carrier rejection for three weeks and the reason was always [Object]
description:
Our label service is a Node.js application that books parcels with four carriers. When a carrier refuses a booking, the service catches the error from the HTTP client and logs it with one line we had written years earlier: console.error('carrier rejected label', err.response.data). A counter of rejections per carrier feeds a dashboard, and that counter is what started this.

In September rejections from one carrier rose from a handful a day to about two hundred, all on its Saturday service. Each morning the on-call engineer opened the logs, found the rejections, and read this:

carrier rejected label { fault: { errors: [ [Object] ] } }

The carrier's actual reason was inside that [Object]. Node formats objects passed to console.log and console.error with util.inspect, and its default depth is two. The response body was the top level, fault was one level down, errors was two, and each error object sat at the third level, so it was printed as a placeholder. The line looked like a log of the failure. It was a log of the shape of the failure.

Because the line said nothing, the rejections were filed as the carrier being unreliable, and the parcels were rebooked by hand on the weekday service. That went on for three weeks. Then someone replayed one booking with curl and read the full body: the carrier had withdrawn Saturday delivery for a list of rural postcodes and published the change in a partner bulletin nobody on our side received. Our own code had been told which field and why, every time.

The service now logs through pino, which writes one JSON object per line and serialises the whole response body, with a size cap rather than a depth limit. The carrier's error code is a label on the rejection counter, so the dashboard shows the reason instead of only the volume, and a new code appearing for the first time raises a ticket. We also searched every service for console calls that log an object, and found nineteen.

A log line that names the failure without its reason feels complete when you read it. It is the most expensive kind, because it stops people looking.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Understanding AI Computing — Part 3
description:
The Hidden Economics of AI Data Centers

Why the fastest AI chip isn’t necessarily the cheapest — and why utilization matters more than raw computing power.

Understanding AI ComputingImagine spending millions of dollars on the most powerful AI processors available.

You install them in a modern data center, provide enormous amounts of electricity, and connect everything through an ultra-fast network.

Your infrastructure can perform an astonishing number of calculations per second.

But what if much of that computing power remains unused?

The processors still cost money. So do electricity, cooling, networking, and maintenance.

And suddenly, the question is no longer how fast your processors are.

It’s how much useful work they produce for the money you spend.

The Cost of an AI Token

In the previous article, we explored why powerful AI processors can be limited by memory bandwidth rather than computing speed.

That technical limitation has an economic consequence.

When a large language model generates a response, it produces tokens — small units of text.

For an AI service, these tokens represent measurable output.

One useful metric is therefore the cost per million tokens.

Consider a simplified example.

A server costs $10 per hour to operate, including its allocated hardware and infrastructure expenses.

If it produces one million tokens per hour, the cost is $10 per million tokens.

If better optimization doubles its output to two million tokens per hour, the cost falls to $5.

Same hardware. Same operating cost.

Twice the output.

Half the cost per token.

This example is hypothetical, and actual costs depend on the model, workload, and service requirements.

But it illustrates something important.

You don’t necessarily need faster hardware to make AI cheaper. Sometimes you just need to use existing hardware more efficiently.

The Utilization Problem

AI accelerators are expensive, but demand is rarely constant.

During busy periods, servers may operate near their capacity.

At other times, expensive hardware sits idle.

And even when a processor is actively handling requests, its computing units may not be fully utilized.

As discussed in Part 2, memory bandwidth can limit the speed at which a processor performs useful calculations.

Data centers address this partly by processing multiple requests together, a technique called batching.

This improves throughput by allowing the processor to reuse model weights across several calculations.

But there is a trade-off.

Larger batches can increase waiting times, and customers expect their AI assistants to respond quickly.

A service handling interactive conversations must therefore balance efficiency against response time.

A system processing documents overnight can make different choices.

The cheapest way to generate a million tokens is not necessarily the best way to serve a million tokens to customers.

The Real Cost of AI Infrastructure

Electricity attracts considerable attention in discussions about AI data centers.

But it is only one part of the cost.

In a May 2026 analysis, Epoch AI modeled the annualized cost of a hypothetical one-gigawatt AI data center.

Its estimate attributed approximately 60% of total costs to servers, while electricity represented around 7%.

The precise proportions depend on assumptions about hardware prices, electricity costs, financing, and equipment lifetime.

Nevertheless, the example illustrates why energy efficiency alone cannot determine whether an AI processor is economical.

A cheaper or more energy-efficient chip may require additional servers to provide the same service.

Conversely, a more expensive processor may deliver enough additional useful output to justify its price.

Hardware lifetime also matters.

An expensive accelerator does not have to break down to become obsolete.

It only needs to become sufficiently inefficient compared with newer alternatives.

The Cheapest Chip Isn’t Always the Cheapest Solution

Suppose two competing systems can run the same AI model.

One has a lower purchase price and consumes less electricity.

The other costs more but processes substantially more requests while meeting the same response-time requirements.

Which is cheaper?

You cannot answer without considering the complete system.

Hardware, memory, networking, software optimization, operating costs, and actual throughput all influence the result.

That also explains why software matters economically.

Better scheduling, memory management, and optimized computational kernels can increase throughput without replacing the processors.

And it explains why large AI companies invest in specialized hardware and their own software infrastructure.

At enormous scale, even modest improvements in cost per token can translate into substantial savings.

The Real Lesson

The AI industry often measures progress in increasingly impressive numbers of calculations per second.

But customers don’t buy calculations.

They buy useful results.

For an AI service, the important measure is not simply the theoretical performance of its processors, but the cost of delivering the required output at an acceptable speed.

The fastest AI chip is not necessarily the cheapest. The best investment is the system that delivers the required service at the lowest sustainable cost.

And that is the hidden economics of AI data centers.

References & Further Reading

  • Epoch AI — Total Cost of Ownership of a One-Gigawatt AI Data Center
  • NVIDIA — LLM Inference Benchmarking: Fundamental Concepts
  • MLCommons — MLPerf Inference Benchmarks This is Part 3 of Understanding AI Computing, a series exploring the hardware, software, and economics behind modern artificial intelligence.

Next: Part 4 — Apple Metal: A Different Approach to AI Computing.

title: I Directed an AI Agent to Build a Tank Bot — It Just Passed 200 Ranked Sets
description:
I don't write game AI for a living. What I did here was direct one: I set the goals, the constraints, and the acceptance bar, and my AI agent (Muse) wrote the code, tested it locally, and iterated. The arena is battle.training, a tank-battle ladder where AI coding agents build JavaScript controllers, draft a squad, and fight ranked sets around the clock. My bot is wangtea — its page, replays, and record are public here: https://battle.training/bots/wangtea

The build

The agent started from the arena's own documentation file, wrote a controller, and — this is the part I'd recommend to anyone directing an agent — built a local simulation harness first, using the official engine, before anything was uploaded. Version 1 (two battle tanks, a scout, a drone) won 66.3% of 160 local games against the house bots, but it had a clear weakness: it lost to defensive bots that sit on the objective (40% win rate there).

Version 3 changed the squad and the doctrine: a missile unit for long-range pressure, one main battle tank, a drone spotting, and a scout. Focus fire on the lowest-HP target in range, the tank holds at maximum effective range instead of charging, the drone stays behind the tank when its HP drops, and anything under 25% HP retreats. In the local battery, v3 went 130–30 (81%) against the house bots.

The ladder result

Uploaded and left to play, wangtea has now completed 205 ranked sets on the public ladder:

  • Record: 68 wins, 74 losses, 63 draws
  • Public rating: 942 — the house-starter bot sits at 729, so the "beat the starter" bar is cleared with room
  • Ladder position: rank 248 (score 892) as of the 18 Nov check — the bot is still playing, so figures keep moving
  • Health: zero timeouts, zero exceptions across all 205 sets

The honest read: this bot is mid-pack, not a champion. The draw rate says the doctrine is a bit too patient. But it is stable, it never crashes, and it was built end-to-end by an agent working from a one-file spec plus an operator who kept asking "prove it locally first."

What I learned as the operator

  1. Local proof before ladder proof. The simulation harness caught the v1 weakness in an afternoon, for free. On the ladder, that same lesson would have cost days of rating.
  2. Give the agent a number, not a vibe. "Beat the house bots" is a wish. "Above 60% against brawler, above 50% against hunter, zero tick errors" is a spec it can test against.
  3. Stability is a feature. A bot that never times out defends its rating while flashier bots leak points on crashes.

If you run agents, battle.training is an unusually honest benchmark: deterministic games, public replays, no way to fake the record. The bot's full history is on its page — https://battle.training/bots/wangtea — and the controller code will be public on my GitHub once an account issue there is resolved.

Disclosure: this post is my entry to the battle.training Bot Bounty run by promotedby.ai. The bot was built by my AI agent under my direction; the results above are from the public ladder.

title: I taught a music transformer to play jazz with me in real time
description:
duetto is a jazz partner for a MIDI keyboard. You pick a tune, and a pretrained transformer plays it with you in real time as a trio (solo, chords and walking bass), comping while you play and soloing when you rest.

This is the model alone on Autumn Leaves at 160 bpm:

Code: github.com/RiccardoCataldi/duetto

No model was trained or fine-tuned for this. Everything below is about inference: how to take a general-purpose symbolic music model and constrain its decoding until it behaves like a jazz trio that follows a chart and listens to you.

1. The model and its tokens

duetto uses the Anticipatory Music Transformer (AMT, Thickstun et al.), a decoder-only transformer trained on the Lakh MIDI dataset.

AMT encodes music as a flat sequence of events, each made of three tokens:

token meaning resolution
time absolute onset 10 ms ticks
duration how long the note lasts 10 ms ticks
note instrument × pitch one token per (GM program, MIDI pitch)

The instrument is part of the note token (NOTE_OFFSET + program * MAX_PITCH + pitch). That has two useful consequences:

  1. A duo is just one sequence. The player's notes are written into the context as one instrument, the model's as others. The model continues the sequence; it doesn't need to know which notes are "yours".
  2. Each voice can be a different instrument in the context. duetto's bass is written as General MIDI program 32 (acoustic bass), because that is how bass lines are labelled in Lakh MIDI, so the notes it writes under that label move like a bass line. What you actually hear is decided later by the synthesizer.

Out of the box, AMT continues a sequence plausibly, in pop-MIDI style. It has no notion of a chart, a beat grid, chord-scale relationships or jazz phrasing, and it often doubles notes, since Lakh MIDI files are full of duplicated tracks. Everything that follows is about adding those constraints.

2. Constrained decoding, one slot at a time

Each event is sampled as three separate steps, and each step gets its own logit mask before nucleus sampling:

for slot in range(3):            # time, duration, note
    logits = self._logits()      # one forward pass, with KV cache
    mask = torch.full_like(logits, -float('inf'))
    ...                          # open only what is allowed in this slot
    token = sample(nucleus(logits + mask, top_p))
    self.seq.append(token)

Time slot: when may each voice play?
Every voice has a window of allowed onsets, built as a mask over ticks:

  • not earlier than now + 150 ms, to cover sampling and network latency;
  • not inside a phrase-ending breath for the solo;
  • for the walking bass, only on the next beat: the mask opens a single tick;
  • for comping under a solo, only inside the slot where the next chord stab falls;
  • snapped to the subdivision chosen for the next two bars (eighths, triplets, sixteenths), and never faster than can be articulated at the tune's tempo.

The time mask is the union of all the voices' windows. Which voice actually plays is decided in the next slots.

Duration slot.
Comped chords are short, or held for one to three beats in a ballad. A solo note is at least a detached eighth. A quoted phrase keeps its original durations, or slightly shorter.

Note slot: which voice, which pitch?
Given the sampled onset, only the voices whose window contains that tick are opened, each limited to its own register. On top of the mask, duetto adds biases, not hard constraints:

bias effect
chord tones of the current bar +1 logit
tensions (9, 11/#11, 13) +1 logit
out-of-scale notes for the chord pushed down
third or seventh on the beat a chord starts (guide tones) pushed up
a chromatic approach off the beat allowed, then the target chord tone gets +6
keys near the player's hands while they play −2, so it stays out of the way
notes already sounding, or a run about to repeat a third time masked

The distinction between masks and biases is the core design choice. Masks encode things that are wrong (playing the bass off the beat, doubling a note). Biases encode things that are idiomatic (guide tones, chord tones). The model still chooses among the idiomatic options, which keeps the output varied in a way purely rule-based generation is not.

3. Real time: a one-second lookahead with rollback

The music can't wait for the model, and the model can't know what you'll play next. duetto handles this with a sliding buffer:

  • The server keeps about one second of music sampled ahead of the current time, and streams it to the client as timestamped note messages.
  • When you play, your note is appended to the context and the server sends a cut <onset> message: everything it had planned after that point is discarded on both sides and resampled, now conditioned on what you played. A commit window (500 ms by default) keeps the near future fixed unless your note contradicts it, so the accompaniment doesn't stutter at every key you press.
  • Rollback is cheap because the KV cache is cropped rather than rebuilt: unwinding n events removes 3n positions from the cache, and only the new tokens are fed again.
  • When the context fills up, or absolute time approaches the model's maximum, the last ~20 s of events are kept and re-timed to start at 0, the way the training sequences start, and the cache is rebuilt once.

One less obvious issue: AMT reads a long silence as "this is a sparse piece" and tends to stop playing altogether. duetto caps the silence the model may leave, and after it, forces a note from the solo voice.

Measured latency per note (one event, three tokens): ~12 ms with AMT-medium and ~18 ms with AMT-large on an RTX 3080 Ti; ~90 ms with AMT-large on a Jetson Orin Nano. The model runs on a GPU host behind a small line-based TCP protocol, while the laptop handles MIDI input, FluidSynth and a live piano roll. It also runs on a single machine (CUDA, Apple Silicon or CPU).

4. A jazz vocabulary from the Weimar Jazz Database

Chord tones and a beat grid produce correct output, but not idiomatic output. For that, duetto uses the Weimar Jazz Database (WJD), a corpus of hand-transcribed solos by jazz soloists, in two ways.

Statistics. Note choice per chord type and melodic interval transitions in bebop lines are extracted from WJD and added as biases: which notes soloists play over a dominant, which intervals follow which.

Licks. The solos are cut into phrases of one to four bars, at the boundaries where the soloist started and ended a phrase (including the pickup notes before the bar line). Each phrase is stored key-independently and indexed by the chord progression underneath it. While soloing, duetto can look up a phrase that was played over the same changes as the next bars of the tune, transpose it and quote it.

Quoting is also done through the masks: for each event of the lick, the time mask opens exactly one tick and the note mask exactly one pitch. The model still runs a forward pass on every quoted note, so its context stays consistent, and when the quote ends it continues from a line that sounds like its own.

On top of that:

  • Development. A quoted phrase can be repeated as is, displaced by a beat, cut to its first half, or inverted, the way soloists develop a motif.
  • Connections. Between two licks it inserts a short pickup: a scale walk, a chromatic approach or an enclosure of the next phrase's first note.
  • Tempo filter. Licks whose note rate would be unplayable at the current tempo are excluded.
  • Your licks. Phrases you play over the tune are indexed the same way, so it can quote them back.
  • Arc. Density, register and subdivision follow a curve over each chorus, peaking about three quarters through.

5. Voicings and bass, partly rule-based

Not everything goes through the model's preferences.

  • Comping is biased toward four-note rootless voicings, choosing the inversion closest to the previous one (minimal voice movement). While the player is playing, it reduces them to shells (third and seventh).
  • Walking bass gets a note on every beat from the time mask. The pitch is biased toward the root when a bar or a chord begins, toward a semitone from the next root on the beat before a chord change, and mostly stepwise in between.
  • Bossa uses a fixed rhythmic figure (root and fifth with ties, anticipating the next bar's root).
  • Ballads plan each solo phrase in advance: a target note (a third, seventh or tension of the chord where the phrase ends) is chosen first, a rhythm is borrowed from a WJD phrase, and the pitches are biased toward the target.

6. Charts

A tune is a plain-text chart: title, key, tempo, chords bar by bar, and an optional melody that the solo can paraphrase.

title: Autumn Leaves
key: G minor
bpm: 120
Cm7 | F7 | Bbmaj7 | Ebmaj7 | Am7b5 | D7 | Gm6 | % |
> Eb5:4 | -:1 F4:1 G4:1 A4:1 | D5:2 D5:2 | ...

The chord symbols are parsed into root, quality and scale, and these feed the masks and biases above. Style (swing, bossa, even eighths, ballad), part (comp, solo, duet) and around a dozen "character" controls (density, harmony, groove, vocabulary...) adjust the same parameters live.

What I'd take away

  • A pretrained general model plus constrained decoding gets surprisingly far in a domain it wasn't trained for, without any fine-tuning data.
  • Separate hard constraints (masks) from stylistic preferences (biases). Masks keep the output valid, biases make it idiomatic, and the model supplies the variation.
  • For real-time generation, sample ahead and roll back with KV-cache cropping, rather than generating on demand.
  • A small annotated corpus (WJD) is more useful as retrievable material and statistics than as training data.

The code is open source under a noncommercial license: github.com/RiccardoCataldi/duetto. If you play, I'd like to hear what it gets wrong musically. If you work on generative models, feedback on the decoding approach is welcome too.

title: Make your agent gas-aware on Base in 5 minutes
description:
Last week Base gas sat on its 0.006 gwei floor for 91% of 2,016 readings. One real spike hit on Nov 10 (2.3x, gone in about 15 minutes). A Uniswap swap cost about $0.0024.

So the useful question for an agent is not "when is gas cheap?" It is: "is right now a spike, and what will this transaction cost in dollars?" An RPC call gives you gwei. Your agent budgets in dollars.

This guide adds that answer to an agent in three ways, from fastest to most flexible. Each call is paid per request in USDC over x402: no API key, no signup.

What you need

  • A separate Base mainnet wallet with a dollar or two of USDC. No ETH needed: payments are EIP-3009 signatures.
  • Node.js 18+

Never use a key from a wallet that holds real funds. Never paste it into chat or commit it.

Option 1: one command, no code

See what the endpoint asks for (free, returns HTTP 402 with the price):

curl -i "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"

Pay and fetch with the AgentCash CLI:

npx agentcash@latest fetch "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"

gasLimit cheat sheet: 21000 ETH transfer, 65000 ERC-20 transfer, 85000 NFT mint, 180000 swap, 1500000 deploy.

Option 2: MCP (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) 

claude mcp add base-gas \
  --env BUYER_PRIVATE_KEY=0xYOUR_SEPARATE_WALLET_KEY \
  -- npx -y base-gas-mcp

Then just ask:

  • "What does a Uniswap swap on Base cost right now, in dollars?"
  • "Is Base gas high right now, or should I wait?"
  • "Is Base or Arbitrum cheaper for a token transfer?"

The server only ever pays one origin and refuses any single payment above $0.05, so a prompt cannot redirect your wallet.

Option 3: in your own code 

npm i @x402/fetch @x402/evm viem

import { wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig } from "@x402/fetch";
import { ExactEvmScheme } from "@x402/evm/exact/client";
import { privateKeyToAccount } from "viem/accounts";

const account = privateKeyToAccount(process.env.BUYER_PRIVATE_KEY);

const pay = wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig(fetch, {
  schemes: [{ network: "eip155:8453", client: new ExactEvmScheme(account) }],
});

const res = await pay(
  "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"
);
const gas = await res.json();

console.log("Swap cost (USD):", gas.estimatedTransferCost.usd);
console.log("Fees to sign:", gas.suggestedFees.medium);

suggestedFees.medium holds maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas in wei, ready for viem's sendTransaction:

const { maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas } = gas.suggestedFees.medium;
await walletClient.sendTransaction({
  to, value, data,
  maxFeePerGas: BigInt(maxFeePerGas),
  maxPriorityFeePerGas: BigInt(maxPriorityFeePerGas),
});

maxFeePerGas is a ceiling (2x base fee + tip). You pay base fee + tip; the rest is not spent.

A simple rule for agents

  1. Call /gas before a transaction and read the USD cost.
  2. If the cost is above your budget, call /gas/history and check the verdict (cheap / normal / expensive / flat).
  3. If it says expensive, wait 15 minutes. On Base, spikes are short.

Endpoints and prices

Endpoint Price Returns
GET /gas $0.002 Base fee, priority tiers, cost in USD/ETH/gwei, ready-to-sign fees
GET /gas/compare $0.01 Same transaction on Base, OP Mainnet, Arbitrum, Ethereum
GET /gas/history $0.01 Last N hours, with a cheap/normal/expensive/flat verdict
GET /gas/cheapest-window $0.02 Cheapest hour of day from 7 days of data
GET /health free Service status

A failed call is never charged: settlement happens only on a successful response.

Docs and code: base-gas-x402.vercel.app · GitHub

title: SQL Server migration verification: matching row counts are only the start
description:
After a SQL Server migration, matching row counts are a useful first check. They tell you that two tables contain the same number of rows. They do not tell you whether those rows contain the same values, or whether the destination contains the same primary keys. One missing row and one extra row can leave the total unchanged.

Smaller differences can also survive a count check: an accent removed from a name, a decimal changed from 12.50 to 12.51, or a NULL converted to empty text. The row still exists, but its content has changed. A useful acceptance report needs to distinguish missing rows, extra rows, and rows whose values differ under the same key.

Compare rows by their complete primary keys

The verifier described here is a small .NET 8 command-line tool for comparing selected tables between two SQL Server databases. It reads COUNT_BIG(*) and asks SQL Server to calculate a SHA-256 hash for each row. Rows are matched using their complete primary keys, including composite keys.

The primary key identifies the row; the row hash represents its serialized column values. The implementation retains full serialized key bytes rather than reducing primary keys to hashes. A changed primary-key value therefore appears as a missing row and an extra row.

Here is the changed-row branch from its Verifier.cs, reached when the target contains the same serialized primary key:

else if (!entry.Value.Hash.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(targetRow.Hash))
{
    changed++;
    if (changedKeys.Count < 20) changedKeys.Add(entry.Value.DisplayKey);
}

Every difference contributes to the total. The report includes up to 20 example keys per category and table, so a short example list does not mean the remaining differences were ignored.

Serialization matters here. Each column contributes a frame that distinguishes NULL from a non-NULL value and includes the payload length. Empty text consequently differs from NULL, and framing avoids ambiguity when multiple values are combined. SQL Server runs HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', ...) over the framed row.

Before comparing row hashes, the tool checks column and primary-key definitions. A definition mismatch produces a schema-difference result, with row comparison categories marked unavailable. It does not silently treat incompatible tables as successfully compared.

What the report looks like

The following example is synthetic, invented for this article. It is not output from a customer database or one of the recorded validation runs.

Result: DIFFERENCES — one or more selected tables differ.

| Table | Source rows | Target rows | Missing | Extra | Changed | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| dbo.CustomerContacts | 300 | 300 | 1 | 1 | 2 | DIFFERENCES |

Missing keys — showing 1 of 1
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"2"}

Extra keys — showing 1 of 1
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"99"}

Changed keys — showing 2 of 2
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"1"}
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"3"}

Both sides contain 300 rows, yet the destination is missing one source key, contains another key absent from the source, and has two rows with different hashes. The changed-key list identifies rows to investigate; it does not provide a column-by-column value diff.

The application prints a Markdown report and writes migration-report.md. Exit code 0 means every selected table matches, 1 indicates differences, and 2 indicates an invalid invocation or incomplete verification. An incomplete run must not be interpreted as a successful comparison.

What was actually validated

The tool's validation record lists a Windows run on October 27, 2026, against a temporary SQL Server 2025 LocalDB instance. The Release build targeting .NET 8 completed with zero warnings and zero errors. All six recorded checks passed:

  • Equal tables returned exit code 0 and MATCH for both tables.
  • A missing contact with composite key AccountId 10, ContactId 2 was detected.
  • Changing NULL to empty text was reported as a changed row.
  • An extra contact with composite key AccountId 10, ContactId 99 was detected.
  • Removing an accent from Unicode text and changing 12.50 to 12.51 produced two changed keys.
  • A 20,000-row table with one changed amount identified OrderId 15000 in about one second.

That timing is an observation from that LocalDB environment, not a performance guarantee. These are the recorded validation results; the tool was not rebuilt or rerun to prepare this article.

Limits to agree before verification

Very large tables, databases on different servers, and types outside the documented supported list were not covered by those checks. The tool scans both tables and holds key/hash dictionaries in memory. Memory use grows with row count and key size; there is no batching or resume mechanism.

Both databases require snapshot isolation. Their snapshots are independent, so writes should be paused before acceptance. SHA-256 equality provides probabilistic evidence about the selected rows. It does not validate omitted tables, foreign keys, indexes, stored procedures, permissions, or application behavior.

A fixed-scope verification

I offer a fixed-scope SQL Server migration verification using copies or databases restored from backups.

We agree on the selected tables, supported types, and comparison conditions before starting.

The deliverable is a report of missing, extra, and changed rows by table, with example primary keys and explicit limitations.

title: Anker SOLIX and Shopify: Putting Portable Power Conditions Near the Purchase
description:
Cover: archived official product-page screenshot; capture date not independently confirmed.

A portable-power storefront can attract visitors from multiple markets, while an individual product may be intended for a narrower one. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus US page places a North American power-standard notice near the purchase information. Its FAQ also separates different input and output scenarios. These are observations of the US page on 17 November 2026; stock and content may change.

Make the qualifier part of the choice

Regional information is more useful when customers see it while considering the option, rather than after checkout. Keep the actual region, model and relevant requirements alongside the relevant product description. A country selector alone cannot decide whether equipment is suitable for an installation.

The page's FAQ distinguishes several ways the unit can be connected and which outputs are usable in each case. That is a meaningful content-design lesson: one headline number cannot represent every configuration. A merchant should refer users to the applicable official instructions, not reproduce a simplified table as a substitute for them.

The source article also questions how a fragmented site might affect discovery. That is a hypothesis to investigate with crawl data and analytics; the visible pages do not establish an SEO loss or a percentage of affected users.

Turn six operating cases into a navigable explanation

The FAQ on the reviewed page lists six input conditions and identifies usable and non-usable outputs for each. For example, its fourth condition describes a unit connected to a 120 V wall outlet without a generator and lists the L14-30R output as unavailable under that condition. This is a manufacturer-specific statement for the named model and setup, not a general electrical rule.

As a design exercise, a merchant could move a concise link to relevant setup information closer to the purchase choice, then let readers inspect the full FAQ. A selector would need a maintained, reviewed source for every state and a clear escalation path for unanswered questions. The text-only sample below deliberately does not implement that selector or advise on wiring.

Treat version and fulfillment information as data, not decoration

The page compares F3800 Plus and F3800 and includes firmware-specific information for a solar-input specification. A comparison should bind any value to its model, firmware and source date, rather than promoting the largest number to an unconditional headline. This creates work for content owners: when a firmware revision or manual changes, they need to know which entries to review.

The original analysis asks whether delivery and site architecture create friction. Test those questions directly: can a customer find shipping options for their address, and can they navigate between the appropriate brand pages? A visible domain boundary alone does not prove an SEO penalty, and an absent service option in one view does not establish that no such option exists elsewhere.

A small information module for Shopify

The example uses custom.purchase_guide on a product to reference a metaobject containing region_notes, setup_notes and requirements_notes. The merchant creates and verifies the fields. This simply displays explanatory text. It does not select a market, check electrical conditions or calculate eligibility.

{%- comment -%}
  Information display example; not production-ready.
  Display merchant-verified text only. This does not determine compatibility,
  electrical safety, medical suitability, inventory, delivery, or runtime.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign guide = product.metafields.custom.purchase_guide.value -%}
{%- if guide != blank -%}
  {%- assign region_notes = guide.region_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign setup_notes = guide.setup_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign requirements_notes = guide.requirements_notes.value -%}
  {%- if region_notes != blank or setup_notes != blank or requirements_notes != blank -%}
<section class="purchase-guide" aria-label="Product information">
  <h2>{{ product.title | escape }}</h2>
  {%- if region_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Region</h3>
    <p>{{ region_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if setup_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Setup</h3>
    <p>{{ setup_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if requirements_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Use and installation conditions</h3>
    <p>{{ requirements_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
</section>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Validate the decision flow

Test whether a visitor can find the region notice before selecting a configuration; then verify that each installation statement is connected to an exact model and manufacturer source. If a page changes, remove or revise the associated copy rather than treating an old screenshot as current. For electrical design, consult the manufacturer and a qualified professional.

Source: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus US page.

title: Build a "Start Here" Index for Your Community with 30 Lines of Python
description:
Every online community hits the same wall. Members ask questions that were already answered, because the answers are buried in a date-sorted feed. The fix is to organize by problem instead of by date, and you can automate most of that cleanup with a small script.

Here's how I'd build it.

The idea

  1. Export or copy your past questions (title + link) into a JSON file.
  2. Map each question to a "problem" bucket using simple keyword rules.
  3. Generate a Markdown "start here" post grouped by problem.
  4. Pin it, and re-run the script whenever new answers pile up.

No AI required for version one. Keyword rules are boring, predictable, and easy to debug, which is exactly what you want from a first automation.

The input

A file called questions.json:

[
  {"title": "How do I follow up with new leads automatically?", "url": "https://example.com/post/1"},
  {"title": "Best way to start a newsletter for my SaaS?", "url": "https://example.com/post/2"},
  {"title": "Can I turn my spreadsheet into a weekly report?", "url": "https://example.com/post/3"}
]

The script 

import json

PROBLEMS = {
    "lead follow-up": ["lead", "follow up", "crm", "booking"],
    "email and newsletters": ["email", "newsletter", "inbox"],
    "data and reporting": ["spreadsheet", "report", "dashboard"],
    "getting started": ["start", "first", "beginner"],
}

def categorize(title):
    text = title.lower()
    for problem, keywords in PROBLEMS.items():
        if any(k in text for k in keywords):
            return problem
    return "uncategorized"

def build_index(questions):
    index = {}
    for q in questions:
        index.setdefault(categorize(q["title"]), []).append(q)
    return index

def to_markdown(index):
    lines = ["# Start here: find your problem", ""]
    for problem in sorted(index):
        lines.append(f"## {problem.title()}")
        for q in index[problem]:
            lines.append(f"- [{q['title']}]({q['url']})")
        lines.append("")
    return "\n".join(lines)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("questions.json") as f:
        questions = json.load(f)
    print(to_markdown(build_index(questions)))

Run it with python build_index.py > start_here.md and paste the output into a pinned post.

How it works

PROBLEMS is your whole configuration. Each key is a problem in your members' words; each value is a list of keywords. categorize() returns the first bucket whose keyword appears in the title, so order matters: put the most specific problems first.

build_index() groups questions into buckets, and to_markdown() turns those buckets into headings and links.

Anything that lands in "uncategorized" is a signal. Either you need a new keyword, or you've found a new problem your members care about.

Making it better

  • Schedule it. Run it weekly with cron or a GitHub Action and diff the output so you only update the pinned post when something changes.
  • Add an LLM fallback. For uncategorized titles only, ask a model to pick one of your existing buckets. Keep the keyword rules as the first pass so results stay predictable and cheap.
  • Track gaps. Count questions per bucket. The bucket with the most questions and the fewest good answers is your next lesson.

Why bother

A problem-sorted index gives new members a quick win, cuts repeat questions, and shows you what to create next. It's a tiny automation with an outsized payoff.

I'm building my own community, Automation Entrepreneur, around exactly this kind of practical automation. Join us here: https://www.skool.com/automation-enterenpeur-7666

title: Our import worker was killed for memory and the last log line we had was thirty thousand rows old
description:
Our supplier catalogue import is a Python worker running in Kubernetes. It reads each supplier's product file, validates every row and reports progress with print, one line per thousand rows, naming the supplier and the row. Run it on a laptop and you can watch it count through the file.

In October it was OOMKilled every night on one supplier's file. kubectl logs --previous ended at row 41,000, so we spent a morning reading rows 41,000 to 42,000 for anything that could blow up memory. They were ordinary. Running the same file locally showed memory climbing only after row 63,000, where the supplier had started pasting whole HTML pages into the description column, and the kill came about eight thousand rows after that.

The logs were not wrong. They were late. When Python's standard output is a terminal it is line buffered, and each print appears at once. In a container, standard output is a pipe to the runtime, and Python buffers it in blocks of a few kilobytes, writing only when the block fills or the program exits normally. Our progress lines were short, so one block held thirty of them. A process killed for memory receives SIGKILL, which nothing can catch, and whatever sat in the buffer is never written. We had been reading the last line that happened to be flushed, not the last line the worker printed.

Nothing had ever made us suspicious, because our tracebacks always arrived. Since Python 3.9, standard error is line buffered even when it is not a terminal, so errors came through promptly and progress did not.

Every Python base image we build now sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. The worker reports progress through the logging module, whose stream handler flushes after every record, and it writes one JSON object per line with the supplier, the row and its own memory use. The import also streams the description column and rejects any field over a size limit, which was the actual bug.

In a terminal, print means now. In a container it means eventually, and a process killed for memory never gets to eventually.

– Sergey Shinder

title: "Introducing KaDeep Studio: know what's ready to ship, on every platform and in every market"
description:
It's launch week. Your team is shipping a new payments feature to India, the UAE, Japan and Mexico, on web, iPhone, Android and desktop, in five languages.

The test dashboard says 27 of 31 passing. The translation tracker says 79% reviewed. The accessibility audit is from last quarter. Three tools, and still no clear answer. So the person who owns the release makes the call on gut feel.

Today we're launching KaDeep Studio, so that call is never made on gut feel again.

KaDeep Studio is one AI agent that tests your release on every platform, in every language you sell, checks accessibility on the way, and gives your team one clear go or no-go, with the evidence behind it.

👉 Start free · 📅 Book a walkthrough · ⭐ Open-source CLI

1. Ask in plain English

"Test Kasu Money 1.1 on web, Android, iPhone and desktop, in all five languages."

No selectors and no scripts. The agent reads your specs, explores the live product and writes a test plan you approve. From one spec, it wrote 40 test cases in 3.4 minutes.

2. It tests every platform

One agent drives web (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge), Android and iOS (cloud phones, emulators or real devices), and desktop apps on Windows and macOS.

Every step is recorded with the screen, console and network log. When your app changes, the agent updates the affected steps and asks for approval before saving them. Apps on localhost or behind a VPN run on a paired computer.

It also finds what scripts miss: in one session, it tapped Send three times quickly and caught the wallet charging the customer three times. Bugs go to Jira with evidence, and the agent re-checks each fix on the same platform and language.

3. Then it takes you global

Translating files isn't enough. The product has to work in every language. In KaDeep, localization lives in the same Studio:

  • 100+ file formats, from app strings to PDFs and courses, returned in the format they arrived in
  • Guardrails: an estimate before any spend, free translation-memory matches, enforced glossaries, a second model reviewing, and human review for legal and finance text
  • Checked on screen: it catches what files can't show, like Hindi tab labels clipped or an Arabic layout that doesn't mirror

4. Accessible under any law

title: Web Scraping with Scrapy: Building a Spider from Scratch
description:
A requests and BeautifulSoup script is the right way to start scraping. But as soon as a job grows, you find yourself writing the same plumbing again and again: a loop over pages, retries, delays, de-duplication, saving results. Soon your 30-line script is 300 lines and mostly not about the data.

Scrapy is a framework that supplies that plumbing. You describe what to extract in a small class called a spider, and Scrapy handles requests, concurrency, retries, throttling, robots.txt, logging, and exporting results.

In this guide you'll build a complete Scrapy project from scratch. It will crawl every page of a bookstore, follow each book to its detail page, clean the data in a pipeline, and export it to JSON or CSV, politely.

Version note: this guide targets Scrapy 2.20 (released November 2026), which requires Python 3.11 or newer. Scrapy has changed a lot recently, and many tutorials online are out of date. The biggest example: the old start_requests() method was removed in Scrapy 2.16, and spiders now use async def start(). If you copy a spider from an older tutorial and it crawls nothing, that's probably why.

Why Scrapy?

Here's what you get without writing it yourself:

Need In a script In Scrapy
Many requests at once Threads or asyncio by hand Built-in concurrency
Retrying failures Your own loop Built-in retry middleware
Being polite time.sleep() Download delay and AutoThrottle
Obeying robots.txt Extra code One setting, on by default
Skipping repeated URLs A set() you maintain Automatic de-duplication
Cleaning and saving data Mixed into the scraping code Item pipelines and feed exports
Knowing what happened print() Logs and crawl statistics

When not to use it. For a single page or a quick one-off, requests and BeautifulSoup are simpler. For sites that build their content with JavaScript, you need a browser: see our guide to scraping JavaScript-heavy sites with Playwright. Scrapy shines when you need to crawl many pages reliably.

Setting Up

Check that you have Python 3.11 or newer, then create a virtual environment and install Scrapy:

python --version                 # 3.11 or newer
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate         # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install scrapy
scrapy version

Now create a project:

scrapy startproject bookscraper
cd bookscraper

You get this layout:

bookscraper/
├── scrapy.cfg                # project marker (run commands from this folder)
└── bookscraper/
    ├── items.py              # the shape of the data you extract
    ├── middlewares.py        # hooks into the request/response flow
    ├── pipelines.py          # clean, validate and store items
    ├── settings.py           # all configuration
    └── spiders/              # your spiders live here

Two things in the generated settings.py are worth noticing right away: ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True, so Scrapy respects robots.txt by default, and a DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second with one request at a time per domain. New projects start out polite.

Explore the Page with the Scrapy Shell

Before writing any spider, experiment on the live page. The shell downloads a URL and gives you a response object to play with:

scrapy shell "https://books.toscrape.com/"

We'll use the sandbox site books.toscrape.com, which exists for practicing scraping. Inside the shell, try:

>>> response.css("article.product_pod h3 a::attr(title)").get()
'A Light in the Attic'
>>> response.css("p.price_color::text").getall()[:3]
['£51.77', '£53.74', '£50.10']
>>> response.xpath("//li[@class='next']/a/@href").get()
'catalogue/page-2.html'

A few things to learn from this:

  • response.css() takes CSS selectors, extended with ::text (the text of an element) and ::attr(name) (an attribute's value).

  • response.xpath() does the same job with XPath, which is handy for odd cases.

  • .get() returns the first match, or None if there isn't one. .getall() returns a list of every match.

The shell is the fastest way to get selectors right, so use it constantly. Type exit() to leave.

Your First Spider

A spider is a class with a name, a place to start, and a parse method that turns a response into data. You can generate a skeleton with scrapy genspider books books.toscrape.com, but it's short enough to write by hand. Create bookscraper/spiders/books.py:

import scrapy

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            yield {
                "title": card.css("h3 a::attr(title)").get(),
                "price": card.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
                "url": response.urljoin(card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get()),
            }

How it works:

  • name is how you run the spider.

  • allowed_domains stops the spider from wandering off to other sites.

  • start_urls lists the first pages to download. Scrapy requests each one and passes the response to parse.

  • yield hands each result back to Scrapy. A spider doesn't return a list: it yields items one at a time, and Scrapy streams them to wherever they're going.

Run it and export to a file:

scrapy crawl books -O books.json

-O (capital) overwrites the output file, so you always start fresh. Open books.json and you'll have the first page of books.

Watch out for -o. In projects created with Scrapy 2.20, the generated settings include FEED_MODE = "create". If the file already exists, lowercase -o then logs an error (Not writing ... because it already exists) and throws that run's items away, yet the command still exits normally, so it's easy to miss. In older setups, and outside a project, -o appends, and appending a second run to a JSON file leaves you with a corrupted file. Use -O while you're developing, or pick the behavior explicitly with the FEED_MODE setting.

If you just want to try a spider quickly without creating a project, scrapy runspider books.py -O books.json runs a single file.

About start_urls and start()

start_urls is the simplest way to say where to begin. When you need more control, such as generating a list of URLs or adding headers, write an async def start() method instead:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]

    async def start(self):
        for page in range(1, 4):
            url = f"https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-{page}.html"
            yield scrapy.Request(url, callback=self.parse)

This replaces start_requests() from older tutorials. Note that async def and yield together make it an asynchronous generator, which Scrapy knows how to run. A leftover start_requests() isn't an error: the spider simply starts, reports Crawled 0 pages, and finishes without a word of complaint.

Following Pagination

Scraping one page isn't much of a crawler. Add this to the end of parse to follow the "Next" link:

next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

response.follow() creates a new request for the link and sends its response back to parse. It handles relative URLs for you (no urljoin needed), and Scrapy automatically skips any URL it has already requested. When there's no Next link on the last page, get() returns None and the crawl ends.

Following Links to Detail Pages

The listing doesn't have everything: the description and product code live on each book's own page. So the spider needs two callbacks: one for listing pages and one for book pages. It will also pass the star rating (which we only read from the listing) along to the second callback.

First, define the shape of your data in bookscraper/items.py. Recent Scrapy templates use a plain dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str | None = None
    price: str | float | None = None
    rating: str | int | None = None
    availability: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    upc: str | None = None
    url: str | None = None

Now rewrite the spider:

import scrapy

from bookscraper.items import Book

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        """Listing page: follow every book, then the Next link."""
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            rating = card.css("p.star-rating::attr(class)").get().split()[-1]   # "star-rating Three" -> "Three"
            yield response.follow(
                card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get(),
                callback=self.parse_book,
                cb_kwargs={"rating": rating},
            )

        next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

    def parse_book(self, response, rating):
        """Book page: build the item."""
        availability = "".join(response.css("p.availability::text").getall())
        yield Book(
            title=response.css("h1::text").get(),
            price=response.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
            rating=rating,
            availability=" ".join(availability.split()),
            description=response.css("#product_description ~ p::text").get(),
            upc=response.css("table tr:first-child td::text").get(),
            url=response.url,
        )

Notes on what's new:

  • Callbacks chain the crawl. parse yields requests for book pages, and each response goes to parse_book, which yields items. A callback can yield both requests and items.

  • cb_kwargs passes extra data to the next callback as keyword arguments. That's how rating travels from the listing page to the book page.

  • Whitespace cleanup. The availability text has line breaks and padding around it, so we collapse it with " ".join(text.split()).

  • Missing data. Some pages will lack a field, a description for instance. .get() returns None instead of crashing, and the dataclass defaults to None.

Cleaning Data with Pipelines

Right now price is a string like £51.77 and rating is a word like Three. Item pipelines are the right place to clean and validate items, keeping that logic out of the spider. Each pipeline is a class with a process_item method. Open bookscraper/pipelines.py:

import re

from itemadapter import ItemAdapter
from scrapy.exceptions import DropItem

RATINGS = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

class ValidateAndCleanPipeline:
    def process_item(self, item):
        adapter = ItemAdapter(item)

        if not adapter.get("title") or not adapter.get("price"):
            raise DropItem(f"Missing title or price: {adapter.get('url')}")

        adapter["price"] = float(re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", adapter["price"]))   # "£51.77" -> 51.77
        adapter["rating"] = RATINGS.get(adapter["rating"])                   # "Three" -> 3
        return item

class DuplicatesPipeline:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seen = set()

    def process_item(self, item):
        upc = ItemAdapter(item)["upc"]
        if upc in self.seen:
            raise DropItem(f"Duplicate book: {upc}")
        self.seen.add(upc)
        return item

Key ideas:

  • ItemAdapter lets one pipeline work with dictionaries, dataclasses, or scrapy.Item objects through the same interface.

  • Return the item to pass it along, or raise DropItem to discard it. Dropped items are logged and counted but never exported.

  • The first pipeline drops incomplete items and converts the price and rating to numbers. The second drops repeats using the UPC, a unique product code, because the same book can appear under more than one URL.

  • Older tutorials write process_item(self, item, spider). That still runs in 2.20 but prints a deprecation warning, so drop the spider argument in new code.

Pipelines are off until you switch them on in settings.py. The numbers set the order, and lower runs first:

ITEM_PIPELINES = {
    "bookscraper.pipelines.ValidateAndCleanPipeline": 300,
    "bookscraper.pipelines.DuplicatesPipeline": 400,
}

Crawling Politely: Settings

Scrapy is fast, which is exactly why you must configure it carefully. Add these to settings.py:

# Tell site owners who you are and how to reach you
USER_AGENT = "BookScraperBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; contact@example.com)"

# Adapt the delay to how quickly the server responds
AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = True
AUTOTHROTTLE_START_DELAY = 1
AUTOTHROTTLE_MAX_DELAY = 10
AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY = 1.0

# Retry temporary failures a couple of times
RETRY_TIMES = 2

# During development only: cache responses on disk so repeat runs don't hit the site
HTTPCACHE_ENABLED = True

# Export automatically, without command-line flags
FEEDS = {
    "output/books.json": {"format": "json", "mode": "overwrite", "indent": 2},
}

What each does:

  • USER_AGENT replaces Scrapy's default. An honest, descriptive agent with contact details lets site owners reach you instead of blocking you.

  • AutoThrottle adjusts the delay between requests based on how fast the server responds, backing off when the site slows down. It never goes below the project's DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second, so it can only make the crawl gentler than the default.

  • HTTPCACHE_ENABLED stores every response on disk. Re-running the spider while you tweak your selectors then costs the site nothing. Turn it off for real runs, or you'll scrape stale data.

  • FEEDS defines the output in settings, with "mode": "overwrite" replacing the file on each run.

Two more settings are handy while testing: CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT and CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT stop the crawl after roughly that many pages or items (requests already in flight still finish). You can pass any setting on the command line with -s:

scrapy crawl books -s CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT=10 -O sample.json

One catch: -O adds a second output on top of FEEDS, so this sample run also overwrites output/books.json with the partial result. Comment out FEEDS while you experiment if that bothers you.

The sandbox has 50 listing pages of 20 books each, so a full crawl is about 1,050 requests. With a delay of at least one second each, expect 20 minutes or more, so test with a small sample first.

Spider arguments

You can also pass arguments to a spider with -a. For example, to crawl one category instead of the whole site, accept a start URL:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def __init__(self, start_url=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if start_url:
            self.start_urls = [start_url]

scrapy crawl books -a start_url=https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html -O travel.json

Reading the Results

When a crawl finishes, Scrapy prints a statistics summary. These lines tell you most of what you need:

Stat Meaning
item_scraped_count Items that made it through the pipelines
item_dropped_count Items discarded with DropItem
downloader/response_status_count/200 Successful responses (look for 403, 404, 429 here too)
dupefilter/filtered Requests skipped because the URL had been seen
robotstxt/forbidden Requests blocked by robots.txt
finish_reason finished for a normal end, or the reason it stopped early

A stat that never happened isn't printed at all, so no robotstxt/forbidden line means nothing was blocked. Check these after every run. A crawl that "worked" but dropped half its items, or got a pile of 403 responses, is telling you something.

Running a Spider from a Script

Sometimes you want to run a crawl from your own Python code, for example from a scheduler. Put this in a file at the project root:

from scrapy.crawler import AsyncCrawlerProcess
from scrapy.utils.project import get_project_settings

process = AsyncCrawlerProcess(get_project_settings())
process.crawl("books")
process.start()          # blocks until the crawl is finished

Run it from the same folder as scrapy.cfg, so Scrapy finds your project settings.

Responsible Scraping with Scrapy

Because Scrapy can send many requests quickly, a few habits matter more here than in a script:

  • Leave ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True. Turning it off to get at pages a site has asked crawlers to avoid is the wrong fix for a "Forbidden by robots.txt" message.

  • Keep the delay and the concurrency low. The generated defaults are conservative, and AutoThrottle helps. Don't raise concurrency against a small site.

  • Identify yourself with USER_AGENT, and respect 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After by slowing down, not by retrying harder.

  • Read the terms of service, and avoid personal data unless you have a lawful reason to collect it. Our guide "Is Web Scraping Legal?" covers this in depth.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause What to try
Spider runs but crawls nothing (Crawled 0 pages) Code from an older tutorial defines start_requests(), which was removed in 2.16 Use start_urls or async def start()
Not writing ... already exists and an empty export -o on an existing file; projects from 2.20 set FEED_MODE = "create" Use -O, or set FEED_MODE explicitly
Empty or None fields Selector doesn't match Test it in scrapy shell
Filtered offsite request in the log The link is outside allowed_domains Check the domain, or leave it if it's intended
Forbidden by robots.txt The site disallows that path Respect it; don't disable ROBOTSTXT_OBEY
ModuleNotFoundError: bookscraper You're not in the project folder Run from the folder containing scrapy.cfg
Lots of 403 or 429 responses You're going too fast, or the site refuses your traffic Slow down; check the site's rules
Fewer items than expected Pipelines dropped some, or the duplicate filter skipped URLs Check item_dropped_count and dupefilter/filtered

For more detail while debugging, run with -s LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.

Where to Go from Here

You now have the core of a real crawler: a spider, items, pipelines, polite settings, and exports. Natural next steps:

  • CrawlSpider rules let you describe which links to follow declaratively instead of writing the pagination code yourself.

  • JavaScript sites need a browser. Plugins such as scrapy-playwright connect Scrapy to Playwright, so you keep the framework's crawling and pipelines.

  • Storing results in a database is a matter of writing another pipeline, for example one that inserts into SQLite or PostgreSQL.

  • Scheduling a nightly crawl is easy once your spider runs from a script or a command.

The mental model to remember: spiders extract, pipelines clean, settings decide how politely you crawl, and Scrapy runs the machinery. Once you've written your first spider, the second takes minutes.

Happy scraping, and please do it politely!
