title: We Moved Our Branch Shared Drives Into Azure and Nine Branches Could Not Reach Them Because Their Broadband Blocked One Port
description:
Each of our branches has a shared drive for the documents that do not belong in any system: cutting lists for the timber saw, photographs of damaged deliveries, the yard rota, the price lists suppliers send as spreadsheets. For years these lived on a small server in each branch. Last spring we retired the servers and moved the drives to Azure Files, which presents cloud storage as an ordinary Windows network drive.

We piloted it at head office and at our two largest branches, and it was excellent. Drives mapped at sign in and files opened quickly. We scheduled the remaining branches over three weekends.

On the Monday after the second weekend, nine branches rang to say their drive had gone. Windows reported that the network path could not be found. The branches that worked and the branches that did not had the same PCs, the same build and the same settings.

They did not have the same internet. Our larger sites connect over a private network that reaches Azure through our own link. The smaller branches use business broadband with direct internet access, and the nine that failed were all with one provider. Azure Files speaks SMB, the Windows file sharing protocol, over TCP port 445, and that provider blocks port 445, as many do. The port was abused by worms for years, and SMB was never designed to cross the open internet. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this, in a section we had not read because our pilot sites never needed it.

For two days those branches emailed files to one another while we arranged a fix. Each branch router now builds a VPN tunnel to our Azure network, and the drives are reached through a private address inside it, so the broadband provider sees only encrypted VPN traffic. That is how it should have been designed from the start.

Our migration checklist now records how every site connects to the internet, and every pilot includes at least one site of each kind. We had tested the product well. We had tested it only from the places where it was always going to work.

– Serguey Shinder

title: The IBS effect in ETFs: section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies, replicated in Python and R
description:
This is a standalone version of an article first published on quantstr.at. The Python and R code, the data files and the line-by-line walk-through are in the original.

TL;DR

  • Strategy: Section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies sorts ETFs by Internal Bar Strength (IBS), where the close sits within the day's range, and bets on mean reversion the next day.
  • What we did: an attempt to replicate Pagonidis (2014), The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs, on Yahoo Finance data for 31 of its 33 ETFs (two are no longer available), first over the original window to 5 December 2013 and then on the 13 years since.
  • Result in the original window: the average next-day return after the lowest IBS bucket was 0.353% and after the highest −0.134% (original: 0.350% and −0.126%). A long-short rule earned 30.8% a year per ETF before costs.
  • Since 2013: the gap between the lowest and highest bucket fell from 0.49 to 0.19 percentage points a day. The same rule earned 9.2% before costs and −0.1% after 5 basis points per trade.
  • The book's decile rule: 38.6% a year before costs since 2013, 16.4% at 2 basis points and −10.4% at 5. It turns over its portfolio about 3.5 times a day, so the cost assumption decides the result.

The idea

IBS = (Close − Low) / (High − Low). It is 0 when the close is the low of the day and 1 when it is the high. Pagonidis finds that ETFs that closed near their low tend to rise the next day and those that closed near their high tend to fall.

IBSi​(t)=racPiC​(t)−PiL​(t)PiH​(t)−PiL​(t)

The single-ETF rule goes long when IBS is 0.2 or below and short when it is 0.8 or above, for one day. The book's version ranks the ETFs each day, buys the lowest tenth and sells the highest tenth with equal weights.

Replication: average next-day return by IBS bucket (%)

0 to 0.2 0.2 to 0.4 0.4 to 0.6 0.6 to 0.8 0.8 to 1
Pagonidis (2014), to 5 Dec 2013 0.350 0.096 0.025 −0.032 −0.126
Ours, to 5 Dec 2013 0.353 0.099 0.032 −0.048 −0.134
Ours, after 5 Dec 2013 0.142 0.072 0.025 −0.005 −0.044

Gap between lowest and highest bucket: 0.49 points in the original window (original: 0.476). Probability of a positive next day: 57.2% after the lowest bucket and 46.4% after the highest (original: 56.8% and 46.2%).

The rule, before and after 2013

Average annual return per ETF of the long-short rule (compounded):

After 2013 the effect is positive in 29 of 31 ETFs but weaker, and trading costs matter: at 5 basis points per trade the rule is about break-even.

IBS as a filter for RSI

Pagonidis combines IBS with Cutler's RSI(3): buy below 10, hold while RSI(3) is 40 or below, and in the filtered version hold only while IBS is 0.5 or below. The sum of daily returns without the filter is 121.9% in the original window (original: 119.0%); with the filter 119.4% (original: 128.6%), in about half the days. We reproduce the halving of time invested but not the improvement in return in that window. After 2013 the filter helps: 30.4% against 20.3%.

The book's decile rule

Annual growth rate of the dollar-neutral decile rule, before and after costs:

Cost per unit traded To 5 Dec 2013 After 5 Dec 2013
None 337.9% 38.6%
2 bps 268.3% 16.4%
5 bps 184.1% -10.4%
10 bps 84.1% -42.1%

Break-even cost is roughly 3.9 basis points. Fills at the close are assumed, which is idealised because the final IBS is only known once the close is set.

Limitations

  • Yahoo adjusted prices differ from the vendor in the original, and two ETFs (GXG, RSX) are missing. The ETFs that remain survived to today.
  • This is an attempt to replicate; where choices were not stated (range and volume medians, tie-breaking, the cost model) they are ours and are listed in the original article.
  • No bid-ask spread, market impact or borrow costs in the replication tables. Not investment advice.

Conclusion

The IBS effect reproduces closely in the original window: next-day returns after low-IBS days were 0.49 percentage points higher than after high-IBS days. Since 2013 the gap has narrowed to 0.19, and whether anything is left after trading costs depends on assumptions a backtest cannot settle.

Reference: Pagonidis, A. S. (2014). The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs. Working paper, NAAIM. Book: Kakushadze, Z. and Serur, J. A. (2018), 151 Trading Strategies, Section 4.4.

The full article, with the Python and R code: https://quantstr.at/quant-strategies/mean-reversion/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=syndication

title: Your Service Has Stopped Responding and You Have Never Taken a Thread Dump
description:
The service is still running. The process is there, the memory looks normal, and the CPU is almost idle. But every request hangs until it times out, and the logs stopped twenty minutes ago without a single error. Someone suggests restarting it. Before you do, spend one minute capturing what every thread inside it is doing right now. That snapshot is called a thread dump, and once you have read one, you will never want to restart a stuck service blind again.

On the Java virtual machine there are three common ways to take one. Run jstack followed by the process id. Or run jcmd with the process id and Thread.print. Or send the process a quit signal with kill -3, which makes the JVM write the dump to its own standard output, so in a container it appears in the logs. Take three dumps about ten seconds apart. A thread that is in the same place in all three is stuck, not busy.

Each thread appears with a name, a state and a stack trace. The state tells you a lot. RUNNABLE means it is doing work, or waiting on the network. BLOCKED means it is waiting to enter a synchronized section that another thread holds. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING mean it is parked until something wakes it.

Now look for patterns rather than reading every line. Are two hundred request threads all waiting at the same line, inside the method that borrows a database connection from the pool? Then the pool is empty, and the interesting question is who is holding the connections. Are several threads BLOCKED on the same lock, with one thread holding it while it waits on a slow external call? There is your problem. If two threads are each waiting for a lock the other holds, jstack will often say so plainly, with a line saying it found a Java level deadlock.

Other runtimes have the same idea. For Python, py-spy dump with a process id prints the stack of every thread without stopping the program.

Practise on a calm day. Take a dump of a healthy service, find your own code in it, and learn what normal looks like. Then, during the next incident, capture first and restart second. The restart fixes today. The dump tells you how to stop it happening again.

– Asael Shinder

title: Your Rust Code Sets an Environment Variable and the 2024 Edition Calls That Unsafe
description:
The service had one line
at the top of main:

std::env::set_var("TZ", "UTC");

Harmless for years.

Then the team
moved the crate
to the 2024 edition.

It stopped compiling.

The compiler said
set_var is an unsafe function
and needs an unsafe block.

One environment variable.

Unsafe.

Here is the mechanism.

On Linux and most Unix systems,
the environment is a plain C array
owned by the C library.

setenv can move it,
or free old entries,
while it changes it.

getenv reads it
with no lock that Rust controls.

Rust's own std::env functions
take a lock.

C code does not.

And C code
reads the environment
all the time.

Time zone lookups.

DNS resolution.

Locale setup.

Any C library
your crate links.

So one thread sets a variable
while another resolves a hostname,
and the reader can follow a pointer
into memory that was just freed.

A crash.

Or wrong data.

Or nothing,
for months,
and then a crash
nobody can reproduce.

Rust's promise
is that safe code
cannot cause that.

set_var could.

So Rust 1.85,
in February 2025,
shipped the 2024 edition
with set_var and remove_var
marked unsafe.

Older editions still compile them
as safe.

The bug was always there.

The edition only
makes you sign for it.

cargo fix --edition
will wrap the calls
in unsafe blocks for you.

Do not stop there.

An unsafe block
is a promise
that no other thread
can touch the environment.

Check whether you can keep it.

Better moves:

Set the variable
before your program starts,
in the unit file,
the container,
the shell.

Pass configuration
as arguments or structs,
not through the environment.

For child processes,
use Command::env,
which sets it
for the child only.

If it must happen in-process,
do it first thing in main,
before the async runtime,
before any thread,
and write down why.

The 2024 edition
is not adding a danger.

It is pointing at one
your code already had.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Kengele: an alarm for when an activist goes missing, that nobody can switch off
description:
When an activist disappears, the first hours matter.

In Kenya, the national human rights commission counted more than 80 abductions and enforced disappearances after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, several abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry. Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan activist Agather Atuhaire were freed after their detention in Tanzania became public.

Speed of public pressure is what gets people out. Today the alarm depends on someone noticing and phoning around, over networks that can be watched or switched off. Uganda and Tanzania both shut down the internet around their elections.

So I'm building Kengele (Swahili for "bell"), an open-source alarm for when an activist goes missing.

Not for real use yet. Kengele is in the design and early build stage. Nobody should rely on it until an independent security review is done.

How it works

  1. Watch windows. Before a protest, a court visit or a risky trip, the activist sets check-ins, for example every 90 minutes from 2pm to 8pm.
  2. The alarm lives on the guardians' phones. Each check-in is a signed, encrypted message to 3 to 5 guardians (family, a lawyer, an organisation). If one doesn't arrive, every guardian's app raises the alarm on its own. Seizing the activist's phone stops nothing.
  3. Duress PIN. If someone forces the activist to check in, the duress PIN shows a normal screen and quietly raises the top-level alarm.
  4. Guardians confirm first. Nothing goes public until 2 of 3 guardians confirm. The alert text is locked under a key split among the guardians (Shamir secret sharing), so one guardian, even a coerced one, cannot publish early.
  5. Public alert and legal packet. Once confirmed, the activist's pre-written alert is published on Nostr, and the lawyer gets a ready habeas corpus packet.
  6. A captor can't call it off. After an alarm starts, the activist's own all-clear ends nothing. Only guardians, after a voice or video check, can stand it down.

Built for shutdowns

  • The clock only runs while the network is up. In a blackout, deadlines pause instead of firing hundreds of false alarms, then the alarm fires the moment the network returns.
  • Encrypted SMS fallback. Every message is exactly 228 bytes and fits in two SMS. A panic looks identical to a normal check-in on the wire.
  • Carry and deliver later. Messages are signed and encrypted, so any phone can carry them and deliver them when it finds a network, with the original signed time intact.
  • Per-route clocks. An SMS only proves SMS works. Each activist's clock pauses only when every route they use is down.

What it deliberately doesn't do

No servers to switch off. No custody of anyone's money. No GPS trail. No accounts or phone numbers. And it doesn't prevent an abduction. It shortens the time between a disappearance and public pressure.

Where it is

Written in Go, on Nostr (NIP-44 encryption, NIP-59 gift wrap) and BIP-340 signatures. So far:

  • a published threat model, written before the code
  • the signed, encrypted message format
  • the guardian watcher with the shutdown-aware clock
  • Nostr transport that hides sender and timing from relays
  • the SMS spec
  • 2-of-3 guardian confirmation and the coerced all-clear rule

Ten pull requests merged, every one race-tested.

Next: the Android app, OpenTimestamps proof, a legal fund guardians can unlock, Bluetooth mesh through bitchat, and an independent security review.

Prior art

The closest tool, Círculo by Guardian Project and ARTICLE 19, says on its site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It needed the internet and its own servers. Amnesty's Panic Button was retired after false alarms. Kengele is designed around both lessons.

Get involved

Security reviewers, Go and Android developers, Nostr folks and Swahili translators are all welcome. Start with the Start here issue.

Code: github.com/altradits/kengele (MIT)

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. If you go quiet, the bell rings.

title: Your Go Function Returned a Nil Error and the Caller Saw an Error Anyway
description:
The order service
had a validation step.

It returned an error
if the quantity was wrong,
and nothing if it was fine.

type QtyError struct{ Qty int }

func (e *QtyError) Error() string {
return fmt.Sprintf("bad quantity %d", e.Qty)
}

func validate(o Order) error {
var err *QtyError
if o.Qty <= 0 {
err = &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return err
}

The caller did the usual thing:

if err := validate(o); err != nil {
reject(o, err)
}

Every order was rejected.

Including the good ones.

Then the log line
that printed the reason
crashed with a nil pointer dereference.

Here is the mechanism.

In Go,
an interface value has two parts.

A type.

And a value.

It equals nil
only when both are empty.

validate returns error,
which is an interface.

Inside, err was a *QtyError
that happened to be nil.

Returning it
put the type *QtyError
into the interface,
with a nil pointer as the value.

Type filled in.

Value empty.

So err != nil
was true.

An interface holding a nil pointer
is not a nil interface.

The Go FAQ has a whole entry on it,
titled
"Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?"

And Error() ran
on a nil *QtyError,
reached for e.Qty,
and panicked.

The fix is small.

Return the interface,
not the concrete pointer:

func validate(o Order) error {
if o.Qty <= 0 {
return &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return nil
}

That nil
is the untyped kind,
and it reaches the caller
as a true nil.

The rule underneath:

never declare a variable
of your own error type
and return it as error.

Declare it as error,
or return nil by name.

The same trap waits
anywhere a nil pointer
is handed to an interface.

A nil *bytes.Buffer
passed as an io.Writer.

A nil *Config
stored in an any.

Each one
looks like nothing
and compares as something.

When a check says
something is there
and you can see nothing,
ask what type
it was wrapped in.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: idl-codegen: عميلان بأنواع محددة لـ TypeScript و Dart من Anchor IDL
description:
برنامج Anchor يصف نفسه في ملف IDL: تعليماته (instructions)، وحساباته، وأنواعه، وأحداثه، وأخطاؤه، وبذور (seeds) عناوين الـ PDA. جهة البرنامج تولّدها لك macros الخاصة بـ Anchor. أما جهة العميل (client) فمنها يبدأ العمل اليدوي. على أحدهم أن يكتب الدالة التي تحوّل الوسائط بترميز Borsh، وتضع أمامها الـ discriminator المكوّن من 8 بايتات، وترتّب الحسابات بالترتيب الصحيح مع أعلام signer وwritable الصحيحة، وتشتق عناوين الـ PDA من نفس البذور التي يستعملها البرنامج.

كتابة ذلك مرة واحدة أمر مقبول. لكن كتابته مرتين، بـ TypeScript لتطبيق الويب وبـ Dart لتطبيق Flutter، تعني نسختين يجب أن تبقيا متطابقتين مع البرنامج ومع بعضهما. وبايت واحد خاطئ في إحداهما يعطي معاملة تفشل على السلسلة برسالة خطأ لا تشرح الكثير.

idl-codegen يقرأ ملف Anchor IDL (مواصفة 0.30 وما بعدها) ويكتب العميلين معًا. والـ README يبدأ بتحذير يجب ذكره هنا أيضًا: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني. العملاء المولَّدون يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون ترميز الحسابات، ولا يوقّعون ولا يرسلون شيئًا. راجع الكود المولَّد مقابل برنامجك قبل استعماله مع أموال حقيقية، وجرّب على devnet أولًا.

ماذا يقدّم

أمر واحد ينتج مجموعتين من الملفات:

  • TypeScript: الملفان <name>.ts وborsh.ts، ويعتمدان على @solana/web3.js v1.
  • Dart: الملفان <name>.dart وborsh.dart، ويعتمدان على package:crypto، وهما موجّهان لتطبيقات Flutter.

كل عميل يحتوي نفس المكوّنات.

معرّف البرنامج. الثابت PROGRAM_ID في TypeScript و<name>ProgramId في Dart.

الأنواع. في TypeScript تحصل على interfaces، وعلى الـ enums في شكل اتحادات { kind: ... }، وعلى دوال encodeX / decodeX. وفي Dart تحصل على أصناف (classes) فيها encode وstatic decode. الـ enums التي بلا بيانات تصبح enum عادية في Dart، والتي تحمل بيانات تصبح أصنافًا من نوع sealed.

بناء التعليمات. الدالة createXInstruction(accounts, args) تُرجع TransactionInstruction في TypeScript. ونسخة Dart تأخذ وسائط مسمّاة وتُرجع Instruction. الحسابات التي لها address ثابت في الـ IDL، مثل System Program، تأخذه كقيمة افتراضية. والحسابات الاختيارية تأخذ معرّف البرنامج كقيمة افتراضية، وهذا عُرف Anchor للتعبير عن "None".

فك ترميز الحسابات. الدالة decodeXAccount(data) تتحقق من الـ discriminator قبل الفك، وفي TypeScript توجد أيضًا isXAccount.

الأحداث (events). الدالة decodeXEvent(data) في اللغتين.

دوال PDA. الدالة findXPda(...seeds) تُولَّد من pda.seeds في الـ IDL: البذور الثابتة، وبذور الحسابات، وبذور الوسائط، وحالات seeds::program مثل حسابات التوكن المرتبطة (ATA). وعميل Dart يأتي بدالة findProgramAddress خاصة به.

الأخطاء والثوابت. في TypeScript: ERRORS و<Name>Error.fromCode(). وفي Dart: <name>Errors و<Name>Exception.fromCode(). ومعها قيم #[constant] المعرّفة في البرنامج.

تحويل الأنواع يتبع نفس الفكرة في الجهتين: u64 وi64 وu128 وi128 تصبح bigint / BigInt؛ والأعداد الصحيحة الأصغر تصبح number / int؛ وpubkey يصبح PublicKey / Pubkey؛ وbytes يصبح Uint8Array / Uint8List؛ وOption<T> يصبح T | null / T?. أما tuple structs وtuple variants فتصبح values: [...] في TypeScript وfield0, field1 في Dart.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع وشغّل المولّد من مجلد المشروع:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen
cd idl-codegen
pnpm install
pnpm gen target/idl/my_program.json --ts app/src/generated --dart mobile/lib/generated
# or after `pnpm build`:  node dist/cli.js <idl.json> --ts <dir> --dart <dir>

الوسيط الأول هو ملف الـ IDL الذي كتبه anchor build. والخياران --ts و--dart هما مجلدا الإخراج. كود TypeScript المولَّد يحتاج @solana/web3.js v1 في تطبيقك، وكود Dart المولَّد يحتاج package:crypto.

ثم في تطبيق الويب:

import { createIncrementInstruction, findCounterPda } from "./generated/counter_todo.js";
const [counter] = findCounterPda(wallet.publicKey);
const ix = createIncrementInstruction({ authority: wallet.publicKey, counter }, { by: 1n });

ونفس النداء في تطبيق Flutter:

import 'generated/counter_todo.dart';
final (counter, _) = findCounterPda(authority: me);
final ix = createIncrementInstruction(authority: me, counter: counter, by: BigInt.one);

المقطعان يشتقان نفس الـ PDA ويبنيان نفس بايتات التعليمة. التوقيع والإرسال يبقيان في كودك أنت، بالمحفظة وطبقة الـ RPC التي يستعملها تطبيقك أصلًا.

كيف اختُبر

الكود المولَّد لا ينفع إلا إذا وثقت في البايتات، ولهذا يدور أغلب قسم الاختبارات في الـ README حول هذه النقطة.

  • اختبارات golden. كل IDL في test/fixtures/ يُولَّد ثم يُقارن بايتًا ببايت مع test/golden/. الملفات هي counter_todo وescrow، وهما IDL حقيقيان من مشاريع Anchor مجاورة، وkitchen_sink المكتوب يدويًا ليغطي كل الأنواع: مجموعات حسابات متداخلة، وحسابات اختيارية، وenums تحمل بيانات، وtuple structs، وu128/i128، وf64، ومصفوفات ثابتة الطول، وseeds::program.
  • مترجمات صارمة. كود TypeScript المولَّد يمرّ من tsc --strict، وكود Dart المولَّد يمرّ من dart analyze --fatal-infos. ويُتجاوز فحص Dart إن لم يكن dart موجودًا في الـ PATH.
  • السلوك. دوال PDA تطابق PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync، بما فيها عناوين ATA. بيانات التعليمة هي الـ discriminator متبوعًا بوسائط Borsh. والحسابات تمرّ بدورة encode ثم decode وتعود كما كانت، مع التحقق من الـ discriminator.
  • بين اللغتين. برنامج Dart في test/golden/dart/bin/check.dart يبني نفس التعليمات وعناوين PDA وبايتات الحسابات، والاختبار يتحقق من أن ناتجه يطابق عميل TypeScript بايتًا ببايت.

هذا الفحص الأخير كشف خطأً حقيقيًا. على Dart 3.9 VM كانت الدالة BigInt.modPow تُرجع نتائج خاطئة لبعض المدخلات ذات 255 بت، فتعطّل فحص وقوع النقطة على منحنى ed25519 الذي تعتمد عليه findProgramAddress. لذلك يستعمل كود Dart المولَّد الآن خوارزمية square-and-multiply خاصة به.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق. العملاء يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون البيانات فقط، لكن تعليمة خاطئة قد تحرّك أموالًا بعد أن توقّعها. قارن الناتج مع برنامجك وجرّبه على devnet أولًا.
  • الأنواع العامة (generics) مرفوضة. الـ IDL الذي يستعمل generics لا يُولَّد منه شيء.
  • بعض بذور PDA تصبح بايتات خام. البذور التي تقرأ بيانات حساب (path: "list.next_id") أو حقلًا من وسيط من نوع struct تتحول إلى وسيط bytes خام. وإن كانت تعليمة أخرى تشتق نفس الحساب من وسيط بسيط، يستعمل المولّد ذلك الشكل الأبسط.
  • coption لم يُختبر مع برنامج حقيقي. هو مدعوم في الترميز وفك الترميز، لا أكثر.
  • ملفات IDL القديمة تحتاج تحويلًا. ملفات IDL السابقة لـ Anchor 0.30 يجب تحويلها أولًا بالأمر anchor idl convert.
  • web3.js v1. ناتج TypeScript موجّه إلى @solana/web3.js v1.

لماذا بنيته

المشكلة هي التكرار. ملف الـ IDL يحتوي أصلًا كل ما يحتاجه العميل: أنواع الوسائط، وترتيب الحسابات، والـ discriminators، والبذور، ورموز الأخطاء. كتابة العميل يدويًا تعني نسخ هذه المعلومات إلى كود، ثم نسخها مرة ثانية عندما يوجد تطبيق موبايل بـ Dart بجانب تطبيق ويب بـ TypeScript. بعدها يجب تكرار كل تغيير في البرنامج في مكانين، ولا شيء ينبّهك عندما يتأخر أحدهما عن الآخر.

توليد العميلين من نفس الـ IDL يلغي خطوة النسخ، ويجعل اختبار أحد الناتجين مقابل الآخر ممكنًا. إذا أنتج عميل TypeScript وعميل Dart نفس البايتات لنفس المدخلات، ووافق عميل TypeScript مكتبة @solana/web3.js في عناوين PDA، يضيق المجال كثيرًا أمام اختلاف صامت. وخطأ BigInt.modPow مثال جيد على قيمة هذه المقارنة: لا شيء في كود Dart كان يبدو خاطئًا، ولم تكشفه إلا مقارنة البايتات.

الكود

المولّد، وملفات الاختبار، وملفات golden، والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: tx-explainer: اقرأ معاملة Solana بلغة بسيطة
description:
العثور على معاملة (transaction) في Solana سهل، لكن قراءتها صعبة. المستكشف (explorer) يعطيك توقيعًا (signature)، وقائمة من مفاتيح الحسابات، وتعليمات (instructions) بياناتها سلسلة من البايتات. لتعرف ما الذي حدث فعلًا، عليك أن تتذكر أن أول بايت في تعليمة Token هو وسم (tag)، وأن المبالغ أعداد صحيحة بترتيب little-endian وبلا فاصلة عشرية، وأن برنامج Anchor يخفي اسم التعليمة خلف discriminator من 8 بايتات.

tx-explainer يقوم بهذه القراءة مكانك. تعطيه توقيعًا، أو بايتات المعاملة الخام، أو ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا في ملف، فيطبع ما فعلته كل تعليمة في جمل بسيطة، ثم الرسوم، ووحدات الحساب (compute units)، وتغيّرات الأرصدة.

هو أداة فك ترميز للقراءة فقط: لا يوقّع ولا يرسل أي شيء أبدًا. والـ README صريح في حدوده: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني (not audited)، وهو موجّه أولًا إلى devnet وtestnet وlocalnet، والنص المبسّط اجتهاد قدر الإمكان ولا يغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج.

ماذا يقدّم

هذا ناتج الأداة على معاملة حقيقية من devnet موجودة ضمن ملفات الاختبار:

$ tx-explainer --file test/fixtures/devnet-memo.json
Transaction 5zhK…  [legacy]
Status: succeeded
Fee: 0.0000155 SOL (of which priority ≈ 0.0000105 SOL)
Compute units: 26,021 of 70,000 requested

What happened:
  1. [Compute Budget] Set compute unit limit to 70,000
  2. [Compute Budget] Set priority fee to 150,000 micro-lamports per compute unit
  3. [Associated Token Account] Create (if missing) the associated token account Expy…TCA6 for wallet 6a1w…BNqd and mint 4wMp…jY4y, paid by 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer)
  4. [SPL Token] Transfer 1,236.871165 tokens of mint 4wMp…jY4y from 55Xo…AmDQ to Expy…TCA6 (authority 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer))
  5. [Memo] Memo: "helm-payout-v1:…"

Token balance changes:
  55Xo…AmDQ (owner 2VyJ…TeEs): -1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y
  Expy…TCA6 (owner 6a1w…BNqd): +1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y

البرامج المدمجة. الأداة تعرف البرامج التي تظهر في أغلب المعاملات:

  • System: التعليمات CreateAccount وAssign وTransfer وCreateAccountWithSeed، وعمليات الـ nonce، وAllocate وTransferWithSeed.
  • SPL Token وToken-2022: تهيئة الـ mint والحسابات، وTransfer وTransferChecked، وApprove وRevoke وSetAuthority وMintTo وBurn وCloseAccount وFreeze وThaw وSyncNative وغيرها. أما تعليمات امتدادات Token-2022 فتُذكر برقمها فقط.
  • Associated Token Account: التعليمات Create وCreateIdempotent وRecoverNested.
  • Compute Budget: التعليمات SetComputeUnitLimit وSetComputeUnitPrice وRequestHeapFrame وSetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit.
  • Memo (الإصداران v1 وv2)، ويُعرض كنص UTF-8.

أي برنامج Anchor عبر الـ IDL. مرّر ملف IDL الخاص بالبرنامج بالخيار --idl (صيغة Anchor 0.30 وما بعدها)، فتعرض الأداة اسم التعليمة، والوسائط بعد فك ترميز Borsh (structs وenums وvec وoption والمصفوفات)، وأسماء الحسابات، وأسماء الأخطاء المخصّصة إن فشلت المعاملة.

بيانات الـ RPC الوصفية (metadata). عندما يأتي الإدخال من getTransaction، يضمّ الناتج أيضًا الحالة (مع أسماء أخطاء Anchor)، والرسوم، وتقديرًا لرسوم الأولوية (priority fee) يساوي حد وحدات الحساب × سعر الوحدة، ووحدات الحساب المستهلكة، والتعليمات الداخلية (CPIs)، وتغيّرات رصيد SOL، وتغيّرات أرصدة التوكنات بالخانات العشرية الصحيحة.

رسائل legacy وv0. الصيغتان مدعومتان. عناوين جداول البحث (address lookup tables) تُحلّ من meta.loadedAddresses. وفي الإدخال الخام، حيث لا توجد هذه البيانات، تُعرض بالشكل table[index].

ثلاث طرق للتشغيل. نفس منطق فك الترميز متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI)، وكمكتبة TypeScript، وكواجهة ويب صغيرة تعمل كليًا داخل المتصفح وتتصل مباشرة بالـ RPC العام للشبكة المختارة. يضع الـ README رابطًا لنسخة تجريبية حية من هذه الواجهة: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/tx-explainer/.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع ثم ابنِه:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer
cd tx-explainer
pnpm install
pnpm build

ثم شغّل الـ CLI من مجلد المشروع:

node dist/cli.js <signature> --cluster devnet           # fetch via getTransaction
node dist/cli.js <signature> --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899
node dist/cli.js --raw <base64-or-base58 tx bytes>      # offline, no metadata
node dist/cli.js --file saved-getTransaction.json --idl target/idl/my_program.json
node dist/cli.js ... --json                             # machine-readable
node dist/cli.js serve --port 8787                      # web UI on 127.0.0.1

الشكلان الأولان يجلبان المعاملة من شبكة أو من الـ validator المحلي. الخيار --raw يعمل بلا اتصال على بايتات بصيغة base64 أو base58. والخيار --file يقرأ ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا، وهذا مفيد في تقارير الأخطاء والاختبارات. أما --json فيعطي نفس الشرح كبيانات منظّمة يستطيع سكربت أن يقرأها.

وكمكتبة، ثلاث دوال تغطي الحالة الشائعة:

import { explain, render, fetchTransaction } from "tx-explainer";
const e = explain({ rpc: await fetchTransaction(sig, "https://api.devnet.solana.com") }, { idls: [myIdl] });
console.log(render(e));

الدالة fetchTransaction تجلب المعاملة، وexplain تبني الشرح المنظّم، وrender تحوّله إلى النص الذي رأيته في الأعلى.

كيف يعمل من الداخل

يصف الـ README أربع وحدات صغيرة، ومعرفة هذا التقسيم تفيدك إن أردت إضافة decoder جديد:

  1. الملف message.ts يحلّل صيغة الإرسال (wire format) يدويًا: أطوال compact-u16، والتواقيع، وترويسة الرسالة، ومفاتيح الحسابات، والتعليمات المجمّعة، وجداول البحث في v0. ثم يستنتج من الترويسة إن كان كل مفتاح موقّعًا (signer) أو قابلًا للكتابة (writable).
  2. الملف programs.ts فيه decoder صغير لكل برنامج مدمج. كل واحد يقرأ وسم التعليمة (u32 في System وu8 في Token) وحقولها بواسطة Reader يعمل بترتيب little-endian.
  3. الملف anchor.ts يقارن أول 8 بايتات من بيانات التعليمة مع الـ discriminator لكل تعليمة في الـ IDL، ثم يفك ترميز الوسائط بـ Borsh انطلاقًا من شجرة الأنواع في الـ IDL.
  4. الملف explain.ts يجمع كل ذلك مع بيانات الـ RPC: أرصدة التوكنات تعطي الـ mint وعدد الخانات العشرية، والتعليمات الداخلية تعطي الـ CPIs، والأرصدة قبل وبعد تعطي الفروقات.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق، والناتج اجتهاد. الجمل وسيلة مساعدة لقراءة المعاملة. لا تغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج، ولا ينبغي أن تبني عليها وحدها قرارًا يخص أموالًا حقيقية.
  • امتدادات Token-2022 تُعرض برقمها فقط. رسوم التحويل، والتحويلات السرّية، وباقي تعليمات الامتدادات لا تُحوَّل إلى جمل.
  • بعض البرامج يُذكر اسمها فقط. تعليمات Stake وVote وAddress Lookup Table والـ loader تُعرَّف بالاسم دون فك ترميزها.
  • رسوم الأولوية تقديرية. تُحسب بالصيغة ceil(limit × price / 1e6). وإن لم تحدّد المعاملة حدًّا، تفترض الأداة القيمة الافتراضية: 200 ألف وحدة حساب لكل تعليمة.
  • الإدخال الخام بلا بيانات وصفية. مع --raw لا توجد حالة ولا رسوم ولا تغيّرات أرصدة ولا تعليمات داخلية، لأن هذه المعلومات تأتي من الـ RPC وليس من بايتات المعاملة.
  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Our tests imported the repository and passed while the package we deployed was missing eleven templates
description:
Our label service is a Python package that turns a consignment into a carrier label. Every carrier zone has a JSON template, and the package ships them inside itself, under labels/templates. setup.py listed them with package_data and the pattern templates/*.json, which had been right since the first carrier.

In September we added the Highlands and Islands zones for a carrier that prices them separately, and the engineer put the eleven new templates in a subfolder, templates/zones. The tests for all eleven passed in CI. The pipeline built a wheel, the image installed it, and the first Highlands label in production failed with FileNotFoundError. Ninety two parcels for Inverness and Skye waited on the dock until the afternoon.

The pattern was easy to blame once we looked. templates/*.json matches files directly inside templates and nothing in a folder below it, so the wheel held every old template and none of the new ones. setup.py did exactly what it said.

The real question was why CI had been green. Our tests ran with python -m pytest from the root of the checkout, and that puts the current directory first on sys.path. import labels found the folder in the repository, holding every file anyone had committed, before it could find anything installed. For four years we had tested the source tree. The wheel that production ran had never been imported by a single test.

We moved the code under src/, so the package cannot be imported from the repository root at all and the tests have to use an installed copy. CI now builds the wheel once, installs it into a clean virtual environment, runs the suite against that, and puts the same file into the image. A short step lists every file under templates in the repository and fails the build if any of them is missing from the wheel. The package_data pattern now covers subfolders, but the check is what we trust.

A green run tells you about the code your tests imported. Ours imported the repository, and we shipped a package.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Designing an RF switch matrix for automated test
description:
A switch matrix looks like a simple box: N inputs, M outputs, and a controller. In practice most of the engineering effort goes into three decisions that are hard to change later — port topology, isolation budget, and control architecture. This note walks through the trade-offs that show up when specifying matrices for semiconductor ATE, satellite payload test benches and EMC labs.

Start from the measurement, not the port count

The first question is not "how many ports" but "what gets measured through the path". A matrix that routes a vector network analyzer to 24 devices under test has different requirements from one that switches a spectrum analyzer between eight antenna feeds.

Two numbers drive everything:

  • Insertion loss budget. Every switch in the path adds loss, and that loss changes the calibration reference. A 4x24 matrix built from cascaded SP6T switches can easily put 1.5 dB between instrument and DUT if the topology is careless.
  • Isolation requirement. Cascaded switches multiply isolation, but only if unused ports are terminated. An open port reflects energy back into the matrix and it shows up as crosstalk on the measured port.

The second point is the one that bites most often. A matrix built from 80 dB switches can measure 60 dB of isolation if a single unused port is left open. Terminating every unused port in 50 ohms is not a refinement, it is part of the specification, which is why the load's return loss and power rating matter as much as the switch.

Reflective or absorptive switching

Mechanical coaxial switches are usually reflective: when a port is deselected the signal bounces back. In a well-terminated matrix that is acceptable, and it keeps cost and insertion loss low.

PIN diode switches come in both flavours. The absorptive version terminates the off port internally so the source always sees a matched load. For receive chains with low noise amplifiers, or any path where a reflection can stress a sensitive front end, absorptive is the safer default. The price is a little more insertion loss and a little more bias current.

Waveguide paths above 26 GHz change the calculus again. Waveguide switches are reflective by construction, and the flange interface matters more than the switch itself: a WR28 switch mounted on a mismatched flange will show worse return loss than the datasheet suggests.

Control architecture, the part everyone underestimates

A matrix is only as good as its driver. Three decisions determine whether the system is pleasant to work with:

  1. Switching element choice. Mechanical switches give low loss and high isolation but switch in milliseconds. When the sequence needs microsecond transitions, the matrix wants PIN diodes on the fast paths and mechanical switches elsewhere, in a hybrid arrangement.
  2. Logic level and latching. TTL inputs can be driven straight from a tester's digital IO. 28 V control is common in industrial and military racks. Latching elements hold state with power removed, failsafe elements return to a defined port. Choosing the wrong one shows up as intermittent path errors months later.
  3. State readback. Without readback the controller cannot tell "commanded" from "actually switched". A matrix that reports its true position saves hours of debugging when a sequence fails at 3 a.m.

Termination, cooling and the boring details

High port count matrices concentrate power. Absorptive switches and terminations dissipate what the DUT reflects, and a rack of 24 ports can turn a few watts of reflected power into a thermal problem. Finned coaxial loads and terminations exist for exactly this reason.

The mechanical details matter as well: connector grade (2.92 mm versus 2.4 mm versus 1.85 mm), torque consistency across operators, and whether the matrix is serviceable when one switch fails. A matrix designed as one sealed unit becomes scrap when a single port dies.

A short specification checklist

  • Port count and topology, with the full path loss budget written down
  • Isolation target, and the termination plan for unused ports
  • Switching speed per path, and whether hybrid mechanical/PIN is needed
  • Control logic, latching behaviour and state readback
  • Connector types and grades, matched across the whole path
  • Worst case power dissipation and the cooling path

Most of these are cheap to get right at design time and expensive to fix once the rack is built. If you are specifying a matrix for a new test bench, the numbers worth arguing about are loss, isolation and termination. The rest follows.

title: Your List Endpoint Runs 101 Queries to Show 100 Orders
description:
Your list endpoint runs 101 queries to show 100 orders.

A list I reviewed loaded 100 orders, then asked the database for each order's customer, one at a time.

1 query for the list.
100 more for the customers.

That is the N+1 problem. The page was slow, the database was busy, and the team's first idea was a bigger database.

What the code usually looks like

The endpoint fetches the orders, then loops over them to fetch each customer:

const orders = await db.query(
  `SELECT id, total, customer_id FROM orders
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100`
);

for (const order of orders) {
  const [customer] = await db.query(
    `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ?`,
    [order.customer_id]
  );
  order.customerName = customer?.name;
}

One query for the list, then one query per row inside the loop. With 100 orders that is 101 queries. With 1,000 orders it would be 1,001. The query count grows with the list, and that is the real problem.

Why it stays hidden for so long

The data is correct. Every order shows the right customer name, so no test fails and no user reports a bug. In development the list has ten rows, so eleven queries feel fast. The problem only shows up when real data arrives, and by then the slow page looks like a database problem, not a code problem.

The wrong fixes

A bigger database pays more for the same 101 queries. The queries are the problem, not the machine running them.

A cache hides the extra queries until the data changes, then the first request after the change pays the full cost again. It also adds a whole new thing to keep correct.

An index makes each of the 101 queries faster, without removing 100 of them. Faster queries that should not exist are still queries that should not exist.

The fix: ask for the data together

One query can return the orders with the customer name already in each row:

SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

One query, 100 rows, the customer name already in each row.

Two details in that query matter.

First, it is a LEFT JOIN, not a plain JOIN. If an order can exist without a customer, a plain JOIN would silently drop those orders from the list. LEFT JOIN keeps every order and leaves the customer name empty where there is no customer.

Second, it has an ORDER BY. Without it, LIMIT 100 returns whichever 100 rows the database happens to find first, and that set can change between requests, which breaks paging. With ORDER BY, the database sorts first and then takes the newest 100 orders.

When a join is the wrong fix

The join above works cleanly because each order has exactly one customer. Joining a many-to-one relation keeps one row per order.

A one-to-many relation behaves differently. Join orders to order_items, and an order with five items becomes five rows. LIMIT 100 now counts rows, not orders, so you might get 30 orders, and the last one can be cut off halfway through its items.

For that case, use two queries instead. Page the orders first, then fetch all their items in one go:

SELECT id, total FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (/* the 100 order ids */);

Then group the items by order_id in your code. That is still two queries for any list size, which is the whole point.

If you use an ORM

Use its eager loading, like include in Prisma or Sequelize. It may run 2 queries instead of 1, and that is fine. What matters is that the query count stays the same as the list grows:

const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({
  take: 100,
  orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' },
  include: { customer: true },
});

The ORM fetches the orders, then fetches the customers for those orders in one more query. Two queries for any list size beats one query per row. This two-query approach is also why ORMs handle one-to-many relations like order items without the row multiplication problem.

How to spot it in your own code

Count the queries per request, not the time per query. Turn on query logging in development, open a list page, and look at the count. Then change the page size from 10 rows to 100 rows. If the query count jumps with the row count, you have an N+1 hiding in that endpoint.

Fix the shape of the query first. Speed comes after, and only where it is still needed.

How many queries does your list endpoint run today? Drop the number in the comments.

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed by me.

title: How AI Visual Search Is Transforming Fashion Apps: Models, Implementation & Costs
description:
Shoppers rarely type the exact product name. They type "black leather ankle boots" or upload a photo and expect the app to find something close. This post shows how to build that with open models, then looks at what it means for a fashion app budget, using Australia as the example market.

Why it matters

Online spending in Australia hit AUD 21.9 billion in April–June 2026, up 14% year on year, according to Australia Post. Fashion catalogues are huge and visual, and keyword search alone misses a lot. Cost guides for ecommerce apps, such as Techugo's breakdown for an app like THE ICONIC, list AI-based search, recommendations and visual discovery among the features that raise development effort.

The core idea: one embedding space for text and images

A CLIP-style model maps images and text into the same vector space. Embed every product photo once, embed each query at request time, and return the nearest vectors.

python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
from PIL import Image

model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")

# 1. Offline: embed the catalogue images
paths = ["boot_01.jpg", "sneaker_02.jpg", "dress_03.jpg"]
img_emb = model.encode(
    [Image.open(p) for p in paths],
    convert_to_tensor=True,
    normalize_embeddings=True,
)

# 2. Online: embed the shopper's text query
query = "black leather ankle boots"
q_emb = model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)

# 3. Retrieve the closest products
hits = util.semantic_search(q_emb, img_emb, top_k=3)[0]
for h in hits:
    print(paths[h["corpus_id"]], round(h["score"], 3))

Passing an image as the query works the same way, which gives you "shop the look" for free.

Architecture in four parts

Ingestion job: embeds new or changed product images on a schedule and writes vectors to an index (FAISS, pgvector or a managed vector database).

Search API: embeds the query, runs a nearest-neighbour lookup, then filters by size, stock and price.

Re-ranking: blends similarity with business signals such as availability, margin or popularity.

App layer: a cross-platform client (Flutter or React Native) is usually enough, because the heavy lifting happens on the server.

Things that go wrong in practice

Domain gap: general-purpose models can confuse close categories such as "midi skirt" and "maxi skirt". Evaluate on your own catalogue and consider fine-tuning.

Stale vectors: if images change and embeddings don't, results drift. Version your index.

Cold start: new shoppers have no history, so fall back to visual similarity and trending items.

Measure it: track recall@k on a small labelled query set, plus click-through and add-to-cart rate online.

What it means for the budget

Reference ranges from the same cost guide, in AUD:

Tier - Budget - Timeline
MVP - 30K – 150K - 3–5 months
Mid-level - 150K – 250K - 5–8 months
Advanced - 250K – 350K - 8–12 months

My suggestion is to ship plain search in the MVP, then add visual search once you have real queries to evaluate against. Beyond the build, plan for:

Hosting: roughly AUD 300–3,000+ per month depending on traffic, with spikes in big sale seasons. Vector search and model inference add to this.

Maintenance: about 15–20% of the initial build cost per year.

Compliance: if you use shopper photos or behaviour data, the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles apply.

Takeaway

Visual search is a small, well-understood pipeline: embed once, search fast, re-rank with business rules. Start with an open model, measure on your own catalogue, and let the data decide whether fine-tuning is worth the cost.

Resources

Sentence Transformers: image search with CLIP

Techugo: cost to build an app like THE ICONIC in Australia

Australia Post quarterly ecommerce update (July 2026)

OAIC: Australian Privacy Principles

Cost figures are indicative estimates from the sources above and vary by vendor, scope and region.

title: Balancing Code Conciseness and Readability in Composite Literals Through Explicit Typing Governance
description:
The Evolution of Syntax: Understanding Composite Literal Type Elision

After a decade-long evaluation cycle, the Go language accepted a proposal allowing developers to omit explicit type parameters in composite literals, letting the compiler infer types directly from context (such as returning zero values like <{}, errors.New(...)> or configuring options structs). The core motivation is the elimination of verbose boilerplate code through compile-time bidirectional type inference resolving untyped composite literal structures against expected context types.

When an engineer reviews code stripped of explicit types, the human working memory mechanism undergoes a distinct structural shift. Without explicit syntactic anchors, developers must perform contextual heuristic scanning—mentally traversing up the abstract syntax tree to the function signature or variable declaration to resolve type provenance. When nesting depth exceeds human working memory limits (typically 3 to 4 levels of nested untyped structs), context retention fails entirely. This causes a sudden spike in cognitive entropy: developers misattribute field types, leading to runtime panics or silent logic bugs during code reviews and onboarding.

To evaluate how engineering teams should approach this feature, we must contrast two primary adoption strategies: aggressive, unconstrained elision for maximum line-level conciseness versus conservative, governed retention of types at architectural boundaries. Unconstrained elision maximizes aesthetic appeal but shatters maintainability by inducing severe onboarding friction; newcomers cannot resolve type provenance without deep IDE symbol tracing, effectively converting static code analysis into a runtime memory burden. Conversely, conservative governance—mandating explicit types for public APIs and complex multi-field initializations while permitting elision solely for simple zero-value returns—optimizes long-term maintainability.

The optimal rule for engineering teams is defined by the boundary of contextual visibility: if an untyped composite literal spans more than a single line or is nested within another literal, explicit typing must be retained. When teams violate this rule and adopt global elision, stylistic fragmentation runs rampant due to divergent individual aesthetic preferences. To prevent instantaneous codebase obfuscation, the Go maintainers made the deliberate architectural decision to exclude any automated go fix migration tool. By omitting this automated refactoring vector, the language ecosystem introduces intentional regulatory friction, forcing teams to debate and codify their own stylistic thresholds manually.
Adoption Strategy Internal Process & Mechanism Observable Effect & Failure Mode
Unconstrained Elision Removes all explicit type anchors, forcing the visual parsing engine to rely entirely on distant contextual declarations. Maximizes line conciseness but triggers cognitive overload, onboarding stalls, and extreme nesting obfuscation.
Governed Retention (Optimal) Retains explicit types at structural boundaries and nested scopes while permitting shorthand solely for zero values. Preserves static type clarity and working memory capacity; prevents team-level stylistic fragmentation.

Ultimately, type elision trades local explicit safety documentation for global contextual reliance, shifting verification overhead from visual parsing to compiler dependency. Without an automated go fix tool to force a uniform ecosystem shift, codebases will diverge based on organizational discipline. Where engineering teams fail to establish strict internal code style linting rules, the lack of automated friction results in silent code rot, proving that syntactic sugar carries a heavy long-term architectural tax.

The Allure of Conciseness: Developer Velocity and Ergonomics

For a decade, Go developers wrestled with a specific brand of visual friction: the mandatory repetition of type names in composite literals. When writing boilerplate-heavy initializations—such as returning zero-value structs like return time.Time{}, errors.New(...) or configuring loggers with &slog.HandlerOptions{...}—the explicit type declaration acts as a rigid syntactic anchor. While this anchor ensures immediate type provenance, it introduces tactile and cognitive drag during rapid feature authoring. By permitting compile-time bidirectional type inference to resolve untyped composite literals against expected context types, the language removes this redundancy, compressing lines of code and accelerating initial authoring speed.

From an information theory perspective, this syntax shift trades byte-level verbosity for higher information density. The mechanical process of typing and reading is streamlined: redundant tokens are stripped, reducing the visual footprint of configuration blocks and allowing the developer's eye to lock onto unique semantic values (like Level: slog.LevelDebug) rather than repeating structural boilerplate. However, this optimization alters how human working memory parses code. Without the explicit type name, visual parsing shifts from local recognition to contextual heuristic scanning—forcing the engineer's brain to mentally traverse up the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to the enclosing function signature or variable declaration to verify what type is actually instantiated.

Evaluating Elision Strategies: Velocity versus Maintainability

Engineering teams evaluating untyped composite literals face a stark architectural choice between unconstrained syntax reduction and conservative governance:

  • Unconstrained Elision: Maximizes line conciseness across all code structures indiscriminately. Failure mode: Shatters maintainability in complex scopes. When nesting exceeds three or four levels, the absence of explicit type markers causes cognitive entropy to spike, leading to field misattribution and silent logic bugs during code reviews.
  • Conservative Governance (Optimal): Restricts elision strictly to shallow, unambiguous contexts—such as single-line zero-value returns or immediate parameter passing where the target type is syntactically adjacent. Mechanism: Preserves local syntactic safety while capturing the ergonomic speed of shorthand syntax.

The optimal boundary rule for engineering workflows is categorical: explicit typing must be retained if an untyped composite literal spans more than a single line or is nested within another literal. When teams violate this rule by applying unconstrained elision across multi-line nested structures, the human parser breaks down under the weight of compiler dependency. Shorthand syntax is a powerful authoring accelerator, but without strict organizational governance, it trades local ergonomics for global codebase obfuscation.

The Hidden Cost: Cognitive Load, Readability, and Maintenance Debt

When Go introduced untyped composite literals—allowing developers to elide explicit type names like time.Time{} down to {}—it traded immediate syntactic brevity for a heavy reliance on contextual compilation. While the Go compiler effortlessly resolves these shorthands via bidirectional type inference against expected context types, the human cognitive architecture lacks a built-in symbol table. This mismatch triggers a profound mechanical shift in how code is read, reviewed, and maintained.

The Breakdown of Visual Anchors and AST Traversal

Explicit types act as visual boundary markers during code inspection. When a developer encounters an explicit type signature, it provides an immediate, localized semantic anchor. Removing these anchors forces a cognitive compensation mechanism: mental Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) traversal. Instead of processing a line locally, the engineer's working memory must actively trace upward through nested function signatures, interface definitions, and variable declarations to reconstruct the missing type provenance.

This process places a heavy tax on human short-term working memory, which typically handles only 4 to 7 distinct elements. When untyped composite literals exceed three to four levels of nesting—such as complex configuration blocks passed into nested builder patterns—working memory saturates. This cognitive entropy causes predictable failure modes: field misattribution, where values are mapped to incorrect struct fields during rapid reviews, resulting in silent logic bugs or runtime panics that bypass static analysis.

Code Reviews and Onboarding Friction

The absence of an automated go fix refactoring tool is not merely an omission; it is a deliberate regulatory friction mechanism designed to prevent instant codebase degradation. However, it transfers the entire governance burden to engineering teams. In codebases with unconstrained type elision, onboarding friction spikes dramatically:

  • Increased IDE Dependency: New engineers cannot evaluate code statically from a pull request diff; they are forced to rely heavily on IDE hover tooltips and symbol-tracing to understand basic data shapes.
  • Reviewer Fatigue: Code reviewers experience diminished oversight capability because verifying correctness requires manual context-switching rather than visual parsing.
  • Stylistic Fragmentation: Different team members apply elision based on subjective aesthetic thresholds, leading to inconsistent code styles that obscure intent.

Governance and Optimal Boundary Rules

Engineering teams must weigh unconstrained elision against conservative governance models:

  • Unconstrained Elision: Maximizes line conciseness and minimizes token count, but shatters long-term maintainability, inflates onboarding time, and maximizes cognitive load.
  • Conservative Governance (Optimal): Restricts untyped composite literals strictly to shallow, unambiguous, single-line contexts—such as zero-value returns (return {}, errors.New(...)) or adjacent parameter passing—while preserving explicit types for public APIs and deep initializations.

The Optimal Governance Rule: If an untyped composite literal spans more than a single line or is nested within another literal, explicit typing must be retained. This boundary preserves working memory capacity, protects static type clarity, and prevents stylistic fragmentation across large engineering organizations.

Governance and Engineering Standards in the Wild

When language evolution strips away syntactic anchors—such as Go's elimination of explicit types in composite literals—the responsibility for maintaining codebase integrity shifts entirely to human engineering processes. Because the Go team deliberately excluded an automated go fix migration tool, engineering organizations cannot rely on automated refactoring scripts to sanitize shorthand syntax. Instead, teams must codify internal style guidelines, linting protocols, and code review boundaries to prevent cognitive overload during pull request reviews.

Without automated guardrails, unconstrained type elision creates an immediate mechanical failure in human code comprehension. When an engineer inspects a deeply nested untyped literal, human short-term working memory—capped at roughly four to seven active elements—must perform mental Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) traversal. The reviewer's brain is forced to trace upward through multiple nested function signatures and variable declarations just to resolve a single field's data type. When nesting depth exceeds three to four levels, working memory saturates, spiking cognitive entropy and directly precipitating field misattribution, silent logic bugs, and runtime panics that evade static compilation checks.

Unconstrained Elision Removes all explicit type anchors, relying entirely on distant contextual declarations and IDE symbol tracing. Maximizes line conciseness at the cost of shattering maintainability; spikes onboarding friction and causes reviewer fatigue during rapid diff analysis.
Conservative Governance (Optimal) Mandates explicit types for public APIs, multi-line declarations, and nested structures; permits elision only for shallow zero-value returns. Preserves static type clarity, protects human working memory capacity, and prevents team-level stylistic fragmentation across growing engineering orgs.

To establish operational stability, organizations must enforce a strict boundary rule: if an untyped composite literal spans more than a single line or sits nested within another literal, explicit typing must be retained. Permitting shorthand strictly for shallow, unambiguous contexts—such as zero-value returns like return {}, errors.New(...) or adjacent parameter passing—maintains ergonomic velocity while cutting off the causal chain of cognitive degradation.

  • If a literal crosses a multi-line boundary: Enforce explicit type declarations to prevent readers from losing contextual tracking across vertical line breaks.
  • If a literal is embedded inside another structure: Mandate explicit types to halt working memory saturation before AST traversal overhead causes field misattribution.
  • If reviewing public API contracts: Reject elision entirely to guarantee that package consumers can identify data shapes without depending on IDE hover tooltips.

Ultimately, treating language features as purely aesthetic shorthand ignores the thermodynamic reality of team codebases. Shifting verification overhead from visual parsing to compiler dependency increases systemic vulnerability unless organizational governance acts as a deliberate regulatory brake.

Ecosystem Lessons: Parallels from Other Language Evolutions

Looking across modern programming ecosystems, the tension between syntactic conciseness and cognitive overhead is a recurring evolutionary bottleneck. When languages introduce type inference or shorthand features—such as automatic type deduction or implicit initialization shorthand in systems languages—they trigger a predictable behavioral shift among developers: local ergonomic optimization quickly overrides long-term maintainability.

In ecosystems where syntactic shorthand was introduced without structural guardrails or automated migration linting, codebases suffered from a distinct failure mode: stylistic fragmentation. Because human short-term working memory is strictly capped at four to seven active elements, removing explicit type anchors forces engineers to execute mental Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) traversal. Comparing these approaches reveals that unconstrained adoption consistently fails under real-world maintenance pressures. The optimal strategy requires explicit boundary rules to prevent cognitive overload. When evaluating whether to drop explicit types from a composite literal, engineering teams must apply a definitive decision rule: If an untyped composite literal spans more than a single line or is nested within another literal, explicit typing must be retained.

Without an automated migration tool to enforce structural limits, the regulatory burden shifts entirely to human convention. Ecosystem lessons demonstrate that voluntary restraint fails without codified team-level policies. Enforcing strict architectural boundaries preserves the compiler's bidirectional type inference benefits while shielding the engineering organization from silent logic bugs, runtime panics, and long-term codebase obfuscation.

Balancing Ergonomics with Sustainability: Conclusion and Future Outlook

The decade-long gestation of Go's untyped composite literal proposal exposes a profound tension in language evolution: the friction between local syntactic velocity and global cognitive sustainability. When language maintainers introduce bidirectional compile-time type inference to strip redundant type names (such as reducing time.Time{} to {}), they remove explicit visual anchors. title: Core Web Vitals po slovensky: LCP, INP a CLS
description:
Core Web Vitals sú tri metriky, ktoré merajú, ako rýchlo a príjemne sa stránka používa. Google ich berie do úvahy pri hodnotení webov.

LCP: za ako dlho sa zobrazí hlavný obsah

Largest Contentful Paint meria čas, kým sa objaví najväčší prvok na obrazovke, zvyčajne hlavný obrázok alebo nadpis. Dobrá hodnota je do 2,5 sekundy.

Čo pomáha: menšie a moderné obrázky, rýchly server, nenačítavať zbytočné skripty pred obsahom.

INP: ako rýchlo stránka reaguje

Interaction to Next Paint meria, ako dlho trvá, kým stránka reaguje na klik alebo ťuknutie. Dobrá hodnota je do 200 milisekúnd.

Čo pomáha: menej JavaScriptu, rozdeliť dlhé úlohy, neblokovať hlavné vlákno ťažkými výpočtami.

CLS: poskakovanie obsahu

Cumulative Layout Shift meria, ako sa obsah počas načítania posúva. Určite poznáte, že chcete kliknúť na tlačidlo a v poslednej chvíli sa odsunie. Dobrá hodnota je do 0,1.

Čo pomáha: vždy uviesť rozmery obrázkov a videí, rezervovať miesto pre reklamy a bannery, správne načítavať písma.

Kde to zmerať

  • PageSpeed Insights ukáže laboratórne aj reálne dáta od používateľov.
  • Search Console má zostavu Core Web Vitals pre celý web.
  • Náš bezplatný sken web prejde aj základné kontroly výkonu.

Poradie krokov

Začnite najväčším problémom. Najčastejšie sú to veľké obrázky a zbytočné skripty. Po každej zmene meranie zopakujte, aby ste videli, čo naozaj pomohlo.

title: Your AI agent copied the web page onto iOS. Start from the platform.
description:
Say you already have a web tool at example.com for logging a site visit, and you ask your AI agent for the iOS screen. The reply is the web page, transplanted: a left sidebar, hover-only extra actions, and a floating button copied from another platform. On a phone held in one hand, the sidebar is gone, and so are the actions that lived on hover.

The agent copied a familiar surface onto the wrong platform.

This is a fictional illustration of how Design Decision Method handles platform guidance, not a case study or a measured result. The product details below are invented for the example.

Start from the platform you are actually building

The live docs already put the device in establish context. When choosing a visual system, they say to keep a system the project already has, and when it has none, to select from the platform. For other web work, the fallback is Material 3. Borrow an interaction pattern when it solves the task. Do not copy another organization's branding.

The docs are plain that this is not a ranking: the procedure routes work across Material 3, platform guidelines, and a project's own rules, among other sources, and does not rank those sources or copy their branding.

What the live introduction does not spell out is how that choice changes on iOS versus Android versus the web. That detail lives in the agent procedure.

What the procedure actually selects

If a suitable existing system, brand, or platform direction is already in place, the procedure says to retain and extend it. A new iOS screen is not automatic permission to invent a second identity.

When there is no existing system, the procedure gives conditional rows, not a favourite:

  • For a native Apple interface, use Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and system controls for the supported OS and SDK. Do not mandate the newest material or an OS upgrade.
  • For Android or Compose, use Material 3, and only use Expressive options where the brief or project calls for them and the installed library supports them.
  • For other web or cross-platform work, Material 3 is the fallback, with implementation support checked.

The routing guidance is just as direct for a native mobile screen: use the platform's guidance for navigation and controls. Avoid mimicking one platform's material on another.

A short note for the example.com iOS screen might look like this:

Platform: A native iOS screen, not a wrapped copy of the website.
Keep: The product's existing brand colour roles, if they already exist.
Follow the platform: System navigation and controls for the supported OS and SDK. Every action that existed on the web stays reachable without hover.
Do not copy: The web sidebar, hover-only overflow, or a floating action pattern brought over from another platform.
Do not add: A new visual material the brief did not ask for, or a required OS upgrade.

Choose the visual system still starts with what the project already has. Platform selection is the next question: which conventions this surface should actually follow.

Brand can travel. Chrome often should not.

Choosing the visual system is separate from borrowing an interaction pattern. The procedure's visual-system reference adds a practical split: native platform conventions can coexist with brand typography and imagery when behaviour stays coherent. The site-visit log can keep its colours. It should not keep a sidebar that iOS does not use, or actions that disappear without a pointer.

The same split runs the other way. A later Android screen should not be dressed in iOS chrome to look "consistent." A web page should not assume a gesture that only exists on a phone. Rebuild the pattern in the target stack — meaning, behaviour, focus, and feedback — instead of pasting another platform's markup.

Structure each view already asks the agent to adapt the layout to the device without dropping a capability the task needs. Hover-only actions on an iOS screen fail that test.

Keep it proportional

Name the platform, keep a suitable existing brand, and write down the conventions you will not transplant. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. It does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee a better native screen. What it gives you is a place to catch a copied surface before it ships on the wrong platform.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Visual-system adoption checks
  • Repository README and install notes

title: 5 Database Performance Checks for Mining IT Teams
description:
Our Mining database performance checklist
Enterprise applications, asset management platforms and reporting tools depend on databases that remain available and responsive. A slow application may be caused by inefficient queries, storage contention, missing maintenance or infrastructure capacity rather than an issue in the application itself.
For mining businesses operating across sites and offices, the following checks help IT teams prioritise database reliability.
1. Check query and workload performance
Review slow-running queries, execution plans, locking, wait events and changes in peak usage. Establish a performance baseline for each critical workload and identify whether recent changes have increased response times.
Ask: Can we identify the queries responsible for the largest performance impact?
2. Review capacity and resource contention
Assess CPU, memory, storage latency, disk utilisation and database growth. Check that capacity forecasts reflect seasonal processing, reporting and planned application changes. Cloud database sizing should be reviewed alongside cost.
Ask: Do we know when our critical environments will reach capacity thresholds?
3. Verify backup and restore capability
Successful backup jobs do not prove that recovery will meet business requirements. Test restores, confirm recovery point and recovery time objectives, and verify dependencies such as encryption keys, configuration and connectivity.
Ask: When was the last successful recovery test, and what did it prove?
4. Review patching, versions and privileged access
Identify unsupported database versions, delayed security patches, unnecessary privileges and configuration drift. Plan upgrades around application compatibility, maintenance windows and rollback procedures.
Ask: Which databases present the greatest security or support risk today?
5. Confirm proactive monitoring and ownership
Ensure alert thresholds reflect business-critical services, not just server availability. Document who receives alerts, who investigates them and how incidents escalate outside business hours.
Ask: Would our team detect degradation before users report it?
What to do next
Record each check as Pass, Needs attention or Not assessed. Prioritise systems by business criticality and assign an owner and target date to each finding.
