title: A prompt change is a code change. Gate it in CI with 60 lines of node:test
description:
Agents and AI features change in a way normal code doesn't. Someone tweaks a prompt, bumps the model version, or adds a line of context, and the code review shows a three-line diff. The tests pass. Nothing in the pipeline knows that the summaries now invent refund amounts.

We review code changes by reading them. We can't review prompt changes that way, because the effect isn't in the diff. It's in the outputs. So the review has to run the outputs.

Here is the small harness we put in front of every AI feature before it ships. It's plain node:test, a JSON file of cases, and about 60 lines. No eval framework, no dashboard. It fails CI when the answers get worse, which is the only job it has.

1. Write cases from real inputs

Start with 20 to 50 real inputs, taken from logs or support tickets (with personal data removed). For each one, write down what a good answer must contain and must not contain. You're not writing the perfect answer. You're writing the things that make an answer wrong.

[
  {
    "id": "refund-amount",
    "input": "Hi, order 1182 arrived broken. I paid $42.50. Please refund me.",
    "mustInclude": ["$42.50", "refund"],
    "mustNotInclude": ["angry"],
    "maxChars": 300
  },
  {
    "id": "no-amount-given",
    "input": "Order 1182 never arrived. I want my money back for order 1182.",
    "mustInclude": ["refund"],
    "maxChars": 300
  }
]

The second case matters as much as the first. The customer didn't give an amount, so the right summary doesn't contain one. Cases where the correct answer is "I don't know" are where models most often make things up.

2. Check what can be checked in code

You can't check in code whether a summary is good. You can check a surprising number of ways it's bad:

// evals/check.js
export function check(output, c) {
  const problems = [];

  for (const s of c.mustInclude ?? []) {
    if (!output.includes(s)) problems.push(`missing "${s}"`);
  }
  for (const s of c.mustNotInclude ?? []) {
    if (output.includes(s)) problems.push(`contains "${s}"`);
  }
  if (c.maxChars && output.length > c.maxChars) {
    problems.push(`too long (${output.length} chars)`);
  }

  // Every number in the answer must appear in the input.
  for (const n of output.match(/\d[\d,.]*\d|\d/g) ?? []) {
    if (!c.input.includes(n)) problems.push(`invented number ${n}`);
  }
  return problems;
}

The last check is the one that earns its keep. Any number in the output that isn't in the input was invented: an amount, a date, an order ID. It's strict and occasionally flags something harmless, like "2 items" when the input said "two items". That's a fair trade for catching the summary that tells your support team to refund $45.00 instead of $42.50.

3. Gate on the pass rate, not on every case

Models aren't deterministic, and a few cases will be borderline. If every case has to pass, the suite turns red on noise and people learn to ignore it. Gate on the overall rate instead:

// evals/summary.test.js
import test, { after } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { summarizeTicket } from "../src/summarize.js";
import { check } from "./check.js";

const cases = JSON.parse(await readFile(new URL("./cases.json", import.meta.url)));
const MIN_PASS_RATE = Number(process.env.EVAL_MIN_PASS_RATE ?? 0.9);
const results = [];

for (const c of cases) {
  test(c.id, async (t) => {
    const output = await summarizeTicket(c.input);
    const problems = check(output, c);
    results.push({ id: c.id, ok: problems.length === 0 });
    if (problems.length) t.diagnostic(`${problems.join("; ")} | output: ${output}`);
  });
}

after(() => {
  const passed = results.filter((r) => r.ok).length;
  const rate = passed / results.length;
  console.log(`evals: ${passed}/${results.length} passed (${(rate * 100).toFixed(0)}%)`);
  assert.ok(rate >= MIN_PASS_RATE, `pass rate ${rate.toFixed(2)} is below ${MIN_PASS_RATE}`);
});

Each case still prints its problems and the actual output, so when the gate fails you can see why without rerunning anything. With a version of summarizeTicket that invents the amount, the run looks like this and exits with code 1:

# missing "$42.50"; contains "angry"; invented number 45.00 | output: Customer wants a refund of $45.00 and is angry.
# evals: 0/2 passed (0%)
  error: 'pass rate 0.00 is below 0.9'

Start the threshold where your current prompt actually scores, then raise it as you fix cases. The point is that it can only go up.

4. Run it only when it matters

Every eval run calls the model, which costs money and takes a minute. There's no reason to run it on a CSS change. Trigger it on the files that change model behaviour:

# .github/workflows/evals.yml
name: evals
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/prompts/**"
      - "src/summarize.js"
      - "evals/**"
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci
      - run: node --test evals/*.test.js
        env:
          MODEL_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MODEL_API_KEY }}

Do the same thing by hand before switching model versions. When your provider retires the version you tested on, this suite is the difference between a one-day upgrade and finding out from customers.

5. Add a case for every bug

When someone reports a bad answer in production, don't just fix the prompt. Add the input as a case first, watch it fail, then fix the prompt until it passes. It's the same habit as writing a regression test for a bug, and it's how the suite grows from 20 cases to the 200 that actually describe your users.

What this doesn't replace

Code checks catch answers that are wrong in ways you predicted. They don't tell you whether an answer is helpful, well-toned or complete. For that you still need a person reading a sample every week, or a second model grading against a rubric, which is its own post.

But the gate comes first. It's an afternoon of work, it runs on infrastructure you already have, and it means a prompt change gets the same treatment as a code change: it doesn't merge until something has checked what it actually does.

I'm Mayursinh, founder of Redlio Labs. We add AI features to custom software for mid-size companies, and this harness goes in before the first prompt does. The harness above was run with Node 22, against a good and a deliberately broken summarizer.

title: How to catch an expiring or broken SSL certificate before your visitors do
description:
Many TLS certificates now live 90 days, and the maximum lifetime for all public certificates is dropping in steps (200 days since March 2026, 47 days by 2029). Auto-renewal handles most of it, until a DNS change, a moved server or a forgotten subdomain breaks the renewal and nobody notices until visitors see a browser warning.

Here is what to check, how to do it for free with tools you already have, and how to run the same checks on a long list of domains.

The four problems to look for

1. Expiry. The certificate is past its end date, or will be soon. You want a warning weeks ahead, not on the day.

2. Wrong name. The certificate is valid but does not cover the name the visitor typed. Typical after a migration: example.com is covered, www.example.com or shop.example.com is not.

3. Broken chain. The server does not send its intermediate certificate. Desktop browsers often repair this on their own, so the site "works for me", while API clients, payment callbacks and bots fail.

4. Self-signed or private CA. Fine on an internal tool, a problem on anything public.

Option A: openssl for one host

openssl is installed on most Linux and macOS machines and ships with Git for Windows:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -enddate -ext subjectAltName

This prints who the certificate is for, who issued it, its end date and every name it covers. -servername matters: without it, a server hosting several sites may hand you the wrong certificate. To check the chain, look for Verify return code: 0 (ok) in the output of the first command alone.

Option B: a short Python script for a list

Python's standard library can do a strict check, the same way an API client would, with no extra package:

import socket, ssl
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def check(host, port=443, warn_days=30):
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()  # verifies the chain and the hostname
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=10) as sock:
            with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host) as tls:
                cert = tls.getpeercert()
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        return f"BAD {host}: {e.verify_message}"
    except OSError as e:
        return f"ERR {host}: {e}"
    end = datetime.fromtimestamp(ssl.cert_time_to_seconds(cert["notAfter"]), timezone.utc)
    days = (end - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).days
    return f"{'OK ' if days > warn_days else 'BAD'} {host}: {days} days left"

for line in open("domains.txt", encoding="utf-8"):
    if line.strip():
        print(check(line.strip()))

Expired certificates, wrong names, self-signed certificates and missing intermediates all end up in the BAD branch with the reason. One limit: when verification fails, Python does not give you the certificate, so you see why it failed but not its dates or names. For that, fall back to the openssl command above. Run the script daily from cron or a scheduled task and you have a basic monitor.

Option C: a hosted checker for bulk jobs

Disclosure: this one is ours. We publish SSL Certificate Checker on Apify. You paste a list of domains, host:port pairs or full URLs, and it does one TLS handshake per host, up to 100 in parallel. Unlike the script above, it still reads and reports the certificate when it is not trusted.

from apify_client import ApifyClient  # pip install apify-client

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("extas_corp/ssl-certificate-checker").call(
    run_input={"domains": ["example.com", "smtp.example.com:465"], "warnDays": 21})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if not item["ok"]:
        print(item["host"], item.get("daysLeft"), item["warnings"], item["error"])

A certificate served for the wrong host comes back like this (shortened):

{
  "host": "wrong.host.badssl.com",
  "ok": false,
  "trusted": false,
  "trustError": "Hostname mismatch, certificate is not valid for 'wrong.host.badssl.com'.",
  "subject": "*.badssl.com",
  "daysLeft": 45
}

Each row also has the issuer, validFrom / validTo, all alternative names, a wildcard flag, the TLS version and cipher. ok is true only when the certificate is trusted, not expired and not expiring within warnDays. DNS, connection and timeout errors are reported on their row and do not stop the run.

It is free during launch: you only pay Apify's own platform usage, which the free monthly credit covers for normal use. Limits: it is not a full TLS security scan (no cipher enumeration, no vulnerability tests), revocation is not checked, STARTTLS ports such as SMTP 587 are not supported, and a CDN may serve a different certificate in another region than the one the check runs from.

What to put on the list

  • Every hostname, not only the main domain: www, apex, api, mail, old marketing subdomains.
  • Mail and other TLS services on their own ports (465, 993).
  • The vendors you depend on: an expired certificate on a payment or webhook endpoint breaks your site too.

Run it daily, alert only on BAD, and the next expiry becomes a ticket instead of an outage.

title: Don't ask the model to be brief. Cut it in code, and count what you cut.
description:
DevReview, the AI code reviewer I'm building, never posts more than eight comments on a pull request [src:facts]. That limit isn't something the model is asked to respect. It's a constant in the application code, applied after the model has finished talking.

I've mentioned that design before, in one line: a prompt is a request, a slice() isn't. This post is the longer version of that line, because when I actually wrote down why, the reasons turned out to be more specific than "models don't always follow instructions." There is also one consequence I didn't expect: once the limit lives in code, the prompt has to say the opposite of what you'd normally write.

The obvious version, and why I didn't ship it

If you want an AI reviewer that doesn't bury a pull request in comments, the first thing you reach for is the prompt:

Only report the most important issues. Keep it to a handful of comments.

That works in the sense that the output usually gets shorter. For a demo, that's enough. I didn't keep it, and not because I measured it failing. I haven't measured how often a prompt-only limit gets ignored, and I don't want to invent a number for it. I dropped it because of what the limit is when it lives in the prompt, regardless of how well the model follows it.

There are four problems with it. Only the first one is about compliance.

1. A request has no failure mode you can see

When the limit is a sentence in the prompt, "the model followed it" and "the model mostly followed it" look the same until someone counts. If a review comes back with too many comments, nothing in the system notices. There's no exception, no log line, no failing check. You find out when a user complains that the tool is noisy, which is the exact complaint the limit was supposed to prevent.

It also drifts. A prompt that produces short output with one model, one set of sampling settings and one style of diff may not do the same after any of those change. You can re-test after every change, but what you're re-testing is a tendency, not a rule.

A limit in code has an obvious failure mode: the number of comments posted is greater than the constant. That can be asserted, and an assertion either passes or it doesn't.

2. The model chooses what to drop before anything is ranked

This is the one that actually decided it for me.

If the model is told to keep the list short, it does the trimming while it writes. Whatever it decided not to say never makes it into the output. So the selection, the most important decision in the whole review, happens inside the generation, in an order I don't control and can't inspect.

What I wanted instead was a fixed rule that I can read:

  1. Collect every finding.
  2. Sort by severity: BUG, then WARN, then NIT, then PRAISE [src:facts].
  3. Within the same severity, keep the order the model produced them in.
  4. Keep the top of the list up to the cap. Count the rest.

The rule isn't clever. Its value is that it's the same rule on every review, and when someone asks "why was this comment cut and that one kept?", the answer is a sentence, not a guess about what the model was weighing at the time.

A side effect is that the ranking is across the whole pull request, not per file. When you ask a model to be brief, you have no idea whether it's being brief across the PR or per file, or front-loading whatever it saw first. With a sort over the full list, a bug in the last file outranks a nit in the first one by construction.

3. You can't disclose what was never written

When DevReview cuts comments, it says so in the review: how many remarks were suppressed to keep the review focused, and (since a change I'll get to below) what severities they were. I call that the Noise Report.

That disclosure is only possible because the cut happens in code. The code has the full list and the shortened list, and the difference between their lengths is a number it can print.

If the model trims itself, there's no full list. The things it chose not to say don't exist anywhere. You can't count them, you can't show them, you can't tell the reader "there was more, and here's roughly what kind." A quiet review and a review that missed something look identical from the outside, and a prompt-side limit makes it impossible to tell them apart even in principle.

This is also why I don't describe DevReview as having nits "off by default." It doesn't. NITs are generated and kept like any other finding, and they're shown if they fit under the cap [src:facts]. They're just the first thing to go when the list is long, and when they go, they're counted.

4. The pull request is in the same context as your instruction

An AI reviewer reads text written by the PR author: the title, the description, the diff. All of that lands in the same context window as the instructions. If the limit is an instruction, then "keep it short" is one sentence competing with whatever else is in that window, including text written by someone you don't control.

I don't want to overstate this. The prompt tells the model to treat PR content as material to review, not as instructions, and that's the main defense. But for the specific question of "how many comments can end up on this PR," I'd rather the answer not depend on that defense holding. With the cap in code, the most any text in the PR can do to the count is fill it.

The part I didn't expect: the prompt has to say the opposite

Once the cap was in code, I had a prompt that still asked the model to be selective. That's two limits stacked on top of each other, and the combination is worse than either one alone.

Walk through it. The model trims itself to a short list, silently. The code then sees a list that's already under the cap, cuts nothing, and reports that nothing was suppressed. The review looks complete and disclosed, but the selection happened in the one place that can't be counted. The Noise Report says zero while the model has quietly dropped things. The code-side limit is still enforced, but the honesty it was supposed to buy is gone.

So the prompt now says the reverse. The relevant rule tells the model to report every genuine finding, and then:

DevReview enforces the comment budget in code — do not self-limit, but do not pad the list either. Only real findings.

Both halves matter. "Do not self-limit" is there so the code gets the full list and the count means something. "Do not pad" is there because the obvious way for "report everything" to go wrong is a model inventing filler to look thorough. The rest of the prompt pushes in the same direction: a list of common false positives to avoid, and an instruction to downgrade or skip anything it's not sure is a bug.

The split of responsibilities ends up clean:

  • The model decides what is a real finding and how severe it is.
  • The code decides how many get posted, in what order, and reports what it cut.

The model is good at the first job and has no reason to be trusted with the second.

What the code-side limit doesn't fix

Putting the limit in code moves the problem. It doesn't remove it. These are the costs and gaps I know about.

The ranking trusts the model's severity labels. The sort is deterministic, but the input to it isn't. If the model labels a real bug as a NIT, the code will faithfully rank it with the NITs and, on a long review, cut it. The code enforces the count, not the judgment. The best it can do is make the cut visible, so a reader who sees "suppressed: some NITs" at least knows there's something to expand.

The cap can cut a bug. If a pull request has more genuine bugs than the cap, some of them don't get posted. Sorting puts bugs first, so you see the worst of it, but "the cap never hides a real bug" is not something I can claim. I used to describe the suppressed comments as "lower-priority," and I removed that word for exactly this reason: when the list is all bugs, what gets cut is also a bug. The note now lists what severities were cut instead of characterizing them.

The order of filters decides what the count means. Counting suppressed comments is only honest if everything that removes a finding is counted, and if invalid findings don't compete for slots with valid ones. I got that wrong once: findings that pointed at files not in the PR were filtered after the cap, so they could take slots and then disappear, and in the worst case the review showed a green check. I wrote that up separately in When a Code Review Says "No Issues" but Found Bugs. The short version: the path check now runs before the cap, and discarded findings are counted too. A code-side limit doesn't make the pipeline honest by itself. It makes it possible to be honest, and then you have to check every filter.

You pay for findings you throw away. If the model reports everything and the code keeps a fraction, the tokens spent on the rest are spent for a number in the Noise Report. I think that's the right trade, since the count is part of what makes the review trustworthy, but it's a real cost and it grows with the size of the PR.

Why the cap is eight [src:facts] is a separate question. This post is about where the limit is enforced, not about its value. I don't have measured data on the value to share yet, so I'm not going to argue for it here.

Because it's code, it can be tested like code

The practical payoff of all this is that the limit stops being a behavior you evaluate and becomes a property you assert.

Testing a prompt-side limit means running the real model on a set of PRs and looking at the distribution of comment counts. That's useful, but it's an evaluation: it tells you how the model tended to behave on those inputs at that time.

Testing a code-side limit means faking the model's response and checking what the pipeline does with it. The model is out of the loop, so the result is the same every run. This is roughly the shape of the test (the helper name here is illustrative, not a file you'll find in the repo):

test("cap is enforced in code and overflow is counted", async () => {
  // Fake model output: more findings than the cap, severities mixed and
  // deliberately out of order, all pointing at files that exist in the PR.
  const findings = [
    ...Array.from({ length: MAX_COMMENTS }, (_, i) => nit(`a.ts`, i + 1)),
    bug("b.ts", 10),
    warn("b.ts", 20),
    praise("a.ts", 30),
  ];

  const result = await reviewWithFakeModel({ comments: findings });

  // 1. Never more than the constant.
  expect(result.comments.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_COMMENTS);

  // 2. Severity order wins over model order: the bug and the warning
  //    the model listed last are posted first.
  expect(result.comments[0].severity).toBe("BUG");
  expect(result.comments[1].severity).toBe("WARN");

  // 3. Nothing disappears without being counted.
  expect(result.comments.length + result.suppressedCount).toBe(findings.length);
});

Three assertions, and each maps to one of the reasons above:

  1. The count is a rule, not a tendency.
  2. Selection follows a fixed order that I wrote down, not one the model chose while generating.
  3. Everything that was cut is disclosed. If a future change adds a filter that drops findings without counting them, the third assertion is the one that should catch it.

The third one is the assertion I care about most, and it's the one a prompt-side limit can't have at all, because there's no "findings.length" to compare against when the model never wrote them.

Since the change I described in the post on the false green check, the review function has been tested end to end with faked responses from the model and from GitHub. The block above shows the idea, not a copy of that suite. The budget itself is also pinned by a plain unit test that feeds generated findings straight into the pure rank-and-slice function, so the cap, the order and the suppressed count don't depend on any model call at all. Before that, I relied on a demo pull request with an expected review written down before running it. One of its pass conditions was that the suppressed count equals the number of generated findings minus the cap. That's the same invariant as the third assertion, just checked by hand.

When a prompt-side limit is fine

None of this means "never put limits in prompts." I'd still use one when:

  • Nobody downstream relies on the limit. If longer output is just a bit annoying and nothing breaks, a prompt instruction is the cheapest thing that mostly works.
  • There's no list to cut. Free-form prose doesn't have a natural unit to slice. Truncating a paragraph in code is worse than asking for a shorter one.
  • You don't need to tell anyone what was left out. If there's no equivalent of the Noise Report, the strongest argument for doing it in code goes away.

For a code reviewer, none of those apply. The output is a list, the reader relies on it being short, and the reader also needs to know whether short means "nothing else" or "more, cut on purpose." That's what pushed the limit out of the prompt.

The rule I'd keep

If an LLM produces a list and something about that list has to be true every time (a maximum length, an order, a guarantee that nothing vanishes without a count), enforce it in code after generation and test it with a faked response. Use the prompt for the part only the model can do: deciding what goes on the list. Then make sure the prompt isn't quietly enforcing the same limit too, because a limit nobody can count is the one you were trying to get rid of.

I'm building DevReview at getdevreview.com. It's a GitHub App that ranks review comments by severity and caps them in code, and there's a free tier if you want to see what a capped review looks like on your own PRs. If you've solved the "the model trims itself before your code can count" problem differently, I'd like to hear how.

title: A Link You Can Just Open
description:
This essay was first published on the Zyaku blog.

Here is a small scene I keep imagining.

It's late in the evening and the power has been out for an hour. In a family group on someone's phone, a cousin forwards a link: a local reporter's post about which roads are under water and which bridge is closed. The phone has one bar. The person holding it taps the link.

A page loads, slowly. It doesn't show the post. It shows a form. Email. Password. Confirm password. A code is on its way to your inbox. The bar flickers, and the code never comes. They close the tab, go back to the group and ask, "What does it say?" Then they wait for someone with better signal to type it out.

Nothing in that scene is broken. Every part works the way somebody designed it. That's what bothers me about it.

This week we changed it on Zyaku. When someone shares a public post with you, you can now read it without signing up. Zyaku asks you to join only when you want to do more than read: like, comment, follow or save. And anyone, with an account or without one, can report a post.


A forwarded link should open to the words, not to a form.

The wall in front of the words


Most links lead to a gate before they lead to anything else.

Most apps put the sign-up wall right in front of the content, and I understand why. Every visitor who turns into an account is something a team can point to at the next meeting. A link someone opens, reads and closes counts for nothing. So the wall goes up early, and its cost lands on the person who only wanted to read one thing.

I've stood on the wrong side of that wall more times than I can remember. Usually it costs me a minute. On a bad connection, in a bad hour, it can cost the whole point of the link. A shared post is often a message from someone you trust: I think you should see this. Turning that into a registration form is a strange way to treat a recommendation.

So now the post comes first. You see who wrote it, their words and pictures, and the labels Zyaku puts on posts: whether something was made with AI, whether media was altered, whether a claim is disputed, and how sure Zyaku is about the post itself. If you want to join the conversation, Zyaku asks you then, and after you sign up it brings you straight back to the post you were reading.

For people who do join, there's a small new welcome too. New accounts now get a Start here card on Home for their first couple of weeks, with one first step that fits what they said they do. Creators can practise posting with no signal: write something, switch the connection off and on, and watch what Zyaku would show while a real post waits. The practice post is never sent. I like that a first lesson can be a rehearsal with nothing at stake.

Ask at the counter


Anyone can read the rates on the wall. The paperwork waits for the counter.

Before I built software, I spent years in finance. One habit from that world took me a long time to see clearly. You ask for someone's papers when money is about to move, not when they walk through the door.

Anyone can stand in a bank and read the rates on the board. The identity checks, the forms and the signatures come at the counter, when there's something real to protect. Ask too early and you don't make anything safer. You make people leave, and you end up holding information you had no reason to collect.

That's how a shared post works now. Reading asks for nothing. Doing something that touches other people, like a comment or a follow, asks you to be someone.

We took the idea one step further than I first expected to. When you open a shared post without an account, Zyaku sets no cookie, keeps nothing in your browser and doesn't count your visit. We also ask search engines not to list these previews, so a post shared with a few people doesn't quietly become a page for the whole web.

That last part has a cost, and I'd rather name it. We won't know how many people opened a link and left. Somebody building a growth chart would love that number. I decided I'd rather not have it than take it from people who never agreed to anything.

Some doors stay shut


Opening one door made us decide which ones stay closed.

Opening the door for reading made us think hard about what should never sit behind it.

Not every post opens without an account. Emergency and crisis messages don't, and neither do posts tied to a place during a crisis. A message someone wrote in a frightening moment, saying where they are, wasn't written for strangers, and a forwarded link can travel much further than its author ever meant it to. Posts by anyone under eighteen don't open this way either. Nor do followers-only posts, mature posts or paid work. A comic chapter is still something readers pay for, and creators still get paid for the chapter they unlock.

Anything outside those rules gets the same short answer as a post that doesn't exist: this post can't be shown here. It doesn't explain why, on purpose. Sometimes the reason itself gives something away.

And while I'm on safety, the line I repeat in every one of these essays: Zyaku is not an emergency service. If you're in danger, call your local emergency number first.

In the language you read in


An open door helps more when you can read what's behind it.

An open door doesn't help much if what's behind it is in a language you can't read. So the other half of this week was about language.

Any journalism article on Zyaku can now be read in any of the languages Zyaku offers, and your choice is remembered for next time. Posts on your screen are now translated together, so they show up in your language much sooner. The shared-post preview, the Start here card and the Zyaku AI screen now appear in every language we support, not only in English.

When Zyaku translates a post, it says so. You can see that the translation was made by AI and what language it came from, and the original is one tap away. I care about that label as much as the translation. A reader deserves to know when the words in front of them aren't the words the writer chose.

This one is personal. I think in a mix of Hindi and English, like a lot of people I grew up with, and most software has treated that as a mistake to correct. A report written in one language by a reporter in one town should be able to reach a reader somewhere else without either of them doing anything special. That's the whole job.

What isn't finished


Some of this is done. Some of it is still on the bench.

Plenty.

Only ordinary posts, pictures, videos and clips open without an account for now. Comics and paid pieces still ask you to sign in, and some of that is deliberate rather than unfinished.

Reports from people without an account can be misused. We limit how often they can come from one place, and they go into the same queue as every other report. I don't think that's the final answer, and I'll keep watching it.

The phone apps aren't public yet, so everything here is about a link opened in a browser. And signing up on one bar of signal is still heavier than it should be. Letting people read first fixes the first minute. It doesn't fix every minute after that.

Underneath all of this, the offline core keeps moving too. HoldSend, our open-source library for writing offline and publishing exactly once, is public under the Apache license, and an early version is now on npm for anyone to try. Its interface may still change, and its own README says plainly that it isn't ready for production.

The first thing we ask


Read first. Decide later.

The first thing a product asks of a stranger says a lot about it. For a long time the answer across most of the internet has been: tell us who you are. I'd like Zyaku's answer to be: nothing yet.

Back in that dark room, the link opens. The post is there. The person reads which bridge is closed, types it into the family group, and goes back to waiting for the lights. Nobody had to make an account to be useful to each other.

So here's my question for you. What's the last link you gave up on because it wanted an account before it would show you anything? I'm curious what you were trying to read, and whether you ever found it another way.

Rohit Kashyap

Founder & CEO, Zyaku · Founder, TAMVEL

What's new on Zyaku · About the founder

title: Server-Side Pagination Looked Easy. It Took Me Longer Than Any React Concept Yet.
description:
This week I learnt server-side pagination, and omo, it humbled me.

On paper it's simple: instead of fetching every product and using .slice() like in client-side pagination, you ask the server for only the page you need. In practice I hit 13 bugs, and this is the longest I've ever spent on one concept.

I was building with dummyjson.com and the plan grew in stages: pagination, then search, then debouncing, then putting everything in the URL. Here are the bugs that taught me the most.

The core idea

For page 4 with 10 products per page:

const skip = (currentPage - 1) * productsPerPage; // (4 - 1) * 10 = 30

https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=10&skip=30

The server also sends back total, so the number of pages is derived, not stored:

const totalPages = Math.ceil(total / productsPerPage);

Bug 1: The URL rule I didn't know existed

When I added search, I found a URL online that looked like https://dummyjson.com/products?laptop. I used it and got a bad request. I changed it to ?search=laptop and it still didn't work the way I expected.

After a lot of back and forth, I learnt that every API has its own request structure, and DummyJSON's search lives on a different endpoint:

https://dummyjson.com/products/search?q=laptop

The Network tab showed 200 OK, yet my products weren't changing. A 200 only means the server handled the request. It doesn't mean it did what I meant. Now I check both the Request URL and the Response body in DevTools, and I read the docs before copying a URL from somewhere.

(Also: user input goes through encodeURIComponent() before it goes into a URL.)

Bug 2: Search only worked after I deleted a letter

This one stressed me, and I'm proud of how I found it. I noticed that when I typed a product name quickly, nothing updated. But when I deleted one letter, the search suddenly ran.

My fetching effect looked like this:

useEffect(() => {
  // fetching logic
}, [currentPage, searchTerm]);

But the URL inside it was built from debouncedSearchTerm. So:

  1. I type "phone" and searchTerm updates.
  2. The effect runs immediately, using the old debouncedSearchTerm.
  3. 500ms later debouncedSearchTerm becomes "phone".
  4. The effect doesn't run again, because debouncedSearchTerm isn't in its dependencies.
  5. I delete a letter, searchTerm changes, and finally a request fires.

The fix:

}, [currentPage, debouncedSearchTerm]);

Lesson: the values that decide what a side effect does must be in that effect's dependencies.

Bug 3: controller.abort vs controller.abort()

To avoid race conditions (an old request finishing after a newer one and showing wrong results), I used AbortController. My cleanup looked fine:

return () => {
  controller.abort;
};

It cancelled nothing. I never called the function. That's a JavaScript problem, not a React one: a function reference is not a function call. I wasn't paying attention to detail, and it cost me time.

The part I loved: URL search parameters

Moving page and search into the URL with useSearchParams was the most practical thing I learnt this week.

I expected refresh to reset to page 1, like it did with useState. Instead the page survived refresh, and I can now share a link like localhost:5173/?page=3&search=phone and the other person lands on exactly what I was looking at.

My final design:

  • Local state: searchTerm, for instant typing feedback
  • 500ms debounce: wait until typing stops
  • URL: the committed search and page
  • Fetching effect: requests products using the URL values

Once the URL became the source of truth, debouncedSearchTerm no longer needed its own state. That was my own call, and I'm getting better at asking "does this value really need to exist on its own?" before adding more state.

Stage 7 was the most frustrating, and Bug 13 stressed me the most

Combining the URL, debouncing and pagination broke things in ways I didn't expect: updating one parameter wiped another, every keystroke reset the page, Back created junk history entries, and shared links reset themselves to page 1 after 500ms.

Bug 13 was the worst. I'm on ?search=laptop, press Back, and the URL returns to ?search=phone, but the input still says "laptop". My debounce effect sees the mismatch, thinks it's a new search, and overwrites the URL with "laptop" again.

The fix I settled on is to sync the input whenever the URL changes:

useEffect(() => {
  setSearchTerm(urlSearchTerm);
}, [urlSearchTerm]);

Honest note: I haven't tested every Back/Forward case with this fix yet. I'd already spent too long on one concept, so I moved on. I'm sharing it as "reasonable, not verified", and it's on my list to test.

What this week taught me

  • Trace your code's execution properly. Almost every bug here (stale dependencies, effects firing on mount, mismatched state) was found by walking through what runs, in what order, with which values. This can't be over-emphasized.
  • Finding the bug is half the work, and the fix needs real reasoning too. The first fix that comes to mind often creates the next bug.
  • React is getting past syntax. I'm entering the stage where you have to think and think. I even got tired at some point.
  • Wondering aloud: I kept thinking about developers who learnt this without AI and wondering how deeply they must have reasoned. I can't prove they were sharper, but it made me want to make sure that, with AI around, I'm still doing the tracing myself.

What I'd do next

Test Back/Forward properly, then think about how to get rid of the useEffect that syncs input from the URL.

If you've handled debounced search plus URL state in a cleaner way, I'd love to hear how.

안녕하세요.

인프랩에서 모의면접 서비스를 개발/운영하고 있는 약풍이라고 해요.
최근에 SNS에 오늘의 면접질문 컨텐츠를 연재하고 있었는데, 인프런에도 해당 컨텐츠를 업로드 해달라는 요청들이 있었어요.

오늘부터 주기적으로 이곳에도 5분내로 읽을 수 있는 면접질문을 하나씩 업로드하려고 해요.
재미있게 읽어주시면 감사하겠습니다 🙇

오늘의 백엔드 질문
결제 API에 동일한 요청이 두 번 들어왔을 때, 중복 결제를 어떻게 막으시겠어요?

이력서/포트폴리오에 결제나 주문, 쿠폰 발급이 있으면 나올 수 있는 질문이에요.
실제로 이런 일이 발생할 수 있을까? 싶기도 하지만, 실무에서 종종 발생하는 이슈에요.

이 질문은 결제 요청이 한 번만 온다는 전제로 코드를 짰는지,
혹은 결제 요청이 여러번 전송되어도 한 번만 처리되도록 로직을 작성했는지 검증하는 질문이에요.

답변 키포인트
멱등키(Idempotency-Key)를 누가 만들고 어디에 저장할지
멱등키에 DB 유니크 제약을 걸어 최종 방어선을 설정했는지
처리중과 완료 상태를 구분해 저장하고, 완료면 이전 응답을 그대로 돌려주는 것
재시도와 원요청이 동시에 처리될 때의 경합
외부 PG 응답이 유실됐을 때의 대사(reconciliation)

"버튼 비활성화"처리 만으로는 아쉬운 이유
중복 결제를 이야기할 때 "프론트에서 버튼을 비활성화한다"에서 끝나면 아쉬운 답변이에요.
버튼은 언제든 클라이언트에 의해 조작될 수 있어서, 실제 방어 로직은 서버와 DB에 있어야 하거든요.

같은 키로 들어온 두 번째 요청을 새 결제가 아니라 이미 처리한 요청의 조회로 취급하는 구조인지, 두 요청이 동시에 들어와도 유니크 제약이 하나를 확실히 막아주는지를 같이 설명할 수 있게 준비하는 게 좋아요.

면접에서는
면접에서 이 질문을 받았다면 "재시도 자체를 없앨 수는 없으니, 요청이 여러 번 들어와도 결과는 한 번만 처리한다"라는 식으로 답변을 시작하면 좋아요.

그다음에는 아래 순서로 이어서 설명하면 돼요.

주문마다 멱등키를 만들고, 그 키에 유니크 제약을 건다.
두 번째 요청은 새로 처리하지 않고 저장된 결과를 반환한다.
PG 응답 유실처럼 서버가 통제할 수 없는 경우에는, 주기적인 대사 과정으로 데이터를 보정한다.
이러한 중복 요청 처리 방안은 결제 외에도 다양한 적용할 수 있어요.
쿠폰 발급, 포인트 적립, Kafka의 at-least-once 소비 이슈 모두 연관된 질문으로 나올 수 있어요.

꼬리질문
다음의 꼬리질문도 생각해보세요.

멱등키는 클라이언트와 서버 중 어디에서 생성하는 것이 좋을까요?
DB에서 주문을 조회 후 없으면 insert 하는 방식에는 어떤 문제가 있나요?
같은 멱등키의 요청 두 개가 동시에 들어오면 두 번째 요청에는 어떤 응답을 주시겠어요?
첫 요청이 아직 처리 중일 때 들어온 재시도는 대기시키는 것과 에러를 반환하는 것 중 어느 쪽이 낫나요?
PG에는 결제가 성공했는데 우리 서버가 응답을 받지 못했다면 어떻게 복구하나요?

AI 모의면접으로
나의 면접 스킬을 체크해보세요
프론트엔드,백엔드,FDE 기술면접부터 문화면접까지,
개발자 면접 준비를 실전처럼 연습해 보세요.

직무/문화면접 보러가기

title: Autoscaling Adds Waiters, Not Ovens. Here's What Actually Breaks at 10x Load
description:
A signed enterprise deal or a viral campaign puts the same pressure on a platform: 10x the normal traffic, arriving faster than anyone budgeted for. The instinct is to trust autoscaling to absorb it, and autoscaling does its job exactly as designed. The problem is what it was designed to scale. It adds more stateless application instances, which were already the most elastic part of the system, and does nothing for the database connection pool, the cache origin, or the shared job queue underneath them. Manoj Yerrasani, VP of Global Platform Engineering at NBCUniversal, put it plainly after operating at Super Bowl scale: "auto-scaling is a lie." More app servers just means more processes competing for the same fixed set of database connections, and that competition is where the outage actually starts.

Four questions that predict where a platform breaks first

The Load Shape Audit is four diagnostic questions, not a tool you install:

  • Request shape: how many backend calls does a single user action trigger? A page load that fans out to six API endpoints multiplies your real request volume by six before traffic even grows.
  • Data shape: how many different access patterns are competing on one database? Write-heavy configuration writes and read-heavy analytics queries fighting over the same connection pool degrade both.
  • Tenant shape: does one large tenant's workload saturate a shared resource, connection pool, job queue, cache, search index, and degrade service for every smaller tenant on the same infrastructure?
  • Failure shape: when something has to give, is there a predetermined priority order, or does the system degrade randomly?

Signal 3 is the one most platforms discover the hard way. Neon's production analysis and the AWS whitepaper on SaaS tenant isolation both document the same pattern: one noisy tenant degrading everyone sharing its infrastructure.

The pattern that fixes the most common request-shape failure

When a cache misses under load, the naive implementation lets every concurrent request for that same uncached key hit the database independently, ten simultaneous cache misses become ten identical queries. The fix is request collapse, also called singleflight: the first request triggers the real query, and every other request for the same key waits on that one result instead of firing its own.

const inFlight = new Map();

async function getWithSingleflight(key, fetchFn) {
  if (inFlight.has(key)) {
    return inFlight.get(key); // piggyback on the request already running
  }
  const promise = fetchFn()
    .finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
  inFlight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}

That's a handful of lines, and it turns a thundering herd of duplicate queries into one query with N waiters. It's also exactly the kind of fix that autoscaling can't provide, because the problem was never a shortage of application instances.

Isolating the noisy neighbor, in order of cost

Tenant-shape problems get fixed in escalating stages, and jumping straight to the most expensive one wastes engineering time you don't have during an incident:

  • Row-level isolation at the database layer. PostgreSQL row-level security enforces tenant boundaries in the database itself, not in application code that a future developer might bypass.
  • Per-tenant connection pools and job queue lanes. A large tenant gets its own lane instead of competing with everyone else for the same shared pool.
  • Full tenant silo. Dedicated infrastructure per tenant, the most expensive option, reserved for the tenants whose load actually justifies it.

What this looked like on a real platform

Brocoders rebuilt Adact's platform on Node.js and Nest.js with a split database layer, PostgreSQL for write-heavy campaign configuration, MongoDB for read-heavy analytics, so the two access patterns stopped fighting over the same connection pool. Server-side rendering behind CloudFront collapsed what had been multiple API calls per page load into a single request. That architecture held through a campaign that generated 18,000 leads in 10 days and sustained over 2 million requests at peak across more than 3 million visitors in six months, without the app-server layer being the thing that mattered most. We run full-stack delivery with our own DevOps, no outsourced infra, so the team building the feature is the same team that has to answer when a connection pool saturates at 2am.

Pre-launch checklist before you trust autoscaling with a 10x event

  • Run expected load in staging at least twice before launch, not once, and not in production.
  • Freeze configuration changes the week of launch. Ben Maurer's 2015 analysis of Facebook outages found human error during change windows was a leading cause, not raw traffic.
  • Map every shared resource: connection pools, caches, job queues, search indexes, and who else is competing for each one.
  • Write explicit traffic-tier priorities before you need them: what's protected (checkout, auth), what degrades gracefully (recommendations), what gets dropped with a message.
  • Set numeric thresholds for architectural work, not vibes: "at X concurrent users the read path splits, at Y tenants we move to per-tenant pools."
  • Don't build the full silo model preemptively. Every extra service boundary adds deployment surface and on-call pages before the load that justifies it arrives.

If you're staring down a 10x traffic event and want a second technical opinion on which layer actually breaks first, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.
