title: Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot
description:
Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot

Go's module system uses go.sum files and the public checksum database to make repeated downloads of a module version reproducible. A downloaded module can be checked against a recorded hash, and the checksum database supplies a signed, append-only record for public modules. The model is strong for public dependencies. It becomes more nuanced when an organization introduces private module paths and internal proxies.

The Go modules reference states that when a module is matched by GOPRIVATE or GONOSUMDB, or when the checksum database is disabled with GOSUMDB=off, the go command accepts the hash and adds the file to the module cache without verifying it against the public database. The build can still be reproducible if go.sum already contains the expected hash. The first download of a private module depends on the private source and the organization's controls around it.

Know which verification source applies

For a public module, the default GOPROXY points to the Go module mirror and then to direct. The checksum database verifies newly added sums, and the module cache records downloaded content. If a proxy mirrors the checksum database, the go command may use that mirrored data instead of connecting to the public service. The proxy becomes part of the trust path and should have its own integrity, availability and access controls.

For a private module, GOPRIVATE acts as a default for GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB. A private module can be fetched through an internal proxy, directly from a version-control server or from a local replacement. The checksum database cannot compute hashes for content it cannot see. The organization needs a private source of truth for the expected commit or artifact, plus a review process for the first version that enters the build.

Do not use GOSUMDB=off as a convenient fix for a proxy problem. It disables checksum verification for every module that is not already recorded in go.sum, which is broader than the private path that caused the failure. GOINSECURE is also not a general integrity bypass: the documentation says it permits insecure fetching for direct dependencies, but it does not by itself disable checksum database validation.

Treat replace directives as build policy

A replace directive can point a module to a local directory, a fork or a different version. That is useful during development and dangerous when it enters a release build without review. The release pipeline should inspect the effective module list, including replacements, and reject a path that is outside the approved source set.

The same review should cover pseudo-versions and local module cache state. A pseudo-version identifies a commit, but the build still needs a trusted mapping from that commit to the source repository and the expected content. A cache check is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for a policy about which source is allowed.

go mod verify checks that cached module files and extracted directories have not changed since they were added to the cache. The Go reference warns that it does not download missing modules and does not use go.sum to verify module content. A clean cache after a build can therefore be consistent with a bad first download. Record the source, version and hash that the build actually used.

Build a private-module control

Configure a private proxy with authenticated access, immutable version storage and audit logs. Protect the credentials used by CI so that a compromised job cannot publish a new private version. Require review for module path changes, new replacements and first-time private dependencies. Run the same configuration in developer and CI environments so that a local GOPRIVATE setting does not hide a production path.

Go's checksum design does not claim to decide whether a dependency is appropriate. It protects the identity of a module version against later substitution. The operator still needs dependency review, source authorization and a policy for modules outside the public transparency log.

References

  • Go Modules Reference
  • How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks

title: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications
description:
Introducing Xanout: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications

I've been working on Xanout, a lightweight, TypeScript-first server router designed to make backend development simpler and more flexible.

The idea behind Xanout is straightforward: provide developers with a clean routing system built around web standards without introducing unnecessary complexity.

What is Xanout?

Xanout is a server-side routing library for building HTTP applications and backend services.

It provides a simple foundation for handling HTTP requests, defining routes, and organizing server-side application logic.

What can you build with Xanout?

Xanout can be used as a foundation for building:

  • REST APIs — Create structured APIs for web and mobile applications.
  • Authentication systems — Implement login, registration, authorization, and session-based authentication.
  • Backend services — Build application backends and business logic.
  • API gateways — Organize and manage HTTP endpoints.
  • Microservices — Develop lightweight HTTP-based services.
  • Middleware-driven applications — Handle authentication, logging, validation, error handling, and request processing.

Why Xanout?

Some of the ideas behind the project:

  • TypeScript-first development.
  • Lightweight routing architecture.
  • Web-standard APIs and interfaces.
  • Flexible middleware handling.
  • Simple and developer-friendly API design.

I want developers to focus on building their applications rather than dealing with unnecessary framework complexity.

Project Links

  • Website & Documentation: https://xanout.devnax.com/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/devnax/xanout

What's Next?

Xanout is still evolving. I'm working on improving its architecture, developer experience, and overall capabilities.

If you're interested in TypeScript, backend development, or open-source projects, I'd appreciate your feedback.

Feel free to explore the project, share your thoughts, or contribute.

Thanks for reading!

title: One button sent people to the wrong page. We checked all 41, and 14 didn't go where they said.
description:
On Tuesday morning I opened the page a small clothing shop was about to get from us: a short video of one of their products, and under it a single button that said "Make one with your own character."

It was a product, not a character. And the button didn't open anything that makes a video. It opened the page where you build a new character from scratch.

This post is about that one button, the 40 others we checked because of it, and the rule we wrote so it stops happening.

TL;DR
We audited all 41 calls to action on our site and in our emails. 14 didn't go where their words said. We fixed 7 the same day, 7 sit on pages we froze on purpose, and a test now fails the build if a button drifts.

The words said one thing and the link did another

I build RefVid, a small tool where you upload a few photos of a product or a character once, then make short videos that keep it looking the same in every shot. Every finished video gets a public share page, and that page has one job: let whoever watches it make their own.

The share page picked its words from a fallback. When a video wasn't made from a template, the page assumed it was about a character, wrote "Keep your own character the same in every shot", and pointed the button at the character builder (we call saved characters and products "elements").

So a shop owner watching a video of their own product would read "character" and land on a form asking them to create one. Nothing on that page says "video".

My first fix sent it to a second wrong page

The obvious patch: read the subject's type. If the clip shows a product, say "Make one with your own product". That went in at 11:15 UTC.

Then I looked at where it actually led. With no template recorded, the new button opened our marketing page for product videos. The words were right now. The destination was a page that explains the thing instead of starting it.

That fix lasted 22 minutes. The second one, at 11:37, is what this post is really about, because by then the question had changed from "why is this button wrong?" to "how many buttons are wrong?"

So we listed every button on the site: 41 of them

We went through every page type and every email we send, and wrote down each call to action as a row: the file, the words, where it goes for a signed-in visitor, and where it should go.

41 rows. 27 were fine. 14 were not. These are the 7 we fixed that day:

Words on the button Where it lives Went to Now goes to
Make one with your own character Share page, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make one with your own product Share page, product clip, no template Marketing page New video
Make one with your own subject Gallery, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make your own series Series index, episodes, making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
Try it in the studio Prompt blocks on making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
(sign in) Invite welcome sheet, no template Character builder New video
Make another "Your video is ready" email That subject's page New video, same subject

The part that surprised me: the same action, "start a new video", was written four different ways in the code. One helper went to the builder, one component opened a photo picker first, one link went to the marketing page, and the email linked to the subject's own page. Every one of them made sense on the day it was written. Together they meant a visitor couldn't predict where "make one" would take them.

Not one label changed in the fix. The words were already right in all 7 languages we ship. Only the destinations moved.

The rule: one label, one destination, defined once

We wrote it down as four rows, and every button on the site now has to be one of them:

The button means Example words Goes to
Make one like this (template known) "Use this template" New video with that template filled in
Start a new video (no template) "Make one with your own…", "Try it", "Make another" New video, nothing preset
Create a character or product Only words that say so: "New element" The builder
Go to the studio "Studio", "Open the studio" The studio home

And each row is built by exactly one function. "Start a new video" is one helper call; nothing else in the codebase is allowed to assemble that link by hand. If you want to see the "make one like this" row working, any card in our template gallery goes straight into a new video with that template filled.

The same bug, in an email, cost a user 124 credits

The same morning a support email arrived. A user had signed up on their phone, added their own photo, and somehow never started a video. Our follow-up email said, more or less: the photo you added is already saved; open the link and press Generate.

The link carried their saved photo in the URL:

/studio/t/product-black-friday?subject=<their photo>

They opened it in their mail app, signed out. Our middleware redirected them to sign in and rebuilt the destination from the path only:

/login?intent=template:product-black-friday

The subject was gone. After sign-in, the template page did what it does when you have no photo: it loaded the template's sample product, a perfume bottle. They pressed Generate, exactly as the email told them, and 124 of their 129 signup credits went into a sample perfume ad they never asked for.

We refunded the credits and added extra, and fixed the redirect so the intent keeps everything it was given:

template:<slug>[:fresh][:subject-<id>]

In the 30 days before, 72 people got that exact "your photo is already saved" email. One of them hit this. That's a small number, and it is also every credit that person had.

It's the same mistake as the button, one layer down: the words promised a destination, and something between the click and the page threw part of it away.

Tests now fail the build if a button drifts

A rule I have to remember will fail again. So the rule is a test. cta-one-destination.test.ts reads the source and fails when:

  • any file outside a short allow-list sends someone to the builder (each allowed file has a one-line reason next to it),
  • a start link is assembled by hand instead of through the one helper,
  • the share page points at a marketing page,
  • a share button says "product" and opens the builder, or says "character" and opens a product page, checked in all 7 languages.

A second test follows the email link as a signed-out visitor through the sign-in redirect and checks that the saved photo is still in the URL where sign-in lands.

What we haven't fixed yet

7 of the 14 wrong buttons are still wrong, on purpose, for now.

They sit on pages we froze on 8 November: our home page, our pricing page and our cartoon series hub. Those are the pages an AI assistant had started sending visitors to, and we decided not to touch them at all while we watched whether that traffic held. We are now unfreezing pages one at a time, each change measured against its own before-numbers. These three haven't had their turn.

Words on the button Page Goes to today Should go to
Make one with your own subject Home, gallery Character builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, header Photo picker, then builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, closing block Photo picker, then builder New video
Generate (own photos, no template) Home, composer Builder with the photos New video with the photos
Make this (an ad format) Home, ad strip The sample subject's page New video with that prompt
Start free Pricing Studio home New video
One clip Pricing Studio home New video

The guard test knows about the three that open the builder: their files sit on its allow-list, each marked "frozen page". When a page thaws, its line comes off the list and the test forces the fix; the other four are on the audit list waiting for the same day. Until then, if you land on our home page and press one of those, you'll see the old behaviour.

A question for you

If you searched your own app today for every button that says "start", "try" or "make one", how many different places would they lead, and would you be able to say which one is right?

title: A server that almost never says no
description:
Most servers are taught to say no. Bad request? 400. Unknown shape? 422. You're strict, you're correct, and somewhere a client fixes its bug and tries again.

vitals-receiver almost never says no, because for this server "no" means "delete this forever". This post is the long version: how it's put together, why each piece is shaped the way it is, and the things that went wrong on the way to the public repo. There's real code below, copied from the repo with comments trimmed.

What it is

It's a small self-hosted receiver for Apple Health exports. An iPhone app of mine (not public yet) sends batches of HealthKit samples over the home network. The receiver stores them in SQLite, outside the repo, and serves two pages on the machine itself: a fitness page with activity rings, the week and a card per metric, and an ops page that tells you whether the pipe is still alive.

It's TypeScript on Node 22, with Fastify, better-sqlite3 and zod. MIT-licensed. You can try it without a phone:

npm ci && npm run demo

That seeds a synthetic store from a fixed seed in the system temp directory and serves it. npm run demo -- --groups=sleep shows one metric group, --groups= shows the empty state. Ctrl-C stops it cleanly. Every number you'll see there is generated. No real reading has ever been in the repo.

The one rule

The phone never reads our response body. What it does next depends only on the status code:

  • No answer, 408, 425, 429, any 5xx: the batch stays in an outbox on the device and is retried under the same exportId and batchSequence, backing off from 15 minutes to an hour, for up to seven days.
  • 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, a bare 413, any 3xx: the batch is dropped the moment we answer. Nothing on the phone ever tries it again.

So on this endpoint a 4xx isn't feedback. It's a delete button, and the server is the one pressing it. Everything else in the design follows from that.

Two doors, never connected

One process, two Fastify instances, one store:

const ingest = buildIngestServer({ config, store, token, log });
const read = buildReadServer({ store, config });

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await ingest.listen({ host: config.ingestHost, port: config.ingestPort });
  await read.listen({ host: config.readHost, port: config.readPort });

Look at the arguments. The ingest door gets token. The read door doesn't, and that's on purpose. Ingest faces the LAN, accepts POST, and checks the phone's credential. The read door is bound to loopback, serves the pages, and has no way to reach the credential, because it was never handed one. It can't leak what it never holds.

The split exists so two credentials never meet. If you put a reverse proxy with its own login in front of the dashboard, the proxy only ever points at the read door. Then the proxy password can't be replayed into ingest, and the phone's token can't read the data back. The README is blunt about it: the day you route a proxy to ingest is the day both separations stop being true.

The read door also enforces "read-only" in code instead of just promising it:

  app.addHook("onRequest", async (req, reply) => {
    if (req.method !== "GET" && req.method !== "HEAD") {
      void reply.header("allow", "GET, HEAD");
      await reply.code(405).send({ ok: false, error: "read-only listener: GET and HEAD only" });
      return reply;
    }
    return undefined;
  });

The ingest door mirrors it: any non-POST gets a 404 that says "this port accepts POST only", and that request still gets a row in the delivery log.

The token

The credential is 32 random bytes, hex, written to a file with mode 600. npm run token:mint makes it and never prints the value. The server re-reads the file only when its mtime changes, so rotating the token needs no restart. If there's no token at startup, the server refuses to start: a LAN-facing listener with no credential is worse than no listener.

The comparison:

export function tokenMatches(expected: string | null, provided: unknown): boolean {
  if (expected === null || expected.length === 0) return false;
  const candidate = Array.isArray(provided) ? provided[0] : provided;
  if (typeof candidate !== "string" || candidate.length === 0) return false;
  const a = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(expected).digest();
  const b = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(candidate).digest();
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

timingSafeEqual throws if the two buffers differ in length, and a length check before it would itself leak the length. Hashing both sides first gives two 32-byte digests every time. The comparison is constant-time and the length can't be measured either.

The ingest path, step by step

The handler is a short ladder. Every rung that would normally be a 4xx is a 200 here.

First, Fastify's body parsing goes away. If the framework parses JSON, a broken body becomes Fastify's 400 before our code ever sees it, and the batch is lost. So the body is taken as a raw string, whatever the Content-Type says:

  app.removeAllContentTypeParsers();
  app.addContentTypeParser("*", { parseAs: "string" }, (_req, body, done) => done(null, body));

Then:

  1. Credential. A wrong or missing one gets a 401. This is one of the two errors the server allows itself, because it's a configuration mistake the owner has to see. That batch is lost, and the README says so in bold.
  2. JSON. Bytes we can't parse are still health data. They go to quarantine and the phone gets a 200.
  3. Schema version. The wire contract says "reject unknown versions". We don't. 
    let parsed: unknown;
    try {
      parsed = JSON.parse(ctx.raw);
    } catch (err) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unparseable-json", err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err));
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }

    const version = (parsed as { schemaVersion?: unknown } | null)?.schemaVersion;
    if (version !== SCHEMA_VERSION) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unknown-schema-version", `schemaVersion=${JSON.stringify(version)}`);
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }
  1. Envelope shape. zod, with loose objects everywhere, because the contract only ever adds fields within version 1. A mismatch goes to quarantine with every zod issue written into detail.
  2. Probe. The app's "test connection" button sends connectivityTest: true with no samples. That gets a delivery row and nothing else. A probe that somehow carries samples is treated as an export. We never throw samples away over a flag.
  3. Samples, one at a time. The envelope's samples is typed unknown[] on purpose, and each sample is validated on its own. One malformed sample goes to quarantine instead of costing the 999 good ones beside it.

The only other error is 413, for a body over 2 MB. The phone caps a batch well under that, so if it ever fires, the fix is to raise the cap, not to shrug. And there's a 500 for real bugs. It's survivable because the phone retries a 5xx, but its body isn't kept, so the README calls it "a defect, not weather".

The store

Five tables in one SQLite file, WAL mode, migrations tracked by user_version:

  • samples: one row per HealthKit sample, keyed on its uuid, with the original JSON kept in raw.
  • runs and batches: one row per export run and per batch. Run aggregates are recomputed from batches on every ingest, so a re-delivered batch can't inflate them.
  • deliveries: every request that reached us, including the refused ones.
  • quarantine: the bytes we couldn't turn into samples. 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS quarantine (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  received_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  remote_addr TEXT,
  reason      TEXT NOT NULL,
  detail      TEXT,
  headers     TEXT NOT NULL,
  body        TEXT NOT NULL,
  bytes       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  delivery_id INTEGER
);

The headers are stored minus the credential. The token appears nowhere in the database file. That was checked against the real database file of a running server, not by reading the code.

deliveries is the table I'd keep if I could keep only one. The sender can't hear us, so this is the only place our side of every conversation is written down: status, bytes, how many samples were stored, how many were duplicates, how many were rejected, and how long it took.

The pages

/ is the fitness page: three rings, a Monday-first week strip, a card per metric with data. It has no scripts and no images, plus a CSP that allows exactly one same-origin stylesheet. /pipe is the ops page: the delivery log, export runs with their real span, how fresh each data type is, and quarantine. /api/summary and /api/fitness serve the same models as JSON, through the same code path, so the page and anything reading it can't drift apart.

/healthz answers 200 or 503, and it's the one read route that writes. It upserts a probe row into the store, so dbWritable is proven on every call instead of assumed. It also reports startedAt, and I'll come back to why.

What went wrong

The rule above sounds tidy. Getting the code to actually keep it took longer. These are the real problems, in the order we hit them.

1. The receiver was counting wrong, quietly. The first store reported stored: N for every sample it was handed, whether it already had it or not. Its upsert on uuid let a re-delivered batch rewrite the provenance of rows that were already correct. Worse, HealthKit was observed re-minting the uuid for identical heart-rate content, about 12 rows per real reading. The fix: insert-once, plus a partial unique index for that one type only.

ON CONFLICT(uuid) DO NOTHING
ON CONFLICT(content_id) WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate' DO NOTHING

Why only that type? For the other types the content id collides by design. In one measurement, 720 real samples carried 195 distinct ids, and a global unique index would have kept 195 and thrown away 525. Stored, duplicate and rejected also became three separate counters. Before, "we already had it" and "we couldn't store it" were the same number, and they need opposite reactions.

2. The test suite was testing the calendar. Two days later, npm test gave 102 pass and 9 fail on a commit that had been green. The day before, the same command on the same commit gave 104 and 7. Nothing had changed but the date. The unit tests pinned a clock, but the HTTP server read the wall clock, so pages built from fixtures dated on the 19th correctly reported "these numbers are from the 19th, not today". The product was honest and the tests were wrong. The fix makes the clock a dependency:

  now?: () => Date;

  const now = deps.now ?? (() => new Date());

It's a function, not a Date: a server that outlives its requests would otherwise freeze "today" at boot. It's optional, so production passes nothing and doesn't notice the seam. The comment in the repo says it better than I can: a suite that reads the wall clock is a suite that tests the calendar, and the calendar always wins eventually.

3. Half the delivery log was crying wolf. The ops page flagged "run metadata drift" whenever a batch disagreed with its run's first batch on generatedAt or the time window. But for one export mode, the window is each batch's own bracket and differs by design. The real store showed 201 of 420 deliveries carrying a false drift note. The fix compares only what the contract says is identical across a run, and keeps the run's window as the real extent of its batches. Before that, /pipe showed a one-hour window for a run that actually spanned 190 hours.

4. An invariant with nothing behind it. The fitness model has a rule: today is partial, always, and never counts toward an average. It was enforced in four places, and only one of them, steps, was tested. For each of the other three, the reviewer flipped partial: day === today to partial: false and the suite still passed, 123 of 123. So each site got a test that fails if you flip it. The repo also had no CI at all. Now it has a workflow that runs typecheck and the suite on every push and pull request.

5. The founding rule was written wrong. The first commit said the phone "never retries", so any non-2xx at all was data loss. Reading the app's source showed otherwise. It retries no answer, 429 and 5xx from an outbox for seven days, and drops only the permanent codes. That changes the meaning of a 500 from "lost" to "retried". Four stale comments had to be rewritten, and a README truth pass checked every claim against the code. A good rule with a wrong reason is a bug waiting for someone to "simplify" it.

6. A silent day had two possible meanings. Some days had zero deliveries. Was the receiver down, or did the phone just not send? The store couldn't say, because it only records what arrives. The fix was one log line and one field:

  return `vitals: started ${new Date(startedAt).toISOString()} commit ${rev}`;

The same instant shows up as startedAt on /healthz. With it, a gap reads as a receiver gap (started after it) or a phone gap (up the whole time). The investigation that prompted it found the phone silent in all three gaps, except one 63-minute slice when the machine was simply powered off. A small silence:check script, meant to run hourly, asks /healthz from the outside and speaks only when the phone has gone quiet.

7. Shutdown that wouldn't shut down. The first shutdown closed both servers, checkpointed the WAL and exited. A probe showed the hole: a request that had sent headers and 11 of its 500 body bytes, then SIGTERM, and the process was still alive more than 25 seconds later. Even a finished request held it open, because its keep-alive socket wasn't idle when close() ran, and Node's default keep-alive is 72 seconds. Now the drain is capped at 10 seconds by default (VITALS_DRAIN_CAP_SECONDS). Because every store write is synchronous inside one transaction, a request cut by the cap is cut before its handler runs, so there's nothing half-written to roll back.

Where it is now

The first version landed in one day, in five slices, with 42 tests. A two-line mutation (dropping uuid normalisation, conflating claimed with stored counts) made two of them fail, so we knew the suite bites. By the time it went public it had a README written for strangers, a vendored copy of the payload contract so the fixture checks run on a clean clone, an identity scrub and an MIT licence. That was 126 tests. At the last count it was 216, all green, with typecheck in CI.

It's a monitor with a store attached, not an analytics product. If you need a boring, honest pipe from your phone to your own disk, and you'd rather it keep the weird bytes than refuse them, take it. The code is public on GitHub under the MIT licence.

title: In an audit, a green test means the bug is real
description:
An audit report says "this route lets anyone find out which accounts exist". The team reads it, nods and moves on to the next ticket. A test shows the request and the response. Anyone can run it again on their own machine.

TL;DR: in an audit, I write tests that pass as long as the flaw exists. A green test proves the problem, with the exact request and response. Everything runs on an isolated test database, with made-up accounts, never touching production. Once the flaw is fixed, the test is flipped and becomes a regression test. The report keeps its paragraphs for what the tests do not prove.

This article is for developers and leads who order a security audit, or receive one. No security background needed.

The setup: a white-box audit of an API

In September, I ran a white-box audit of an API. Two questions drove the work. Can someone without an account find out who is registered? Can a logged-in user touch another account's data?

The core of the audit was five HTTP tests. An HTTP test sends a real request to the API and checks the response. The five held 21 assertions. An assertion is one precise check, like "the status code is 200".

All five tests were green. That was the bad news.

Here I cover the public routes, the ones that work without an account. The other tests targeted another account's IDs sent in the request body, the topic of a separate article.

An audit test passes when the flaw exists

Usually a green test means the code works. I have written before that a green test only proves what it actually checks. In an audit, I make it check the dangerous behavior on purpose.

Each test describes the flaw as if it were the expected behavior. For example, "with a wrong token, the API returns the profile". If the test passes, the flaw is real. If it fails, the flaw was not reproduced under these conditions. Check the fixtures, configuration and actual response before drawing a conclusion.

That is the big difference with a paragraph. A paragraph can be wrong and nobody notices. A test makes the evidence reproducible. Tests can be wrong too, so review their assertions.

The example: "forgot password" answers 200 or 422

Take the "forgot password" route. You send an email address, and the API sends a link to change the password. Nothing could be more ordinary.

In this API, the response depended on the address. A registered address got a 200 status code, which means "OK". An unknown address got a 422, which means "request rejected".

That difference is enough for account enumeration. Someone tries a list of addresses and keeps the ones that answer 200. They now know who has an account, without any password.

And the route had no explicit rate limit. Nothing slowed down mass attempts.

Here is the audit test, simplified for this article. The API was written in PHP with Laravel, but the idea works in any language.

// Audit test: green means the flaw exists.
public function test_forgot_password_reveals_which_emails_exist(): void
{
    User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(200);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(422);
}

The test creates a fake account, then sends two requests. It passes if the two status codes differ. Green means the flaw exists.

This is not a rare case. In 2026, several CVEs describe exactly the same flaw. Here are two, checked in the official registry.

  • CVE-2026-24468, in the open source project OpenAEV. The /api/reset route answered 400 for an unknown email and 200 for a valid one. It is fixed in version 2.0.13.
  • CVE-2026-58503, in the Frappe web framework. The enumeration went through the reset_password route. It is fixed in versions 15.106.0 and 16.16.0.

Everything happens far from production

An audit must not cause the incident it is looking for. So no test touched production. Not a single request went to it.

The tests ran in a temporary Docker environment. That environment had no access to the outside network. Even a mistake in a test could not reach a real server.

The database was an isolated MySQL test database. The accounts and records were synthetic. Synthetic means made up for the test. No real person is behind them.

During the audit, I did not change the project's code. The proof tests were not added to its repository.

This setup has one more benefit. Anyone on the team can replay the tests, with no production access and no real data.

The report says what the tests do not prove

A test proves one precise thing, and nothing else. The report has to say so. That is where paragraphs really earn their place.

Take the "verify email" route. For an active account, it returned the profile with any non-empty token. That profile also held the account's internal ID.

Combined with "forgot password", this made a chain. You test addresses, then you collect the IDs of the accounts you found. Yet the report states the limit. It works one address at a time, from a guessed list. The audit found no route that hands out every account at once.

The report also splits two lists. On one side, flaws confirmed by a test. On the other, leads seen in the code but not tested. A lead stays a lead until a test confirms it.

Finally, the tests cover the local code, not the deployed application. And the project already had a test checking that one account was denied access to another's data. It passed too. Its green said nothing about the routes my tests targeted.

Once the flaw is fixed, the test flips

The cycle has four steps: reproduce the flaw, fix the code, see the proof fail, then write the protective test.

Green proves the flaw, then the same test keeps it closed. During the audit, the test passes as long as the route answers 200 or 422 depending on the address. After the fix, it expects the same answer for both.

A green audit test is an alarm. It should not stay green. After the fix, it fails, and that is the signal you want.

You then rewrite it the other way around. It becomes a regression test that replays the same request on every code change. For "forgot password", both addresses must receive the expected generic response. Two identical errors are not enough.

// Regression test: green means the flaw stays closed.
public function test_forgot_password_answers_the_same_for_every_email(): void
{
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::fake();
    $user = User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $known = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test']);
    $unknown = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test']);

    // This example's API contract is 200 with this exact generic response.
    $expected = ['message' => 'If the account exists, a reset link will be sent.'];
    $known->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    $unknown->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertSentTo(
        $user, \Illuminate\Auth\Notifications\ResetPassword::class
    );
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertCount(1);
}

This example uses Laravel’s standard notification, intercepted by Notification::fake(). Adapt the status, message and notification to your API. This test does not measure response time. OWASP also asks for a constant response time. Otherwise the delay gives the address away. The rate limit deserves its own test too.

I did this flip on the "verify email" route. After the fix, I added a test that sends a wrong token. It expects a 422 rejection, with no profile data in the response. A second test checks that an unknown account gets the same error.

Why a test beats a paragraph

A report gets read once. A test lives in CI and runs again on every change. It keeps working after the auditor has left.

The test establishes the observed behavior. Severity still depends on the exposed data, required permissions and deployed configuration.

Finally, it sets the expected result without dictating the fix. The team chooses how to fix it. The test only says when it is done.

The checklist

In an audit, every confirmed flaw gets its test. Once the flaw is fixed, that test flips and stays in CI.

  • [ ] Write each suspected flaw as a test that passes if the flaw exists
  • [ ] Run the tests on an isolated test database, never on production
  • [ ] Use only made-up accounts and data
  • [ ] Cut network access from the test environment
  • [ ] Keep flaws confirmed by a test apart from leads seen in the code
  • [ ] Write in the report what each test does not prove
  • [ ] On "forgot password", compare the status code and message for a known and an unknown email
  • [ ] Test response time and rate limiting separately
  • [ ] After the fix, flip each test and keep it in CI

The takeaway

In an audit, green changes meaning. It no longer says "it works". It says "the flaw is here, and here is how to replay it".

Then the same test switches sides. Flipped, it keeps the flaw closed, long after the audit.

Want an audit that delivers proof your team can replay? See my audit and hardening offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Laravel, testing notifications · CVE-2026-24468 (OpenAEV) · OpenAEV, advisory GHSA-v6rg-hf9w-f8ph · CVE-2026-58503 (Frappe) · OWASP, Forgot Password Cheat Sheet · OWASP WSTG, testing for account enumeration · CWE-204, Observable Response Discrepancy

title: Which post-quantum key exchanges does a server actually support?
description:
Every post-quantum migration starts with the same question: does this server support a post-quantum key exchange yet? It sounds like a yes or no. It isn't, because the honest answer depends on which client is asking.

I built pqc-probe to answer it from real handshakes instead of configuration files or advertised lists. It connects to a server over TLS and SSH, tries each key exchange one at a time, and reports which ones actually complete. Version 0.1.0 is out this week as a CLI, a web service, a Docker image and a GitHub Action.

This post covers what the tool measures, how to read its output, and what it found across the 1,000 most popular sites. Later posts in the series go deeper into the surprises along the way.

Offered is not negotiated

A TLS client sends a list of key exchange groups it can use, and the server picks one. A normal connection tells you only which group won, not which others the server would have accepted. So pqc-probe offers one group at a time and records whether the handshake completes:

openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -4

If that handshake succeeds, the server supports X25519MLKEM768. If it fails, the server does not, whatever any configuration page claims. The probe repeats this for seven groups: four classical (X25519, P-256, P-384, P-521) and three ML-KEM hybrids (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024).

SSH needs a different trick. The server sends its full list of key exchange algorithms before any encryption starts, so pqc-probe reads that packet directly. Then, for each post-quantum algorithm both sides know, it runs a real key exchange and marks the row ok (tested) only when the exchange completes. Being on the server's list is not enough.

Two clients, one diff

Which client asks matters, so pqc-probe asks with two:

Mode TLS client SSH client Answers
vanilla stock OpenSSL 3.5 stock OpenSSH What a normal production client gets today
experimental OpenSSL + oqs-provider OQS-OpenSSH What the Open Quantum Safe algorithms unlock

--mode both runs the two side by side and prints a diff. A group that only the experimental client can negotiate means the server supports something your users' clients cannot use yet. A group both can negotiate is deployable today.

There is one catch, and the tool flags it. OpenSSL 3.5 already supports ML-KEM hybrids out of the box. When the stock client is itself post-quantum capable, an empty diff says little about the server, so the report adds a note saying exactly that.

Reading a real report: github.com

Here is GitHub, probed from the Docker image with both protocols and both client stacks (trimmed):

$ docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
    pqc-probe probe github.com --protocol both --mode both

TLS KEMs (vanilla  vs  experimental):
  offered                   vanilla           experimental
  X25519                    ok                ok
  P-256                     ok                ok
  P-384                     -                 -
  P-521                     -                 -
  X25519MLKEM768            -                 -
  SecP256r1MLKEM768         -                 -
  SecP384r1MLKEM1024        -                 -

SSH KEX (server offer × client support):
  server offers                         mainline ssh      OQS-OpenSSH
  mlkem768x25519-sha256                 ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512                ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com    ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  curve25519-sha256                     ok                ok
  ...

SSH diff:
  Mainline ssh and OQS-OpenSSH negotiate identically on this target.

Two services on the same domain give opposite answers:

  • TLS (port 443): only X25519 and P-256 complete. The stock OpenSSL 3.5.7 offered ML-KEM, and GitHub's front end declined it. At the time of this run, a browser connecting to github.com got a classical key exchange.
  • SSH (port 22): three post-quantum key exchanges complete with both clients, so git push over SSH is already post-quantum.

The SSH diff is empty because the image's stock client is OpenSSH 10.0, which already supports these algorithms. The same probe from an older laptop with OpenSSH 9.6 showed two of them as "only experimental". That is the client changing, not the server.

What the top 1,000 sites do

Tranco list K9YYW, top 1,000, scanned 2026-11-06 with pqc-probe scan · one vantage point, IPv4 only · data and method in results/ in the repository]

Among the most popular sites that answer over TLS 1.3, post-quantum key exchange is already the majority. Read "accepts" strictly: the handshake completes when X25519MLKEM768 is offered alone, which shows support, not that the server prefers it.

The 305 sites without a handshake say nothing about post-quantum support either way: most are list entries with no DNS answer or no web server on port 443. The full dataset, the retry passes and the charts are in results/.

Three things that surprised me

  1. The SSH debug log cut the server's offer in half. My first version read the server's algorithm list from ssh -vv. On a test server with a long list, the line simply stopped mid-name: OpenSSH truncates debug lines at about 1 KB. Reading the key exchange packet directly fixed it.
  2. Testing too fast produced false negatives. OpenSSH 9.8 and later penalise addresses that open many short connections (PerSourcePenalties). My test server's log showed a 16-second penalty kicking in, after which real support looked like failure. The probe now tests at most 8 algorithms, one per second.
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum. OpenSSL 3.5 and OpenSSH 10 ship ML-KEM by default, so the classic "vanilla versus experimental" comparison is shrinking. Where it still shows a gap, the gap is usually an old client, not the server.

Each of these gets its own post in this series.

Try it

The Docker image carries both client stacks, so it is the quickest start:

docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
  pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both --mode both

With Rust 1.89 or later, the CLI installs from crates.io and uses the openssl and ssh already on your machine:

cargo install pqc-probe
pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both

Static Linux binaries are on the GitHub release page.

To check your own hosts on every deploy, the GitHub Action keeps a JSON report per host and can fail the job when a host has no post-quantum key exchange:

- uses: asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe@v0.1.0
  with:
    targets: api.example.com, git.example.com:2222
    require-pq-ssh: "true"

Every report follows a published JSON schema, which only ever gains fields within a version, so you can build on it. Please probe hosts you are responsible for.

What's next

The rest of this series:

  1. Your SSH debug log is truncating the server's offer
  2. Probing SSH without getting penalised
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum
  4. Shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way (#210, #211)
  5. Running a scanner for strangers: SSRF, DNS rebinding and rate limits

pqc-probe is the first project of three. pqc-bench measures what post-quantum TLS costs in performance, and a migration dashboard built on pqc-probe's reports comes next.

The code is on GitHub under MIT or Apache-2.0. Issues and results from your own servers are very welcome.

title: Three States for Async Product Image Jobs: Accepted, Downloaded, Approved
description:
AI-generated tutorial from CartVisual, based on the cited vendor documentation. The job states below are an illustrative integration design.

An image-edit job can be accepted before the edited file exists. In a catalog pipeline, confusing those events can cause two problems: a duplicate paid request when polling is slow, or a broken SKU image when a status URL ends up in the asset table.

Keep the job receipt separate from the asset

Store the provider job ID and the immutable source revision together as soon as the API acknowledges the request. Keep the lookup URL in the task record. Claid’s async image-editing documentation, for example, distinguishes the task lookup from the completed result’s output object. If the response does not include a lookup URL, the documented route also accepts the task ID.

Make the merchant approval a distinct transition

Transition Required evidence
Submitted to accepted A provider job ID that can be looked up
Accepted to downloaded A completed response and a file your worker actually read
Downloaded to approved A check against the SKU, dimensions and source reference

If polling times out after acceptance, keep the receipt and reconcile that job. A local timeout does not tell you that the provider stopped. If the download fails after completion, retry the download according to the provider’s documented access and expiry rules. Both paths avoid submitting another generation merely to recover a file.

A useful test for your worker

Create a fake status response pointing to a fake task lookup. Assert that the worker never writes that URL into the product’s live image field. Then feed it a completed response with a fixture file and confirm that the file reaches a review state. You can test both branches with local fixtures and without making a paid provider request.

For a worked Claid example and the documented field names, see CartVisual’s async image handoff guide and the official Claid async API reference.

title: Fix Go Goroutine Leaks & Scale ClickHouse Monoliths
description:
💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

At 02:30 AM, production metrics on our modular monolith system suddenly spiked. The memory consumption graph in our monitoring dashboard showed an unrelenting upward linear curve, culminating in pod crashes driven by the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer. The root cause was not a traditional heap memory leak, but rather the accumulation of thousands of hanging Go goroutines caused by unhandled context cancellation within analytical background workers processing millions of daily telemetry rows.

At the enterprise level, when telemetry data volume hits hundreds of millions of rows per day, row-oriented storage architectures like PostgreSQL hit severe physical bottlenecks. Even with advanced optimizations, query aggregation latencies remained unacceptable before we adopted BRIN indexes in PostgreSQL. However, for high-volume real-time analytics, that approach alone falls short. We needed a fundamental shift in both our storage layer and application concurrency management.

Architectural Dilemma: PostgreSQL vs ClickHouse in Modular Monoliths

Within a modular monolith architecture, isolating analytical modules without falling into the full complexity of microservices is an art of balance. The core challenge lies in executing heavy aggregation queries that trigger massive table scans, holding database connections hostage and triggering client timeouts. When clients disconnect, Go background workers frequently keep running due to the absence of strict context propagation.

Below is a comparative evaluation of enterprise-scale data aggregation performance between traditional PostgreSQL and the ClickHouse columnar engine:

Benchmark Parameter PostgreSQL (Row Store) ClickHouse (Columnar Engine) Performance Lift
100M Rows Aggregation 4.82 Seconds 0.08 Seconds ~60x Faster
Peak RAM Consumption 14.2 GB 1.1 GB 92% Memory Saving
p99 Query Latency 3200 ms 45 ms Sub-second Latency
CPU Utilization 98% (Multi-core bottleneck) 35% (Vectorized execution) High Efficiency

The table above demonstrates the absolute operational necessity of transitioning to ClickHouse for high-performance data pipelines.

Goroutine Leak Mitigation Flow & Context Propagation Design

To halt hanging threads or goroutines, every I/O operation and database query must strictly adhere to the context.Context lifecycle. The following diagram illustrates a leak-safe concurrency handling architecture:

flowchart TD
 A[Client Request / API Gateway] -->|HTTP / gRPC Request| B[Go Modular Monolith Router]
 B -->|Context with Timeout & Cancel| C[Worker Pool Manager]
 C -->|Spawn Worker with ctx| D{Worker Execution}
 D -->|Client Disconnect / Timeout| E[Trigger ctx.Done()]
 E -->|Abort Query Instantly| F[ClickHouse Columnar Engine]
 D -->|Success| G[Return Result to Client]
 F -->|Release Connection & Goroutine| H[Zero Memory Leak]

Through this architecture, context cancellations instantly abort query execution at the database level while deterministically reclaiming goroutine memory allocations.

Code Implementation: Leak-Free Goroutine Worker with ClickHouse

Here is a production-ready Go code snippet implementing strict context propagation to prevent goroutine leaks when interacting with the ClickHouse driver:

package telemetry

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    _ "github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-go/v2"
)

type TelemetryWorker struct {
    db *sql.DB
}

func NewTelemetryWorker(db *sql.DB) *TelemetryWorker {
    return &TelemetryWorker{db: db}
}

// FetchAggregatedData performs real-time aggregation with strict context cancellation protection
func (w *TelemetryWorker) FetchAggregatedData(parentCtx context.Context, tenantID string) ([]map[string]interface{}, error) {
    // Define a strict timeout to prevent workers from hanging indefinitely
    ctx, cancel:= context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    query:= `
 SELECT event_date, count(*) as total_events, avg(latency_ms) as avg_latency
 FROM enterprise_telemetry
 WHERE tenant_id =? AND event_date >= today() - 7
 GROUP BY event_date
 ORDER BY event_date DESC
    `

    // Execute query bounded by the request lifecycle context
    rows, err:= w.db.QueryContext(ctx, query, tenantID)
    if err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to execute ClickHouse query: %w", err)
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var results []map[string]interface{}
    for rows.Next() {
 // Check if context was cancelled midway through large dataset iteration
 if err:= ctx.Err(); err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("operation aborted to prevent goroutine leak: %w", err)
 }

 var eventDate time.Time
 var totalEvents uint64
 var avgLatency float64

 if err:= rows.Scan(&eventDate, &totalEvents, &avgLatency); err!= nil {
 return nil, err
 }

 results = append(results, map[string]interface{}{
 "date": eventDate,
 "total_events": totalEvents,
 "avg_latency": avgLatency,
 })
    }

    if err:= rows.Err(); err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("row iteration error: %w", err)
    }

    return results, nil
}

Within large-scale distributed systems, the underlying infrastructure powering this pipeline plays a critical role. To maintain pod stability and high I/O throughput, deploying services on Hostinger KVM VPS infrastructure provides consistent virtualized compute efficiency. Implementing Traefik v3 API gateway architecture also assists in managing incoming traffic before it hits the Go modular monolith cluster.

Infrastruktur di atas mendukung skalabilitas proses operasional jangka panjang.

Architectural Conclusion

The combination of ClickHouse real-time columnar aggregations and context propagation-driven goroutine management successfully eliminated OOM anomalies in our production environments. By offloading heavy analytical workloads from transactional databases to dedicated columnar engines, our modular monolith systems now seamlessly handle 10x traffic spikes without ballooning infrastructure footprints.

title: The Receiver Should Refuse the Second Copy — Your Retry Loop Never Will.
description:
Yesterday's fix was on the sending side. A slow receiver took 2.5 seconds to answer, the sweeper checked every second, heard silence, and sent the same order three times. The fix was a claim row: one row per delivery key, claimed once, so the second and third ticks had nothing to send. Three deliveries became one.

Then itsvicmoreno asked the question that undoes that fix, politely, in the comments. What if the acknowledgement is lost AFTER the write? The receiver has already taken the order, already charged the card, already sent the email. The sender never hears back, decides the delivery failed, and sends it again. The claim row cannot help you there. The sender did its job, the row says done or it says nothing useful, and a second copy is already on its way. Does the fix live only in the sweeper, or does the receiving end have a say?

I ran that exact case on my own machine. One event, evt-1042, a $29.00 payment confirmation for order ORD-1042. The same event delivered twice, the second send waiting for the first reply, so the second copy arrives after the first write has fully landed. Two receivers, side by side, with the same side effects: a charge line, a confirmation email line, and one stock decrement each time a delivery is accepted. The only difference is that one of them keeps a table of keys it has already processed, and checks it before doing anything else.

My claim is simple, and I expect some of you to disagree with it. A smarter retry loop will never be enough. The receiver has to be able to say no to the second copy, because the receiver is the last place where a duplicate can still be stopped before it becomes a second charge.

Problem 1: the plain inbox charged twice for one order

The plain receiver has no duplicate check at all. Every delivery it accepts is a real delivery, as far as it knows. Here is what two copies of evt-1042 did to it:

Plain inbox Receiver with a processed-keys table
Deliveries received 2 2 (1 accepted, 1 refused)
Charges 2, $29.00 twice, $58.00 in total 1, $29.00
Confirmation emails 2 1
Stock decrements 2, stock 10 down to 8 1, stock 10 down to 9
Second copy's reply 200, processed 200, duplicate, refused

Both runs gave the same numbers, twice each, at 00:07:04 and 00:07:08 for the plain receiver, 00:07:06 and 00:07:11 for the one with the table. The plain receiver logged two deliveries for one order, charged $58.00 for a $29.00 order, sent the customer the same confirmation twice, and took two items out of stock for one sale. Nothing about the second copy looked wrong when it arrived. It had the same key, the same order, the same amount, and it arrived after a perfectly normal gap. A receiver that cannot recognise a key it has already seen has no way to know it has been paid twice.

That is the shape of the bug itsvicmoreno pointed at. The sender-side claim is a good fix for the slow case, and I am not taking that back. But the lost-acknowledgement case walks straight past it. The sender believes the first delivery failed. From the sender's side, resending is the correct, careful thing to do. The duplicate is not a mistake in the retry logic. It is the retry logic working as designed, on wrong information.

Problem 2: the table works, and the order of the two steps is the whole trick

The second receiver keeps a small table, one row per delivery key. When a delivery arrives, it checks the table first. If the key is already there, it refuses the copy before any side effect runs, and still answers 200, so the sender stops retrying. If the key is new, it writes the key into the table first, and only then charges, emails, and decrements stock.

The reply matters as much as the refusal. The second copy got {"status":"duplicate","refused":true} with a 200 behind it. A refused copy that answers with an error would look like another failed delivery, and the sender would send it a third time, then a fourth. A refusal has to sound like success to the sender, because from the sender's point of view the order did go through. It went through the first time.

And the order of the two steps inside the receiver is the whole trick. Key first, then side effects. If you charge first and write the key second, there is a gap between the two, and a crash in that gap leaves a charge with no record of it. The next copy arrives, the table says it is new, and the customer is charged again. Writing the key first closes that gap in one direction: a crash after the write leaves a recorded key with no charge, which is a missing charge you can reconcile, not a double charge you have to refund. One of those is a bookkeeping problem. The other is a customer with two charges on their statement.

The check itself is small. In the receiver, before anything else happens:

if (keys.includes(evt.delivery_key)) {
  // refuse: already processed, no side effects
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'duplicate', refused: true }));
  return;
}
// record the key FIRST, then charge, email, decrement stock
writeKeys([...keys, evt.delivery_key]);

That is the entire defence. A lookup, a refusal, and a write that happens before the money moves.

Problem 3: the table does not remove the duplicate, only its cost

Be honest about what the table buys you. The second copy still arrives. It still costs a delivery, a lookup, and a reply. On a bad day, when every acknowledgement is being lost, the table does not reduce the traffic at all. It reduces the damage the traffic can do. Two copies still cross the wire. Only one of them touches money, email, or stock.

That is a narrower win than the headline version, and it is worth saying plainly, because it decides where this fix belongs. The table is not a replacement for the sender-side claim. It is the second layer, the one that catches the copy the claim could not stop. The claim stops the sweeper resending a delivery that is still in flight. The table stops the receiver acting on a delivery that already landed. You need both, because they guard different moments, and the lost-acknowledgement case is the one that slips between them.

Problem 4: the honest limits of this test

Three limits, because the test was small. First, my two copies arrived one after the other, in order, never at the same instant. Two copies landing at the exact same moment, both checking the table before either has written, were not tested, and a race like that is exactly where a simple lookup breaks. A real table wants the check and the write to happen as one step, not two, and I did not test that step.

Second, the crash window I described above, between writing the key and running the side effects, was not tested either. I know the order matters. I did not prove what happens when the receiver dies inside it. A real table wants the key write and the side effects in one transaction, or a reconciliation pass that finds recorded keys with no charge. My test had neither.

Third, I reset the table before each run. Whether the keys survive a receiver restart, and for how long they should be kept before they are cleared, are both open questions my test does not answer. A table that forgets is a table that charges twice, just later.

So the claim stands, narrowed to what the numbers support. The sender-side claim fixed the slow receiver. It does not fix the lost acknowledgement, because in that case the sender is right to resend. The receiver-side table does fix it: the second evt-1042 was refused, one charge instead of two, one email instead of two, stock 9 instead of 8. The fix belongs at the receiving end, in a table checked before the money moves, with the key written before the side effects run.

If you run webhooks, you have met this one. What did your duplicate cost you, a double charge, a double email, a customer asking why they got two copies of the same thing? And what caught it in the end, a table like this one, a claim on the sending side, or something else entirely?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Decoupling HTTP Clients in Vue 3: Extracting API Modules and Converting PendingSubmissionsPill to TypeScript
description:
A common anti-pattern in frontend development is calling HTTP client libraries (like axios or native fetch) directly inside Vue UI components. When components perform raw network calls, testing becomes cumbersome, endpoints cannot be reused, and frontend code is coupled to specific networking libraries.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3201, closing Issue #880), I migrated the PendingSubmissionsPill navigation component to TypeScript and extracted its API interactions into a dedicated, typed client module.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of decoupling HTTP interactions from components and testing them cleanly in Vitest.

1. The Anti-Pattern: Direct Axios Calls Inside Components

In the navigation bar, PendingSubmissionsPill.vue displays a badge showing how many community submissions (blog posts, talks, events) are pending reviewer approval.

Previously, the component called axios directly:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
import axios from 'axios';
import { ref } from 'vue';

const count = ref(0);

const fetchCount = async () => {
  try {
    const { data } = await axios.get('/api/v1/submissions/count');
    count.value = data.count;
  } catch {
    error.value = true;
  }
};
</script>

Why this is problematic:

  1. Coupling: The UI component is tightly coupled to Axios. Migrating to another client or adding global interceptors requires touching multiple Vue SFCs.
  2. Brittle Mocking: Unit tests had to mock global axios.get calls using URLs as magic strings ('/api/v1/submissions/count'), making tests fragile when endpoints evolve.
  3. No Contract Validation: Response data was untyped, leaving data.count unchecked by the compiler.

2. Step 1: Extracting a Typed API Service Layer

We created a dedicated client module in ~/api/submissions.ts, leveraging generated OpenAPI response types:

// app/javascript/api/submissions.ts
import axios from 'axios';
import type { GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse } from '~/api/generated';

export async function fetchSubmissionsCount(): Promise<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse> {
  const { data } = await axios.get<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse>(
    '/api/v1/submissions/count'
  );

  return data;
}

We accompanied this with an isolated unit test in api/submissions.spec.ts:

import axios from 'axios';
import { PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE } from '~/spec/mockFactories';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from './submissions';

describe('fetchSubmissionsCount', () => {
  it('gets and returns data from the submissions count endpoint', async () => {
    const get = vi.spyOn(axios, 'get').mockResolvedValue(PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE);

    const result = await fetchSubmissionsCount();

    expect(get).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/api/v1/submissions/count');
    expect(result).toBe(PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE.data);
  });
});

3. Step 2: Refactoring the Vue Component

With the network layer isolated, PendingSubmissionsPill.vue became a pure presentation component focused exclusively on UI state and browser lifecycle events:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BBadge, BNavItem } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import { computed, onMounted, onUnmounted, ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from '~/api/submissions';
import { useSubmissionsRefresh } from '~/common/useSubmissionsRefresh';
import { useVueData } from '~/common/useVueData';

const { pendingSubmissionsCount } = useVueData();
const count = ref(pendingSubmissionsCount);
const error = ref(false);

const fetchCount = async () => {
  try {
    const data = await fetchSubmissionsCount();
    count.value = data.count;
    error.value = false;
  } catch {
    error.value = true;
  }
};

// Re-fetch when user switches back to the tab
const onVisibilityChange = () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'visible') {
    void fetchCount();
  }
};

onMounted(() => {
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', onVisibilityChange);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  document.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', onVisibilityChange);
});
</script>

Notice void fetchCount();: explicitly voiding the floating promise in event handlers keeps @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises satisfied.

4. Cleaner, High-Level Testing in Vitest

Because axios is no longer imported by the component, PendingSubmissionsPill.spec.ts mocks the domain function fetchSubmissionsCount directly using vi.mocked():

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { flushPromises, shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from '~/api/submissions';
import { useSubmissionsRefresh } from '~/common/useSubmissionsRefresh';
import { createAxiosError, createVueData } from '~/spec/mockFactories';
import PendingSubmissionsPill from './PendingSubmissionsPill.vue';

vi.mock('~/api/submissions');

describe('when tab becomes visible again', () => {
  it('refetches the latest count', async () => {
    createWrapper(3);
    vi.mocked(fetchSubmissionsCount).mockResolvedValue({ count: 7 });

    // Trigger window visibility event
    document.dispatchEvent(new Event('visibilitychange'));
    await flushPromises();

    expect(fetchSubmissionsCount).toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('7');
  });
});

Tests are no longer concerned with HTTP verbs or URLs—they verify application behavior and user outcomes directly.

Key Takeaways

  1. Extract Network Calls to API Services: Never call axios.get directly in Vue components. Keep components focused on rendering and UI state.
  2. Type API Responses with OpenAPI Contracts: Typing service functions with generated contracts (Promise<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse>) prevents subtle property mismatches.
  3. Mock Domain Functions, Not HTTP Clients: Mocking fetchSubmissionsCount() rather than axios.get('/api/...') makes unit tests clearer, more resilient, and easier to maintain.

title: Aligning Vue 3 Components with OpenAPI Types: Converting CurrentYearTable to TypeScript
description:
In full-stack web applications, frontend models can easily drift out of sync with backend APIs when types are manually redefined or left untyped. By integrating OpenAPI schema generators into the build pipeline, client applications can consume authoritative backend models directly in their Vue components.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3218, closing Issue #868), I converted the CurrentYearTable leaderboard component to TypeScript.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we typed props using generated OpenAPI contracts, applied the withDefaults macro, and constructed tests using model factories.

1. The Challenge: Generic Array Props

In the original implementation, CurrentYearTable.vue received leaderboard records using generic JavaScript options:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
import { computed } from 'vue';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
  fromDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
  toDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

While functional, type: Array gave zero insight into what properties a contributor record contained (such as user handles, merged MR counts, or bonus points). If the backend API renamed or removed a property, the frontend would fail silently at runtime.

2. Deriving Prop Types from OpenAPI Specs

Rather than hand-crafting a duplicate Contributor interface that could drift over time, the project generates TypeScript contracts directly from openapi.yaml.

In CurrentYearTable.vue, we imported GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse and indexed its records:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse } from '~/api/generated';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = withDefaults(defineProps<{
  contributors: GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'];
  fromDate?: string;
  toDate?: string;
}>(), {
  fromDate: '',
  toDate: '',
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

<template>
  <ContributorsTable
    :contributors="contributors"
    :filter-data="filterData"
  />
</template>

Why this is a best practice:

  1. Single Source of Truth: The TypeScript type GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'] is generated directly from the backend Rails API definition. If an API contract changes, vue-tsc immediately flags any breaking changes across all views.
  2. withDefaults Macro: Provides idiomatic default values for optional string props (fromDate?: string, toDate?: string) without runtime object overhead.

3. Writing Resilient Specs with Model Factories (ADR 005)

Per the project's architectural guidelines (ADR 005: Model Factories in Specs), test fixtures should not be hard-coded object literals with incomplete shapes. Instead, tests use factory functions that populate complete, valid schema defaults.

In CurrentYearTable.spec.ts:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';
import { createLeaderboardContributor } from '~/spec/factories/leaderboard';
import CurrentYearTable from './CurrentYearTable.vue';

// Factory generates a valid, complete OpenAPI leaderboard record
const mockContributor = createLeaderboardContributor();

let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = shallowMount(CurrentYearTable, {
    props: {
      contributors: [mockContributor],
      ...props,
    },
  });
};

const findContributorsTable = () => wrapper.findComponent(ContributorsTable);

it('renders ContributorsTable with contributors and default filterData', () => {
  createWrapper();

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('contributors')).toEqual([mockContributor]);
  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '',
    toDate: '',
  });
});

it('renders ContributorsTable with custom fromDate and toDate in filterData', () => {
  createWrapper({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });
});

Using createLeaderboardContributor() ensures that our test mocks strictly adhere to the OpenAPI schema without breaking when new fields are introduced.

Key Takeaways

  1. Leverage Generated API Types: Import types directly from OpenAPI or GraphQL code-generators (Response['key']) to eliminate manual duplication and catch breaking API updates.
  2. Use withDefaults(defineProps<{ ... }>(), { ... }): The standard Vue 3 pattern for combining compile-time type definitions with default prop values.
  3. Adopt Model Factories in Tests: Test helpers like createLeaderboardContributor() ensure test mocks always reflect production API contracts.
