title: The path to AI FDE #17: Lists and dictionaries: holding many values
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Yesterday you wrapped code in functions. Today you learn to hold many values at once, instead of one variable per value.

Python has two containers you’ll use every day. A list keeps things in order, like a numbered queue. A dictionary keeps things by name, like a form with labelled boxes. Put them together, a list of dictionaries, and you get the exact shape of most data that AI tools send and receive. By the end you’ll have a small script that sums up a made-up playlist.

Part A · Lists

1. A list keeps items in order, and counts from 0. Make a list with square brackets and commas. Save this as lists.py in your sandbox folder:

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[2])
print(fruits[-1])
print(len(fruits))

Run it with python3 lists.py (Windows: python lists.py):

apple
cherry
cherry
3

Each item has a position number called an index, and Python starts counting at 0. So fruits[0] is the first item and fruits[2] is the third. A negative index counts from the end: fruits[-1] is always the last item. len() tells you how many items there are.

Because counting starts at 0, the last index is one less than the length. Ask for fruits[3] and you get:

IndexError: list index out of range

That “one too far” slip is called an off-by-one error. It’s the most common list mistake there is.

2. Add, count, slice and sort. Lists can grow and change. Try this:

scores = [7, 3, 9]
scores.append(5)
print(scores)
print(len(scores))
print(scores[1:3])
print(scores[:2])
print(sorted(scores))
print(scores)
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)

[7, 3, 9, 5]
4
[3, 9]
[7, 3]
[3, 5, 7, 9]
[7, 3, 9, 5]
[9, 7, 5, 3]

Line by line:

  • .append(5) adds one item to the end.
  • Slicing, scores[1:3], gives a new list from index 1 up to but not including index 3. Leave out the first number and it starts at the beginning, so scores[:2] is the first two items.
  • sorted(scores) gives back a new sorted list and leaves the original alone, which is why the next line still prints [7, 3, 9, 5].
  • .sort() sorts the list itself. reverse=True (a keyword argument, from yesterday) sorts from biggest to smallest.

One trap: .sort() changes the list and returns None. So result = scores.sort() leaves result as None. If you want a sorted copy, use sorted().

Part B · Dictionaries and friends

3. A dictionary stores values under names, called keys. Use curly braces, with a key, a colon, and a value for each entry:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book["title"])
book["pages"] = 320
book["year"] = 2020
print(book)
print(len(book))

Moon Garden
{'title': 'Moon Garden', 'author': 'A. Rao', 'year': 2020, 'pages': 320}
4

You look a value up by its key, not by position: book["title"]. Assigning to a new key, book["pages"] = 320, adds an entry. Assigning to a key that already exists replaces its value, because each key appears only once. And the dictionary remembers the order you added the keys.

Ask for a key that isn’t there and Python stops with:

KeyError: 'rating'

A list is for “the third one”. A dictionary is for “the one called title”.

4. Read safely with .get(), and loop with .items(). When a key might be missing, use .get() instead of square brackets:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book.get("rating"))
print(book.get("rating", "no rating yet"))
print("year" in book)
for key, value in book.items():
    print(key, "->", value)

None
no rating yet
True
title -> Moon Garden
author -> A. Rao
year -> 2019

.get("rating") gives None for a missing key instead of crashing, and .get("rating", "no rating yet") gives the fallback you choose. in checks whether a key exists. .items() hands you each key and value as a pair, so a for loop can unpack both at once.

A simple rule: use square brackets when the key must be there (a crash tells you something is wrong), and .get() when it might be missing.

5. Tuples are fixed, and sets drop duplicates. Two more containers, each with one special trick:

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
tags = {"sci-fi", "classic", "sci-fi"}
print(len(tags))
print("classic" in tags)
print(sorted(set(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])))

3 4
2
True
['a', 'b', 'c']

A tuple uses round brackets. It’s like a list you can’t change after it’s made, which suits values that belong together, such as a point’s x and y. x, y = point unpacks it into two names. Try point[0] = 10 and you get TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.

A set uses curly braces without colons. It keeps each value only once, so the repeated “sci-fi” counts once and len(tags) is 2. That makes sets great for “which different values are there?” Sets have no order, so there’s no tags[0]; use sorted() when you want to show them in order. One gotcha: {} on its own makes an empty dictionary, so an empty set is set().

6. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON. Put dictionaries inside a list and you can hold a whole table of records:

import json

books = [
    {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019},
    {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023},
]
print(books[1]["title"])
for b in books:
    print(b["title"], b["year"])
print(json.dumps(books))

Paper Boats
Moon Garden 2019
Paper Boats 2023
[{"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}, {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023}]

Read books[1]["title"] from left to right: position 1 in the list, then the key “title” in that dictionary. The for loop visits each record in turn.

The last line uses Python’s built-in json module (you’ll learn how import works in issue #20). json.dumps() turns the data into JSON text, the format web APIs, and the AI tools later in this series, send and receive. It looks almost the same as Python. The differences: JSON always uses double quotes, True becomes true, and None becomes null. Tomorrow you’ll read and write JSON files.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create playlist.py, a made-up playlist as a list of dictionaries: 
playlist = [
    {"title": "Morning Run", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 4},
    {"title": "Rainy Bus", "artist": "Paper Cups", "minutes": 6},
    {"title": "Late Tea", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 3},
]

total = 0
titles = []
artists = set()
for song in playlist:
    total = total + song["minutes"]
    titles.append(song["title"])
    artists.add(song["artist"])

print("Songs:", len(playlist))
print("Total minutes:", total)
print(sorted(titles))
print(len(artists), "artists")
print(playlist[0].get("year", "unknown"))
  1. Run python3 playlist.py. You should see: 
Songs: 3
Total minutes: 13
['Late Tea', 'Morning Run', 'Rainy Bus']
2 artists
unknown

“The Toys” appears twice, but the set keeps it once, so there are 2 artists. None of the songs has a "year" key, so .get() gives the fallback.

  1. Change the last line to print(playlist[0]["year"]). Read the last line of the error: KeyError: 'year'. Change it back.
  2. Add print(playlist[3]). You get IndexError: list index out of range: three songs means indexes 0, 1 and 2. Remove the line.
  3. Find the longest song with a loop. Start with longest = playlist[0], then for each song, if song["minutes"] > longest["minutes"], set longest = song. Print longest["title"]. You should get Rainy Bus.

Check your understanding: (a) In ["a", "b", "c"], what’s the index of "c"? (b) What’s the difference between book["rating"] and book.get("rating") when there’s no rating? (c) What does sorted() do that .sort() doesn’t?

Answer: (a) 2, because counting starts at 0 (or -1, counting from the end). (b) Square brackets raise KeyError; .get() returns None (or the fallback you give it). (c) sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone; .sort() changes the list itself and returns None.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Off-by-one: using len(x) as an index. The last item is x[len(x) - 1], or just x[-1].
  • Expecting a slice to include the end: x[1:3] stops before index 3.
  • KeyError from square brackets on a key that might be missing. Use .get(), or check with in first.
  • Writing x = x.sort(), which leaves x as None.
  • Writing {} for an empty set. That’s an empty dictionary; use set().

Takeaway

A list keeps items in order and counts from 0. .append(), len(), slicing and sorted() cover most of what you’ll do with one. A dictionary stores values under unique keys: square brackets when the key must exist, .get() when it might not, .items() to loop. Tuples are fixed and sets keep each value once. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Almost every AI tool I’ll call takes a list of dictionaries in and hands a dictionary back, so reading data[0]["text"] without thinking is a skill worth drilling now. Tomorrow: strings, files and JSON, so that data can come from a file and go back to one.

Over to you: think of something you track, such as books, runs or recipes. Reply with one record as a Python dictionary, like {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}.

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “An Informal Introduction to Python”, Lists (indexing from 0, negative indexes, slicing, len(), .append()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists
  2. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, More on Lists (.append(), .sort(), list methods). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#more-on-lists
  3. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Tuples and Sequences (tuples, unpacking) and Sets (duplicates removed, set() for an empty set). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#tuples-and-sequences
  4. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Dictionaries (keys are unique, insertion order, in, KeyError) and Looping Techniques (.items()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#dictionaries
  5. Python docs, “Built-in Types”, dict.get (returns the default, or None, for a missing key). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict.get
  6. Python HOWTO, “Sorting Techniques” (sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; reverse=True). https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html
  7. Python docs, “json” (json.dumps(), and how Python types map to JSON). https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (IndexError, KeyError, TypeError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up (the books, songs and artists are invented) and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

title: The path to AI FDE #16: Functions: reusable pieces of logic
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Last week your code learned to decide and repeat. Today you learn to name a piece of code and reuse it, so you write it once and call it whenever you need it.

That named piece of code is a function. You’ve already used other people’s functions: print(), len(), type(). Today you write your own. By the end you’ll have a small script that shares pizzas fairly between friends, built from two tiny functions.

Part A · Building a function

1. def defines a function; calling it runs it. Save this as greet.py in your sandbox folder:

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Asha")
greet("Ben")

Run it with python3 greet.py (Windows: python greet.py):

Hello, Asha
Hello, Ben

The first two lines are the definition. def starts it, greet is the function’s name, (name) lists its inputs, and the line ends with a colon. The indented lines under it are the function’s body, just like the blocks in last week’s if and for.

Defining a function doesn’t run it. Python just remembers it under the name greet. The body runs only when you call the function: its name followed by brackets, greet("Asha"). Two calls, two greetings. Python reads your file from top to bottom, so put the def above the first line that calls it.

2. Parameters are the input slots; arguments are the values you put in them. A function can take more than one input:

def area(width, height):
    print(width * height)

area(3, 4)
area(10, 2)

12
20

width and height are the parameters: the names in the definition. 3 and 4 are the arguments: the values you pass when you call it. Python matches them in order, so the first argument goes into the first parameter. Inside the body, width is 3 and height is 4.

Leave one out, with area(3), and Python stops with:

TypeError: area() missing 1 required positional argument: 'height'

The message names the slot you left empty. People mix up the two words all the time, and it rarely matters, but now you know which is which.

3. return sends a result back. Without it, you get None. Our area prints the answer, but the rest of your program can’t use it. Change print to return:

def area(width, height):
    return width * height

total = area(3, 4) + area(10, 2)
print(total)

32

return hands a value back to the line that called the function. You can picture area(3, 4) being replaced by 12, so the line becomes total = 12 + 20. That’s the difference: print shows a value to a human; return gives it to your code.

Forget return, and the function still runs but hands back None (Python’s “no value here” from issue #14):

def double(n):
    n * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)

None

The function worked out 10 and then threw it away. return also ends the function immediately: any lines after it in the same block never run.

Part B · Functions that are easy to use

4. Defaults and keyword arguments let callers skip or name inputs. Give a parameter a default value with = in the definition, and callers can leave it out:

def make_tea(cups, sugar=1, milk=True):
    return f"{cups} cup(s), {sugar} sugar, milk: {milk}"

print(make_tea(2))
print(make_tea(2, sugar=0))
print(make_tea(milk=False, cups=1))

2 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: True
2 cup(s), 0 sugar, milk: True
1 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: False

The first call uses both defaults. The second passes a keyword argument, sugar=0, which sets that one input by name. The third names every input, so the order no longer matters. Names make calls easier to read too: make_tea(2, sugar=0) says more than make_tea(2, 0). One rule: arguments without names come first. make_tea(sugar=0, 2) gives SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument. Later in the series you’ll see the same shape in AI code, such as a function that splits text with a default size=500.

The one trap: never use a list as a default. The default is created once, when Python reads the def, and then shared by every call:

def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item("apple"))
print(add_item("pear"))

['apple']
['apple', 'pear']

The second call “remembers” the apple. (append adds an item to the end of a list; lists get their own issue tomorrow.) The fix is to default to None and make a fresh list inside:

def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

Now the two calls print ['apple'] and ['pear'].

5. Scope: names made inside a function exist only inside it. Each call gets its own private workspace. Names created there disappear when the function ends:

def bake():
    dough = 200
    print("inside:", dough)

bake()
print(dough)

inside: 200
NameError: name 'dough' is not defined

(Python prints a few more lines above the NameError, called a traceback. You’ll learn to read those in issue #19.) The part of a program where a name exists is its scope. dough is a local name: it belongs to bake.

The other direction is softer: a function can read a name defined outside it. With greeting = "Hi" at the top of the file, a function can use greeting. But if a function assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local for the whole function. So this fails:

count = 0

def bump():
    count = count + 1

bump()

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

The clean habit: pass values in as arguments and return results out.

def bump(n):
    return n + 1

count = 0
count = bump(count)
count = bump(count)
print(count)

This prints 2. (Python has a global keyword that lets a function change an outside name. You’ll rarely need it; passing in and returning out is easier to follow.)

6. Give each function one job, and a name that says what it is. Small functions are easier to read, test and reuse. Here, one function does the maths and another builds the sentence:

def to_fahrenheit(c):
    """Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit."""
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

def describe(c):
    f = to_fahrenheit(c)
    return f"{c}°C is {f}°F"

print(describe(100))
print(describe(-40))
print(to_fahrenheit(0) == 32)

100°C is 212.0°F
-40°C is -40.0°F
True

Three habits are packed in here:

  • One job each. to_fahrenheit only converts. describe only words the answer, and it reuses to_fahrenheit instead of repeating the formula.
  • A quick check. to_fahrenheit(0) == 32 prints True, so you know the maths is right. Because the function returns a value instead of printing it, it’s easy to test. That’s where proper tests (lesson 4.6) start.
  • A docstring. The string in triple quotes on the first line of the body says what the function does. Many editors show it when you hover over the name.

Give functions names that say what they do, in snake_case, the Python style guide’s choice for function names: to_fahrenheit, make_tea, add_item. If you can’t name a function without using “and”, it’s probably doing two jobs.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create pizza.py, for sharing made-up pizzas between friends: 
def slices_each(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many whole slices each person gets."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) // people

def leftover(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many slices are left after a fair share."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) % people

print(slices_each(3, 5), leftover(3, 5))
print(slices_each(2, 4, per_pizza=6), leftover(2, 4, per_pizza=6))
print(slices_each(people=7, pizzas=1))
  1. Run python3 pizza.py. You should see: 
4 4
3 0
1

Three pizzas of 8 slices is 24; shared by 5, that’s 4 each with 4 left over. (// and % are whole-number division and remainder, from issue #14.)

  1. Delete the word return in slices_each (keep the maths) and run it again. The first number on each line becomes None. Put it back.
  2. Add print(slices_each(3, 0)) at the end. Read the last line of the error: ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero. You can’t share between nobody. (Handling errors like this properly is issue #19.) Remove the line.
  3. Write a third function, pizzas_needed(people, slices_each=3, per_pizza=8), that returns how many pizzas to order. Hint: -(-a // b) rounds a division up. With 10 people, it should return 4.

Check your understanding: (a) In def area(width, height):, are width and height parameters or arguments? (b) What does a function return if it has no return line? (c) Why did the second add_item("pear") call also show the apple?

Answer: (a) Parameters: the names in the definition. The values you pass in a call are the arguments. (b) None. (c) A list default is created once, when the def runs, and every call shares it. Use None as the default and make a new list inside.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Forgetting return, then wondering why the result is None.
  • Printing inside a function when the caller needs the value. Return it, and print outside.
  • Defining a function and never calling it (no brackets, no run).
  • Using a list or dictionary as a default (def f(x=[])). It’s shared between calls.
  • Trying to change an outside variable from inside a function. Pass it in and return the new value.

Takeaway

def names a block of code, and calling it runs it. Parameters are the input slots, and arguments are the values you put in. return hands a result back; without it you get None. Defaults and keyword arguments make calls short and clear. Names made inside a function stay inside. Keep each function to one job.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Every AI app I build later is a stack of small functions: one to load text, one to call a model, one to check the answer. Tomorrow: lists and dictionaries, the two containers that hold almost all the data you’ll touch.

Over to you: what’s a task you’d turn into a function? Reply with its name and its inputs, like make_tea(cups, sugar=1).

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, Defining Functions (def, the body is indented, a function without return returns None; docstrings). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions
  2. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, More on Defining Functions (default argument values, “the default value is evaluated only once”, keyword arguments, positional arguments before keyword arguments). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#more-on-defining-functions
  3. Python glossary, “parameter” and “argument” (the difference between the two). https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-parameter
  4. Python reference, “Execution model”, Naming and binding (a name assigned inside a function is local to it). https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding
  5. Python FAQ, “Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError when the variable has a value?” and “Why are default values shared between objects?”. https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-am-i-getting-an-unboundlocalerror-when-the-variable-has-a-value
  6. PEP 8, “Style Guide for Python Code” (function names are lowercase, with words separated by underscores). https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#function-and-variable-names
  7. PEP 257, “Docstring Conventions” (what a docstring is; triple double quotes). https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (TypeError, NameError, UnboundLocalError, ZeroDivisionError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

title: I Benchmarked Vexlo Cloud India Singapore and USA Nodes Against Railway ($5 vs $45 a month)
description:
Let us be real for a second. Usage-based cloud pricing sounds cute until your side project gets a tiny traffic spike and Railway or Render hits you with a $60 bill for vCPU seconds and outbound bandwidth.

I wanted to see if a flat-rate PaaS could actually hold up across global regions without throttling containers, so I benchmarked Vexlo Cloud over the weekend.

What I Tested

I deployed a Dockerized Node.js backend, a Next.js frontend, and a managed Redis plus Postgres stack. Here are the raw numbers from the run.

  • Cold GitHub Push to Live HTTPS took 42 seconds using their automated build pipeline.
  • Global Edge Regions include India (Mumbai) at 14ms regional ping, plus dedicated Singapore and USA nodes for international traffic.
  • Monthly Cost stayed locked at ₹149 a month via instant UPI in India, or $5 a month in USD and 16 other global currencies with zero egress overage fees.

The Bill Shock Math

If you want to see the exact price gap for your own stack, play around with the Railway Pricing Calculator and the Render Pricing Calculator they built. Seeing per-seat fees and RAM multipliers side by side makes it pretty obvious why indie devs are moving back to predictable flat-rate containers.

One Click Self Hosted Stacks

Instead of manually writing Traefik labels and SSL configs on a raw Ubuntu VPS, their 1-Click Open Source Templates let you deploy self-hosted tools in under a minute across India, Singapore, or USA servers. I tested Deploy n8n on Vexlo and Deploy Uptime Kuma and both spun up with persistent volumes and valid TLS automatically.

Backups are automated out of the box, the infra team already manages hosting for 1,500+ developers, and you can export your data anytime with zero lock-in. Check out their Developer Docs and Runbooks if you are debugging Docker OOM errors or Indian payment gateway webhooks.

title: Preserving Visual UI Stability with TypeScript Snapshot Testing in Vue 3: The LegacyCategoryLegend Component
description:
During large-scale frontend modernization efforts, teams frequently convert dozens of components from JavaScript to TypeScript. While stateful components require deep assertions on reactive state, mutations, and API calls, pure static presentation components—such as legends, badges, and informational tooltips—serve a different purpose: preserving visual markup and design token consistency.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3195), I converted the LegacyCategoryLegend component to TypeScript and established an automated snapshot test suite using Vitest.

Here is an architectural look at how lightweight snapshot testing protects visual UI elements during progressive migrations.

1. The Component: Historical Contributor Tier Badges

On the Top Annual Contributors leaderboard, the platform honors historical contribution milestones (prior to the current point-based scoring system).

LegacyCategoryLegend.vue displays color-coded badges mapping to historical recognition tiers:

  • SuperStar (Warning badge): More than 75 merged MRs
  • Star (Info badge): Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  • Enthusiast (Secondary badge): Between 5 and 10 merged MRs 
<!-- LegacyCategoryLegend.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BBadge } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
</script>

<template>
  <div class="text-muted small mt-2">
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="warning">SuperStar</BBadge> More than 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="info">Star</BBadge> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span>
      <BBadge variant="secondary">Enthusiast</BBadge> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
    </span>
  </div>
</template>

Adding <script setup lang="ts"> ensures typed integration with bootstrap-vue-next component exports without any runtime overhead.

2. Fast, Deterministic Snapshot Testing with Vitest

For static presentation components without props or reactive state, writing redundant DOM query assertions for every badge text can be unnecessarily verbose.

Instead, a deterministic snapshot test using shallowMount provides 100% coverage while locking down the exact HTML structure and CSS utility classes:

// LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import LegacyCategoryLegend from './LegacyCategoryLegend.vue';

const createWrapper = () =>
  shallowMount(LegacyCategoryLegend, {
    global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true },
  });

it('matches the snapshot', () => {
  expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});

Why this pattern works well:

  • Instant Regression Detection: Any unintentional change to Bootstrap badge variants (warning, info, secondary), spacing classes (me-3, mt-2), or milestone descriptions is immediately flagged by the Vitest snapshot runner.
  • Stub Slot Rendering: Using global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true } ensures that child slot content (like "SuperStar") is preserved inside <b-badge-stub> rather than discarded.
  • Zero Boilerplate: The spec is concise, clean, and runs in milliseconds.

3. Snapshot Output Verification

When executed, Vitest records the rendered template in __snapshots__/LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts.snap:

// Vitest Snapshot v1
exports[`matches the snapshot 1`] = `
"<div class="text-muted small mt-2">
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="warning">SuperStar</b-badge-stub> More than 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="info">Star</b-badge-stub> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span>
    <b-badge-stub variant="secondary">Enthusiast</b-badge-stub> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
  </span>
</div>"
`;

This guarantees visual and structural stability as the underlying UI library upgrades across minor and major versions.

Key Takeaways

  1. Use Snapshot Tests for Pure Presentational UI: When a component has no internal logic or conditional branching, snapshot testing offers high confidence with minimal test maintenance.
  2. Always Enable renderStubDefaultSlot: In Vue Test Utils, shallow mounting child components can hide slot text unless renderStubDefaultSlot: true is configured.
  3. Every Component Counts: Converting even small UI components to TypeScript ensures the whole codebase maintains 100% type coverage without gaps.

title: Let your coding agent ask a QA agent: connect TestOptim over MCP with one sign-in
description:
Your coding agent says the change is done. A QA agent can check that. TestOptim runs AI tests on your web app and logs each failure as an issue with steps to reproduce. Its remote MCP server lets an MCP client list your projects, start test runs and read those issues.

Until now you had to create an API key and paste it into the client config. Since Nov 10 you can sign in with OAuth instead. Here is the full flow, step by step.

What we tested

We ran this flow with the MCP Inspector (v2.15.0, MCP protocol 2025-11-25). Other clients that support OAuth sign-in for remote servers use the same flow, but we did not test them for this post.

1. Add the server with only its URL

  • Transport: Streamable HTTP
  • URL: https://api.testoptim.com/api/mcp
  • No Authorization header.

The server answers the first request with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header that points to its OAuth metadata. The client finds the sign-in page from there and registers itself. You do not enter a client ID.

2. Sign in and approve

The client opens TestOptim in your browser. Sign in, then read the consent page. It names the client and lists what it can do:

  • See your projects
  • Start and stop test runs, and read their results
  • Read the issues TestOptim found
  • Start explorations of your app

Select Allow. Only the Owner or an Admin of the organization can approve.

3. The client connects

The browser returns to the client, and the server shows as connected. The client lists 8 tools: list_projects, start_test_run, get_test_run, stop_test_run, list_issues, get_issue, start_exploration and get_exploration.

4. Ask for results

We called three tools:

  1. list_projects returned our 2 projects.
  2. list_issues on one project returned the open issues, with severity and status.
  3. get_issue returned one issue in full: description, 5 steps to reproduce, expected and actual behaviour, the page URL and a screenshot link.

In a coding agent, the same calls look like this: "Run the QA tests on the checkout project and show me the critical issues." The agent calls start_test_run, waits with get_test_run, then reads the results with list_issues and get_issue. A test run uses your plan's test executions, the same as a run started in the app.

5. Remove access when you are done

Each OAuth connection appears in TestOptim under Settings → API keys, named after the client, for example "MCP Inspector (OAuth)". Disconnecting in the client does not remove it. To stop access, revoke it there.

API keys still work

If your client does not support OAuth sign-in, create an API key under Settings → API keys and send it as Authorization: Bearer topt_.... The setup for each client is in the TestOptim MCP README.

TestOptim plans start at $19 a month after a 7-day free trial that needs a card. testoptim.com

title: Building Type-Safe Multi-Facet Search in Vue 3: Converting LanguageFilter to TypeScript
description:
In community-driven open-source portals like GitLab, developers explore issues based on their technical skills—whether they write Go, Ruby, Vue/TypeScript, or Python. Providing clean, multi-select search facets allows contributors to filter hundreds of opportunities down to the exact technologies they care about.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3198), I converted the LanguageFilter component and its test suite to strict TypeScript.

Here is a look at building type-safe multi-select filters in Vue 3, managing two-way array state, and ensuring robust test coverage.

1. Multi-Select State: Moving Beyond Primitive Models

Single-value inputs (like text boxes or radio buttons) usually bind to string or number. However, multi-select facet filters manage dynamic string arrays (string[]).

Previously, LanguageFilter.vue used generic runtime options:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
defineProps({
  availableLanguages: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
});

const selectedLanguages = defineModel('selectedLanguages', {
  type: Array,
  required: true,
});
</script>

While this validated that the prop was an Array, it did not enforce the element type of the array. Passing an array of numbers, objects, or null values would satisfy runtime validation but cause rendering glitches in the dropdown chips.

2. Compile-Time Type Safety with Vue 3.4 Macros

By converting to <script setup lang="ts">, we typed both the available options and the reactive selection collection:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BFormGroup } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import 'vue-select/dist/vue-select.css';

// Strictly typed array of language names (e.g. ['Ruby', 'Go', 'Vue'])
defineProps<{
  availableLanguages: string[];
}>();

// Strongly typed two-way model binding
const selectedLanguages = defineModel<string[]>('selectedLanguages', {
  required: true,
});
</script>

<template>
  <BFormGroup label="Language">
    <VueSelect
      v-model="selectedLanguages"
      multiple
      :options="availableLanguages"
    >
      <template #no-options="{ search, searching }">
        <template v-if="searching">
          No issues in {{ search }}
        </template>
        <template v-else>
          No languages available
        </template>
      </template>
    </VueSelect>
  </BFormGroup>
</template>

Key Benefits:

  • Element-Level Type Safety: Both availableLanguages and selectedLanguages are guaranteed to be string[]. The compiler flags any attempt to push non-string entities.
  • Named Two-Way Model: defineModel<string[]>('selectedLanguages', { required: true }) creates a contract where the parent must bind v-model:selectedLanguages, automatically typing the event payload for update:selectedLanguages.

3. Strict Event and Slot Testing with Vitest

In LanguageFilter.spec.ts, we eliminated loose typing in test helpers and refined emitted event assertions:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import LanguageFilter from './LanguageFilter.vue';

describe('LanguageFilter', () => {
  const defaultProps = {
    availableLanguages: ['Ruby', 'Go'],
    selectedLanguages: [],
  };

  let wrapper: VueWrapper;
  const createWrapper = (props = {}) =>
    wrapper = shallowMount(LanguageFilter, {
      props: { ...defaultProps, ...props },
      global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true },
    });

  const findSelect = () => wrapper.findComponent(VueSelect);

  // Safe helper to render the child component's custom no-options slot
  const findNoOptions = (slotProps: Record<string, unknown>) =>
    shallowMount({
      render: () => findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps),
    });

  it('emits updated language selection when an option is picked', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findSelect().vm.$emit('update:modelValue', ['Ruby']);

    // Checking exact emit structure: [[['Ruby']]]
    expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')).toEqual([[['Ruby']]]);
  });

  it('renders helpful message when searched language has no issues', () => {
    createWrapper();

    const noOptionsWrapper = findNoOptions({ search: 'Haskell', searching: true });
    expect(noOptionsWrapper.text()).toContain('No issues in Haskell');
  });
});

Notice the event assertion:

expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')).toEqual([[['Ruby']]]);

Rather than asserting wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')[0], matching the entire emitted event array verifies both the payload and the exact call count in a single check.

Key Takeaways

  1. Type Array Elements, Not Just Array: In TypeScript SFCs, always specify string[] or T[] rather than generic Array to prevent bad data downstream.
  2. Harmonize Filter Facet APIs: Keeping filter components uniform (LanguageFilter, ProjectFilter) with consistent named models (selectedLanguages, selectedProjects) makes parent filter bars clean and modular.
  3. Full Event Array Assertions: In Vue Test Utils, asserting against the entire emitted event array (expect(wrapper.emitted('event')).toEqual([[payload]])) guards against unexpected duplicate emissions.

title: I Built an AI Loop That Finds "Lost My Work" Bugs and Fixes Them Until the Test Passes
description:
We've all done it. You fill in a long sign-up form, a job application, or a checkout, press Back or Refresh, and everything you typed is gone. These "lost my work" bugs are everywhere, and unit tests rarely catch them because they only show up in a real browser.

For the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI, I built StillHere: a loop that catches these bugs in a real browser and keeps fixing them until the test passes.

What it does

StillHere runs a closed loop:

  1. Find it. Kane CLI drives a real Chrome session through a journey described in plain English: fill in a checkout, open another page, press Back, press Refresh, and check the cart, details, and current step are still there.
  2. Fix it. If anything is wiped, Kane's failure report becomes a repair prompt for the Codex coding agent, which fixes the app without weakening the test.
  3. Prove it. The exact same Kane objective re-runs, unchanged, until it passes.

It works for any form or multi-step flow via --objective, not just checkout.

How I built it

Node.js with no dependencies. StillHere calls Kane CLI with --agent, parses its NDJSON result, writes a failure report with evidence and screenshots, and pipes a repair prompt to codex exec. A sample shop with a real Back/Refresh bug is included, and npm run demo:loop resets the bug so you always see fail, fix, pass. Built solo with Codex.

What Kane caught

In the recorded run, pressing "Back to checkout" wiped the order: the cart, the customer's details, and the review step were all gone. Codex fixed it by saving state in sessionStorage plus browser history and restoring it on load and Back. Kane then passed through both Back and Refresh. The test was never changed to make it pass.

Challenges

Chrome crashed when launched from a sandbox, so Kane runs from a normal terminal. Long Kane runs timed out, so the default timeout became 300 seconds. I also made sure a run with no final Kane result counts as incomplete, not as a failure for the agent to "fix."

What I learned

Verifying in a real browser catches bugs a mock never would, and keeping the test fixed is what makes an AI fix trustworthy.

What's next

A GitHub Action that runs the loop on every pull request, plus ready-made objectives for sign-up, login, and multi-step forms.

Try it

  • Code and setup: https://github.com/Mzee04/stillhere
  • Demo: https://youtu.be/4R3yvR5oKvg

title: Typing Untyped Vue 3 Libraries and Named defineModel in TypeScript: The ProjectFilter Migration
description:
When converting legacy Vue applications to TypeScript, third-party component libraries often become a stumbling block. Some popular ecosystem packages still lack first-party TypeScript definitions or ship incomplete @types packages, resulting in TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module errors during build time.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3199), I converted the ProjectFilter component to strict TypeScript.

Here is how we handled untyped third-party dependencies with ambient declarations, implemented Vue 3.4's named defineModel macro, and tested scoped slot rendering.

1. Handling Untyped Libraries with Ambient Declarations (.d.ts)

The ProjectFilter component integrates the popular vue-select dropdown package to allow contributors to filter community issues across dozens of GitLab projects.

Because vue-select does not ship built-in type definitions, importing it in a TypeScript SFC produces compiler errors:

import VueSelect from 'vue-select'; // ❌ TS7016: Could not find declaration file

Instead of bypassing type checking with // @ts-ignore, the idiomatic TypeScript solution is creating an ambient module declaration in the project's source root (app/javascript/vue-select.d.ts):

declare module 'vue-select' {
  import type { DefineComponent } from 'vue';

  const component: DefineComponent<Record<string, unknown>>;
  export default component;
}

Why this approach works:

  • Zero Suppression Comments: The compiler recognizes vue-select as a valid Vue component without polluting component files with suppressions.
  • Global Availability: vue-tsc picks up all *.d.ts files included in tsconfig.json, enabling any other component across the codebase to import vue-select safely.

2. Implementing Named Two-Way Binding: defineModel('selectedProjects')

In Vue 3.4+, components can bind multiple models or use custom model names using the first argument of defineModel().

In ProjectFilter.vue:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BFormGroup } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import 'vue-select/dist/vue-select.css';

defineProps<{
  availableProjects: string[];
}>();

// Strongly typed named model with required flag
const selectedProjects = defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { 
  required: true 
});
</script>

<template>
  <BFormGroup label="Project">
    <VueSelect
      v-model="selectedProjects"
      multiple
      :options="availableProjects"
    >
      <template #no-options="{ search, searching }">
        <template v-if="searching">
          No projects matching "{{ search }}"
        </template>
        <template v-else>
          No projects available
        </template>
      </template>
    </VueSelect>
  </BFormGroup>
</template>

Improvements:

  • defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { required: true }) automatically types both props.selectedProjects and emits update:selectedProjects with a payload of string[].
  • Prop validation for availableProjects is enforced at compile time without verbose runtime type objects.

3. Testing Scoped Slots in Vue Test Utils

A unique testing pattern in ProjectFilter.spec.ts is verifying custom template slots like #no-options="{ search, searching }".

In TypeScript, accessing $slots on a child component's vm requires proper typing and optional chaining:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import ProjectFilter from './ProjectFilter.vue';

describe('ProjectFilter', () => {
  let wrapper: VueWrapper;
  const findSelect = () => wrapper.findComponent(VueSelect);

  // Type-safe slot helper rendering the child's scoped slot
  const findNoOptions = (slotProps: Record<string, unknown>) =>
    shallowMount({
      render: () => findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps),
    });

  it('emits updated projects when selection changes', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findSelect().vm.$emit('update:modelValue', ['gitlab']);

    // Emits are typed as Array of argument arrays
    expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedProjects')).toEqual([[['gitlab']]]);
  });

  it('renders matching text when search has no results', () => {
    createWrapper();

    const noOptionsWrapper = findNoOptions({ search: 'non-existent', searching: true });
    expect(noOptionsWrapper.text()).toContain('No projects matching "non-existent"');
  });
});

Using optional chaining findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps) prevents runtime TypeError when a component's slot is undefined during mounting.

Key Takeaways

  1. Ambient Declarations for Untyped Packages: Create clean .d.ts declaration files instead of relying on @ts-ignore when working with untyped npm packages.
  2. Named defineModel<T>('name'): Leverages Vue 3.4's macro to type non-default model bindings cleanly and succinctly.
  3. Safe Scoped Slot Testing: Use typed inline render helpers with optional chaining to mount and assert custom slot templates in Vue Test Utils.

title: YouTube's transcript panel gives you the full transcript — I scrolled three videos to prove it
description:
I built a YouTube transcript exporter, and one design question kept coming back: when the timedtext endpoint won't cooperate, is the on-page transcript panel a real fallback — or does it only hold the rows currently on screen?

On 2026-11-15 I measured that YouTube's timedtext endpoint returns empty bodies from datacenter IPs (curl: HTTP 200 with 0 bytes, then 429; real browser: json3 through srv3 all empty, no challenge page). Real users on residential IPs should be fine, but my test environment could not verify that path. So the panel became the question that mattered. I originally wrote that the panel "only gives the currently rendered rows, not the full transcript." That was an untested assumption. I tested it properly this week, at three scales.

How I measured it

Headless Chrome 154 with a local CONNECT relay, loading the real youtube.com watch page. For each video I opened the transcript panel, counted the rows, then scrolled the panel container to the bottom twice and counted again. I also ran my extension's own YTE_GET_TRANSCRIPT (source: panel) before and after scrolling, so the panel DOM and the extension's reading of it were checked against each other.

Results

Video Length Rows before scrolling Rows after 2 scrolls Cues (extension) Characters
Rick Astley — Never Gonna Give You Up (dQw4w9WgXcQ) 3:33 24 24 24 2,066
TED — Do schools kill creativity? (iG9CE55wbtY) 20:03 163 163 163 17,412
Randy Pausch — The Last Lecture (ji5_MqicxSo) 76:27 713 713 713 65,510

First cue to last cue covered the whole video in each case (0:01–3:23, 0:27–19:19, 0:17–1:15:26). The panel container's scrollHeight was far larger than its clientHeight (e.g. 39,870 vs 299 on the 76-minute video), so there was real scrolling to do — the row count simply did not change. The extension's transcript was identical before and after scrolling in all three runs.

What changed in my design

The panel is now the default full-transcript source (verified up to 76 minutes / 713 cues). timedtext is demoted to a backup for when the panel is unavailable. The panel DOM itself also changed recently: the old ytd-transcript-segment-renderer selector returns zero rows now; the current rendering uses <transcript-segment-view-model> with timestamps in .ytwTranscriptSegmentViewModelTimestamp and text in span[role="text"]. My reader tries the new DOM first and falls back to the old one.

Honest caveats

  • I have not tested 2-hour-plus videos or 1,000+ cue transcripts. If a virtualization threshold exists, it can only be at a larger scale than 713 cues.
  • My DOM probe truncated each row to 80 characters, so its character totals (1,776 / 11,471 / 49,505) are lower than the extension's (2,066 / 17,412 / 65,510). That is a probe-method difference, not a data difference.
  • The 2026-11-15 claim that "the panel only gives the currently rendered rows" is overturned at all three scales tested. It was wrong because I had not scrolled before writing it.

Status

YouTube Transcript Export v0.1.0 is in review on Microsoft Edge Add-ons and cannot be installed yet. The Pro tier (planned ¥19.90 one-time, Afdian activation code) is not on sale. Privacy page: https://alapha888.github.io/yt-transcript-export-privacy/

title: Swagger UI is from 2011. It’s Time to Upgrade to Scalar.
description:
You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe APIs, and everything working perfectly.

Then someone opens your /docs endpoint.

And there it is. The same old Swagger UI.

Don't get me wrong. Swagger UI is great and has served developers for years. But API documentation can look and feel much better.

That's where Scalar comes in.

What Is Scalar?

Scalar is an open-source API documentation tool that gives your OpenAPI documentation a cleaner, more modern interface.

Think of it as Swagger UI, but with a better developer experience.

Here's what makes it interesting:

  • Modern UI: Clean layout, dark mode, and customizable themes.
  • Built-in API client: Test endpoints directly without switching to Postman.
  • Code snippets: Generate request examples in JavaScript, Python, Go, and more.
  • Authentication: Support for Bearer tokens, API keys, and other OpenAPI security schemes.
  • OpenAPI support: Works with your existing OpenAPI specifications.

And the best part?

You don't need to change your backend or rewrite your API schemas.

Swagger UI vs. Scalar

Here's a quick comparison:

Feature Swagger UI Scalar
UI Design Traditional accordion layout Modern, clean interface
Dark Mode Requires customization Built-in
API Testing Basic Try it out Integrated API client
Code Snippets Configurable request snippets Multiple languages and clients
Authentication Bearer, API keys, OAuth2 Bearer, API keys, OAuth2
Search Endpoint filtering Integrated reference search
Customization CSS and configuration Built-in themes and configuration
OpenAPI 3.1 Supported Supported
Open Source Yes Yes

Both tools do the job, but Scalar focuses more on the overall developer experience, especially when exploring and testing APIs.

How Easy Is It to Integrate?

If you're using Fastify with @fastify/swagger already configured, it's just a few lines.

Install Scalar:

npm install @scalar/fastify-api-reference

Register it in your Fastify application:

await fastify.register(
  import('@scalar/fastify-api-reference'),
  {
    routePrefix: '/docs',
    configuration: {
      theme: 'purple',
    },
  }
);

Now open:

http://localhost:3000/docs

That's it. Your existing OpenAPI specification now has a modern documentation interface.

Scalar also supports NestJS, Express, Next.js, and other frameworks.

Should You Replace Swagger UI?

Not necessarily.

Swagger UI is still actively maintained and supports OpenAPI 3.1, authentication, and interactive requests.

Scalar simply offers a different, more polished experience for exploring and testing APIs.

If you're happy with Swagger UI, there's no reason to rush.

But if you want better-looking, developer-friendly API documentation without much effort, Scalar is definitely worth trying.

Final Thoughts

We spend hours improving our backend architecture, performance, and code quality.

Why not give the same attention to our API documentation?

A great API deserves a great developer experience.

Give Scalar a try on your next project.

What do you use for API documentation — Swagger UI, Scalar, or something else?

title: Fixing Modal Keyboard Traps in GitLab UI: Conditional Escape Key Propagation in GlTokenSelector
description:
In design systems, composite input components—such as tag pickers, autocomplete dropdowns, and token selectors—often handle internal keyboard events to navigate suggestion lists. However, when a component aggressively stops event propagation (event.stopPropagation()), it can inadvertently break surrounding containers like modal dialogs, drawers, and overlay popups.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Pajamas Design System (MR !6678, closing Work Item #3762), I resolved a keyboard accessibility barrier in @gitlab/ui's GlTokenSelector that prevented modal dialogs from closing on Escape.

Here is an architectural look at the problem, how WAI-ARIA recommends handling nested keyboard contexts, and how we solved it in Vue.

1. The Bug: Trapped Inside the Modal

GlTokenSelector is the multi-selection token input used across GitLab to assign labels, users, milestones, and security tags.

Inside GlTokenSelector, the text input had an inline event modifier attached to catch keypresses:

<!-- Before in GlTokenSelector.vue -->
<input
  ref="input"
  @keydown.stop="$emit('keydown', $event)"
  ...
/>

The .stop modifier in Vue unconditionally invokes event.stopPropagation().

The Real-World Breakdown

When GlTokenSelector is embedded inside a modal dialog (GlModal), users expect standard keyboard navigation:

  1. Focus Input: The user types to search for tokens. A dropdown opens with suggestions.
  2. Press Escape (1st time): The suggestions dropdown should dismiss, returning focus to the input.
  3. Press Escape (2nd time): Because the dropdown is closed, the Escape key should bubble up to GlModal and close the dialog!

Because @keydown.stop caught and swallowed every Escape keydown event, the event never reached the modal container. Users had to manually reach for their mouse to close the modal—violating WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard Accessible) and frustrating power users.

2. The Solution: Conditional Event Propagation

According to the W3C WAI-ARIA Dialog Pattern, when an active input inside a modal does not have its own popup or combobox menu open, pressing Escape must close the dialog.

To resolve this, we removed the blind @keydown.stop modifier and implemented programmatic event propagation:

<!-- After in GlTokenSelector.vue -->
<input
  ref="input"
  @keydown="handleKeydown"
  ...
/>

In the component's script:

handleKeydown(event) {
  if (event.key === 'Escape') {
    this.handleEscape(event);
    return;
  }

  // Non-Escape keys remain contained inside the token selector
  event.stopPropagation();
  this.$emit('keydown', event);
},

handleEscape(event) {
  if (this.dropdownIsOpen) {
    // 1st Escape: Close dropdown and prevent bubbling to parent modal
    event?.stopPropagation?.();
    this.closeDropdown();
  } else {
    // 2nd Escape: Dropdown already closed, let Escape bubble up to GlModal!
    this.$emit('keydown', event);
  }
}

How It Works:

  • When Suggestions are Open: event.stopPropagation() fires, cleanly closing the dropdown without triggering the parent modal.
  • When Suggestions are Closed: Propagation is not stopped. The event bubbles up the DOM tree, allowing GlModal's root key listener to catch Escape and close the dialog as expected.

3. Unit Testing Keyboard Propagation

To safeguard against regressions, we added unit test suites in token_selector.spec.js using Jest/Vue Test Utils to verify propagation states:

describe('when Escape key is pressed', () => {
  it('stops propagation when suggestions dropdown is open', () => {
    createComponent({ dropdownIsOpen: true });
    const stopPropagation = jest.fn();

    findInput().trigger('keydown', {
      key: 'Escape',
      stopPropagation,
    });

    expect(stopPropagation).toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it('allows propagation to bubble to parent when dropdown is closed', () => {
    createComponent({ dropdownIsOpen: false });
    const stopPropagation = jest.fn();

    findInput().trigger('keydown', {
      key: 'Escape',
      stopPropagation,
    });

    expect(stopPropagation).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});

Key Takeaways for Design System Engineers

  1. Be Cautious with .stop Modifiers: Avoid applying @keydown.stop or @click.stop indiscriminately on inputs. Child components frequently live inside composite parents (modals, drawers, dropdowns) that rely on event bubbling.
  2. Follow Layered Escape Ergonomics: An Escape press should peel back one UI layer at a time: active tooltip $\rightarrow$ autocomplete menu $\rightarrow$ modal dialog.
  3. Accessibility is Built in the Small Details: Fixing keyboard traps and ensuring predictable focus behavior makes design systems truly accessible to everyone.

title: Bringing the Semantic Web to GitLab Pages: Implementing RFC 9110 Content Negotiation in Go
description:
The Semantic Web and Linked Open Data (LOD) initiatives rely on a foundational principle: a single persistent URI (e.g., https://example.com/alice or https://example.com/ontology) should be accessible to both humans in their web browsers and machines consuming semantic data models.

Through HTTP Content Negotiation, a browser requesting Accept: text/html receives a styled HTML page, while an RDF crawler or knowledge-graph ingestion pipeline requesting Accept: text/turtle or Accept: application/ld+json receives machine-readable triples from the exact same URI.

In my recent contribution to GitLab Pages (MR !1384, closing Issue #1135), I designed and implemented RFC 9110-compliant content negotiation for static sites hosted on GitLab Pages.

Here is an engineering deep-dive into how we implemented media-type negotiation, specificity weighting, and cache safety in Go.

1. The Problem: Extensionless URLs in Static Hosting

Historically, GitLab Pages mapped extensionless HTTP requests (GET /research-paper or GET /) exclusively to .html (or index.html).

For scientific organizations, academic publishers, and open-data projects hosting ontologies on GitLab Pages:

  • A browser requesting /schema received schema.html.
  • A machine or graph database sending Accept: application/rdf+xml or Accept: text/turtle still received HTML or a 404 error.

Because static sites couldn't resolve semantic file variants without forcing users to type explicit extensions like schema.ttl, GitLab Pages could not serve Linked Data in compliance with W3C best practices.

2. Designing an RFC 9110 Compliant Accept Parser in Go

HTTP content negotiation is defined in RFC 9110 (Section 12.5.1). A robust content negotiation parser must handle:

  1. Quality Values (q): Entries with higher weights (q=1.0 vs q=0.5) take priority. Zero quality (q=0) rejects the type.
  2. Specificity Weighting:
    • Exact type/subtype: application/ld+json (highest precedence)
    • Subtype wildcards: text/* (medium precedence)
    • Global wildcards: */* (lowest precedence)

We built a parser that parses candidate media types and orders them by quality and specificity:

type MediaRange struct {
    Type       string
    Subtype    string
    Quality    float64
    Specificity int
}

When a client sends:

Accept: text/html;q=0.8, text/turtle;q=0.9, */*;q=0.1

The parser evaluates text/turtle ($q=0.9$) first, followed by text/html ($q=0.8$), and finally the wildcard fallback.

3. Mapping Media Types to Semantic File Extensions

GitLab Pages now recognizes common Linked Data and Semantic Web formats:

MIME Media Type File Extension Format Description
text/turtle .ttl Terse RDF Triple Language
application/ld+json .jsonld JSON for Linked Data
application/rdf+xml .rdf Resource Description Framework XML
application/n-triples .nt N-Triples
text/n3 .n3 Notation3
application/owl+xml .owl Web Ontology Language
text/html, application/xhtml+xml .html HyperText Markup Language

Resolution Algorithm:

  1. When receiving a request for /dataset:
  2. Inspect the client's Accept header.
  3. For each candidate media type in descending preference order, test if the corresponding file exists on disk (e.g., dataset.ttl, dataset.jsonld, dataset.rdf).
  4. If a match is found, serve that file with the matching Content-Type header.
  5. If no semantic file matches or no Accept header is provided, safely fall back to the default dataset.html.

4. Cache Correctness: Why Vary: Accept is Crucial

In static web hosting and CDNs, caching responses correctly is just as important as serving them.

If a CDN caches dataset.html for GET /dataset, a subsequent request from an RDF crawler with Accept: text/turtle would mistakenly receive the cached HTML from the CDN edge server!

To prevent cache poisoning:

  • Whenever content negotiation takes place, GitLab Pages appends: 
  Vary: Accept
  • This instructs CDNs, reverse proxies, and browsers that the cached representation depends strictly on the incoming Accept header.
  • Direct extension requests (e.g., GET /dataset.ttl) bypass negotiation and do not emit unnecessary Vary headers.

5. Testing & Verification

The feature is covered by unit tests and end-to-end integration tests in TestReader_ContentNegotiation:

  • Directory Indexes: GET / with Accept: application/rdf+xml serves index.rdf.
  • Quality Fallbacks: Verifying that q=0.9 wins over q=0.7.
  • Graceful HTML Fallback: If an unsupported media type is requested, standard HTML is delivered without breaking normal user navigation. 
go test -v ./internal/vfs/zip -run '^TestReader_ContentNegotiation$'

Conclusion

With this contribution, thousands of static websites hosted on GitLab Pages can now serve both human-friendly documentation and Linked Open Data from identical canonical URLs.

Special thanks to the GitLab Pages maintainers for their thorough reviews and guidance throughout this implementation!

title: URL-Synchronized Pagination in Vue 3: Typing RoutePagination and Testing External Behavior
description:
In data-heavy dashboards, tables, and issue trackers, pagination should always synchronize with the browser's URL query parameters. Storing the active page number in ?page=X enables users to share direct links, bookmark filtered views, and use browser back/forward buttons seamlessly.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3200), I migrated the shared RoutePagination component and its unit test suite to TypeScript.

Beyond adding type annotations, this migration provided an opportunity to modernize the component's two-way binding using Vue 3.4's defineModel() macro and refactor the test suite from inspecting internal component state to asserting user-facing behavior.

1. Modernizing Two-Way Binding with defineModel<number>()

Previously, RoutePagination.vue relied on runtime prop definitions and untyped model declarations:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  totalRows: { type: Number, required: true },
  perPage: { type: Number, required: true },
});

const currentPage = defineModel({ required: false, type: Number });
const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage) => {
  router.push({ query: { ...route.query, page: newPage } });
};
</script>

The TypeScript Refactoring

In the migrated version, we introduced compile-time type declarations and handled asynchronous router promises cleanly:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import { onMounted } from 'vue';
import { useRoute, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { numberParam } from '~/common/QueryParams';

const props = defineProps<{
  totalRows: number;
  perPage: number;
}>();

// Strongly typed two-way v-model binding
const currentPage = defineModel<number>();

const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage: number | string) => {
  const query = route.query;
  // Explicitly void floating navigation promise
  void router.push({ query: { ...query, page: newPage } });
};

onMounted(() => {
  const page = numberParam(route.query.page) || 1;
  currentPage.value = page;
});
</script>

Key Technical Details:

  • defineModel<number>(): Replaces manual modelValue prop and update:modelValue emit declarations with Vue 3.4's type-safe macro.
  • Handling Floating Promises (void router.push): Calling asynchronous routing methods without await can trigger @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises. Adding void explicitly marks the promise as intentionally unawaited in event callbacks.

2. Refactoring Specs: Testing External Contracts, Not Internal State

In older specs, unit tests frequently inspected component internals using wrapper.vm:

// ❌ Old Anti-Pattern: Checking private component internals
expect(wrapper.vm.currentPage).toBe(2);

While wrapper.vm works in JavaScript, relying on it creates fragile tests that break whenever internal variable names change. It also creates typing friction in TypeScript because wrapper.vm is not strictly typed unless heavily annotated.

The Modernized Spec

In RoutePagination.spec.ts, we refactored assertions to observe what the user and parent components actually observe:

  1. Child Props: Verifying what the underlying <BPagination> component receives.
  2. Emitted Events: Verifying what update:modelValue emits to the parent.
  3. URL State: Verifying what router.currentRoute.value.query reflects. 
import { flushPromises, mount, type VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import type { Router } from 'vue-router';
import { createTestRouter } from '~/spec/testHelpers';
import RoutePagination from './RoutePagination.vue';

const defaultProps = { totalRows: 10, perPage: 5 };

let router: Router;
let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = mount(RoutePagination, {
    props: { ...defaultProps, ...props },
    global: { plugins: [router] },
  });
};

const findBPagination = () => wrapper.findComponent(BPagination);
const findPage2Button = () => findBPagination().find('button[aria-posinset="2"]');

beforeEach(async () => {
  router = await createTestRouter('/leaderboard');
});

describe('changing page', () => {
  it('updates route and emits current page', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findPage2Button().trigger('click');
    await flushPromises();

    // Asserting actual URL query change
    expect(router.currentRoute.value.query).toStrictEqual({ page: '2' });

    // Asserting child UI received modelValue update
    expect(findBPagination().props('modelValue')).toBe(2);
  });
});

Key Takeaways

  1. Use defineModel<T>(): Simplifies component code by replacing separate prop/emit definitions with a single typed reactive reference.
  2. Handle Router Promises: Use void router.push(...) in event handlers where awaiting the navigation is unnecessary.
  3. Test the Black Box: Test emitted events and child component props rather than private wrapper.vm properties. Tests will be sturdier and easier to type.

title: A Practical Stack Checklist for Small-Business Web Apps (Next.js, Node.js, SQL or MongoDB)
description:
Most small-business web apps I see share the same shape: a handful of forms, a dashboard, some user roles, and a few integrations (payments, email, maybe WhatsApp or SMS). The hard part is rarely the code. It's picking a stack that a small team can ship quickly and still maintain two years later.

Here is the checklist I use before writing the first line.

1. Start from the data, not the framework

Sketch the core entities and their relationships first: customers, orders, invoices, bookings, whatever the business runs on.

  • Mostly relational data (orders → line items → products, strict reporting needs): reach for SQL (MySQL or PostgreSQL). Joins and transactions will save you later.
  • Flexible, document-shaped data (form submissions with varying fields, content blocks, activity logs): MongoDB is a comfortable fit.
  • Both? That's normal. Keep the transactional core in SQL and store loosely structured data as JSON columns or in a separate collection.

2. Pick a rendering model per page, not per project

With Next.js you don't have to choose one strategy for the whole app:

Page type Good default
Marketing pages, blog Static generation (fast, SEO-friendly)
Product/catalogue pages Static + revalidation
Dashboards behind login Client or server components fetching per request
Admin tables with filters Server-side data fetching + pagination

Public pages get the SEO benefits, and the authenticated app stays dynamic.

3. Keep the API boring

For a small team, a plain Node.js REST API (or Next.js route handlers) with clear resource names beats a clever architecture. A few rules that pay off:

  • Validate every request body at the edge (Zod or similar).
  • Return consistent error shapes: { error: { code, message } }.
  • Paginate every list endpoint from day one.
  • Log with request IDs so support issues can be traced.

4. Authentication and roles early

Retro-fitting roles is painful. Even if version one has only "admin" and "staff", model roles and permissions as data, not as if (user.isAdmin) scattered through the code.

5. Plan for the second integration

The first integration (say, a payment gateway) usually goes straight into a route handler. The second one is the signal to introduce a small service layer and a queue or background job runner, so slow third-party calls don't block requests.

6. Make it observable and backed up

Before launch, confirm you have:

  • [ ] Automated database backups and a tested restore
  • [ ] Error tracking on both frontend and backend
  • [ ] Uptime monitoring on key pages
  • [ ] Environment variables kept out of the repo

Wrapping up

None of this is exotic, and that's the point. Small-business software succeeds when it is predictable, easy to hand over, and cheap to change. A React/Next.js front end, a Node.js API, and the right database for your data shape cover the vast majority of these projects.

What's on your checklist that I've missed? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

I'm Haseeb Ullah, a software developer building web applications, SaaS products and custom business software. You can see more of my work on my portfolio.

title: Which Companies Use AWS? Real-World Examples Across Industries
description:
A beginner-friendly look at well-known companies that run on AWS, grouped by industry, and why they chose it.

tags: aws, cloud, beginners, devops

vishalcloudjourney

When I started learning AWS, one question kept coming back to me: is anyone actually using this at scale, or is it just a certification topic?

The answer is that AWS runs a huge share of the internet, from streaming and banking to space agencies and healthcare. In this post I've grouped well-known companies by industry and noted what they use AWS for.

1. Streaming and Entertainment

  • Netflix runs its streaming platform, recommendation engine and data analytics on AWS (EC2, S3, DynamoDB).
  • Disney+ uses AWS for video delivery and scaling during big launches.
  • Twitch uses AWS for live video and chat at global scale.
  • Epic Games hosts the backend for Fortnite and its game services on AWS.
  • Formula 1 uses AWS for race data analytics and machine learning insights.

2. E-commerce, Travel and Social Platforms

  • Airbnb runs its booking and search platform on AWS (EC2, S3, RDS).
  • Expedia Group moved a large part of its travel platform to AWS.
  • Pinterest uses AWS for content storage and recommendation systems.
  • Reddit uses AWS for hosting and media delivery.
  • Slack relies on AWS for messaging infrastructure at scale.
  • Lyft runs its ride-sharing platform on AWS.

3. Banking, Fintech and Finance

  • Capital One went "all in" on AWS and shut down its own data centers.
  • Goldman Sachs uses AWS for data and analytics workloads.
  • Nasdaq uses AWS for market data and cloud-based trading infrastructure.
  • Coinbase runs its crypto exchange platform on AWS.
  • Intuit (TurboTax, QuickBooks) uses AWS for its financial software products.

4. Healthcare and Pharma

  • Pfizer uses AWS for research and data processing.
  • Moderna used AWS for drug discovery and data analysis.
  • Johnson & Johnson uses AWS for cloud and analytics workloads.
  • Philips uses AWS for its HealthSuite digital health platform.

5. Automotive and Manufacturing

  • BMW Group uses AWS for its connected car and data platform.
  • Toyota uses AWS for connected vehicle and mobility services.
  • Siemens uses AWS for industrial IoT workloads.
  • GE uses AWS for industrial and digital services.

6. Technology and Software

  • Adobe runs parts of Creative Cloud and its marketing products on AWS.
  • Samsung uses AWS for services supporting its devices and apps.
  • Zillow runs its real estate data platform on AWS.

7. Government and Science

  • NASA / NASA JPL uses AWS to store, process and share space mission and image data.
  • Public sector bodies use AWS through dedicated regions, including AWS GovCloud (US).

Why Do These Companies Choose AWS?

  1. Scalability: capacity grows with demand, like a show launch or a big sale.
  2. Global reach: many Regions and Availability Zones put apps close to users.
  3. Pay-as-you-go pricing: no need to buy hardware up front.
  4. Breadth of services: compute, storage, databases, AI/ML, analytics and security in one place.
  5. Security and compliance: support for many industry standards.

What This Means for Beginners Like Me

Seeing these names made the learning feel more real. The same services I practice with, such as EC2, S3, IAM, VPC and RDS, are the building blocks behind apps used by millions of people. If you're starting your AWS journey, you are learning skills the industry actually uses.

Note: Companies change their cloud setups over time, and many use multi-cloud. For the latest details, check the AWS Customer Success Stories page.

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

title: Refactoring Vue 3 Unit Tests: Moving from Mutable beforeEach State to Functional Factory Helpers in TypeScript
description:
When migrating large Vue codebases to TypeScript, static typing often exposes patterns in our test suites that are brittle or unnecessary. One common pattern in older Vue Test Utils specs is storing a mutable let wrapper variable in the test scope and initializing it inside beforeEach().

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3204), I converted the Labelathon page's DetailsSection component to TypeScript and refactored its unit test suite to use functional factory helpers.

Here is a look at why this refactoring improves test clarity, type inference, and test isolation.

The Component: DetailsSection.vue

The DetailsSection component renders instructions and event guidelines using accordion components from bootstrap-vue-next alongside a custom MarkdownRenderer:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { BAccordion, BAccordionItem } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import MarkdownRenderer from '~/common/components/MarkdownRenderer.vue';
</script>

<template>
  <BAccordion class="mt-4">
    <BAccordionItem title="Rules & Guidelines">
      <MarkdownRenderer :markdown="guidelines" />
    </BAccordionItem>
    <!-- Additional accordion items -->
  </BAccordion>
</template>

Adding lang="ts" ensures strict compilation of imported third-party components and child component props.

The Spec: Mutable beforeEach vs. Pure createWrapper

The Old Pattern (JavaScript)

Previously, the spec relied on an outer mutable reference:

// Before (DetailsSection.spec.js)
describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  let wrapper;

  beforeEach(() => {
    wrapper = shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });
  });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(wrapper.html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why avoid this pattern in TypeScript?

  1. Unnecessary State Mutation: A global let wrapper introduces shared state across tests. Tests should be isolated and idempotent.
  2. Type Ambiguity: In TypeScript, declaring let wrapper; defaults to any unless explicitly typed (VueWrapper<InstanceType<typeof DetailsSection>>), which adds boilerplate.
  3. Execution Overhead: If some test cases only test static exports or helpers, beforeEach still mounts the component unnecessarily.

The Modern Pattern (TypeScript)

In DetailsSection.spec.ts, we eliminated beforeEach and the mutable variable in favor of a concise factory helper:

// After (DetailsSection.spec.ts)
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import DetailsSection from './DetailsSection.vue';

describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  const createWrapper = () =>
    shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why this is better:

  • Automatic Type Inference: createWrapper() naturally returns a typed VueWrapper, avoiding manual type annotations.
  • Pure & Self-Contained: Each test explicitly invokes createWrapper() with optional prop overrides when needed, preventing test leakage.
  • Seamless Snapshot Migration: The Vitest snapshot was smoothly renamed from DetailsSection.spec.js.snap to DetailsSection.spec.ts.snap without breaking snapshot verification.

Key Takeaways

  1. Favor Factory Functions over beforeEach: Pure createWrapper = (props = {}) => ... functions result in cleaner, more readable specs compared to mutating a shared let wrapper variable.
  2. Leverage Type Inference in Tests: By using inline factory functions, Vue Test Utils and Vitest automatically infer wrapper types without verbose casting.
  3. Clean Codebases One Slice at a Time: Converting small presentation components and their specs in focused merge requests keeps review cycles fast and eliminates maintenance debt.
