title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them

Understanding ACH Return Codes: A Developer's Guide

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A transaction you thought was settled comes back rejected, and you need to know why and what to do next. The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) publishes a standardized set of return codes—R01 through R85—that tell you exactly what went wrong. This article breaks down the most common ones and how to handle them in code.

The Big Three: R01, R03, and R10

R01: Insufficient Funds

What it means: The recipient's account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit. This is the most common return code.

When it fires: 1–2 business days after the ACH debit is initiated, during the bank's settlement window.

How to handle it:

  • Log the return with timestamp and amount.
  • Mark the payout as "returned" in your database, not "failed"—there's a difference.
  • Notify the recipient (usually via email or in-app).
  • Offer retry options: wait 3–5 business days and retry, or switch to a different payout rail (e.g., Visa Direct for faster settlement). 
async function handleR01Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);

  payout.status = 'returned';
  payout.returnCode = 'R01';
  payout.returnedAt = new Date();
  payout.retryCount = (payout.retryCount || 0) + 1;

  if (payout.retryCount <= 2) {
    // Schedule retry in 5 business days
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5));
    await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
      subject: 'Payout returned — will retry',
      message: `Your $${payout.amount} payout was returned due to insufficient funds. We'll retry on ${addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5).toDateString()}.`
    });
  } else {
    // Max retries exceeded; escalate
    payout.status = 'manual_review';
    await notifySupport(payout);
  }

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
}

R03: No Account / Account Closed

What it means: The account number or routing number is invalid, or the account has been closed.

When it fires: 1 business day after initiation (banks catch this quickly).

How to handle it:

  • This is a permanent failure. Do not retry.
  • Flag the recipient's bank details as invalid.
  • Require the user to update their account information before attempting another payout.
  • Consider blocking future payouts to that account until verified. 
async function handleR03Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);
  const recipient = await db.recipients.findById(payout.recipientId);

  payout.status = 'failed';
  payout.returnCode = 'R03';

  // Mark bank account as invalid
  recipient.bankAccount.status = 'invalid';
  recipient.bankAccount.invalidReason = 'No account or account closed';
  recipient.bankAccount.requiresUpdate = true;

  await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
    subject: 'Bank account information is invalid',
    message: 'The account you provided does not exist or is closed. Please update your bank details.'
  });

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
  await db.recipients.save(recipient);
}

R10: Unauthorized / Unauthorized Debit

What it means: The account holder did not authorize this debit, or the authorization is outside the agreement terms.

When it fires: Up to 60 days after the original debit (this is a consumer dispute).

How to handle it:

  • Investigate immediately. This may indicate fraud or a customer complaint.
  • Halt further payouts to that recipient until resolved.
  • Contact the customer to verify legitimacy.
  • If legitimate, you may need to resubmit with corrected authorization.

  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);

  payout.status = 'disputed';
  payout.returnCode = 'R10';
  payout.requiresInvestigation = true;

  // Freeze recipient pending review
  const recipient = await db.recipients.findById(payout.recipientId);
  recipient.status = 'frozen_pending_review';

  await escalateToSupport({
    payoutId

title: Building Type-Safe Presentation Components in Vue 3: Converting ContributorSocialLinks to TypeScript
description:
In frontend design systems, presentation components-small, focused components responsible solely for displaying data—are the building blocks of clean UI architecture. However, when these components accept raw arrays without strict contracts, optional fields like social links, profile URLs, and handles can easily lead to template errors or broken links.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3194), I migrated the ContributorSocialLinks component and its test suite to strict TypeScript.

Here is a quick breakdown of how typing lightweight presentation components improves maintainability and test reliability.

1. The Challenge: Loose Array Props

Originally, ContributorSocialLinks.vue accepted contributors through standard runtime prop validation:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
});

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Why was this problematic?

  1. Missing Shape Contract: The compiler had no knowledge of what attributes a "contributor" held. A parent passing an object with linkedin (lowercase 'i') or discord_handle would fail silently.
  2. Untyped Filter Results: contributorsWithSocials held elements of type any, preventing type checking across the component template (such as icon rendering or URL generation).

2. Strong Type Contracts with interface

By adding lang="ts" and exporting a discrete Contributor interface, we created a clear contract for both the component and its consumers:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
export interface Contributor {
  name: string;
  gitlabUsername?: string;
  linkedIn?: string;
  discord?: string;
}

const props = defineProps<{
  contributors: Contributor[];
}>();

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Advantages:

  • Type-Only defineProps: Eliminates verbose runtime object definitions. Vue 3 automatically validates props at compile time based on the TypeScript definition.
  • Reusable Interface: Parent components (e.g., contributor lists, award cards) can import type { Contributor } directly to ensure prop compatibility.
  • Safe Filtering: TypeScript's type checker now verifies that .discord and .linkedIn exist on the Contributor model.

3. Strict Type Safety in Unit Tests

In ContributorSocialLinks.spec.ts, untyped factory helpers were replaced with typed parameters using the exported interface:

import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import type { Contributor } from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';
import ContributorSocialLinks from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';

describe('ContributorSocialLinks', () => {
  const createWrapper = (contributors: Contributor[]) =>
    shallowMount(ContributorSocialLinks, {
      props: { contributors },
    });

  it('does not render when no contributors have socials', () => {
    const wrapper = createWrapper([
      { name: 'Test User' }, // Fully conforms to Contributor interface
    ]);

    expect(wrapper.find('p').exists()).toBe(false);
  });
});

Spec assertions are now resilient against future schema changes, ensuring that mock objects always mirror realistic application data.

Key Takeaways

  1. Export Component Prop Interfaces: When a component receives structured domain data (like a user, contributor, or product), export its interface so parent views and test suites remain in sync.
  2. Favor Type-Only defineProps: defineProps<{ data: T }>() is cleaner and offers better IDE autocompletion compared to JavaScript options-based prop validators.
  3. Keep Spec Helpers Strongly Typed: Passing typed parameters into helper functions like createWrapper prevents accidental drift between test fixtures and production models.

title: The Error That Escaped Without A Collar
description:
One exit for every error of every transport: a mapped code instead of Unknown, a fixed message instead of internal text, and a panic that becomes Internal instead of taking the process with it.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The exit guard is built into the shared library and is on by default in its gRPC server chain; its tests, benchmarks and leak checks were run as targeted runs with the race detector. How often the old leak happened in production I did not measure, and I do not claim a number.

This is part 3 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Every animal that leaves an enclosure in our zoo wears a collar. The collar says whose animal it is and where it belongs. Keepers put it on at the gate, every time, by hand.

One morning Nora finds Biscuit, our dog, trotting along the main path with no collar at all. "Whose dog is this?!" Biscuit, very pleased with himself, answers the only thing he can: "Unknown! Woof!"

It gets worse. A dog without a collar does not know what not to say. Biscuit happily tells every visitor what he saw behind the scenes: "Table seven, row forty-two!" Miso hisses "Shh! Nobody asked you" - but by then the visitors have heard it.

The zoo's fix is not "keepers, please remember the collar". The fix is a keeper at the one gate everybody leaves through. Nobody leaves without a collar - even Biscuit. And when somebody faints at the gate, the gate keeper does not panic either: the animal is carried out with a plain tag that says "internal", and the zoo stays open.

The mapper you had to remember

In our services, a handler turns a domain error into an answer for the caller. For gRPC that is a status code with a reason; for HTTP a status and a body; for a consumer a decision to drop the message or try again. The library has a builder for exactly that mapping, and for a long time each handler called it itself.

That is the keeper who has to remember the collar. The library's changelog describes what happened when one did not: the forgotten call handed the caller Unknown with the internal text of the error, and a panic in a consumer flew into the goroutine of the resource that ran it. Two failures, one cause: the last step of every error was optional.

One gate for three transports

The library now has one exit for errors, with three doors on it. In the shape of the code - names shortened, the meaning is what matters:

// one exit for every transport - a form
guard.Answer(ctx, err)        // gRPC / HTTP: a mapped status, never raw text
guard.Recover(ctx, p)         // a panic -> Internal, a fixed message, the span marked
guard.Settle(ctx, msg, err)   // a consumer: drop the message, or retry it

Answer is the collar. Whatever error a handler returns, it goes through the mapping on the way out, so a forgotten mapper is no longer a leak - the gate maps it.

Recover is the keeper at the gate when someone faints. A panic in a handler becomes Internal with a fixed message, the trace span is marked, and the process keeps serving everyone else.

Settle is the consumer's door. A message whose error code is in the drop list - by default InvalidArgument and its neighbours, errors that will not get better by trying again - is dropped; anything else is retried. Before, that decision was another thing each consumer had to remember.

The guard is on by default in the chain of the library's gRPC server. A service does not import it to get it - which is why the count of services that import it directly is zero, and the count that run it is every service on that server.

Door Before After
gRPC the handler maps, or the caller gets Unknown with internal text the gate maps every error
HTTP the same, by hand per handler the same gate, the same mapping
consumer a panic flies into the resource goroutine Internal, span marked, process alive
consumer decision each consumer decides drop or retry one rule: drop codes are dropped, the rest retried

What the caller sees

The difference is easiest to see from the outside. The same failure, as a caller received it before and after the gate - shapes only, with the internal text replaced by a placeholder:

before:  code = Unknown
         message = "<internal error text: query, table, row>"

after:   code = <the mapped code, e.g. NotFound / FailedPrecondition>
         reason = <a reason code the caller can branch on>

panic:   code = Internal
         message = "<a fixed panic message>"     # the span is marked, the process lives

The caller of the first answer can do nothing but log it and give up, and the text in it belongs to the service, not to the caller. The caller of the second can branch on the reason. The third answer is the important quiet one: a single broken request no longer takes the process down with it.

Tested at the gate

A gate is only worth something if it holds under load and under races. The tests, benchmarks and goroutine-leak checks for the guard were written in a pass over several prompt sets and run as targeted runs with the race detector.

What went wrong

Two real leaks, both from the same design: the last step of an error was the handler's job. A forgotten mapper sent Unknown with internal text to a caller - the dog without a collar, telling visitors about table seven. A panic in a consumer escaped into the goroutine of the resource that ran it - the animal fainting in the middle of the path instead of at the gate.

The lesson is the one this whole series keeps repeating. A rule that every handler must remember is not a rule; it is a hope. The fix was not a review checklist or a linter warning but a gate in the one place every error passes, on by default.

What I do not claim

  • Not how often the leak hit callers before the gate. I did not count it.
  • Not that every service already runs the newest guard. It is on by default for services on the library's server.
  • Not that the drop list fits every consumer. It is the default.
  • Not a full load test. The guard has benchmarks and race runs, not a production measurement.

What of this is method

  • The last step of every error lives at one gate. Not in each handler.
  • A panic is an answer, not an exit. Internal, a fixed message, the span marked, the process alive.
  • Drop or retry is decided once. By the error's code, in one place.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 3. Next: One Ticket, Punched Once.

If your handlers map their own errors, how would you find the one that forgot? If you recover panics, where - per handler, or at one gate? If your consumers decide drop or retry, is that decision written once or many times? What did your last error without a collar say to a caller?

title: Every Heist Needs a Mastermind. So Does Your Backend.
description:
Every app you use runs a small heist behind the scenes.

Say you order a pair of shoes. One part of the system checks that the shoes are in stock. Another takes your payment. A third ships the box. Each one is a service, a small program with one job. Think of them as a crew: the inside guy, the safecracker and the driver.

Now picture that crew with no plan. They just message each other and hope it works out. The stock check says yes, the payment is still pending, and the driver leaves anyway. Nobody notices anything went wrong until the customer calls asking about an order they were never charged for, or one that never showed up.

Every heist needs a mastermind. In software, that’s called an orchestrator.

The orchestrator holds the plan and tells each service when to move. The driver doesn’t leave until the payment clears. If the payment fails, it tries again. If it still fails, the shoes go back on the shelf so you don’t end up shipping something nobody paid for. And every move is written down, so when something goes wrong, you can see exactly what happened and when.

That’s orchestration. It isn’t about making each service smarter. It’s about having one place that knows the whole plan.

Unmeshed is the orchestrator for your backend. If your services are talking to each other and hoping for the best, take a look at how it works:
Unmeshed Workflows

title: Protección y Recuperación de Datos NoSQL: Backups Automatizados con MongoDB Atlas, GitHub Actions y Render Copiar
description:
Introducción

En el desarrollo de sistemas informáticos, almacenar información correctamente es fundamental. Sin embargo, existe un aspecto igual de importante que muchas veces pasa desapercibido: ¿qué sucede cuando los datos se pierden, se eliminan accidentalmente o la base de datos presenta un problema?

Una aplicación puede funcionar perfectamente y, aun así, estar expuesta a pérdidas de información si no dispone de una estrategia adecuada de respaldo y recuperación.

Como parte del curso de Base de Datos II de la Universidad Privada de Tacna, desarrollamos en equipo una aplicación web que utiliza MongoDB Atlas como base de datos NoSQL y que incorpora mecanismos automatizados para generar, verificar y recuperar copias de seguridad.

Para completar la solución, integramos GitHub Actions como herramienta de automatización y Render como plataforma de despliegue.

En este artículo presentaré cómo organizamos nuestra solución, las tecnologías utilizadas, el funcionamiento de los respaldos y los aprendizajes obtenidos durante su implementación.

Enlaces del proyecto

  • Repositorio público: https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy
  • Aplicación desplegada: https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com
  • Base de datos: MongoDB Atlas.
  • Automatización: GitHub Actions.
  • Despliegue: Render.

1. La importancia de proteger los datos en una aplicación NoSQL

Cuando una aplicación utiliza una base de datos alojada en la nube, es posible pensar que la información está completamente protegida gracias a la infraestructura del proveedor.

Sin embargo, disponer de un sistema de replicación no significa necesariamente contar con una copia de seguridad independiente.

Por ejemplo, si un administrador elimina accidentalmente los documentos de una colección, esa operación puede propagarse a las réplicas de la base de datos.

Por esta razón, es necesario implementar mecanismos que permitan recuperar información almacenada en un momento anterior.

Durante nuestro proyecto trabajamos con tres conceptos fundamentales:

Respaldo (Backup): consiste en generar una copia de los datos que pueda utilizarse posteriormente.

Restauración (Restore): permite recuperar la información desde un respaldo previamente generado.

Recuperación ante desastres: comprende los procedimientos necesarios para restablecer la información y los servicios después de un incidente.

Nuestro objetivo fue integrar estos mecanismos en una aplicación funcional y demostrar que es posible automatizar procesos de recuperación utilizando herramientas de desarrollo modernas.

2. Descripción de la aplicación desarrollada

Para implementar y demostrar nuestra estrategia construimos una aplicación web que representa una pequeña tienda.

El sistema utiliza Node.js y Express para gestionar las solicitudes HTTP y MongoDB Atlas como servicio de almacenamiento documental.

La aplicación permite registrar productos, consultar sus datos, eliminarlos y administrar determinados procesos de respaldo.

Principales funcionalidades

  • Registro de productos con nombre, precio y cantidad disponible.
  • Visualización de los productos almacenados.
  • Eliminación de registros.
  • Comunicación con MongoDB Atlas.
  • Generación de respaldos desde una interfaz administrativa.
  • Consulta de información sobre los respaldos generados.
  • Verificación del estado de conexión con la base de datos.

Para el manejo de los respaldos, la aplicación incorpora operaciones protegidas mediante un token de administrador, evitando que cualquier solicitud pueda acceder directamente a esas funciones.

La interfaz web sirve como demostración práctica del funcionamiento de la base de datos y de los procedimientos de protección implementados.

3. Tecnologías y arquitectura del sistema

Seleccionamos un conjunto de tecnologías que nos permitiera integrar desarrollo web, almacenamiento NoSQL, automatización y despliegue continuo.

Tecnología Función
MongoDB Atlas Almacenamiento de documentos NoSQL
Node.js Ejecución del código JavaScript del servidor
Express Desarrollo de la API web
Docker Empaquetado de la aplicación
GitHub Control de versiones
GitHub Actions Pruebas, backups y automatización
Render Publicación de la aplicación
OpenSSL Cifrado de los archivos de respaldo

¿Cómo se relacionan estos componentes?

Cuando un usuario accede a la aplicación, Render entrega la interfaz y ejecuta el servidor Express.

El servidor establece una conexión con MongoDB Atlas para realizar operaciones sobre las colecciones.

De manera independiente, GitHub Actions ejecuta procesos programados para generar respaldos, probar su restauración y almacenar los archivos resultantes como artefactos.

Esta separación es importante porque la aplicación y el sistema de respaldos no dependen del mismo proceso de ejecución.

Además, utilizamos Docker para facilitar la configuración y reproducción del entorno de desarrollo.

4. Diseño de nuestra estrategia de respaldo

Uno de los primeros pasos fue establecer qué características debía cumplir el mecanismo de protección.

Decidimos implementar un sistema de respaldo lógico automatizado, en el que los documentos de MongoDB se exportan a archivos que pueden almacenarse y recuperarse posteriormente.

Esta decisión estuvo relacionada con el uso del clúster gratuito M0 de MongoDB Atlas, que no proporciona las mismas funciones de backup administrado disponibles en determinadas modalidades de pago.

Objetivos de recuperación

Para organizar nuestra estrategia consideramos dos indicadores:

RPO (Recovery Point Objective):

Representa la cantidad máxima de datos recientes que estamos dispuestos a perder ante un incidente.

Establecimos como objetivo un RPO de 24 horas, mediante la programación de un respaldo diario.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective):

Representa el tiempo máximo esperado para recuperar el servicio después de una interrupción.

Nuestro objetivo de diseño fue realizar una recuperación en menos de cinco minutos para el conjunto reducido de datos de demostración.

Estos valores representan metas del proyecto. Su cumplimiento real depende de factores como la ejecución del respaldo, la disponibilidad de los archivos y el tiempo efectivo de restauración.

Aplicación del principio 3-2-1

También tomamos como referencia la conocida estrategia 3-2-1, que propone mantener varias copias de los datos, utilizar medios de almacenamiento diferentes y conservar al menos una copia fuera del entorno principal.

En nuestra solución, la información original reside en MongoDB Atlas, mientras que los respaldos automatizados se almacenan como artefactos de GitHub Actions.

Estos artefactos también pueden descargarse y conservarse en otro almacenamiento para completar una estrategia con una tercera copia independiente.

De esta manera, evitamos depender exclusivamente del proveedor que aloja la base de datos.

5. Implementación del respaldo lógico

El componente principal de la estrategia se encuentra en el archivo:

src/backup-lib.js

Este módulo contiene la lógica utilizada para crear respaldos, restaurar documentos, calcular verificaciones de integridad y administrar la retención.

¿Por qué utilizamos Extended JSON?

MongoDB trabaja con tipos BSON que no siempre pueden conservarse correctamente utilizando una conversión tradicional a JSON.

Por ejemplo, existen tipos como:

  • ObjectId: identificadores de documentos.
  • Date: valores de fecha.
  • Decimal128: números decimales de alta precisión.

Para preservar estos tipos utilizamos Extended JSON (EJSON) en su representación canónica.

Un fragmento del código implementado es:

async function* lineas() {
  for await (const doc of cursor) {
    documentos++;
    yield EJSON.stringify(doc, {
      relaxed: false
    }) + '\n';
  }
}

Este procedimiento recorre los documentos de una colección y los transforma a EJSON.

Posteriormente, la información se comprime utilizando gzip:

await pipeline(
  Readable.from(lineas()),
  zlib.createGzip(),
  fs.createWriteStream(archivo)
);

El resultado es un archivo comprimido con extensión .jsonl.gz por cada colección.

Esta implementación permite procesar los documentos mediante flujos de datos, evitando cargar toda la colección simultáneamente en memoria.

6. Integridad de los archivos y metadatos

Crear archivos de respaldo no es suficiente. También necesitamos comprobar que la información pueda recuperarse correctamente.

Para solucionar este problema, implementamos verificaciones mediante SHA-256, un algoritmo criptográfico que permite calcular una huella digital de los archivos.

Cada respaldo incorpora un archivo llamado:

metadata.json

Este archivo registra información como la identificación del respaldo, el nombre de la base de datos, las colecciones exportadas, la cantidad de documentos, los índices y sus respectivos checksums.

¿Para qué sirve el checksum?

Supongamos que un archivo de respaldo se modifica accidentalmente o sufre una corrupción durante su almacenamiento.

Cuando intentamos restaurarlo, el sistema vuelve a calcular su hash SHA-256 y lo compara con el valor registrado originalmente.

Si ambos valores son diferentes, el archivo se considera alterado y se rechaza la restauración.

Un fragmento utilizado en nuestro proyecto es:

const actual = await sha256(
  path.join(dirBackup, info.archivo)
);

if (actual !== info.sha256) {
  throw new Error(
    `Checksum inválido en la colección "${nombre}"`
  );
}

Una característica importante es que esta verificación se realiza antes de iniciar la modificación de los documentos de destino.

Así reducimos el riesgo de utilizar respaldos dañados durante un proceso de recuperación.

7. Proceso de restauración de MongoDB

Una parte esencial del proyecto fue implementar el procedimiento inverso: recuperar los documentos almacenados en un respaldo.

Para ello desarrollamos el script:

scripts/restore.js

Este componente utiliza las funciones de restauración disponibles en nuestra biblioteca.

Etapas de recuperación

Primera etapa: validación del respaldo

Se comprueba la existencia de los archivos y se verifican sus checksums SHA-256.

Segunda etapa: lectura de documentos

Los archivos comprimidos se descomprimen y los documentos EJSON se convierten nuevamente a sus tipos correspondientes.

Tercera etapa: inserción de registros

La restauración organiza los documentos en lotes de hasta 1000 registros para insertarlos en MongoDB.

Cuarta etapa: recuperación de índices

Se recrean los índices registrados en los metadatos, conservando estructuras importantes para las consultas.

Quinta etapa: verificación final

Se compara el número de documentos restaurados con el número registrado durante el respaldo.

De esta manera, el procedimiento no termina únicamente después de insertar información, sino que incorpora una validación adicional.

Importante: la restauración predeterminada elimina los documentos existentes en las colecciones incluidas en el respaldo antes de volver a insertarlos. Por ello, debe ejecutarse sobre una base de datos de prueba o bajo un procedimiento de recuperación previamente autorizado.

8. Pruebas automatizadas del sistema

Para demostrar que los respaldos funcionan, incorporamos pruebas automatizadas utilizando las herramientas de Node.js.

Estas pruebas se encuentran en:

test/backup.test.js

Una de las pruebas genera una colección de 2501 documentos, incluyendo valores especiales de MongoDB.

Después crea un respaldo, elimina la colección de prueba y ejecuta la restauración.

Finalmente, verifica que se hayan recuperado correctamente los documentos, sus tipos y el índice configurado.

También incorporamos otras pruebas para comprobar:

  • Que la política de retención conserve únicamente la cantidad de respaldos configurada.
  • Que un archivo modificado sea rechazado por una verificación SHA-256 incorrecta.
  • Que los registros recuperados mantengan los tipos de datos originales.

El comando para ejecutar estas pruebas es:

npm test

Estas verificaciones son importantes porque permiten identificar errores en el proceso de recuperación antes de utilizar el sistema con información relevante.

Una de nuestras principales conclusiones técnicas fue que un respaldo es realmente útil cuando se ha comprobado que puede restaurarse.

9. Automatización de backups mediante GitHub Actions

Una vez implementado el sistema de respaldo, el siguiente objetivo fue evitar que su ejecución dependiera de una persona.

Para ello configuramos GitHub Actions mediante el archivo:

.github/workflows/backup.yml

Este workflow utiliza una programación automática:

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 5 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

La expresión cron programa el respaldo diariamente a las 05:00 UTC, equivalente a las 00:00 en Perú.

También incorporamos workflow_dispatch, que permite iniciar manualmente el proceso desde GitHub.

¿Qué hace el workflow?

El flujo realiza las siguientes actividades:

  1. Descarga el código desde el repositorio.
  2. Prepara Node.js e instala las dependencias.
  3. Se conecta a MongoDB Atlas y genera el respaldo lógico.
  4. Restaura el respaldo en una instancia temporal de MongoDB para verificarlo.
  5. Prepara un archivo comprimido y aplica cifrado AES-256 cuando está configurada la contraseña de respaldo.
  6. Publica el archivo como artefacto de GitHub Actions, con una retención configurada de 30 días.

La conexión a MongoDB Atlas utiliza credenciales almacenadas en GitHub Secrets.

Para el cifrado se utiliza el secreto BACKUP_PASSPHRASE.

En la configuración actual, el workflow permite continuar sin cifrar si ese secreto no está definido y genera una advertencia. Para un entorno de producción sería recomendable exigir obligatoriamente su configuración y detener la publicación cuando falte.

Esta automatización representa una mejora importante respecto a generar respaldos manualmente, porque permite incorporar el procedimiento a una rutina programada y verificable.

10. Integración continua y despliegue en Render

Además de los respaldos, desarrollamos un segundo workflow encargado de realizar pruebas y automatizar la publicación de la aplicación.

Este archivo se encuentra en:

.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

El proceso comienza cuando se realizan cambios en el repositorio.

Funcionamiento del pipeline

1. Validación del código

GitHub Actions prepara un entorno de ejecución y ejecuta las pruebas automatizadas contra un servicio temporal de MongoDB.

2. Construcción con Docker

Cuando las pruebas finalizan satisfactoriamente, se construye una imagen Docker como comprobación de que la aplicación puede empaquetarse correctamente.

3. Despliegue automatizado

Si el cambio corresponde a la rama principal, GitHub Actions utiliza el deploy hook de Render para solicitar una nueva publicación.

4. Verificación del servicio

El pipeline consulta el endpoint:

/health

Este endpoint permite verificar que el servidor responda y pueda establecer comunicación con MongoDB.

Gracias a este procedimiento, la publicación está vinculada al resultado de las pruebas.

Aplicación desplegada

Nuestra aplicación utiliza MongoDB Atlas como servicio de base de datos y Render para ejecutar el servidor Node.js.

Se puede acceder desde:

https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com

La configuración de infraestructura de Render se encuentra declarada en render.yaml, lo que facilita reproducir la configuración del servicio.

11. Cómo ejecutar el proyecto localmente

El repositorio incluye un entorno configurado con Docker Compose.

Para obtener el proyecto se puede utilizar:

git clone https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy.git

cd NoSQL-Backup-Strategy

Posteriormente, se inicia la aplicación y la base de datos local:

docker compose up -d --build

Para cargar los datos de demostración:

docker compose exec app node scripts/seed.js

El sistema incorpora cinco productos de ejemplo, como una laptop, un monitor y accesorios informáticos, además de registros de clientes.

Después podemos ingresar a:

http://localhost:3000

Para comprobar el funcionamiento de las pruebas automatizadas dentro del contenedor:

docker compose exec app npm test

También es posible generar un respaldo manual:

docker compose exec app npm run backup

Y restaurarlo en una base de datos local independiente, evitando modificar los registros originales:

docker compose exec -e DB_NAME=tienda_restaurada app npm run restore

Estos comandos permiten explorar el funcionamiento del proyecto y comprender el ciclo de respaldo y recuperación utilizando un entorno de desarrollo aislado.

12. Resultados y aprendizajes obtenidos

El desarrollo de esta solución nos permitió integrar diferentes conocimientos del curso de Base de Datos II.

Entre los principales resultados alcanzados destacan:

  • Implementación de una aplicación web conectada a MongoDB Atlas.
  • Desarrollo de mecanismos de respaldo lógico de documentos NoSQL.
  • Conservación de tipos BSON utilizando EJSON.
  • Compresión de respaldos y verificación mediante SHA-256.
  • Recuperación de documentos e índices.
  • Pruebas automatizadas para validar integridad y restauración.
  • Configuración de procesos programados mediante GitHub Actions.
  • Integración de Docker y despliegue automatizado en Render.

Uno de los aprendizajes más importantes fue comprender que la protección de datos no consiste únicamente en guardar archivos.

Es necesario considerar la frecuencia de los respaldos, la seguridad de las credenciales, la integridad de la información y los procedimientos que se seguirán ante una pérdida de datos.

También identificamos oportunidades de mejora, como incorporar alertas ante fallos de ejecución, exigir siempre el cifrado y almacenar copias adicionales en servicios independientes.

Para escenarios de mayor escala también sería necesario evaluar mecanismos de respaldo que proporcionen garantías de consistencia durante escrituras concurrentes y opciones de recuperación a un punto específico en el tiempo.

13. Conclusiones

El desarrollo de este proyecto nos permitió comprender la importancia de implementar estrategias de respaldo y recuperación para bases de datos NoSQL alojadas en la nube.

En primer lugar, comprobamos que MongoDB Atlas puede integrarse con aplicaciones web desarrolladas mediante Node.js y Express, ofreciendo una plataforma adecuada para gestionar información documental.

En segundo lugar, la implementación de respaldos mediante EJSON, compresión gzip y verificaciones SHA-256 nos permitió conocer diferentes mecanismos que contribuyen a preservar la información y detectar posibles alteraciones.

Finalmente, la incorporación de GitHub Actions y Render demostró cómo las prácticas de automatización pueden aplicarse tanto a la publicación de aplicaciones como a los procedimientos de protección de datos.

La experiencia nos ayudó a fortalecer nuestros conocimientos sobre bases de datos NoSQL, desarrollo web, integración continua, despliegue automatizado y recuperación ante fallos.

El principal aprendizaje es que una estrategia de backup no debe limitarse a generar copias, sino que también debe garantizar procedimientos verificables para recuperar la información cuando sea necesario.

Referencias y documentación

Para comprender las tecnologías utilizadas, pueden consultarse las siguientes fuentes oficiales:

  • MongoDB Documentation — Bases de datos, BSON, respaldos y restauración.
  • GitHub Actions Documentation — Automatización de workflows y ejecución programada.
  • Render Documentation — Despliegue de servicios web y configuración de infraestructura.
  • Node.js Documentation — Desarrollo de aplicaciones y procesamiento de archivos.

Créditos del proyecto

Artículo elaborado por: Ana Cecilia Esteban Ramos.

Proyecto desarrollado en equipo por:

  • Ana Cecilia Esteban Ramos.
  • Saúl José Alvarado Urbano.

Curso: Base de Datos II.

Institución: Universidad Privada de Tacna.

Repositorio del proyecto: https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy

Aplicación desplegada: https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com

Este proyecto fue desarrollado como una experiencia práctica para aplicar conceptos de bases de datos NoSQL, estrategias de respaldo, restauración y automatización de servicios en la nube.

¡Gracias por leer! Espero que nuestra experiencia resulte útil para estudiantes y desarrolladores interesados en implementar mecanismos de protección y recuperación de datos mediante tecnologías modernas.

title: TypeScript `Omit` vs `Pick` vs `Exclude` in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing
description:
TypeScript Omit vs Pick vs Exclude in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers reach for Omit when they need Pick, apply Exclude to object types that need Omit, and ship code that compiles cleanly but accepts any string literal as a property name. TypeScript provides six property-manipulation utilities that look similar but operate on fundamentally different input shapes. The confusion costs hours in debugging sessions where the compiler stays silent while the runtime produces undefined values.

The root problem is naming. Pick and Omit transform object types. Exclude and Extract filter union types. No visual or naming convention signals which category each utility belongs to, so developers test by trial until the compiler accepts the syntax. The correct approach groups utilities by input shape first, then checks whether the operation adds or removes members.

Key Takeaways

  • Pick and Omit operate on object types by selecting or removing properties; Exclude and Extract operate on union types by filtering members.
  • Omit accepts any string literal without checking if the property exists, allowing typos to compile successfully while producing incorrect types.
  • Decision framework: check the input shape (object vs union) before choosing the utility, then decide whether the operation should include or remove members.
  • Strict variants from type-zoo (PickStrict, OmitStrict) enforce property existence at compile time, catching typos and refactoring oversights.
  • Object utilities preserve structure and return new object types; union utilities return new unions with fewer or different members.

Pick vs Omit: Object Property Selection

Pick<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by selecting a subset of properties from an existing object type. The operation requires two inputs: the source object type and a string literal or union of string literals naming the properties to extract. TypeScript introduced Pick in version 2.1 alongside Partial, Readonly, and Record.

interface UserAccount {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  lastLogin: Date;
  preferences: Record<string, unknown>;
}

type PublicProfile = Pick<UserAccount, "id" | "email" | "createdAt">;

const profile: PublicProfile = {
  id: "usr_123",
  email: "user@example.com",
  createdAt: new Date("2026-01-15"),
};

The pattern fits API response types where the backend returns a subset of database columns. GraphQL resolvers often return fragments that match a Pick type exactly. The alternative approach requires duplicating property definitions across multiple interfaces, which creates maintenance burden when field types change.

Omit<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by removing specified properties from an existing object type. TypeScript added Omit in version 3.5 as the inverse of Pick. The operation accepts the same input types but produces the complement set of properties.

type UserUpdatePayload = Omit<UserAccount, "id" | "createdAt">;

function updateUser(userId: string, updates: UserUpdatePayload) {
  // Implementation accepts all fields except immutable ones
}

The comparison reveals a structural difference beyond inclusion versus exclusion. Pick forces developers to list exactly what the new type contains. Omit forces developers to list what the new type excludes. The cognitive load shifts based on whether the remaining properties or the excluded properties form a shorter list.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Pick Object type Select named properties New object type with subset API responses, public interfaces
Omit Object type Remove named properties New object type without exclusions Update payloads, sensitive data removal

The decision between Pick and Omit depends on which list is shorter and which intent is clearer. A type that needs 2 properties from a 10-property interface uses Pick. A type that needs 8 properties from a 10-property interface uses Omit. Neither choice affects runtime behavior or compilation output, but the shorter list reduces maintenance surface area.

TypeScript utility types decision matrix

Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filtering

Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers> constructs a new union by removing all members from UnionType that are assignable to ExcludedMembers. TypeScript introduced Exclude in version 2.8 as part of a set of conditional type utilities. The operation works on union types exclusively and fails when applied to object types.

type HTTPMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";
type ReadOnlyMethod = Exclude<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function fetchData(method: ReadOnlyMethod, url: string) {
  // Only GET requests compile
}

Extract<Type, Union> constructs a new union by selecting all members from Type that are assignable to Union. The operation inverts Exclude by keeping matching members instead of removing them. Both utilities appeared in the same TypeScript release as complementary tools.

type MutatingMethod = Extract<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function modifyResource(method: MutatingMethod, url: string, body: unknown) {
  // GET fails to compile
}

The confusion between object utilities and union utilities stems from overlapping terminology. "Exclude" and "Omit" both remove things. "Extract" and "Pick" both select things. The critical distinction is input shape: object types have named properties, union types have discrete members. TypeScript enforces this boundary at compile time but provides no naming convention to signal the category.

The pattern fits discriminated unions where runtime logic branches on a subset of possible values. State machines often use Extract to constrain valid transitions from a given state. Event handlers use Exclude to prevent certain event types from reaching sensitive code paths.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Exclude Union type Remove matching members New union without exclusions Restricting valid values, state machines
Extract Union type Keep matching members New union with only matches Filtering event types, permission checks

Real-World Code Examples: API Response Types

Backend services often return nested JSON structures where different endpoints expose different subsets of the same entity. TypeScript utility types model these variations without duplicating property definitions. Consider a user service that stores comprehensive account data but exposes sanitized versions through public APIs.

interface DatabaseUser {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  passwordSalt: string;
  totpSecret: string | null;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
  emailVerified: boolean;
  roles: Array<"admin" | "moderator" | "user">;
  loginAttempts: number;
  lastLoginIp: string | null;
  preferences: {
    theme: "light" | "dark";
    notifications: boolean;
  };
}

type PublicUserProfile = Pick<
  DatabaseUser,
  "id" | "email" | "emailVerified" | "createdAt" | "preferences"
>;

type AdminUserView = Omit<DatabaseUser, "passwordHash" | "passwordSalt" | "totpSecret">;

type UserUpdateRequest = Partial<
  Pick<DatabaseUser, "email" | "preferences">
>;

type AuthenticationResponse = Pick<DatabaseUser, "id" | "email" | "roles"> & {
  token: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

The composition demonstrates layering: Pick extracts the base structure, Partial makes fields optional for update operations, and intersection types add authentication metadata. Each derived type maintains a single source of truth for property shapes while modeling different access patterns.

Role-based filtering uses union utilities to constrain valid permission sets. The backend defines an exhaustive permission list as a union type, then uses Extract to model role-specific capabilities.

type Permission =
  | "users:read"
  | "users:write"
  | "users:delete"
  | "posts:read"
  | "posts:write"
  | "posts:delete"
  | "analytics:read"
  | "settings:write";

type UserPermissions = Extract<Permission, `users:${string}`>;
type PostPermissions = Extract<Permission, `posts:${string}`>;
type ReadOnlyPermissions = Extract<Permission, `${string}:read`>;

function checkPermission(
  userRole: "admin" | "moderator" | "user",
  required: Permission
): boolean {
  const rolePermissions: Record<string, Permission[]> = {
    admin: [
      "users:read", "users:write", "users:delete",
      "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete",
      "analytics:read", "settings:write"
    ],
    moderator: [
      "users:read", "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete"
    ],
    user: ["posts:read"]
  };

  return rolePermissions[userRole].includes(required);
}

The pattern works because Extract with template literal types filters by pattern matching. The result maintains type safety while avoiding string manipulation at runtime. Frontend code uses these derived types to conditionally render UI elements based on user permissions.

TypeScript utility types in production code

The Silent Bug: Why Omit Doesn't Catch Typos

Omit accepts any string literal in its second type parameter without verifying that the property exists on the source type. TypeScript designed this behavior intentionally to support mapped types and conditional logic, but the permissiveness creates a maintenance hazard. A typo in the excluded property list compiles successfully and produces an incorrect output type.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Typo: "header" instead of "headers"
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "header">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, // Still required
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The code compiles without warnings. CleanResponse still contains the headers property because Omit silently ignored the nonexistent header property. The bug surfaces only when downstream code expects headers to be absent and receives an unexpected value at runtime. The compiler provides no indication that the exclusion list contains an invalid property name.

Refactoring compounds the issue. When a property name changes in the source interface, Omit calls that reference the old name continue to compile. The type system cannot detect that an excluded property no longer exists because Omit treats the exclusion list as an open set of string literals rather than a constrained subset of known properties.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  responseHeaders: Record<string, string>; // Renamed from "headers"
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Stale reference compiles successfully
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "headers">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  responseHeaders: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The workaround requires strict variants that check property existence at compile time. The type-zoo package provides OmitStrict, PickStrict, and similar utilities that fail compilation when property names do not exist on the source type. These variants add a constraint that maps the exclusion list to actual keys.

import { OmitStrict } from "type-zoo";

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Compilation error: "header" does not exist on ApiResponse
type CleanResponse = OmitStrict<ApiResponse, "header">;

The tradeoff is explicit. Standard Omit supports dynamic property exclusion and conditional types at the cost of safety. Strict variants enforce correctness but require all excluded properties to exist in the source type. Teams must choose between flexibility and type safety based on codebase size and refactoring frequency. For more on union filtering, see TypeScript Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filters Explained.

Practical Decision Framework: Which Utility When

The selection process starts with input shape classification. Object types with named properties use Pick or Omit. Union types with discrete members use Exclude or Extract. Applying union utilities to object types produces compilation errors because union operations expect string literals, not property access patterns.

interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

// Error: Type 'Config' does not satisfy constraint 'string | number | symbol'
type InvalidExclusion = Exclude<Config, "apiKey">;

Once the input shape category is correct, the second decision is inclusion versus exclusion. Count the properties or union members in each set. If the desired output contains fewer members than the exclusions, use the inclusive utility (Pick or Extract). If the exclusions form a shorter list, use the exclusive utility (Omit or Exclude).

The third consideration is change frequency. Types that evolve frequently benefit from inclusion-based utilities because adding a new property to the source type does not automatically add it to derived types. Exclusion-based utilities require explicit updates when new properties should be excluded.

Error messages guide correction. TypeScript reports different errors for category mismatches versus property name issues. Union utilities applied to object types produce constraint violation errors. Pick applied with nonexistent property names produces "does not exist on type" errors, while Omit accepts any string literal without complaint.

Decision factor Pick/Extract Omit/Exclude
List length Desired output is shorter than source Exclusions are shorter than output
Change frequency New properties default to excluded New properties default to included
Type safety Pick enforces property existence Omit accepts any string literal
Maintenance Explicit about included members Explicit about excluded members

The framework applies recursively to composed types. A type that uses both Pick and Partial applies each utility in sequence: first extract the desired properties, then mark them optional. The order matters because Partial operates on whatever type it receives as input.

interface FormData {
  username: string;
  email: string;
  password: string;
  confirmPassword: string;
  agreedToTerms: boolean;
}

// Extract fields, then make them optional
type PartialUpdate = Partial<Pick<FormData, "email" | "password">>;

// Equivalent to:
type PartialUpdate = {
  email?: string;
  password?: string;
};

Strict Variants and Type-Zoo Alternatives

Production TypeScript often combines standard utility types with custom mapped types to enforce stricter constraints. The type-zoo package provides battle-tested implementations of strict variants that catch common errors at compile time. Teams can implement these patterns inline or install the package as a development dependency.

OmitStrict requires that all excluded properties exist on the source type. The implementation uses a mapped type to check each key against the source type's keys before performing the exclusion.

type OmitStrict<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;

interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
}

// Compilation error: "password" is not assignable to "id" | "email" | "passwordHash"
type InvalidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "password">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "passwordHash">;

The constraint K extends keyof T forces TypeScript to verify that every property in K exists in T before allowing the type to compile. This catches typos immediately and fails compilation when refactoring renames properties without updating all Omit callsites.

PickStrict provides similar guarantees for property selection. The standard library's Pick already enforces key existence because it must access those properties to include them in the output type. The strict variant adds no additional constraint but maintains naming consistency with other strict utilities.

Union type filtering benefits from strict variants when the exclusion list might contain invalid members. ExcludeStrict enforces that all excluded members exist in the source union before performing the exclusion. The implementation requires a helper type that checks membership.

type ExcludeStrict<T, U extends T> = Exclude<T, U>;

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected";

// Compilation error: "cancelled" is not assignable to Status
type InvalidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "cancelled">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "rejected">;

The constraint U extends T ensures that every member of the exclusion union U is also a member of the source union T. This prevents situations where exclusion lists accumulate stale values after refactoring removes union members.

Teams should adopt strict variants when the codebase meets two criteria. First, the type system must enforce correctness rather than providing flexibility for dynamic types. Second, compile-time checks must catch refactoring oversights before they reach production. Codebases that prioritize rapid prototyping over type safety may find standard utilities sufficient. For related patterns, see TypeScript Partial, Required, DeepPartial: Optional Properties That Scale.

The installation adds zero runtime overhead because all utility types disappear during compilation. The package provides TypeScript definitions only and contains no JavaScript code. Development teams can audit the implementation by reading the source code, which consists entirely of type aliases and mapped types. For a broader overview, see 10 TypeScript Utility Types That Catch Bugs Before Production.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I use Exclude on an object type instead of a union?

TypeScript produces a compilation error stating that the type does not satisfy the constraint string | number | symbol. Exclude operates exclusively on union types and cannot remove properties from object shapes. Use Omit for object property removal.

Does Pick enforce that all specified properties exist on the source type?

Yes. Pick requires that every property name in the second type parameter exists as a key on the source type. TypeScript enforces this constraint with K extends keyof T, which means attempting to pick nonexistent properties produces a compilation error immediately.

Can Omit remove optional properties from an interface?

Yes. Omit removes any property regardless of whether it was required or optional in the source type. The operation works at the structural level and does not distinguish between required and optional properties when deciding what to exclude.

Why does OmitStrict exist when Pick already enforces key existence?

Pick enforces constraints on included properties because it must access them to construct the output type. Omit accepts any string literal as an exclusion without verification, allowing typos to compile successfully. OmitStrict adds the same constraint that Pick has natively, catching excluded property typos at compile time.

When should I use Extract instead of Pick?

Use Extract when filtering members from a union type. Use Pick when selecting properties from an object type. The operations are incompatible because unions contain discrete values while objects contain named properties. TypeScript enforces this distinction through different generic constraints on each utility.

Conclusion

TypeScript utility types operate on two distinct categories: object types with named properties and union types with discrete members. Pick and Omit transform objects. Exclude and Extract filter unions. The selection process checks input shape first, then counts members to decide between inclusion and exclusion utilities. Standard Omit accepts any string literal without verification, allowing typos and stale property names to compile successfully while producing incorrect types. Strict variants enforce property existence at compile time, trading flexibility for compile-time safety in codebases where refactoring frequency justifies the constraint. Teams that adopt this classification framework stop guessing which utility applies and start building type-safe transformations that catch errors before they reach production.

  • TypeScript: Playground Example - Built-in Utility Types

title: Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.
description:
Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.

Let's be honest. How often do you update your database diagram after changing your database?

You add a table, introduce a relationship, rename a column or refactor an existing module. Your application evolves, your database changes, and your documentation slowly falls behind.

The problem isn't creating database diagrams. There are plenty of tools for that.

The problem is keeping them updated.

A common solution is to export a diagram as an image and commit it to your repository. It works, but the moment your schema changes, the image becomes outdated.

And someone eventually has to remember to replace it.

There is a better approach: put your database diagram directly in your GitHub README and let it update automatically.

Why database documentation gets outdated

Most development teams understand the importance of database documentation.

A diagram helps developers:

  • Understand how tables relate to each other.
  • Explore an unfamiliar codebase.
  • Identify dependencies before changing existing structures.
  • Onboard new developers.
  • Discuss database architecture with the rest of the team.

But maintaining that documentation introduces another task into an already busy development workflow.

Consider a typical Laravel application.

You start with users, roles and permissions. Later, you introduce subscriptions, invoices, payments and notifications.

Your migrations are updated, your application works, and everything gets committed.

But the database diagram?

It still shows the original structure.

Eventually, developers stop trusting it.

Put your database diagram directly in GitHub

With SchemaSketch, you can now embed a live database diagram directly into a GitHub README.

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Create your database diagram

Go to SchemaSketch and create a diagram using DBML.

DBML is a simple language for describing database structures.

For example:

Table users {
  id integer [primary key]
  name varchar
  email varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table projects {
  id integer [primary key]
  user_id integer
  name varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table tasks {
  id integer [primary key]
  project_id integer
  title varchar
  status varchar
}

Ref: projects.user_id > users.id
Ref: tasks.project_id > projects.id

SchemaSketch renders the database structure visually, allowing you to explore tables and their relationships.

You can also export your schema into SQL, Laravel migrations and models, Mermaid or PlantUML.

Step 2: Share your diagram

Once your diagram is ready, open the Share dialog.

Make the diagram publicly accessible and select Copy Markdown.

SchemaSketch generates the Markdown required to embed your diagram.

Step 3: Add it to your README

Open your GitHub repository and edit its README.md file.

Paste the Markdown you copied from SchemaSketch wherever you want the diagram to appear.

Commit your changes.

That's it.

Your database diagram is now part of your repository documentation.

Step 4: Let it update automatically

This is the interesting part.

The embedded diagram is served as an SVG image.

It automatically supports GitHub's light and dark themes, so readers can view it comfortably regardless of their interface settings.

More importantly, when you update your diagram in SchemaSketch, the embedded image updates automatically, usually within approximately five minutes.

You don't need to export another image.

You don't need to replace anything in GitHub.

You don't need another commit just to update the documentation image.

If you make the diagram private or revoke its sharing link, the embedded image is no longer accessible.

What does this look like?

Imagine opening a repository and finding this:

Project Database Architecture

Your actual database diagram, showing users, projects, tasks and all their relationships.

A new developer can understand the database structure without having to open another application or search for an old diagram.

And when the database design changes, the README follows.

No separate image files to maintain.

No manual exports.

No outdated screenshots.

More than just database diagrams

The live README integration is one of several improvements we've recently introduced to SchemaSketch.

There are a few other things worth mentioning.

An open-source DBML renderer

We've released the drawing engine as schemasketch-render, an npm package.

It is MIT licensed, has no dependencies and supports Node.js 18 and above.

You can use it to render DBML into SVG independently.

For example, this makes it possible to generate database diagram images as part of your own development or CI workflows.

Repository and package:

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/schemasketch-render
  • GitHub: https://github.com/SchemaSketch-dev/

More AI coding agent integrations

SchemaSketch also supports more AI coding environments through its agent plugin.

The plugin provides integrations for:

  • Codex
  • Cursor
  • Devin
  • Windsurf
  • Gemini CLI
  • Antigravity

GitHub Copilot CLI and Kiro can use the same plugin's skill, with an additional MCP server configuration.

Claude Code and Claude Desktop already support a one-command setup.

Through the SchemaSketch MCP server, AI agents can work with database diagrams rather than relying entirely on assumptions when generating application code.

More information: https://schemasketch.dev/mcp#clients

Better support for real-world DBML

We've also improved compatibility with DBML structures commonly found in existing projects.

This includes:

  • PostgreSQL-style schemas, such as billing.invoices.
  • Relationships across schemas.
  • Named foreign key constraints.
  • Composite foreign keys.
  • Composite primary keys.
  • UNIQUE constraints.
  • CREATE INDEX statements in SQL exports.

The goal is to make working with existing database designs easier, not just diagrams created from scratch.

Documentation should evolve with your application

A database diagram shouldn't be something you create once, export and eventually forget.

It should be part of your development workflow.

Whether you're maintaining a Laravel application, working with PostgreSQL or building software with AI coding agents, having an accessible and current representation of your database makes a difference.

That's what we're trying to make easier with SchemaSketch.

Try it for free:

https://schemasketch.dev

Your database changes. Your documentation should keep up.

title: A small Node.js fixture for incomplete streaming tool arguments
description:
AI-assisted draft prepared for the AI Relay Check account. The examples below use local fixtures.

Valid JSON can still miss a required tool argument. If a stream ends early, the same tool may never receive a complete invocation. A local fixture separates argument parsing from the backend, and it can be run before testing a paid route.

Start with a tool whose required arguments are a string named label and an integer named count. Use known values and check the results before executing any tool.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

function readFixtureArguments(chunks, complete) {
  if (!complete) throw new Error("Incomplete tool invocation");
  const args = JSON.parse(chunks.join(""));
  if (args.label !== "sample" || args.count !== 2) {
    throw new Error("Unexpected tool arguments");
  }
  return args;
}

assert.deepEqual(readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",', '"count":2}'], true),
  { label: "sample", count: 2 });
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample"}'], true), /Unexpected/);
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",'], false), /Incomplete/);

In a live client, set the completion flag from the actual protocol event and associate fragments with the correct invocation ID. Then return a mock result and confirm the model continues using that result. A transport-level HTTP 200 alone cannot validate the tool workflow.

title: How I Built a Financial Literacy App with React, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL
description:
Tags (pick these four): react, python, webdev, beginners

Body:

I built Compound, a financial literacy app that teaches things like compound interest, investing basics, and fees through short lessons, quizzes, and calculators. Here's how it's put together and what tripped me up along the way.

What it does

• A lesson path with quizzes that explain why each answer is right
• Calculators for compound interest, DCA, FIRE number, fee impact, mortgage breakdown, inflation hedge, and portfolio building
• Completion certificates
• Family accounts

The stack

• Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel
• Backend: FastAPI + PostgreSQL, deployed on Railway
• Auth: JWT
• Content loading: a protected /admin/seed endpoint that loads the lessons

Three things that tripped me up

  1. "vite: command not found" on Vercel.
    My deploy failed with vite build exited with 127. Exit code 127 means "command not found." My app lives in a frontend/ folder, but Vercel was building from the top of the repo, where there's no package.json, so it never even ran npm install. The fix was one setting: Project Settings → Build and Deployment → Root Directory → frontend.

  2. Keep secrets out of the repo.
    I use .env.example files with placeholder values and keep the real values in my host's environment variables. Before sharing the code, I exported a clean copy with git archive and searched it for .env files, keys, and connection strings. It's a quick check and worth doing every time.

  3. Rotate secrets at the source.
    After my hosting provider disclosed a security incident, I replaced my keys and passwords. The lesson: changing a value in your dashboard isn't enough. Revoke the old key with whoever issued it, or it may still work.

Try it

Live demo: https://compound-frontend-seven.vercel.app

If you'd like the source code to learn from or start your own project, it's available here (one-project license): https://dmlrod.gumroad.com/l/hdcon

What would you add? I'd love to hear what other developers would build into a learning app like this.
