title: A Go web service on a free container tier: a 15 MB image and tens of megabytes of RAM
description:
TL;DR: A net/http service with a health endpoint, graceful shutdown and the port read from the environment, built by a two-stage Dockerfile into a 7 MB binary and an image around 15 MB. What it uses at runtime on 512 MB and a quarter of a CPU, how to add a database without adding bloat, how to embed static files in the binary, and what sleep looks like in the logs.

If a free container tier was designed for one language, it was Go. A Go web service compiles to a single static binary, starts in milliseconds and idles in a few tens of megabytes, so 512 MB and a quarter of a CPU is not a constraint, it is a surplus. This guide builds a small HTTP service the way it should be built for a container: a two-stage Dockerfile, a tiny image, a health endpoint, graceful shutdown, and the port read from the environment.

The service

Standard library only. net/http is enough for most services and it keeps the binary small. Go 1.22 and later route by method and path pattern, so no router package is needed for this:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    port := os.Getenv("PORT")
    if port == "" {
        port = "8080"
    }

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /health", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
        w.Write([]byte("ok"))
    })
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /api/time", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"now": time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)})
    })

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:              ":" + port,
        Handler:           mux,
        ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }

    go func() {
        log.Printf("listening on :%s", port)
        if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && err != http.ErrServerClosed {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
    }()

    stop := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    signal.Notify(stop, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
    <-stop

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    log.Println("shutting down")
    srv.Shutdown(ctx)
}

Three things in there earn their keep on a container host. PORT from the environment, so the platform decides the port.

ReadHeaderTimeout, so a slow client cannot hold a connection open forever on a small instance. And the SIGTERM handler: when a container is stopped, or a free container goes to sleep after 15 minutes without traffic, the runtime sends SIGTERM first; a server that shuts down cleanly finishes in-flight requests instead of dropping them.

The Dockerfile 

FROM golang:1-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum* ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates && adduser -D -u 10001 app
USER app
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
  • golang:1-alpine tracks the current Go 1.x release, so the tag does not go stale. Pin golang:1.27-alpine if you want reproducible builds.
  • CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a static binary; -s -w strips symbols and debug info. The service above builds to roughly 7 MB.
  • The final image is Alpine plus certificates plus the binary: about 15 MB. scratch would be smaller still, but Alpine gives you a shell for debugging and the CA bundle for outbound HTTPS.
  • Running as a non-root user costs nothing and is the first thing a security scan looks for.

If you deploy without a Dockerfile, SnapDeploy generates one when it sees go.mod: a two-stage build with CGO_ENABLED=0 onto an Alpine runtime, much like the above. The generated builder uses a Go 1.21 image; if your go.mod declares a newer Go, the toolchain directive downloads it during the build. For control over the version, keep your own Dockerfile.

What it uses at runtime

Measured on the service above: about 10 MB of resident memory idle, under 30 MB while handling a few hundred requests a second, and start-up in well under a second. Against a 512 MB container that leaves room for in-memory caches, a SQLite file for read-mostly data, or an embedded queue, none of which a Node or JVM service could afford in the same box. Wake-up on the free tier is about 60 seconds, but almost all of that is the platform starting the container; the Go process itself is ready as soon as it is scheduled.

If you want to see the numbers yourself, GODEBUG=gctrace=1 prints heap sizes at each collection, and /proc/self/status inside the container shows VmRSS.

Deploying

  1. Push the repository to GitHub with the Dockerfile.
  2. In SnapDeploy, Containers → Deploy from GitHub → choose the repository. Confirm the port (8080 here).
  3. Deploy. Go builds are quick; the first build is a few minutes because the base images are pulled and modules downloaded, later builds reuse the cached module layer.
  4. Hit /health on the containers.snapdeploy.app URL, then /api/time.

When Go still needs more than the free tier

  • It has to answer at any hour. Free containers sleep after 15 minutes without traffic. Always-On Small is $12/month for the same 512 MB; a Go service rarely needs the 2 GB Medium.
  • It needs a database that persists. The container filesystem is ephemeral, so the SQLite trick above is for caches and read-only data. PostgreSQL Mini is $29/month; a $1 DB Sprint Pack gives you 12 hours of it to test against.
  • It needs a custom domain. Always-On again; free containers live on containers.snapdeploy.app.

Adding a database without adding bloat

The one dependency most services need is a database driver. With pgx the binary grows by a few megabytes and the service still idles well under 30 MB. Read the connection string from DATABASE_URL, which a SnapDeploy add-on injects and every other provider gives you to paste, and keep the pool small: a free container will never need more than a handful of connections, and a PostgreSQL Mini allows 50 in total.

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
cfg.MaxConns = 4
pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)

Make the health handler run pool.Ping(ctx) with a one-second timeout. When the container wakes after sleeping, the first request will re-establish the pool; a ping with a timeout turns a hung database into a clear 503 instead of a slow page.

Static files inside the binary

If the service also serves a small front end, the embed package puts the files into the executable, so the image stays one binary and there is nothing to copy or mount:

//go:embed static/*
var static embed.FS

mux.Handle("GET /", http.FileServerFS(static))

Go 1.22 added http.FileServerFS; on older versions use http.FileServer(http.FS(static)). Either way the files are read from memory, which is the fastest static file server you will run on a quarter of a CPU.

What sleep looks like in the logs

Because the service handles SIGTERM, a container going to sleep after 15 quiet minutes leaves a clean trail: shutting down, then the process exits with code 0. A service that ignores the signal is killed after the platform's stop timeout and exits with code 137, which looks like a crash in the logs and drops any request that was in flight. Ten lines of shutdown code are the difference between "sleeps politely" and "keeps dying every night" when you read the runtime log a week later.

Free tier: 4 containers, 512 MB and 0.25 vCPU each, 100 container-hours a month, 10 deploys a day, no card. Details on the free tier docs page; the Docker hosting page covers what happens when you bring your own image instead of a repository.

title: Giga Energy Secures $1 Billion AI Cloud Deal for 60 MW Data Center in Hunting County, Texas
description:
U.S.-based AI data center developer Giga Energy has signed a 10-year, USD 1 billion lease with an unnamed AI cloud provider for Project Clay, a 60 MW GigaBase AI data center campus in Hunt County, Texas.

Giga broke ground on the project in July and will develop, own, and operate the campus, which the customer will use for AI computing capacity. The site is slated to be ready for service in spring 2027.

*GigaBase Targets Faster Data Center Deployment
*
Alongside the lease announcement, Giga officially unveiled GigaBase, its data center system engineered to tackle lengthy construction timelines, heavy water consumption, and strain on local utilities.

As part of its expansion into Data Center Projects in the US, the company says Project Clay will be completed in under eight months, less than half the time of traditional builds.

Power Strategy Taps Underutilized Capacity
A cornerstone of the project is an investment in new electrical infrastructure that draws on underutilized capacity from dedicated power infrastructure in the county.

The design ensures the campus does not pull from distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses.

Giga positioned the project against the priorities laid out by Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has called for data centers to pay for their own power, deploy water-efficient cooling technologies, prevent infrastructure costs from shifting onto residents, and ensure communities benefit from growth.

This is exactly the kind of AI infrastructure Texas needs," said Brent Whitehead, president and co-founder at Giga Energy.

"Communities shouldn't have to choose between economic growth and protecting local resources. We've engineered our GigaBase system and development approach so they don't have to."

Cooling System Runs Independently of Local Water
Project Clay replaces open-loop evaporative cooling with a fully closed-loop system that operates independently of local water supplies, whether municipal or groundwater, to cool its IT equipment.

According to the company, the facility consumes no water for compute operations.
The only local water use will come from sinks and employee bathrooms, comparable to a small business office and on par with the annual usage of two homes. Giga frames this approach as aligning with Texas' growing emphasis on water-efficient data center development in drought-prone regions.

Jobs and Tax Revenue Head to Hunt County

The roughly 30-acre campus will serve hyperscale and AI cloud customers while, according to Giga, generating lasting economic value for the county.

The build phase is expected to create approximately 300 construction jobs, with 24 permanent full-time positions carrying estimated annual salaries of USD 116,000 to USD 180,000.

The project is also projected to generate millions in new recurring annual tax revenue that the company says can help fund local schools, infrastructure, emergency services, and other essential public needs.
"We believe AI infrastructure should leave a community stronger than it found it. That means creating high-paying jobs, expanding the local tax base, and making long-term investments that benefit residents for decades," said Whitehead.

"Hunt County is gaining an economic engine that will support schools, public services, and future growth for generations."

*Off-Site Manufacturing Drives the Schedule
*
At the heart of the GigaBase system is a factory-first construction model in which much of the facility is manufactured off-site before final assembly in the community.

Giga says this approach significantly shortens construction schedules, reduces truck traffic, minimizes disruption to local roads and housing, and allows communities to realize economic benefits sooner.
The company describes the resulting campus as faster to build, lighter on local infrastructure, and purpose-built to be a long-term community partner.

Giga has previously promoted the concept under the banner "shovel-ready to rack-ready in 9 months" when introducing the GigaBase system.

Company Background and the Deal's Significance

Giga Energy is a U.S.-based manufacturer, developer, and operator of modular AI data centers, actively contributing to the growth of data center projects and infrastructure development in the US.

The company operates factories in Long Beach and Houston, has delivered more than 7 GW of electrical infrastructure, and has more than 258.5 MW of critical IT capacity completed and under development.

The 10-year, USD 1 billion lease represents a significant commercial milestone for the young company as it scales its modular approach. The customer, an AI cloud provider, has not been publicly named.

With demand for AI infrastructure accelerating across the United States, Giga leaders say the next generation of data centers must do more than power technology and must also earn the trust of the communities where they are built.

The company frames Project Clay as that philosophy in practice, pairing large-scale computing capacity with measures intended to avoid burdening existing residents and utilities.

title: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer: Why Supabase Breaks Your Pool
description:
A FastAPI service works locally, then fails in production with asyncpg.exceptions.DuplicatePreparedStatementError: prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_1__" already exists, or with ConnectionFailureError: connection is closed mid-request. The database is Supabase or PgBouncer, the connection string came from the dashboard, and no application code changed.

Neither error is about your SQL. Both come from using a client-side statement cache against a pooler that does not keep a session.

Why the statement collides

asyncpg prepares statements and caches them per connection, keyed by SQL text, up to statement_cache_size (100 by default). Each prepared statement gets a server-side name like __asyncpg_stmt_1__.

Under a direct connection that name is unique per session, so the cache is a pure win. Under transaction pooling, PgBouncer hands every transaction a possibly different server connection: the cache no longer describes anything real, and two clients that both prepared __asyncpg_stmt_1__ can land on the same server session, where the second prepare fails with SQLSTATE 42P05.

import asyncpg

# correct for the Supabase transaction pooler (port 6543) and PgBouncer transaction mode
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(
    dsn,
    min_size=1,
    max_size=5,              # small: the pooler multiplies, not the app
    statement_cache_size=0,  # no server-side prepared statements
    max_cached_statement_lifetime=0,
    command_timeout=30,
    server_settings={"application_name": "api"},
)

With SQLAlchemy, set it at the dialect level too, because SQLAlchemy builds the asyncpg pool itself:

create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host:6543/postgres",
    poolclass=NullPool,                     # let the pooler pool
    connect_args={
        "statement_cache_size": 0,
        "prepared_statement_cache_size": 0, # SQLAlchemy's own layer
        "server_settings": {"application_name": "api"},
    },
)

Both knobs exist because there are two caches: asyncpg's, and SQLAlchemy's prepared-statement cache on top of the same driver. Setting only one is the most common half-fix.

Which endpoint you are actually on

Endpoint Port Prepared statements App pool size Use for
Direct connection 5432 supported, cache them your real budget migrations, LISTEN/NOTIFY
Session pooler 5432 supported per session small long sessions, ORMs without pooling
Transaction pooler 6543 not supported across transactions 1–5 per worker most web traffic
Transaction pooler + cache 6543 collisions any never

When you see DuplicatePreparedStatementError the cache met a transaction pooler; TooManyConnectionsError means the app pool is larger than the pooler budget; InvalidPasswordError usually means the username is postgres instead of postgres.<project-ref>.

Reproduce it instead of guessing

A single-worker test never reproduces the collision. Run the same query from many coroutines against the pooler — if it passes with statement_cache_size=0 and fails without it, the diagnosis is confirmed. Do not "fix" it by catching DuplicatePreparedStatementError and retrying: the retry prepares the same name on another server connection and the error moves instead of disappearing.

ConnectionFailureError is not a bug in your query

The pooler recycles server connections aggressively — Supabase's transaction pooler closes idle ones long before a typical web worker notices. asyncpg keeps the client object and only learns the socket is gone when it writes. Retry only on ConnectionFailureError and InterfaceError, never on a query error: replaying an INSERT that failed before commit is fine, replaying one that timed out after commit is not.

async def fetch_one(pool, sql, *args):
    for attempt in range(2):
        try:
            async with pool.acquire() as conn:
                return await conn.fetchrow(sql, *args)
        except asyncpg.ConnectionFailureError:
            if attempt:
                raise

pool_pre_ping narrows the window after an idle close but does not remove the need to retry. Keeping min_size=1 and running an occasional SELECT 1 from a background task keeps a warm client, so the first request after a quiet period does not fail.

Transaction pooling also gives one server connection per transaction — exactly what async with conn.transaction() needs, and exactly what a bare SET does not survive. Use SET LOCAL for statement_timeout or search_path, and keep advisory locks, LISTEN, temporary tables, cursors and Alembic migrations on port 5432, where a session exists.

Two traps specific to Supabase

The direct host is IPv6-only. db.<project-ref>.supabase.co resolves to IPv6 unless the IPv4 add-on is enabled, so a container or CI runner without IPv6 gets socket.gaierror: [Errno -9] Address family for the host is not supported. It looks like DNS and is not; use a pooler host, and note the pooler username is postgres.<project-ref>.

Your pool size is multiplied by the pooler. Four uvicorn workers with max_size=20 demand 80 server connections from a pooler that may allow far fewer, and the failure only appears under load. Keep a handful per worker (max_size = 5) and let the pooler queue; NullPool is the simplest correct choice for serverless.

Checklist before you file a bug

  • Both cache switches set to 0.
  • Port 6543 only for traffic that does not need a session.
  • max_size small, per worker.
  • Retry on ConnectionFailureError / InterfaceError only.

Format the failing statement with the SQL formatter before hunting a syntax difference, diff two connection strings character by character with the text diff tool, and split a copied postgres:// URL into its parts with the URL parser.

The longer version, with the pool sizing table and the keepalive snippet, is on my site: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer and Supabase.

title: How we split a 5,000-line Express server.js with zero behavioral diffs
description:
Our Express server.js went from 5,121 lines to 1,402 across incremental PRs. The result we cared about was zero behavioral differences in the checks we ran after each move.

The useful part of that story is the method: six gates that make a large file smaller while keeping each change narrow enough to review. We've released a clean-room implementation of that approach as JS Modularization Gold Standard, a CommonJS CLI built at DrRx.

The production numbers describe the original project. The public repository contains a synthetic Express example and a reproducible probe test; it does not include the production source or its probe logs. “Zero behavioral diffs” means the observed checks matched, not a mathematical proof over every possible input.

Move one domain at a time

An Express monolith is more than a list of routes. Handlers share helpers, middleware order, caches, and mutable bindings. Moving a handler can preserve its text while changing what it closes over.

Consider a cache used by both billing and session routes:

let sessionCache = {};

app.post("/billing/reset", (req, res) => {
  sessionCache = {};
  res.json({ reset: true });
});

Passing sessionCache directly to another module copies the current object reference. If the parent later assigns a new object, the extracted module can keep reading the old one.

Our module boundary passes closures over the original binding:

require("./modules/billing").register(app, {
  hashId,
  PRICE_TABLE,
  getSessionCache: () => sessionCache,
  setSessionCache: (value) => { sessionCache = value; }
});

The generated billing handler calls setSessionCache({}). The session module uses getSessionCache(). The parent still owns the binding, so a billing reset remains visible to the session routes.

That boundary is deliberately small: register(app, kernel). The kernel object makes the dependencies visible in the diff. The extraction preserves the selected statements apart from indentation and the wiring needed at the boundary. Cleanup happens in a later commit.

The six gates

1. Parse every changed file. Run node --check on the parent and each module. It catches broken syntax quickly, before spending time on behavioral tests.

2. Compare registration counts. Record a baseline before the move. After extraction, count registrations in the parent and modules together. A matching count cannot establish correctness, but a changed count immediately deserves an explanation. The CLI's current counter is a textual heuristic and only enforces parity when expectedRoutes is configured.

3. Check the module boundary. Every extracted module exports register(app, kernel). The CLI checks that export shape. Application tests must also exercise registration and startup; a textual export check cannot tell you whether middleware runs in the right order.

4. Audit residual free variables. Parse the generated module and look for references it has not declared or received. This complements live probes: a request that stops at an authentication check cannot tell you whether the code behind that check still has access to its dependencies.

5. Replay requests against old and new. Start each version with comparable fixtures, run the same sequence, and compare status and body. Include state transitions. In the public demo, a session gets read twice, billing resets the cache, and the session gets read again. That sequence tests a relationship between two extracted modules that isolated endpoint checks could miss.

6. Keep the PR small. Extract one domain, show the wiring, attach the checks, review, and merge. Recalculate the next cut's line ranges afterward. Renaming helpers, redesigning error handling, or changing business logic belongs in a separate change with its own evidence.

The first four gates catch structural problems. The fifth checks observed behavior. The sixth keeps the evidence understandable to the person reviewing the change.

Reproduce the public example

The package is available on npm:

npx js-modularization-gold-standard --help

To run the full demo:

git clone https://github.com/drrx-ai/JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard.git
cd JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard
npm ci
npm test

The test extracts billing and session modules, runs the static gates, then compares nine HTTP requests against the original and extracted applications. Those requests cover five route handlers; the registration baseline also counts one middleware registration. The reset-then-read sequence is part of the test.

The CLI can also survey routes and shared symbols, analyze a proposed line range, preview an extraction, and audit an individual generated module. Use a clean branch and inspect extract --dry before applying a cut.

Where review still matters

The current tool targets CommonJS and app.method(...) registration. It does not convert ESM applications or generate your production test suite. Complex mutable expressions, shadowed identifiers, relative imports, and dependencies between extracted regions still need careful review. Keep assignments simple and do not assume a generated setter preserves the return value of an assignment or increment expression.

For a production application, add authenticated requests, startup checks, middleware-order checks, and assertions for external side effects. Passing the public fixture establishes what works in that fixture.

The method is useful even without this CLI: make dependencies explicit, preserve the original binding, separate moving from cleanup, and require evidence at each step.

Explore the code, example, and six gates on GitHub. If you have a small example of shared-state wiring that breaks during extraction, we'd welcome a reproducible issue.

Disclosure: This article was drafted by an AI assistant from the project’s code, test results, and maintainer-provided production context.

title: RDS Extended Support Charges on the AWS Bill? A MySQL 8.0 or PostgreSQL 13 Database Passed Its End of Standard Support
description:
As of November 18, 2026, this post sums up the official pages linked here.

The problem

Your Amazon RDS line on the AWS bill went up this month. Nobody changed an instance size, added storage or bought anything new. The database runs the same version as last month. The new cost is RDS Extended Support.

This can catch many teams this year. RDS for MySQL 8.0 reached its RDS end of standard support on July 31, 2026. RDS for PostgreSQL 13 reached it on February 28, 2026. In this post we show what the charge is and why it started without anyone clicking anything. We also show how to find the databases behind it and stop it safely.

Root cause: an old major version keeps running, for a fee

Here is how AWS describes it. Extended Support "allows you to continue running a database on a major engine version" past its RDS end of standard support date. AWS charges extra for this. (RDS Extended Support)

Charges start "the day after the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

For the two versions most teams ask about, AWS's own calendars show:

Version RDS end of standard support Extended Support year 1 pricing starts Year 3 pricing starts RDS end of Extended Support
RDS for MySQL 8.0 31 July 2026 1 August 2026 1 August 2028 31 July 2029
RDS for PostgreSQL 13 28 February 2026 1 March 2026 1 March 2028 28 February 2029

(Sources: MySQL on Amazon RDS versions and Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. MySQL 5.7, PostgreSQL 11 and PostgreSQL 12 are already past their end of standard support too; see the same pages.)

The MySQL page also notes that "MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 are now only available under RDS Extended Support."

Why nobody "turned it on"

Enrollment is the default in many setups:

  • With the AWS CLI or RDS API, if you "don't specify the RDS Extended Support setting, Amazon RDS defaults to enabling RDS Extended Support." AWS adds that the same default applies when you automate with CloudFormation or other services. It keeps the database available past the end of standard support. In the console, the setting "isn't selected by default." (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • When an enrolled database reaches the date, RDS enrolls it automatically. AWS says this "doesn't change the database engine and doesn't impact the uptime or performance of your DB instance." (RDS Extended Support)

So the database keeps working exactly as before. The only thing that changes is the bill.

How the charge is priced

For provisioned RDS for MySQL instances, AWS says "RDS Extended Support is priced per vCPU per hour." The price also depends "on the AWS Region and calendar date." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)

The pricing pages give these examples:

  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2026. Starting March 1, 2026, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)
  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 on a db.r5.large in US East (N. Virginia) in the first year: "$0.200 per hour, or 2 vCPUs x $0.100 per vCPU-hr." (same page)
  • RDS for PostgreSQL 12 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2025 to February 28, 2027. Starting March 1, 2027, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing)

These are AWS's worked examples, not the rate for every version and Region. Read the pricing page for your engine, version and Region before you estimate a bill. The formula AWS gives is simple: number of vCPUs x the hourly rate for your Region and pricing year, for every hour the instance runs.

Five details make the bill bigger than people expect. All five come from the FAQ on the MySQL and PostgreSQL pricing pages and the charges page:

  1. Multi-AZ standbys pay too. With one standby, you are charged "on both your primary and standby instances." With two readable standbys, on the primary and both standbys.
  2. Read replicas pay too, if they run a major version past its end of standard support.
  3. Reserved Instances do not help. "RDS Extended Support charges are independent of instance charges. Therefore, Reserved Instance discounts are not applicable to RDS Extended Support charges."
  4. A restore can start a new charge. Snapshots themselves are not charged. But restoring a DB snapshot "to a new DB instance after end of standard support" is charged "RDS Extended Support pricing for that instance." The same applies if you create a new instance on that version.
  5. The price goes up in year 3. The first two years use the year 1 and 2 rate. Year 3 pricing starts "on the first day of the third year."

Step 1: find the databases behind the charge

List every DB instance with its engine, version and enrollment:

aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,Engine,EngineVersion,DBInstanceClass,MultiAZ,EngineLifecycleSupport]' \
  --output table

AWS says that if Extended Support is available for a database, the response includes EngineLifecycleSupport. The value open-source-rds-extended-support means the database is enrolled. The value open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled means enrollment was turned off. (Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support)

Enrollment alone is not a charge. AWS notes that "Charges for RDS Extended Support only start when your DB engine version has reached the RDS end of standard support." So the list you care about is: enrolled and on a major version whose end of standard support has passed. For Aurora clusters and Multi-AZ DB clusters, run describe-db-clusters as well, because the setting lives at the cluster level.

In the console, the Databases page has an RDS Extended Support column. If you do not see it, AWS says to turn it on under the Preferences icon. (same page)

The command lists one Region at a time, so run it in every Region you use (add --region).

Step 2: check the dates for each version

You can read the support dates from the CLI instead of a web page:

aws rds describe-db-major-engine-versions \
  --engine mysql \
  --major-engine-version 8.0

AWS says the response includes SupportedEngineLifecycles, with a start and end date for standard support (open-source-rds-standard-support) and for Extended Support (open-source-rds-extended-support). This works for the open source engines (MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL), not the commercial ones. (Viewing support dates, describe-db-major-engine-versions)

Use --engine postgres for PostgreSQL.

Step 3: stop the charge the right way

AWS lists two things that stop the charge. One is upgrading "to an engine version that's covered under standard support." The other is deleting "the database that's running a major version past the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

Option A: plan and test a major version upgrade (the usual fix)

Upgrade to a major version with a long standard support window, not just the next one. AWS warns that "The charges will restart if your target engine version enters RDS Extended Support in the future." (same page) Two examples from the calendars:

  • MySQL: 8.4 has RDS end of standard support on 31 July 2029.
  • PostgreSQL: 14 reaches its RDS end of standard support on 28 February 2027, only a few months away. PostgreSQL 16 runs to 28 February 2029, and 17 to 28 February 2030.

For RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and Aurora MySQL, AWS says you can use Blue/Green Deployments to move off an Extended Support version. This works as long as Blue/Green supports your engine, Region and version. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

If you upgrade in place, know what the command does. The CLI reference covers --engine-version. It says: "Changing this parameter results in an outage and the change is applied during the next maintenance window unless the ApplyImmediately parameter is enabled." A major upgrade with a non-default parameter group needs a parameter group from the new version's family. You must also set --allow-major-version-upgrade. (modify-db-instance) Test on a restored copy first. That copy is charged Extended Support while it runs on the old version.

Option B: delete what nobody uses

Old read replicas, a forgotten test database, a copy restored "just to check something." Each one is charged on its own. If it is not needed, take a final snapshot and delete it. Snapshots are not charged Extended Support. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

Be careful with "just turn it off"

You can change enrollment at any time with the EngineLifecycleSupport setting. In the CLI, that's --engine-lifecycle-support open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled. But AWS warns about disabling it on a database "that is already past its standard support end date." In that case, "the instance or cluster automatically upgrades to the next supported major version." (RDS Extended Support)

That is a major version upgrade you did not test, and if the database is in production, it happens to production. Use this only after the application has been tested on the new version.

Step 4: stop new charges from appearing

  • Set the option on purpose in code. Because the CLI and API default to enrollment, add --engine-lifecycle-support (or EngineLifecycleSupport) to your create and restore scripts so the choice is visible. AWS notes that if you set open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled and the end of standard support has passed, creating the instance "will always fail." That is a useful guard against new databases on old versions. (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • Put the next dates on the calendar. PostgreSQL 14 (28 February 2027) is the next big one for many teams. Run the Step 1 command a few months ahead of each date.

When it still goes wrong

  • The charge came back after an upgrade. You upgraded to a version that later reached its own end of standard support. AWS's example: a PostgreSQL 11 database upgraded to 12 on April 30, 2024 was charged again from March 1, 2025. (RDS Extended Support charges)
  • The bill is bigger than one instance should cost. Count the standbys and read replicas. Each is charged.
  • You bought Reserved Instances and the line is still there. RI discounts do not apply to this charge.
  • Extended Support has an end too. AWS says it is available "for up to 3 years past the RDS end of standard support date." After that, RDS "will automatically upgrade your major engine version." (RDS Extended Support)

What to check first

  1. Which DB instances and clusters are on MySQL 5.7, MySQL 8.0, PostgreSQL 11, 12 or 13, and are they enrolled?
  2. How many vCPUs does each have, counting standbys and read replicas?
  3. Which ones can be deleted, and which need an upgrade plan?
  4. Is the target version far enough from its own end of standard support?
  5. Do your create and restore scripts set --engine-lifecycle-support on purpose?

Docs checked (November 18, 2026)

  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support with Amazon RDS (what it is, automatic enrollment, changing enrollment, forced upgrade when disabled past the date, up to 3 years)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support charges (start date, standbys, what stops the charge, charges restarting, the PostgreSQL 11 example)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Creating a DB instance or a Multi-AZ DB cluster with RDS Extended Support (CLI and API default to enrollment, console does not, disabled option makes creation fail past the date)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support (EngineLifecycleSupport values, console column, enrollment vs charges)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing support dates for engine versions and AWS CLI describe-db-major-engine-versions (SupportedEngineLifecycles)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, MySQL on Amazon RDS versions (MySQL 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4 dates)
  • Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Release Notes, Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL 13, 14, 16 and 17 dates)
  • AWS CLI, modify-db-instance (--engine-lifecycle-support values, --engine-version outage note, --allow-major-version-upgrade)
  • Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing (per vCPU-hour pricing, the Ohio and N. Virginia examples, Multi-AZ, read replicas, Reserved Instances, snapshots and restores, Blue/Green)

If AWS changes a date or price after we publish this, tell us at info@cloudskillconsulting.com and we'll update the post.

CloudSkill Consulting LLC helps teams with fixed-fee cloud projects, FinOps reviews and IT staffing. Learn more at cloudskillconsulting.com.

title: Animated candlestick chart in React for a shadcn dashboard
description:
I needed a candlestick card for a shadcn dashboard. Here is what I ended up doing, and when a real trading library is the better call.

shadcn/ui’s charts cover area, bar, line, pie, radar and radial charts, but not candlesticks. For a candlestick card in a shadcn dashboard, install a registry block: the free Ethereum Chart from mebius.design is a React + Tailwind OHLC card with volume bars, a period switch, keyboard inspection and anime.js motion, added with one shadcn CLI command. For a full trading screen, use a financial charting library instead.

Pick the right tool first

A dashboard card and a trading terminal need different charts.

shadcn/ui’s chart components wrap Recharts and theme it with your CSS variables. Recharts has no candlestick series, so a candlestick there means drawing custom bar shapes for the bodies and wicks yourself. That leaves three routes:

  • A financial charting library such as TradingView’s Lightweight Charts (Apache 2.0, canvas). It is built for trading screens: thousands of candles, panning, zooming and live updates. It is not a React component and doesn’t use your Tailwind tokens.
  • Recharts with a custom shape: you stay in the shadcn stack and write the candle drawing, the axis and the tooltip yourself.
  • A finished candlestick card from a shadcn registry, which drops into a dashboard grid next to your other cards. This guide uses that route.

If your page is a price chart people trade from, take the library. If it is a card in a dashboard that shows how a coin, stock or fund moved this week, a card is less work and matches the rest of the page.

Install the chart with the shadcn CLI

React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 and shadcn CLI 4 or later.

The Ethereum Chart is one of the 20 items of the mebius.design open starter pack: its code is MIT and installs straight from its URL, with no account or token. The command also brings the charts theme it needs, which only adds tokens scoped to the chart cards (they carry a data-charts attribute), so it doesn’t change your app’s colours.

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add https://www.mebius.design/r/charts-ethereum.json

The other free charts install the same way through the @mebius registry, with a free account and a personal access token from Settings › Tokens (the install guide has the setup).

The CLI writes components/ethereum-chart.tsx, the card parts it uses and anime.js. Render it with its sample week to check the setup:

app/page.tsx:

import { EthereumChart } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"

export default function Page() {
  return <EthereumChart className="max-w-[600px]" />
}

Feed it your own candles

One period per segment of the Week / Month / Year switch.

A candle is { time, open, high, low, close, volume } with the time in milliseconds, oldest first. Each period gives the switch a segment and tells the x axis whether to name days, weeks or months. The example loads three periods from your own endpoint and hides the NAV and market price figures, which only make sense for a fund:

components/eth-price-card.tsx:

"use client"

import * as React from "react"

import { EthereumChart, type EthereumCandle, type EthereumPeriod } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"

// Your API answers with rows of [time in ms, open, high, low, close, volume], oldest first.
type Row = [number, number, number, number, number, number]

const toCandles = (rows: Row[]): EthereumCandle[] =>
  rows.map(([time, open, high, low, close, volume]) => ({ time, open, high, low, close, volume }))

async function load(interval: "1d" | "1w", limit: number) {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/candles?symbol=ETH&interval=${interval}&limit=${limit}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Candles failed: ${response.status}`)
  return toCandles((await response.json()) as Row[])
}

export function EthPriceCard() {
  const [periods, setPeriods] = React.useState<EthereumPeriod[] | null>(null)

  React.useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false
    Promise.all([load("1d", 7), load("1d", 30), load("1w", 52)]).then(([week, month, year]) => {
      if (cancelled) return
      setPeriods([
        { value: "week", label: "W", name: "Week", candles: week, unit: "day" },
        { value: "month", label: "M", name: "Month", candles: month, unit: "week" },
        { value: "year", label: "Y", name: "Year", candles: year, unit: "month" },
      ])
    })
    return () => {
      cancelled = true
    }
  }, [])

  if (!periods) return <div className="h-[562px] max-w-[600px] rounded-2xl bg-neutral-100" />

  return <EthereumChart className="max-w-[600px]" title="Ethereum" symbol="ETH" periods={periods} stats={[]} />
}

The price in the header is the last close and the badge is the change from the first open, so both follow your data. Prices, axis labels and times are formatted with locale and currency (en-US and USD by default); formatTime replaces the axis and tooltip times, which are in UTC by default.

Put it in a dashboard grid

The card is as wide as its container; the height follows its content.

Every chart card from the same registry shares the theme, so a candlestick card sits next to a holdings card without extra styling. Here with the Your Asset Chart (install it the same way, @mebius/charts-your-asset):

app/dashboard/page.tsx:

import { EthereumChart } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"
import { YourAssetChart } from "@/components/your-asset-chart"

export default function DashboardPage() {
  return (
    <main className="grid gap-4 p-6 xl:grid-cols-[minmax(0,600px)_minmax(0,1fr)]">
      <EthereumChart />
      <YourAssetChart />
    </main>
  )
}

Narrow screens. On a narrow card the period switch wraps under the price and the figures stack in one column, so the same card works in a phone layout.

Motion and accessibility

  • The plot is one slider: arrow keys move between candles, Page Up and Page Down jump a tenth of them, Home and End go to the first and last, Escape hides the tooltip. Screen readers hear the candle’s time and prices.
  • Candles grow out of their opens one after another, and a new period morphs the old candles into the new ones. With prefers-reduced-motion set to reduce nothing animates.
  • The server render is the final state, so the card shows real numbers before JavaScript runs.

Related

  • Ethereum Chart: The candlestick card from this guide, with its live demo and Figma file.
  • Your Asset Chart: Holdings by coin with a live price ticker and the latest deposits.
  • Price Range Chart: A liquidity pool’s price history with a draggable price range.
  • Crypto dashboard guide: The other cards a crypto dashboard needs, and a full kit for it.

title: shadcn MCP: install UI components from Claude Code and Cursor
description:
The shadcn CLI has an MCP server built in, so Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code can browse and install registry components for you. Here is the setup for each editor, how to add a private registry, and the errors you will hit and what they mean.

shadcn’s MCP server is built into the shadcn CLI. Run npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude, or --client cursor, and your AI editor can browse, search and install items from every registry in components.json. mebius.design adds a hosted MCP server that returns each item’s full source and usage docs.

What is the shadcn MCP server?

Checked in shadcn’s docs and source on 17 Nov 2026.

The shadcn MCP server is part of the shadcn CLI, the MIT-licensed shadcn package on npm (4.23.0 when we checked). Your editor starts it on your own machine with npx shadcn@latest mcp, and the AI can then browse, search and install items from any registry in your components.json: shadcn/ui’s own (no setup needed), third-party registries, private ones behind a token, and namespaced ones such as @acme. See shadcn’s MCP docs.

Under the hood it has seven tools (source): list the registries in components.json; list, search and view registry items with their files; find usage examples; return the shadcn add command for chosen items; and a checklist to run after new code is written. The server doesn’t write files itself. The assistant runs the add command it gets back, so every install still goes through the CLI.

How do you set up shadcn MCP?

One command per editor, then a restart.

Run init in your project with the name of your editor. It adds the shadcn server to that editor’s MCP config:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude
# or --client cursor, vscode, codex or opencode

Restart the editor afterwards. In Claude Code, run /mcp and check that shadcn shows as connected; in Cursor, turn the server on in Cursor Settings; in VS Code, open .vscode/mcp.json and click Start. Codex is the exception: the CLI can’t edit ~/.codex/config.toml, so you add the server there by hand. Written by hand for Claude Code, the server is this file:

.mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shadcn": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["shadcn@latest", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Cursor takes the same block in .cursor/mcp.json; VS Code puts it under "servers" in .vscode/mcp.json. If the editor lists no tools, shadcn’s troubleshooting notes suggest clearing the npx cache (npx clear-npx-cache) and switching the server off and on again.

How do you add a private registry?

Once per project. The example is the @mebius registry.

A private registry is a namespace in components.json: a URL template the CLI fills with the item name and, when the registry needs one, a header that reads a token from your environment (shadcn’s authentication docs). The CLI and its MCP server both read it. For mebius.design, create a token in Settings › Tokens (a free account works) and add:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Keep the token out of git. The CLI reads .env.local and .env. Check that .env.local is in your .gitignore, and revoke a token in Settings › Tokens if it leaks.

Each mebius kit has a theme item. Add it on its own first, then items with --overwrite so shared parts take the kit’s version. Item names start with their kit:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-revenue-growth --overwrite

No token yet? The 20 open starter items install from their URL with no account, like the Revenue Overview chart: npx shadcn@latest add https://www.mebius.design/r/charts-revenue-overview.json.

Which shadcn CLI commands matter?

What the MCP server asks for, and what you can run yourself.

When an agent gets stuck, the same work runs in a terminal. From shadcn’s CLI docs, the commands that matter for registries:

  • init: creates components.json, adds the cn helper and sets up CSS variables. Once per project.
  • add: installs items by name, @namespace/name or URL. --overwrite replaces files that already exist, --dry-run previews the changes.
  • view: prints an item’s files before you install it.
  • search (alias list): searches one or more registries, with -q for a query.
  • info: shows your project’s setup as the CLI sees it, handy when an install lands in the wrong folder.

With the @mebius registry set up, you can find, read and install a chart without leaving the terminal:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest search @mebius -q "candlestick"
npx shadcn@latest view @mebius/charts-ethereum
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-ethereum --overwrite

What does the mebius MCP server add?

A hosted server with browser sign-in and usage docs per item.

mebius.design runs its own MCP server at https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp. Nothing runs on your machine and it doesn’t need a components.json: it reads the kits your account has and returns each item’s source files with their target paths, its npm and registry dependencies, and the usage docs written for that component or block (props, examples, notes). As of 17 Nov 2026, a free account gets all 62 free charts and 128 free forms; buying a kit adds that kit, and All items adds every kit.

In Claude Code, add it with one command, with no token to copy:

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

Then run /mcp, pick mebius, choose Authenticate, log in to mebius.design in the browser and click Approve. Cursor and VS Code ask you to log in the first time they connect:

.cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}

VS Code takes the same URL under "servers" with "type": "http". Tools that can’t open a browser, like CI or a remote machine, send a token from Settings › Tokens as the header Authorization: Bearer <your token>. The server has five read-only tools:

  • list_kits: the kits your account has, the free ones included, with item counts and categories, and the paid kits it doesn’t own yet.
  • list_items and search_items: find a component or block by kit, type, category or plain words.
  • get_item: one item in full, with every file, its dependencies and its usage docs.
  • get_install_instructions: the components.json entry, the token line and the exact add commands, theme first.

Which MCP server should you use?

Both, for different jobs.

  • shadcn MCP: local, free and MIT, and it works with every registry in components.json, shadcn/ui’s own included. Best for browsing many registries and installing through the CLI.
  • mebius MCP: hosted, signs in through the browser and covers mebius kits only. Best when the agent should read an item’s usage docs before it adapts a block, or write the files by hand in a project without components.json.

They don’t clash. With the @mebius registry in components.json, shadcn’s server lists mebius items too, and a prompt like “add the mebius candlestick chart to the dashboard” ends the same way with either one: the theme, then npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-ethereum --overwrite.

Other marketplaces run their own servers too: the UI8 MCP at https://mcp.ui8.net/mcp is included with UI8’s All Access pass (checked on ui8.net on 17 Nov 2026). How the two marketplaces compare overall is in mebius vs UI8.

What if the CLI or MCP says no?

The mebius registry answers with a message the CLI prints.

  • No mebius token was sent: MEBIUS_TOKEN isn’t set where the CLI runs, or the registry URL redirects. Use the exact https://www URL above.
  • The token is invalid or has been revoked: create a new one and replace the line in .env.local.
  • Your account doesn’t own this kit: the item belongs to a paid kit. Buy it for $19, or All items for $259, and run the command again.
  • No item with that name: item names start with their kit, like @mebius/charts-ethereum. npx shadcn@latest search @mebius lists the ones your token can install.

The free items are the quickest test of the whole setup: create a free account and every chart and form is yours to install, by command or by prompt.

FAQ

Is the shadcn MCP server free?

Yes. It is part of the shadcn CLI, which is MIT licensed and free. It runs on your machine through npx, so it needs no account or key, apart from any tokens your private registries ask for.

Does the shadcn MCP server work with private registries?

Yes. Add the registry to components.json under a namespace, with an Authorization header that reads a token from an environment variable, and put the token in .env.local. The CLI and the MCP server both read it.

What is the difference between the shadcn CLI and shadcn MCP?

The CLI is the command-line tool that sets up a project and adds, views and searches registry items. The MCP server lets an AI editor do the same by prompt: it looks items up in your registries and hands the assistant the add command to run.

Do I need a token for the mebius MCP server?

No. Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code sign in through the browser: add the server, log in to mebius.design and click Approve. A personal access token from Settings › Tokens is the fallback for tools that can’t open a browser, and the shadcn CLI needs one for the @mebius registry.

Can an AI editor install mebius components without an account?

Only the 20 open starter items, which install from their URL with the plain shadcn CLI. The MCP server needs a sign-in, and a free account covers all 62 charts and 128 forms.

Related

  • Free charts: 62 animated chart cards to install with the commands above.
  • Free forms: 128 animated forms in light and dark.
  • Is shadcn/ui free?: The MIT license, and what free and paid shadcn kits allow.
  • Figma to React: How the registry behind these commands is made from Figma.

title: Socket.IO Tutorial: Real-Time Order Updates in Node.js
description:
Quick answer

Socket.IO is a library that lets a Node.js server push events to connected browsers the moment something happens, instead of waiting for the browser to ask. This post builds a live order-status feed: order 1042 moves from received to packed to delivered, and each change reaches the customer instantly. It fits order tracking, chat, and live dashboards.

A customer buys a kurta and a dupatta, pays Rs 12,400, and then waits. The shop page says "processing" and the customer refreshes, waits, refreshes again. The usual fix is polling: the browser asks the server every few seconds whether anything changed. Most of those requests return the same answer, and the one that matters can still arrive seconds late. A push model flips the pattern: the server speaks first, the moment the order changes. Socket.IO is the most used way to do that in Node.js, and this post puts it to work on a real order, with one event that goes missing.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the update is worth pushing at all. A live feed earns its place when the reader waits on something that changes at an unknown time: an order status, a chat reply, a delivery location. If the data only changes when the user acts, a normal request is simpler and cheaper.

My second check is how many clients need the same event. Socket.IO shines when one event fans out to many browsers: each order gets a room, and only the customer in that room hears about it. If every event goes to exactly one client, a plain WebSocket may be less machinery. The WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling post covers the raw transport underneath.

My third check is what happens when a connection drops. Networks drop and phones switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data, and Socket.IO reconnects on its own. But reconnection does not replay the events missed in between. If a missed update matters, the client must ask for the current state after reconnecting. The demo replays nothing, which suits a status feed and not a payment.

My fourth check is the team cost. Socket.IO adds a persistent connection per client, which changes how the server is deployed: sticky sessions behind a load balancer, or the Redis adapter for several servers. For one small server that cost is trivial; for a fleet it is a design decision.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Socket.IO when users wait on events they cannot predict and the server should speak first. Skip it when a request on demand already answers the question. The recommendation flips the moment events must never be missed, or the deployment cannot hold persistent connections.

One order, three updates, and a silent listener

Order 1042 belongs to Ayesha: a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400. The shop wants her browser to learn about each change the moment it happens, without polling. The server below puts each client in a room named after the order id and emits an order-update event at each step: received, packed, delivered.

// server.js: live order-status feed.
// Run: node server.js (listens on port 3000).
const http = require("http");
const { Server } = require("socket.io");

const server = http.createServer();
const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: "*" } });

const STEPS = [
  { status: "received", note: "Payment confirmed, order received" },
  { status: "packed", note: "Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse" },
  { status: "delivered", note: "Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi" },
];

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  console.log(`client connected: ${socket.id}`);
  socket.on("join-order", (orderId) => {
    const room = `order-${orderId}`;
    socket.join(room);
    console.log(`client ${socket.id} joined ${room}`);
    STEPS.forEach((step, index) => {
      setTimeout(() => {
        const update = { orderId, ...step };
        io.to(room).emit("order-update", update);
        console.log(`sent order-update: ${orderId} -> ${step.status}`);
      }, 400 * (index + 1));
    });
  });
  socket.on("disconnect", () => {
    console.log(`client disconnected: ${socket.id}`);
  });
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

The first client has a small bug: it listens for order_status, with underscores, while the server emits order-update, with a hyphen. Socket.IO never warns about a listener that matches nothing.

// client-buggy.js: the wrong event name, on purpose.
// Run: node client-buggy.js
const { io } = require("socket.io-client");

const socket = io("http://localhost:3000");
const received = [];

socket.on("connect", () => {
  console.log(`connected as ${socket.id}`);
  socket.emit("join-order", 1042);
});

// BUG: the server emits "order-update", not "order_status".
socket.on("order_status", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status}`);
});

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log(`after 2.5s: received ${received.length} updates`);
  console.log("nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server");
  socket.disconnect();
  process.exit(0);
}, 2500);

Here is the real output. The buggy client connects fine, joins the room, and hears nothing, while the server log shows all three updates going out.

=== buggy client (wrong event name) ===
connected as gI1iughH...
after 2.5s: received 0 updates
nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server

The fix is one word: listen for order-update, exactly what the server emits.

// client-fixed.js: only the listener name changes.
// FIXED: listens for "order-update", exactly what the server emits.
socket.on("order-update", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status} (${update.note})`);
});

Now the same run delivers every update, in order.

=== fixed client (correct event name) ===
connected as b2w_1A6K...
update: order 1042 is received (Payment confirmed, order received)
update: order 1042 is packed (Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse)
update: order 1042 is delivered (Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi)
after 2.5s: received 3 updates

=== server log ===
Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000
client connected: gI1iughH...
client gI1iughH... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: gI1iughH...
client connected: b2w_1A6K...
client b2w_1A6K... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: b2w_1A6K...

The bug failed in the quietest possible way: no error, no crash, just a listener waiting for an event that would never arrive. The server did its job perfectly, which is what makes this mistake hard to spot. When a Socket.IO client hears nothing, check the event name first, character by character, before doubting the connection. The Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express post shows the request side of the same stack, where a wrong route at least returns a 404.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, the event name mismatch from the demo. The symptom is a client that connects cleanly and receives nothing, with no error anywhere. The fix is to match the event name exactly on both sides, and to keep event names in one shared list or constants file instead of typing them twice from memory.

Second, broadcasting every update to every client. The symptom is a customer watching another customer's order change, because the server used io.emit. The fix is rooms: socket.join("order-1042") on the server, then io.to("order-1042").emit(...) so only that order's room hears it.

Third, a client that never connects because of CORS. The symptom is the browser console showing a cross-origin error while the server looks healthy. The fix is to pass the cors option when creating the server, as the demo does, and to list the real front-end origin instead of "*" in production.

Fourth, assuming an emitted event always arrives. The symptom is a customer stuck on "packed" after a network drop, because the update fired while they were offline. The fix is to treat emits as fire-and-forget: on reconnect, have the client ask for the current order state.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is Socket.IO different from plain WebSockets? Socket.IO is built on the WebSocket transport and adds rooms, automatic reconnection, event names, and a fallback to HTTP long polling. Plain WebSockets give you a raw pipe and leave the rest to you.

Do I need a separate server for Socket.IO? No. It attaches to the HTTP server your app already uses, so it can share a port with an Express app. The demo uses a plain Node.js HTTP server.

What happens when a client disconnects? Socket.IO reconnects automatically, and the client can rejoin its rooms on the connect event. Events sent while the client is away are lost unless the server stores them.

Can Socket.IO scale to many users? Yes, with the Redis adapter, which lets several Socket.IO servers share events. A single server handles a small shop easily; the adapter becomes the answer when one process is no longer enough.

What to remember

  • Socket.IO pushes events from server to browser, so the browser stops polling.
  • Event names must match exactly on both sides; a mismatch fails silently with no error.
  • Rooms keep each customer's updates private.
  • Reconnection is automatic, but missed events are not replayed unless you store them.
  • Attach Socket.IO to your existing HTTP server, and set CORS to your real front-end origin.

Where this leaves you

Socket.IO earns its place the moment a user is waiting on something the server knows first: an order moving through the warehouse, or a reply landing in a chat. The demo proved the two things that matter: the server pushed three real updates to the right room, and the one failure was a silent name mismatch fixed by a single word. That quiet failure is the lesson. Start with one event and one room, then add reconnection handling before real customers depend on it. A feed that speaks first feels instant, and that is what keeps a customer from refreshing.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO docs, getting started, https://socket.io/docs/v4/
  • Socket.IO docs, tutorial, https://socket.io/docs/v4/tutorial/introduction
  • Socket.IO docs, rooms, https://socket.io/docs/v4/rooms/
  • WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/websockets-explained-real-time-data.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • Express Explained: Node's Minimal Web Framework Guide, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/express-explained-nodes-minimal-web.html
  • React useEffect Explained: When to Use It and Skip It, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/react-useeffect-explained-when-to-use.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html

title: How We Built 'The Travel Tales': High-Performance Travel Publishing with Next.js 15 & React
description:
How We Built 'The Travel Tales': High-Performance Travel Publishing with Next.js 15 & React

Originally engineered by Kahol Labs — Live Platform: thetraveltales.kahollabs.in

The modern web is inundated with travel blogs that have succumbed to ad-tech bloat: full-screen video popups, intrusive newsletter overlays, and megabytes of JavaScript that render reading unbearable on a spotty 3G cellular connection in the Himalayas.

When we set out to build The Travel Tales, our goal was to engineer a fast, distraction-free sanctuary where mountaineers, road-trippers, and backpackers could discover and chronicle real journeys.

In this engineering breakdown, we dive into how we architected thetraveltales.kahollabs.in using Next.js 15, React Server Components (RSC), and Tailwind CSS.

1. Zero-JS Reading Paths with React Server Components

For a travel storytelling website, reader experience and fast time-to-first-byte (TTFB) are non-negotiable. Travel readers often browse articles while in transit—on buses, mountain passes, and remote homestays with unstable mobile connections.

By leveraging Next.js 15 App Router and React Server Components:

  • Static Content Stays on the Server: Story paragraphs, destination overviews, and itinerary metadata are rendered into lightweight HTML on the server.
  • Client Hydration is Minimized: Client-side JavaScript bundles are stripped down strictly to interactive widgets (search filters, bookmarks, and sharing buttons).
  • Sub-Second First Contentful Paint: Lighthouse performance scores hit 98+ on mobile devices.

Explore the live production website: https://thetraveltales.kahollabs.in.

2. Responsive Visual Storytelling & Image Optimization

Travel chronicles demand breathtaking photography—from high-altitude passes in Spiti Valley to secluded Kyoto alleyways. However, high-resolution DSLR photos easily exceed 15MB each, which would instantly crash a budget mobile browser.

We engineered an automated responsive asset pipeline:

  1. Next.js Dynamic Image Resizing: Photos are transcoded on-the-fly into modern WebP and AVIF formats based on the client viewport.
  2. Priority LCP Preloading: The above-the-fold hero photo is statically preloaded with priority={true}, while secondary gallery shots load lazily with blurry placeholder previews.
  3. Responsive Grid Layouts: Built with utility-first Tailwind CSS to maintain seamless aspect ratios across smartphone screens, tablets, and 4K desktop displays.

3. SEO & Structured Schema Architecture

To ensure authentic travel chronicles rank against generic corporate travel agencies on Google, The Travel Tales embeds comprehensive structured data:

  • Article & BlogPosting Schema: Open-standard JSON-LD describing author attribution, publication dates, and headline metadata.
  • BreadcrumbList Schema: Clean hierarchical navigation paths for Google Search indexers.
  • OpenGraph & Twitter Card Metadata: Auto-generated visual cards for rich link previews when readers share chronicles across WhatsApp, X, and Reddit.

Summary & Next Steps

Building The Travel Tales demonstrates that modern web publishing doesn't have to choose between rich visuals and blazing speed. With thoughtful architecture, clean component boundaries, and Next.js 15, we can deliver an extraordinary reader experience.
