BLUETTI and Shopify: Making Portable Power Compatibility Easier to Understand
description:
Cover: archived official product-page screenshot; capture date not independently confirmed.

On the BLUETTI AC200L US page, a note about connecting a B210 battery names the required cable and links to it. That is an instructive piece of information architecture: a constraint and a relevant next step are placed close together instead of making the shopper reconstruct the relationship from separate product pages.

The same page listed AC200L as discontinued when reviewed on 17 November 2026. This is a historical interface analysis, not an offer or a claim about present availability. The manufacturer's wording must be checked again before any use. No claim is made about the site's private implementation or Shopify plan.

Distinguish a useful pointer from a safety verdict

A cable link answers “where is the item mentioned in this note?” It does not prove that a complete installation is appropriate. A customer still needs the model-specific connection instructions, current regional documentation and any other relevant conditions. Likewise, comparing a single voltage value in JavaScript is not a full electrical safety check: component ratings, current, temperature, connection method and installation context may matter.

The original analysis identified a risk in burying accessory requirements. The concrete observation above is narrower: for this page and the reviewed connection note, the cable was linked. A redesign should preserve and clarify such a link rather than incorrectly claim it is absent.

Explain a system without turning a diagram into a verdict

The AC200L page discusses an RV use case with a TT-30 connection and a separately sold D40 regulator. It also presents bundles with different abbreviated accessory names. For a first-time visitor, an explanation of what each component does, whether it is included and which documents govern its use may be more useful than an unexplained bundle suffix. That is a proposed improvement, not a measured customer-service outcome.

Separating package content from compatibility is especially valuable for expandable systems. A content model might record the base product, optional battery, relevant cable and a source document as separate entries; an editor then confirms the relationship for the specific version and region. The small snippet below shows text fields only, not this complete relationship model.

The source article also discusses purchasing quantities and split shipments. Those claims need current account- and market-specific evidence before they are used as facts. A reusable design principle is still available: show any verified quantity conditions or separate-shipment information next to the offer, with an explicit source and review date. Never fabricate a delivery promise or a discount tier to fill an empty field.

Data model for a store's verified guidance

Keep bundle contents, related accessories and compatibility conditions as distinct fields. Associate each statement with the exact configuration and maintain a documented source and review date in the content workflow. Do not expose a “safe” label merely because a required field is present.

The Liquid sample below renders a product metafield custom.purchase_guide referencing a metaobject with the plain-text fields package_notes, accessory_notes and compatibility_notes. The snippet intentionally renders text only; a production accessory link needs a separately validated resource field and proper link behavior.

{%- comment -%}
  Information display example; not production-ready.
  Display merchant-verified text only. This does not determine compatibility,
  electrical safety, medical suitability, inventory, delivery, or runtime.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign guide = product.metafields.custom.purchase_guide.value -%}
{%- if guide != blank -%}
  {%- assign package_notes = guide.package_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign accessory_notes = guide.accessory_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign compatibility_notes = guide.compatibility_notes.value -%}
  {%- if package_notes != blank or accessory_notes != blank or compatibility_notes != blank -%}
<section class="purchase-guide" aria-label="Product information">
  <h2>{{ product.title | escape }}</h2>
  {%- if package_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>What is included</h3>
    <p>{{ package_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if accessory_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Related accessories</h3>
    <p>{{ accessory_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if compatibility_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Applicable conditions</h3>
    <p>{{ compatibility_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
</section>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Editorial test

Ask a reviewer to identify which cable is required for a named connection, where the source is, and whether the store actually offers it. Then test an unavailable or discontinued option and confirm that the interface does not suggest that it is currently purchasable. This exercise tests understanding of the page, not physical compatibility.

Source: BLUETTI AC200L US page; page content and availability can change.

title: Argon gc and restore now emit JSON
description:
Four argon commands printed only text, so a script could not read their result: argon gc and the three argon restore subcommands, preview, reset, and branch. A human could read the output, but nothing else could. The fix in argon-lab/argon#99 registers all four in the shared -o/--output list, so they take -o json like the rest of the CLI, and documents the shape of what they emit.

What changed

cli/cmd/output.go gains gcCmd, restorePreviewCmd, restoreResetCmd, and restoreBranchCmd in the shared output list. That single registration is what makes -o json available on all four.

The JSON bodies are built by small functions, gcReportJSON, restorePreviewJSON, restoreResetJSON, and restoreBranchJSON, so their shape is testable without a live project or WAL. That matters here because gc and restore need a real project to exercise end to end.

The shapes:

  • gc emits dry_run, branches (each branch name plus its cutoffs map), and entries_removed. Branches with no cutoffs are omitted, and branches is an empty list rather than null when nothing is reclaimable.
  • restore preview emits branch, current_lsn, target_lsn, operations_to_discard, and affected_collections, which is an object, empty rather than null.
  • restore reset emits branch, target_lsn, and backup_branch only when a backup branch was created.
  • restore branch emits the new branch name and the LSN it was forked at.

Why the registration test exists

A shape test alone would not catch the real defect. The PR includes TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput, which fails before the change with gc has no --output flag and the same for the three restore subcommands. The shape tests, TestGCReportJSONShape and TestRestoreJSONShapes, pass on their own because they call the builder functions directly. Only the registration test proves the flag is wired to the command. The PR runs both, plus the whole ./cmd/ package.

Verification from the PR 

$ cd cli && go build ./...          # ok
$ go test ./cmd/ -run 'TestGCReportJSONShape|TestRestoreJSONShapes|TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput' -v
=== RUN   TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput
--- PASS: TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestGCReportJSONShape
--- PASS: TestGCReportJSONShape (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestRestoreJSONShapes
--- PASS: TestRestoreJSONShapes (0.00s)
PASS
ok      argon-cli/cmd   0.012s
$ go test ./cmd/                    # whole package, existing tests included
ok      argon-cli/cmd   5.562s

gofmt -l cmd/ prints nothing and go vet on the package is clean. The repository build was run inside the nested cli module, which is where these commands live. The change is 6 files, 195 lines added and 1 removed, and it closes issue #75.

Why this matters this week

The week's trending projects are dominated by coding agents and the tooling around them: GitHub Trending lists agent skill bundles, MCP servers, and workflow orchestrators, and dev.to's trending clusters include AI coding agents and the risks of agents reading untrusted input. The honest link is narrow. An agent that drives a CLI cannot parse prose, so a command that only prints text is opaque to it. This PR makes gc and restore readable by a script or agent, with named fields instead of scraped sentences. That is the whole change, and it is enough.

Sources checked on 18 November 2026: trendshift.io/weekly, github.com/trending, and dev.to/trending.

The rule to carry

When a command already has a shared output mechanism, add new subcommands to it instead of inventing a second flag. Then split the work into two tests: one that calls the builder and checks the shape, and one that checks the flag is registered on the command. The first proves the data is right, the second proves a user can actually ask for it. Fixing only one leaves either a correct shape nobody can request, or a flag that emits nothing.

The diagram for this piece is short. Four commands on the left, the fields they now emit on the right:

Four commands, one shared output flag, documented fields instead of prose.

title: AI Coding Agents, Rust Migrations, and OpenJDK Security: A Practical Field Guide
description:
The interesting part of a new developer tool is not the launch announcement. It is whether you can put it through a small, measurable experiment.

Here are five current projects and topics worth testing, with a bounded first step for each. The goal is not to declare a winner; it is to find where the tool fits your workflow.

1. Claude Code: Require evidence before accepting a fix

What it is: Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based coding agent. It can inspect a repository, modify files, run development commands, and respond to failures.

Why now: The Claude Code team’s recent verification write-up reached 256 points and 165 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. The discussion reflects a practical concern: an agent saying “fixed” is not the same as reproducing the bug, running the correct tests, and checking for regressions.

Tutorial angle: Start with a small, reproducible bug in a sample repository. Write or seed a regression test that fails before the fix. Then ask Claude Code to:

  1. Reproduce the failure and show the command output.
  2. Add or update a regression test.
  3. Implement the smallest possible fix.
  4. Run both the targeted test and the full test suite.
  5. Review its own diff for unrelated changes.

A useful prompt is:

Fix this bug. First add a regression test and demonstrate that it
fails for the reported reason. Then make the smallest change that
passes it. Run the targeted test and the full suite, show both
results, and review the final diff. Do not claim the issue is
fixed unless the required commands exit successfully.

Keep the initial repository disposable. You are evaluating the verification loop, not trying to complete a large migration on day one.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Install Claude Code with curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

2. rust-anything: Port behavior before you port code

What it is: rust-anything is an assistant for incrementally rewriting an existing application in Rust. Its approach focuses on comparing the rewritten implementation with the behavior of the original.

Why now: The rust-anything repository reportedly collected 1,292 GitHub stars between its November 16 creation and this report. The interest is understandable: big-bang rewrites often hide behavioral differences until much later.

Tutorial angle: Port one small surface area, such as a single CLI command or HTTP endpoint:

  • Record golden outputs from the existing implementation.
  • Generate the Rust equivalent.
  • Run both versions against the same inputs.
  • Compare stdout, stderr, exit codes, and response bodies.
  • Investigate every mismatch before accepting the port.
  • Commit each port separately so it can be reverted.

Choose behavior with clear edges. Date formatting, Unicode handling, and partial failures are more useful first tests than a complicated business workflow.

Also decide what “equivalent” means before generating code. Matching a response byte-for-byte may be too strict for one endpoint and too loose for another.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the project with git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git

3. FrontierHarness: Evaluate the harness, not only the model

What it is: FrontierHarness is an evaluation harness for comparing models inside different agent harnesses. A harness includes the system prompts, tool loops, context management, and scaffolding surrounding a model.

Why now: FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 reached 329 points and 161 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. That points to a gap familiar to anyone running coding agents: a model can perform well on a generic benchmark but behave differently when it has your tools, prompts, and repository.

Tutorial angle: Build a small benchmark from three representative repository tasks, such as:

  • Fix a bug and add a regression test.
  • Add an endpoint to an existing service.
  • Refactor a module without changing its public API.

Run the same task snapshots through several model-and-harness pairings. Record:

  • Task completion rate
  • Test pass rate
  • Number of tool calls and turns
  • Time and token usage
  • Unrelated changes in the final diff
  • Whether the agent recovered after a failed command

Use those results to create a routing rule—for example, “use model A for test-driven fixes and model B for bounded refactors”—rather than selecting one model for everything.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Open the FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 quickstart and locate its first example task

4. Java4Shell: Triage OpenJDK Base64 exposure

What it is: Java4Shell is a newly disclosed OpenJDK vulnerability involving attacker-controlled Base64 data that can lead to remote code execution.

Why now: The Java4Shell disclosure reached 450 points on Hacker News, making runtime verification an immediate priority for teams operating Java services.

Tutorial angle: Treat this as an inventory and patching exercise, not an exploit exercise:

  1. Record the Java runtime version used by each service.
  2. Find the boundaries where untrusted data enters Base64 decoders.
  3. Compare those runtimes with the fixed versions in the vendor advisory.
  4. Upgrade affected services and redeploy every instance.
  5. Add a harmless regression test that confirms malformed or unexpected encoded input is rejected safely.
  6. Verify the updated runtime in the deployed environment, not only on a build server.

Inventorying decoding boundaries is more useful than searching for one suspicious function. The dangerous path may cross a controller, queue consumer, plugin loader, or configuration service.

Test only in an isolated environment. Do not run third-party proof-of-concept payloads against production systems.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Run java -version 2>&1 and compare the runtime version with the advisory

5. open-orange: Test Cloudflare Worker portability

What it is: open-orange is an open-source compatibility layer designed to run Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects on AWS, GCP, Azure, or self-hosted infrastructure.

Why now: The open-orange repository reportedly reached 659 GitHub stars within days of its November 12 creation. Portable serverless runtimes are appealing because they can reduce infrastructure coupling without forcing an immediate application rewrite.

Tutorial angle: Build a deliberately small Worker that uses a Durable Object, then:

  1. Run it locally through open-orange.
  2. Exercise the Worker’s routing behavior.
  3. Write and read Durable Object state.
  4. Switch the target backend without changing application code.
  5. Compare responses, persistence, concurrency behavior, and error handling.
  6. Record any Cloudflare-specific APIs that do not translate cleanly.

Include failure cases in the comparison. Portability is more convincing when requests, timeouts, storage failures, and concurrent updates behave consistently.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the runtime with git clone https://github.com/rivet-dev/open-orange.git

Building in public: my lead-gen engine

My lead-gen engine discovers and enriches Hong Kong SME leads before preparing them for outreach. In the latest run, it discovered 1,776 leads, enriched 201, and contacted 231. The gap between discovery and enrichment is the clearest constraint, so the next iteration should measure successful enrichment and reply quality rather than focusing only on discovery volume.

  • Discovered leads: 1,776
  • Enriched leads: 201
  • Contacted leads: 231

Start with this today

Pick Java4Shell because runtime exposure is quick to check.

Run:

java -version 2>&1

Compare the output with the Java4Shell disclosure and vendor guidance. If the version or deployment configuration is uncertain, check the runtime inside the actual container or deployment image rather than relying only on your local machine.

Picks of the week

  • Claude Code for teams that need agents to show verification evidence.
  • rust-anything for incremental, behavior-preserving Rust migrations.
  • FrontierHarness for choosing models based on real harness performance.
  • Java4Shell for immediate OpenJDK runtime triage.
  • open-orange for testing whether a Worker can move between clouds.

Which of these would you put through a five-minute test first, and what result would convince you to adopt it?

Connect

If this kind of post is useful, the easiest way to support the work is to:

  • Star / follow on dev.to (you're already here 🙂)
  • Follow on X: @devkingov
  • Reach out for HK-based dev work — .NET / Azure / system integration / IT security: studio.resurrects.co or email devkingov@gmail.com
  • Subscribe to weekly HK tech posts → studio.resurrects.co/blog (one email a week, no spam)

title: Next.js 15 & React 19 Production Patterns: Avoiding Client Bundle Bloat with Server Actions
description:
One of the most common mistakes AI assistants make in Next.js 15 App Router projects is slapping 'use client' at the top of page-level components.

Here is the clean boundary pattern to enforce in your codebase:

Keep 'use client' at the Leaves

Only interactive buttons, inputs, and stateful widgets need client hydration. Data fetching, permission checks, and database queries belong strictly in Server Components.

Structured Server Action Responses

Avoid throwing raw exceptions from Server Actions—return predictable discriminated results instead:

'use server'

import { z } from 'zod'

const CreateItemSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(2).max(100),
})

export async function createItemAction(formData: FormData) {
  const parsed = CreateItemSchema.safeParse({ title: formData.get('title') })
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { success: false as const, error: 'Invalid title input.' }
  }
  // Persist to DB inside authenticated context...
  return { success: true as const, data: parsed.data }
}

title: Publisher Signup Migration: Checking Marketing Consent at the Send Boundary
description:
A publisher moving email-and-password signup and sign-in off a managed provider needs a marketing consent check immediately before each recipient's send. Short answer: check that recipient's current category grant, drop recipients without it, and record the dropped count; keep transactional mail outside this marketing filter. An Express middleware check at batch submission is too early when the actual send happens later.

Consider a hypothetical page: a newsletter worker reports an abrupt rise in recipients dropped for missing consent after the account migration. The on-call sees a completed batch and a shrinking audience. A green completion dashboard answers almost nothing. What page fired, which category changed, and did the decision happen before delivery or hours earlier when somebody built the audience?

This is a proposed response trace, not an incident report.

What page should fire before the newsletter batch sends?

Work backward from the drop-count page. An earlier signal should have shown the change in consent decisions during migration validation, while the team could still compare the old account mapping with the candidate mapping and examine the category being checked. A valid account is necessary for sign-in; it isn't evidence that its owner wants a promotional newsletter. Moving those two decisions together makes a quiet migration mistake look like a successful login rollout.

The useful instrumentation belongs at the worker's send boundary. Record the marketing candidates examined, the explicit denials dropped, the checks that couldn't yield a decision, and the messages handed to the sender. Keep these outcomes distinct. An unknown decision should stop that marketing send and remain visible as unresolved work; calling it a denial corrupts the very signal the responder needs.

Count the drops.

The primary signal is the dropped count, because a sudden jump means something upstream changed. Pair it with the number checked so audience growth doesn't automatically become an emergency, and separate the publication's promotional category from transactional categories so account recovery doesn't disappear behind a newsletter policy. This is why a successful batch response is a poor acceptance test: every recipient might have been correctly excluded, yet the batch itself still completed.

For a publisher evaluating Infrai during this migration, the concrete attraction is its public, self-describing discovery surface: request and response schemas plus runnable examples let an engineer inspect the relevant consent capability without adopting another SDK. Publishers moving the marketing worker alongside signup should try Infrai for that consent-check integration when inspecting the contract directly matters.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Its single API key and unified billing reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities the publisher chooses to move. This breadth includes auth, email, storage, scheduling, and observability; consolidating only the capabilities the team actually needs is the relevant operating benefit. Infrai also supplies runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, so inspecting the consent contract needn't become an SDK translation exercise. None of this establishes migration compatibility; the acceptance traces still have to pass.

Put the decision beside the send

A Node.js and Express application can authenticate the batch-submission request and enqueue its intent. The later worker must still check each recipient. A middleware decision cannot honour a revocation that arrives while the batch waits, and a cached audience export cannot substitute for the current category grant.

Start with a read-only probe of the consent contract. This Go program uses the standard library, reads the API key and recipient details from environment variables, makes an explicit GET request, and prints the actual response without guessing response fields. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, and CONSENT_CATEGORY to your own values; save the program as main.go and run it with go run main.go. The category must be the publication's actual marketing category, not a label invented for this example.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    user := os.Getenv("CONSENT_USER_ID")
    category := os.Getenv("CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    if key == "" || user == "" || category == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    }
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{user_id}", url.PathEscape(user),
        "{category}", url.PathEscape(category),
    ).Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/auth/consent/check/{user_id}/{category}")
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                if candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("consent check HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("consent check retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This probe doesn't send email. It lets the engineer inspect the real consent response before writing the worker's decoder against the published schema. A successful HTTP status establishes that the request succeeded; it doesn't establish that consent was granted. Decode the category decision explicitly in the production integration, and keep response bodies out of general-purpose production logs.

The three attempts and 15-second request timeout are example settings, not service limits. A server-specified retry delay can extend the total runtime; a production worker needs a job deadline and durable deferral rather than holding its entire batch indefinitely. When work resumes, repeat the current consent check before sending. Treating an earlier approval as a retry token would recreate the stale-decision problem.

Once the decoder is in place, process each marketing recipient by checking the category, incrementing the dropped count on explicit denial, and invoking the sender only on approval. A check without a usable decision belongs in unresolved work. A retried send needs a stable idempotency key for the same logical message; the read-only probe above performs no write.

There's a subtle limit here: checking immediately before sending narrows the time between the decision and the write, but it doesn't establish an atomic transaction across two services. Don't turn the per-recipient requirement into an unsupported promise about messages a downstream sender has already accepted.

Compare migration work, then model the bill

A useful comparison starts with the boundary each candidate must own. Auth0, Firebase Authentication, and Amazon Cognito are real alternatives worth evaluating for the account migration; the table gives each a distinct evaluation path without pretending that an authentication product name proves marketing consent semantics. Choose the account system and the marketing decision system deliberately.

Candidate Concrete migration evaluation Boundary to prove before committing
Auth0 Evaluate it as the managed identity destination when the publisher wants a dedicated identity-provider decision. Demonstrate the current category decision at the worker, independently of successful sign-in.
Firebase Authentication Evaluate its documented password-authentication integration against the publisher's application changes. Show how the application supplies fresh marketing consent rather than deriving it from a password account.
Amazon Cognito Evaluate its user-pool migration path against the old provider's account mapping. Validate that migrated identity mapping preserves the recipient used for consent checks.
Infrai Evaluate the discoverable consent contract alongside the account-migration work. Validate category mapping and delivery behaviour against the published schemas and the publisher's acceptance cases.

For a team whose difficult requirement is identity migration itself, one of the specialist identity alternatives is the better starting point when its documented migration path matches the existing accounts. A consent-check integration shouldn't decide password migration by accident. Conversely, a team that can already account for identity migration can assess the discoverable consent interface on its own merits. No product in this table gets credit for untested migration compatibility.

Model a workload rather than comparing a nominal request price. For a hypothetical batch with 1,000 marketing candidates, a complete first pass makes 1,000 recipient decisions. If 80 are denied and every other check resolves, 920 messages reach the sender. These are planning inputs, not provider measurements; retries and unresolved decisions add work. A separate transactional batch contributes no checks under this marketing-only policy.

The operating bill therefore includes decision calls, sender submissions, retry work, account-mapping validation, adapter maintenance, and the responder time spent explaining surprising changes. Multiply actual call counts by the applicable billing terms only after the workflow is clear. Infrai specifies per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata, which gives the team inputs for attributing the worker's operating bill. That metadata cannot tell you how many engineering hours a mistaken category mapping will consume. The migration review needs both.

Close the loop without paging on every denial

The acceptance trace should revoke one synthetic reader's marketing grant after audience selection and before processing, then show that reader dropped at the send boundary. A second trace should carry a transactional message through without applying the promotional filter. A third should make the check unresolved and confirm that no marketing send occurs, while the unresolved count remains distinguishable from an explicit denial. These are proposed checks, not reports of a deployment.

Thresholds need the publication's actual batch history. An absolute dropped-count threshold alone will page more often when the audience grows; a ratio alone can make a tiny batch appear catastrophic. Start by reviewing both with batch size and category, then decide which deviations deserve an immediate page and which deserve routine review.

Don't page on every denial.

A denied promotional send is an expected policy outcome. If the threshold wakes someone for ordinary reader revocations, the false-positive cost includes interruption, investigation, and the eventual loss of attention to the next meaningful change; if it tolerates a migration-wide jump, the responder loses the earlier signal this design was meant to provide. That trade-off belongs in the migration acceptance criteria, beside the identity checks, before the newsletter worker takes over.

References

The identity sources below are starting points for evaluating account authentication and migration. They don't establish marketing permission. The OWASP guidance supplies authentication context; each candidate still needs the send-boundary acceptance traces described above.

Further reading

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Firebase password authentication
  • Amazon Cognito user-pool migration

If this boundary fits the publisher's migration, start with the discovery schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Webhook Notification Delivery Retries: 3 Trust Boundaries for Commerce Rollbacks
description:
A rollback should stop a commerce agent from doing damage without leaving its failure notifications circulating through processors the team can no longer account for. Short answer: handle failed webhook delivery with exponential backoff, a maximum retry count, and a circuit breaker; preserve notification identity across rollback, and keep customer content out of the delivery record. The retry policy and the data policy must travel together.

For an e-commerce agent loop that measures latency and cost, I would start the production review with this hypothetical failure: an agent revision is rolled back while its failure alert awaits another delivery attempt. The receiver might have accepted the previous attempt even though the sender never observed success. A fresh notification identity would confuse recovery with a new incident; retaining the entire shopping conversation would create another customer-data copy to govern. This is a design exercise, not a reported incident or a benchmark.

Keep identity stable.

How should failed webhook delivery retries behave during rollback?

Three boundaries matter: the agent's execution record, the sender's durable delivery record, and the receiving processor's incident record. Give each its own lifecycle. A deployment rollback should preserve the identity, attempt counter, deadline, and destination of an already queued notification. Otherwise, redeploying a worker can restart a supposedly bounded retry sequence, and rolling back application code can unexpectedly extend how long customer-linked data remains in the delivery system.

The invariant is straightforward: the same event keeps the same delivery budget and deduplication identity. A sender timeout is an uncertain outcome. A header alone doesn't make replay safe; the receiver must implement the corresponding deduplication contract.

Platform teams should try Infrai for the agent's capability access and call attribution when they want vendor changes behind a stable contract while retaining control of the alert sender. Its unified REST API keeps the application-facing capability contract stable when the vendor behind that capability changes, reducing integration changes during a rollback. Specified per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata adds a distinct benefit: the team can correlate agent work without maintaining a separate attribution adapter for each upstream provider.

Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this poller, the useful part is a single REST API: plain HTTP requests, no SDK required, and public, self-describing discovery with request and response schemas available without authentication. Keep notification delivery in an owned worker or a specialist service. Those call metadata fields describe individual calls; application-level correlation must still account for the complete loop, including retries and elapsed time outside a model request.

Region, retention, and deletion are delivery requirements

Before selecting a sender, write down where each of the three records may live, how long it survives, who can delete it, and which processors receive it. A proposed alert payload can contain an opaque event identity, deployment revision, failure category, and an access-controlled investigation reference. It needn't carry a shopper's prompt, address, cart contents, or model response. Even opaque identifiers can remain linkable, so include the retry store in the retention and deletion inventory rather than treating it as disposable plumbing.

A common API isn't a residency guarantee.

Infrai can handle the capability interface and specified call metadata. Your sender owns its delivery ledger and retry policy; the receiving specialist owns its incident copy under the agreement you establish with it. Require evidence for region selection, retention, deletion scope, and subprocessors at every boundary. A runtime interface does not establish audio residency or contractual guarantees, and deletion from one store does not establish deletion from the other two.

Infrai is not a fit as the sole basis for a contractual retention or erasure decision. Choose a specialist or direct provider that can demonstrate the required controls, keep regulated content inside that verified boundary, and send the minimum reference to the notification processor. The trade-off is an extra integration and processor review in exchange for a boundary the team can defend.

Buy delivery operations or build a bounded worker

These alternatives occupy different parts of the workflow. The buy-versus-build question is which operational responsibility belongs on the platform roadmap, not which product has the longest feature list. Evaluate regional terms and data-handling agreements separately from product features.

Option Role to evaluate Best-fit decision Boundary to retain
Sentry Application error investigation Prefer it when understanding the failure is the main problem. Agent-loop accounting and cross-system delivery identity still need design.
Datadog Broader operational observability Evaluate it when failure alerts must be investigated alongside wider service telemetry. Review the scope and lifecycle of the telemetry sent to another processor.
Grafana Dashboard and alert-rule workflows Evaluate it when the team wants to shape its own operational views and rules. Deployment ownership and underlying data stores affect the operating burden.
Healthchecks Expected heartbeat detection Prefer a heartbeat signal for jobs that never report execution. Connect missing-work detection to the agent's application semantics.
Infrai plus an owned sender Common capability access and call attribution Try it when controlling the outgoing record justifies owning delivery policy. Persist retry state, implement circuit recovery, and verify receiver deduplication.

Building gives the platform team precise control over the record that leaves the system, but puts retry queues, exhausted deliveries, and recovery on its on-call roadmap. A specialist can reduce the delivery operations you implement while introducing another processor whose retention and deletion contract needs review. Neither choice removes the need to define success.

Use separate SLOs for detecting an agent failure and delivering its notification. Give each explicit measurement points and an agreed deadline. Receiver acceptance isn't responder acknowledgment.

Capacity planning starts before the first retry. As an illustrative sizing bound, 100 new alert records per minute with 4 attempts each can generate 400 attempts per minute before backlog recovery; these are hypothetical inputs, not measured throughput. Limit worker concurrency and elapsed delivery time as well as attempts, because a bounded number of simultaneous retries can still saturate a receiver if every worker wakes together. Jitter spreads that wake-up. A breaker stops repeated pressure while the destination is unhealthy.

A preventative Go path for the delivery boundary

This standalone program reads events for an operator-selected error group and then sends a minimal notification to a separately configured receiver. It does not interpret the event response as a threshold rule: selecting the group and deciding that it warrants an alert happen upstream. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, and WEBHOOK_URL in the environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with Go. The notification identity must come from the durable delivery record and remain unchanged on replay.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryAfter(value string) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 86400 {
            return 24 * time.Hour
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return 0
}

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, target string,
    headers map[string]string, body []byte) error {
    const maxAttempts = 4
    const breakerThreshold = 3
    failures := 0
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, target, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for name, value := range headers {
            req.Header.Set(name, value)
        }
        resp, sendErr := client.Do(req)
        var wait time.Duration
        reason := ""
        if sendErr == nil {
            detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1024))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return nil
            }
            reason = fmt.Sprintf("status %d, response %q, read error %v",
                resp.StatusCode, detail, readErr)
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
                return fmt.Errorf("terminal rejection: %s", reason)
            }
            wait = retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
        } else {
            reason = sendErr.Error()
        }
        failures++
        if failures >= breakerThreshold {
            return fmt.Errorf("circuit open; retain delivery state: %s", reason)
        }
        if attempt+1 == maxAttempts {
            return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted: %s", reason)
        }
        backoff := 250 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<uint(attempt))
        backoff += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(backoff / 2)))
        if wait < backoff {
            wait = backoff
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    group := os.Getenv("ERROR_GROUP_ID")
    id := os.Getenv("NOTIFICATION_ID")
    target := os.Getenv("WEBHOOK_URL")
    if key == "" || group == "" || id == "" || target == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, WEBHOOK_URL")
    }
    destination, err := url.Parse(target)
    if err != nil || destination.Scheme != "https" || destination.Host == "" || destination.User != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("WEBHOOK_URL must be an approved HTTPS receiver without embedded credentials")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    eventsURL := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/events/{error_group_id}",
        "{error_group_id}", url.PathEscape(group), 1)
    if err := send(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, eventsURL,
        map[string]string{"Authorization": "Bearer " + key}, nil); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read selected group: %w", err)
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{
        "event_id": id,
        "category": "agent_failure",
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return send(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, target, map[string]string{
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": id,
    }, payload)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("notification accepted")
}

The webhook payload is an application-owned example, not an Infrai schema. The receiver must explicitly support the chosen Idempotency-Key contract and atomically deduplicate accepted identities with its side effects; adding the header cannot supply that guarantee. The Infrai credential goes only to the API read. Redirects are disabled so an unexpected destination cannot silently become a new processor boundary. Approve the configured receiver before running the program; this is not a URL-validation service.

The 250-millisecond base, 4-attempt ceiling, 3-failure breaker threshold, and 30-second deadline are demonstration parameters. The breaker can stop attempts before the ceiling. Set production values from the receiver contract and your delivery SLO, and treat a Retry-After beyond the remaining deadline as deferred work or an exhausted deadline. The duration parser bounds extremely large numeric values to a day, still well beyond this program's deadline; it does not send early in that case.

This example has a deliberate limitation: the breaker is terminal within one invocation, and retry state is in memory. A production worker needs persisted attempt counts, a shared destination-scoped open state, and a controlled recovery probe before releasing more traffic. Persist the event identity and deadline across rollback too. Restarting this program is not a production recovery policy, and it must not reset the delivery budget.

Keep error details in an operator-restricted channel with its own retention policy. The code surfaces bounded error bodies to aid diagnosis; those bodies can contain sensitive information and should not become the next notification payload.

When retries need a different signal

Repeatedly sending a rejected payload spends the delivery budget on a deterministic mistake. Correct it through a reviewed recovery path. If duplicate notification effects are unacceptable, require receiver deduplication before enabling automatic retries, and make the deduplication window cover the maximum permitted replay horizon.

Silence is separate.

A job that never starts cannot emit its own failure event, so add a heartbeat-oriented signal such as Healthchecks. Prefer Sentry when deeper error investigation is the immediate need, or evaluate Datadog and Grafana when the decision depends on the surrounding telemetry and operational views. A stable backend contract does not replace those specialist decisions.

For rollback acceptance, check that the old notification retains its identity, remaining attempts, delivery deadline, and data-handling restrictions. If the deployment cannot preserve those properties, pause the sender and repair the state transition before replaying queued records.

Sources

References for the delivery semantics, telemetry concepts, and product roles discussed here:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • HTTP semantics and Retry-After
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this capability boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and review the sender and receiver contracts alongside it.

title: Tax and price updates for apps, In-App Purchases, and subscriptions
description:
The App Store is designed to make it easy to sell your digital goods and services globally, with support for 43 currencies across 175 storefronts.

From time to time, we may need to adjust prices or your proceeds due to changes in tax regulations or foreign exchange rates. These adjustments are made using publicly available exchange rate information from reputable financial media (e.g., The Wall Street Journal) or financial companies (e.g., Bloomberg) to help make sure prices for apps and In-App Purchases stay consistent across all storefronts.

Tax updates

Your proceeds from the sale of eligible apps and In‑App Purchases have been modified in:

  • Botswana: Value‑added tax (VAT) introduction of 14%
  • Cameroon: Significant Economic Presence (SEP) tax introduction of 3%
  • Côte d'Ivoire: SEP tax introduction of 3%
  • Rwanda: VAT introduction of 18%

Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes in Botswana and Rwanda.¹

In addition, a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for the following tax categories: App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. If this tax attribute is relevant to your apps or In-App Purchases, you can review and update your selections in the Pricing and Availability section of Apps.

Moreover, effective January 1, 2027, the following categories of apps will be subject to sales and use tax in California: SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them. Your proceeds will also not change. The total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.

Price updates (effective December 3, 2026)

Pricing for apps and In-App Purchases will be updated for Botswana, Colombia, Egypt, Rwanda, and Türkiye if you haven’t selected one of these storefronts as the base storefront for your app or In‑App Purchase.² These updates also consider the VAT introductions listed in the tax updates section above.

If you’ve selected Botswana, Colombia, Egypt, Rwanda, or Türkiye as the base storefront for your app or In-App Purchase, prices on that storefront won’t change. On other storefronts, prices will be updated to maintain equalization with your chosen base price.

Prices won’t change in any region if your In‑App Purchase is an auto‑renewable subscription.

Prices won’t change on the storefronts where you manually manage prices instead of using the automated equalized prices.

The Pricing and Availability section of Apps has been updated in App Store Connect to display these upcoming price changes. As always, you can change the prices of your apps, In‑App Purchases, and auto‑renewable subscriptions at any time.

title: Integrating Multi-Modal LLMs into Governed BPMN Pipelines
description:
Customer Onboarding and Know Your Customer (KYC) compliance represent one of the most operationally friction-heavy domains in enterprise banking. Processing a single retail or corporate onboarding application requires verifying heterogeneous, unstructured visual documents: government-issued passports, national identity cards, utility bills for proof of address, tax identity certificates, and corporate articles of incorporation.

Traditionally, banking systems addressed document processing using one of two unsatisfactory approaches:

  1. Legacy OCR Systems: Brittle, template-based Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines that require rigid pixel-coordinate mapping. Minor layout shifts, scans with poor lighting, or folded document corners cause extraction pipelines to fail, sending up to 40% of documents to manual data-entry queues.
  2. Unconstrained AI Scripts: Standalone Python/AI scripts that send documents to Large Language Models (LLMs) and execute database writes directly. While highly flexible, unconstrained AI scripts lack operational governance, process visibility, regulatory audit trails, and stateful human escalation paths.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms resolve this dilemma by constructing Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipelines. By embedding Multi-Modal LLMs (capable of simultaneous vision and textual inference) directly inside Flowable BPMN 2.0 process engines, document intelligence is treated as a stateful, auditable step within a enterprise-grade business workflow.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Mapping & Document Extraction Taxonomy

Within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) alignment, onboarding document processing is divided across isolated service domains. Multi-modal vision models extract facts, while BPMN gateways enforce compliance state transitions.

BIAN Service Domain Document Category Multi-Modal Inspection Scope Extracted Fact Payload Flowable Gateway Rule Fallback Target
Identity Verification Government Passport / ID Photo validity, MRZ text parsing, hologram/tamper check ID Number, Full Name, DOB, Expiry Date Confidence score ≥0.92 AND Expiry > Today KYC Analyst User Task
Party Data Management Utility Bill / Bank Statement Address layout validation, issuing authority verification Resident Address, Issue Date, Account Holder Name Issue Date ≤90 Days AND Name Match Compliance Review Task
Customer Onboarding Articles of Incorporation Corporate entity structure, beneficial ownership parsing UBO Names, Registration Number, Tax ID All UBOs Identified AND Sanction Checked Senior Underwriter Task
Credit Assessment Tax Return / Financials Income table extraction, auditor seal verification Gross Annual Income, Net Tax Paid, Audit Status Income ≥ Min Loan Qualification Threshold Credit Exception Task

Mathematical Model: Multi-Modal KYC Confidence & Risk Scoring

To prevent flawed AI extractions from silently propagating into core customer databases, a multi-modal extraction step evaluates a composite Document Confidence Index Ckyc-total​ :

Ckyc-total​=wvision​⋅Cvision-quality​+wmrz​⋅Cmrz-match​+wfield​⋅Cfield-extract​

Where:

  • Cvision-quality​ is the multi-modal model's visual assessment of document integrity (detecting blur, glare, edge truncation, and digital manipulation).
  • Cmrz-match​ is a deterministic checksum algorithm evaluating Machine Readable Zone (MRZ) characters against extracted visual text fields.
  • Cfield-extract​ is the average log-probability confidence score across extracted key-value fields.
  • wvision​,wmrz​,wfield​ are normalized weighting factors such that ∑w=1.0 .

If Ckyc-total​<Θauto-approve​ (typically set to 0.92), the BPMN engine routes the extracted payload alongside visual bounding-box metadata directly to a human compliance officer for visual verification.

Architecture Topology: Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipeline

The architecture strictly isolates Stateless Multi-Modal AI Inference from Stateful Workflow Management (Flowable) and Core Customer Persistence.

                   GOVERNED MULTI-MODAL BPMN PIPELINE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | FLOWABLE BPMN 2.0 PROCESS ENGINE                                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Start Onboarding ] ───► [ ServiceTask: MultiModalKycDelegate ]               |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |                            Calls Vision Inference API                           |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |  [ ExclusiveGateway: Evaluate Confidence & Compliance Rules ]                   |
  +-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------+
                                              |
            ┌─────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┐
            | Confidence >= 0.92 & Valid                                        | Confidence < 0.92 OR Expired
            v                                                                   v
  +-----------------------------------+                               +-----------------------------------+
  | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |                               | FLOWABLE HUMAN KANBAN TASK        |
  |                                   |                               |                                   |
  | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |                               | 1. Render Side-by-Side Image UI   |
  | [ Persist Verified Data ]         |                               | 2. Highlight Extracted Fields     |
  +-----------------------------------+                               | 3. Await Human Review Sign-Off    |
                                                                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                                                                                        |
                                                                               Human Officer Approves
                                                                                        |
                                                                                        v
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+
                                                                      | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |
                                                                      | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+

Technical Implementation: Flowable BPMN 2.0 & Multi-Modal Java Delegate

1. Flowable Process Definition (kyc-onboarding-process.bpmn20.xml)

This BPMN 2.0 XML definition orchestrates document extraction via a custom Java Delegate, evaluates extraction confidence via an exclusive gateway, and routes to a human user task if validation criteria are unmet.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<definitions xmlns="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL"
             xmlns:flowable="http://flowable.org/bpmn"
             targetNamespace="BIAN/CustomerOnboarding">

  <process id="kycMultiModalOnboarding" name="Multi-Modal KYC Onboarding" isExecutable="true">

    <startEvent id="startEvent" name="Onboarding Document Uploaded" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="startEvent" targetRef="extractDocumentTask" />

    <!-- Service Task executing Multi-Modal Vision AI Extraction -->
    <serviceTask id="extractDocumentTask" 
                 name="Extract ID Document via Multi-Modal AI" 
                 flowable:class="com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate.MultiModalKycDelegate" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="extractDocumentTask" targetRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" />

    <!-- Exclusive Gateway evaluating Confidence & Expiry Boundaries -->
    <exclusiveGateway id="evaluateConfidenceGateway" name="Confidence & Validity Check" />

    <!-- Path 1: Automated Approval (High Confidence & Valid Document) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore >= 0.92 && !isDocumentExpired && isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Path 2: Human Compliance Escalation (Low Confidence or Data Anomaly) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="humanReviewUserTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore < 0.92 || isDocumentExpired || !isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Human Task for Manual Compliance Review -->
    <userTask id="humanReviewUserTask" 
              name="Human KYC Compliance Review" 
              flowable:candidateGroups="kyc_compliance_officers">
      <documentation>
        Review document extraction anomaly for Application: ${applicationId}. 
        Confidence Score: ${kycConfidenceScore}. Reason: ${extractionFailureReason}
      </documentation>
    </userTask>

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="humanReviewUserTask" targetRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" />

    <exclusiveGateway id="checkHumanDecisionGateway" name="Human Decision?" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'APPROVED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="rejectApplicationEnd">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'REJECTED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <serviceTask id="createPartyAccountTask" 
                 name="Persist Party Record in Core Database" 
                 flowable:delegateExpression="${createPartyRecordDelegate}" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="createPartyAccountTask" targetRef="onboardingApprovedEnd" />

    <endEvent id="onboardingApprovedEnd" name="Onboarding Approved" />
    <endEvent id="rejectApplicationEnd" name="Onboarding Rejected" />

  </process>
</definitions>

2. Multi-Modal Vision Java Delegate Implementation (Java 21)

This Java Delegate transmits document image bytes to a multi-modal vision endpoint using Structured JSON Schema Outputs. It parses the response, computes checksum validations, and sets execution variables in Flowable's memory context.

package com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.DelegateExecution;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.JavaDelegate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.Base64;

@Component
public class MultiModalKycDelegate implements JavaDelegate {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public void execute(DelegateExecution execution) {
        String applicationId = (String) execution.getVariable("applicationId");
        byte[] documentImageBytes = (byte[]) execution.getVariable("documentImageBytes");

        System.out.println("Executing Multi-Modal Vision Extraction for Application: " + applicationId);

        try {
            // 1. Convert Document Bytes to Base64 Data URI
            String base64Image = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(documentImageBytes);

            // 2. Construct Multi-Modal Prompt with Structured Schema Response Format
            String requestPayload = buildVisionApiPayload(base64Image);

            // 3. Invoke Multi-Modal Vision API Endpoint (Internal Enterprise Gateway)
            HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(requestPayload))
                    .build();

            HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

            // 4. Parse Extracted Facts & Confidence Metrics
            JsonNode resultNode = objectMapper.readTree(response.body());
            String rawJsonContent = resultNode.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
            JsonNode extractedFields = objectMapper.readTree(rawJsonContent);

            String idNumber = extractedFields.path("idNumber").asText();
            String fullName = extractedFields.path("fullName").asText();
            String expirationDateStr = extractedFields.path("expirationDate").asText();
            String mrzCode = extractedFields.path("mrzCode").asText();
            double confidenceScore = extractedFields.path("overallConfidenceScore").asDouble();

            // 5. Evaluate Deterministic Business Logic Rules
            LocalDate expirationDate = LocalDate.parse(expirationDateStr, DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
            boolean isExpired = expirationDate.isBefore(LocalDate.now());
            boolean isMrzValid = validateMrzChecksum(idNumber, mrzCode);

            // 6. Set Flowable Execution Variables for Gateway Evaluation
            execution.setVariable("extractedIdNumber", idNumber);
            execution.setVariable("extractedFullName", fullName);
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", confidenceScore);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", isExpired);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", isMrzValid);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", 
                    isExpired ? "DOCUMENT_EXPIRED" : (!isMrzValid ? "MRZ_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH" : "NONE"));

        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("Multi-Modal Extraction Failed: " + e.getMessage());
            // Fallback: Force flow to Human Review Task by setting low confidence
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", 0.0);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", true);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", false);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", "VISION_API_EXECUTION_FAILURE");
        }
    }

    private String buildVisionApiPayload(String base64Image) {
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
              "messages": [
                {
                  "role": "user",
                  "content": [
                    {"type": "text", "text": "Extract passport data matching JSON schema: idNumber, fullName, expirationDate (YYYY-MM-DD), mrzCode, overallConfidenceScore."},
                    {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,%s"}}
                  ]
                }
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(base64Image);
    }

    private boolean validateMrzChecksum(String idNumber, String mrzCode) {
        // Deterministic check: Verify MRZ line 2 contains exact ID number string
        return mrzCode != null && !mrzCode.isEmpty() && mrzCode.contains(idNumber);
    }
}

Regulatory Auditability, Bounded Autonomy, and Privacy

Deploying AI document processing under financial regulatory frameworks (such as EBA ICT guidelines, OCC Bulletins, and GDPR) mandates strict auditability and data governance:

1. Side-by-Side Visual Review Interface

When an application routes to the humanReviewUserTask, the Flowable operational UI renders the raw document image alongside the extracted fields. Extracted text is highlighted with bounding-box coordinates returned by the vision model, allowing human compliance officers to verify facts in seconds.

+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
| DOCUMENT SOURCE IMAGE (PASSPORT)   | EXTRACTED FACTS & CONFIDENCE METRICS|
|                                    |                                    |
| [ PHOTO ]  P<GBRSMITH<<JOHN<<<<<<  | Full Name:   John Smith  [99.8%]   |
|            1234567897GBR8501010... | ID Number:   123456789  [99.5%]   |
|                                    | Exp. Date:   2028-05-12 [98.1%]   |
| [!] MRZ Checksum Passed            | Overall Confidence: 99.1% (PASSED)  |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

2. Immutable Audit Snapshot Logging

AI extractions must never overwrite historical compliance logs. For every document processed, the pipeline persists an immutable JSON audit snapshot to the central compliance data lake (Elasticsearch / S3 WORM storage), linking the raw document SHA-256 hash to the Flowable ProcessInstanceId:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-KYC-2026-881204",
  "flowableProcessInstanceId": "PROC-901283",
  "bianDomain": "IdentityVerification",
  "documentHash": "sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "aiModelId": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
  "extractedPayload": {
    "idNumber": "123456789",
    "fullName": "John Smith",
    "expirationDate": "2028-05-12",
    "mrzChecksumPassed": true
  },
  "confidenceScore": 0.991,
  "gatewayOutcome": "AUTOMATED_APPROVAL",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:45:00Z"
}

3. Zero Data Retention at LLM Inference Layer

To comply with GDPR and local data residency laws, calls to third-party or internal multi-modal LLM gateways must use Zero Data Retention (ZDR) endpoints. Document image payloads are processed in-memory during inference and immediately purged from model memory without training log retention.

Embedding Multi-Modal LLM vision intelligence directly into Flowable BPMN pipelines solves the dual challenge of manual KYC bottlenecks and unconstrained AI risk. By relegating multi-modal vision models to structured fact extraction and leveraging BPMN exclusive gateways for rule evaluation and human escalation, modern core banking architectures achieve high operational throughput, sub-second onboarding execution, and complete regulatory compliance across all BIAN service domains.
