title: Object Storage Service for Storing User Documents with Go Backup Pipelines
description:
A practical decision rule: use Amazon S3 when backup durability, lifecycle depth, and ecosystem coverage dominate; use Cloudflare R2 when an S3-compatible edge-oriented design fits; use Azure Blob when the rest of the estate is already Azure; consider Infrai when the main cost is integrating several backend capabilities and a plain, discoverable REST surface matters. For a fintech tenant-document system, keep every object private, make restore a separate workflow, and treat a large-file transfer as a throughput problem rather than a pricing headline.

The backup invariant is simple: a tenant snapshot is immutable to the restore workflow, a retry cannot create a second logical snapshot, and the restore target is selected explicitly. The storage provider is only one part of that contract. A cheap GB-month does not compensate for an unsafe overwrite or a restore path that cannot explain what happened.

Keep it boring.

What fails first in a tenant backup runbook?

The dangerous signal is not always an outage. It is often a successful-looking job that uploaded some objects, timed out, and ran again. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. Large files make this sharper: a retry can spend time and bandwidth on an upload whose first attempt may already exist. Keep the logical snapshot ID in the database, derive object keys from tenant ID and snapshot ID, and record the checksum and completion state before advertising the snapshot to a restore operator.

I would separate the control plane from the bytes. The control plane owns tenant authorization, snapshot selection, retention decisions, and restore state. The object store owns private bytes and transfer mechanics. That boundary gives the on-call engineer something concrete to verify: database state, object existence, object size, checksum, then restore completion.

Do not use a public ACL for user documents. A private object plus a short-lived presigned URL is the safer delivery shape, and the application must not forward its storage-service Authorization header to the returned URL. This also keeps browser delivery subject to an explicit CORS design; CORS is a browser permission mechanism, not an access-control substitute.

Which object storage service should handle storing user documents?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a direct provider architecture. The application uses S3, R2, or Azure Blob primitives directly, usually with the provider SDK, multipart upload, provider lifecycle rules, and the provider's replication and recovery features. Its invariant is provider-native correctness: the SDK and the provider agree on upload completion, conditional writes, retention, and restore semantics. This is the strongest choice when the backup path is the product and the team is willing to own provider-specific operations.

The second is a unified REST architecture. A service such as Infrai presents storage behind one REST surface, while its discovery endpoint exposes the available capability, request schema, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when the same team is also wiring queues, schedules, or other backend services and does not want each integration to introduce another SDK and credential model. The invariant changes: the application must pin the capability contract it uses, preserve provider-neutral object keys, and keep an exit path through ordinary object-store formats.

Here is the comparison I would put in a design review:

Option Strong fit Boundary to test before adoption
Amazon S3 Broad ecosystem, mature lifecycle and multipart patterns Provider-specific features and configuration become part of the runbook
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible access for workloads already centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required replication, lifecycle, and recovery behavior for the region and compliance model
Azure Blob Storage Teams already operating identities, policy, and monitoring in Azure Validate the translation between Blob semantics and an S3-shaped application layer
Infrai storage A discoverable REST integration and one credential model matter across backend capabilities No public ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration; browser upload CORS is not self-service

For a US/EU fintech project, I would choose the direct provider architecture when the document archive needs WORM controls, provider-native replication, or a migration program with bulk tooling. I would choose the unified shape for a private document workflow whose main engineering constraint is integration surface, provided an external database or compliance store supplies the missing immutability and coordination guarantees.

The live platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth is not a storage guarantee. A storage decision still turns on the bytes, the restore contract, and the controls the archive must prove during an audit.

How should the worker upload and restore safely?

Start with a durable record such as (tenant_id, snapshot_id, state, object_key, checksum, size). The worker claims one pending snapshot, writes to a deterministic private key, and records completion only after the object check passes. A retry reads that record and either resumes the transfer or verifies the already-complete object. It does not invent a new key because the network was uncertain.

For large files, use multipart transfer where the selected provider supports it. Bound concurrency so a restore does not starve ordinary document reads. Treat an incomplete multipart upload as an operational object that needs inspection: a one-day minimum lifecycle may be too coarse for a cleanup policy, and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule in the unified storage option described above.

Infrai's storage surface includes a private object put operation and presigning, and its API is self-describing: discovery is public, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in Go as well as other languages. That makes a new integration easier to inspect before implementation. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the broader platform exposes one key and a common REST convention across its capabilities, including documented idempotency conventions for applicable writes.

This is the smallest useful upload shape for a private object. It keeps the key outside the request body, uses a deterministic idempotency value, checks status codes, and backs off on a rate limit. The exact request schema should still be confirmed from discovery before production rollout.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        panic("usage: put-object <bucket> <key> <file>")
    }
    key, err := os.Open(os.Args[3])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer key.Close()

    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(endpointTemplate, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    endpoint = strings.ReplaceAll(endpoint, "{key}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[2]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, key)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "tenant-snapshot-2026-10-24")
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
                body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
                res.Body.Close()
                panic(fmt.Sprintf("upload failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body))
            }
            res.Body.Close()
            return
        }
        wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
        }
        res.Body.Close()
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
    panic("upload rate-limited after retries")
}

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the application-facing private document transfer and backup orchestration when discovering and wiring one REST capability is more valuable than provider-native storage controls. Keep the snapshot ledger outside it, and choose S3 or Azure Blob instead when object lock, native replication, or a provider-specific compliance control is a hard requirement. That is a real limitation, not a footnote: Infrai is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, WORM retention, or a workflow that needs automatic cross-region copies.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a short runbook, not a dashboard slogan. After an upload, compare the recorded size and checksum with the object metadata, then run a restore into a quarantine namespace for a representative tenant. Check authorization at the application boundary and confirm that the delivered URL is signed and time-limited. Record the request ID and outcome so a duplicate delivery can be distinguished from a second logical snapshot.

Rollback means stopping new snapshot publication, leaving the original private objects untouched, and reverting the control-plane state to the last verified snapshot. Do not promise recovery from an accidental overwrite if the selected service has no object versioning or object lock. For strict concurrent writes, coordinate through the database or a queue because the unified storage option does not provide an If-Match conditional write.

A final trap: lifecycle rules are not a substitute for a retention policy. The unified option has a one-day minimum lifecycle and prefix-only object listing; metadata is not server-side searchable. If operators need legal holds, exact metadata queries, or automatic cross-region copies, that requirement belongs in the architecture decision, not in a late configuration ticket.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the private document storage guide and verify the capability contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Infrai storage documentation

description:
Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets.

Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in.

These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

title: Rigging UI Elements: Bones and IK Outside of Character Animation
description:
Bones are associated with characters, and that association keeps designers from using them where they would save the most time: interface elements that need to bend.

This is a practical guide to the cases, the workflow, and the limits.

What a bone rig actually buys you

A keyframe rig says: at 200ms, this vertex is here. At 400ms, it is there.

A bone rig says: this vertex is 60% influenced by the upper arm and 40% by the forearm. Move the arm and the vertex follows, everywhere, forever.

That indirection is the value. You animate the skeleton — a handful of rotations — and the geometry follows. Change the artwork, and the rig still works. Change the pose, and the skin deforms consistently.

For UI, that means:

  • a mascot that leans, blinks and gestures without re-keyframing every path
  • an illustration that squashes on press without distorting its neighbours
  • a decorative arrow that bends along a curve instead of being redrawn
  • a loading skeleton that breathes with a single parameter
  • a hero object whose parts stay attached when the layout changes

The workflow, in the order it matters

1. Decide what the skeleton is, not what the drawing is.

Look at the artwork and ask: what are the levers? A tail has three. A ribbon has four. An arm has two plus a hand. Bones should be fewer than you think; a rig with twelve bones for a shape that needs three is harder to animate, not easier.

2. Parent the hierarchy properly.

Master bone at the root, children for the limbs or segments, each rotated around a sensible pivot. In Exode this is the master/child bone distinction in the hierarchy panel, and the pivot is what makes a rotation look like a joint rather than a spin.

3. Bind, then weight.

Auto-binding on selection is convenient and destructive if you are not careful — the audit notes on the Exode repo list exactly that problem and the fix that shipped. The safe sequence is: bind the mesh, then paint weights, then test extreme poses before you animate.

Weights are the craft. A vertex at 100% on one bone will crease. A vertex split 50/50 will bend smoothly. The batch weighting and the live weights table exist because doing this one vertex at a time is how rigs get abandoned.

4. Add IK only where you need it.

Inverse kinematics solves the pose from a target: drag the hand, the elbow follows. It is magic for a character reaching for something. It is overkill for a two-bone ribbon you will animate directly.

Exode supports IK chains; the rule is to use them at the end of a chain, not the root, or the whole rig becomes a puppet you cannot pose precisely.

5. Animate the skeleton, never the mesh.

Once the rig is bound, all animation should be bone rotations and root position. If you catch yourself keyframing individual vertices, the rig is wrong.

The UI-specific details nobody tells you

Layout and rigs interact badly if you let them. A bone rig lives in the coordinate space of its container. If the container reflows on a breakpoint, the rig must be positioned by layout, not by absolute coordinates, or it will detach on mobile. This is the single most common bug in "responsive mascot" work.

Rigs need a rest pose that matches the design. If the rig's neutral pose is not the design's default, every state has a permanent offset. Bind at the pose you will ship.

Reduced motion needs a rig-free fallback. A static image at the rest pose is the honest fallback. Do not run a cut-down rig animation for users who asked for less motion; show the still.

Export the rig, not a video. A baked sprite sequence loses the interactivity you built the rig for. If the rig is in the design artefact, the compiled component carries it.

Where the tooling is still catching up

The honest part.

Mesh deformation in Rive and Spine is deeper than in Exode today. If the brief is "a cape that ripples with wind", those tools have more mature free-form deformation and more artist-facing controls.

Exode's rigging audit lists eight gaps it closed — destructive auto-bind, single-vertex selection, read-only weights, edit-mode exit, static weight visuals, destructive re-binding, no independent Bézier handle weighting, and rigid normalisation. That is a real list, and the fact that it is public is a good sign. It is not the same as a decade of character rigs.

So the split I use:

  • Character as art object, shipped inside a canvas or game: Rive or Spine.
  • Character or shape inside a responsive interface, driven by app state: rig it where the layout and state live.

A small example

A brand mark that reacts to a form field:

  • idle: rest pose
  • focus: slight lean toward the field, one bone rotation
  • invalid: a single shake on the root bone, damped
  • success: a squash-and-stretch envelope plus a small bounce

Four states, one rig, two bone rotations and an envelope. No keyframed paths, no per-state redraw, and the whole thing scales with the container because it is inside the layout.

That is the case for bones outside character animation: it turns "redraw it four times" into "rotate a lever".

The rule I would give a team

If an element needs to bend in more than one state, rig it. If it only ever translates or fades, keyframe it and move on. Bones are a multiplier on reuse, and reuse is the only reason they are worth the setup.

UX Baba writes about interaction design and the unglamorous parts of craft. Exode's bone system is part of the editor at exodeui.com.

title: Save Points for Law Firm Intake Forms: A Game Design Lesson
description:
Anyone who played games before autosave remembers losing an hour of progress to a power cut or a missed save point. Modern game design treats that kind of loss as the game's fault. Progress is saved quietly at sensible moments, and a crash costs a few seconds at most.

Law firm intake forms rarely get the same care. A person filling out a criminal defense contact form is often stressed, on a phone, and interrupted. A call comes in, the browser reloads, the screen locks, and everything they typed about the arrest is gone. Some will start again. Many will not. If you build sites for defense firms, a save point in the intake form is a small piece of work with a real payoff, as long as you handle the privacy side carefully.

What games get right about saving

Good save systems share a few habits. They save without asking, so the player never has to think about it. They save at natural checkpoints, such as entering a new area, rather than every frame. They tell the player when a save happened with a small, unobtrusive icon. And they make it easy to start fresh when the player wants to.

Each of those maps onto a form. Save quietly as the user types, at the moment a field loses focus. Show a short "Saved on this device" note. Offer a clear way to wipe the saved data. Restore it automatically if the page reloads.

The privacy problem games do not have

A saved game holds a character's inventory. A saved intake form can hold a description of an arrest, a charge, a court date and a phone number. That changes the design.

The device may be shared. A person might fill out the form on a family computer, a work laptop or a friend's phone. Anything stored in the browser can be seen by the next person who opens it. For that reason, persistent storage that survives closing the browser is a poor fit for defense intake. Session-scoped storage is a better default: in current browsers, sessionStorage data survives a reload but is cleared when the tab is closed, and it is not shared with other tabs.

It also helps to be selective about what gets saved at all. Contact details and simple choices, such as the type of charge from a dropdown, are the fields people most hate retyping. The long free-text description of what happened is the most sensitive. A reasonable compromise is to save the structured fields and leave the free-text box out, or to save it only if the firm decides the trade-off is worth it after discussing it with the lawyers.

A minimal implementation

Here is a small sketch using sessionStorage. It saves listed fields when they lose focus, restores them on load, and clears everything on submit or when the user asks.

const KEY = "intake-draft";
const form = document.querySelector("#intake");
const SAVED = ["name", "phone", "email", "charge_type", "county"];

function save() {
  const data = {};
  SAVED.forEach(n => { data[n] = form.elements[n]?.value || ""; });
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data)); } catch (e) {}
}

function restore() {
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) || "{}");
    SAVED.forEach(n => { if (data[n] && form.elements[n]) form.elements[n].value = data[n]; });
  } catch (e) {}
}

function clearDraft() {
  try { sessionStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
}

form.addEventListener("focusout", save);
form.addEventListener("submit", clearDraft);
document.querySelector("#clear-draft").addEventListener("click", () => { clearDraft(); form.reset(); });
restore();

The try blocks matter. Storage can throw in private browsing modes or when the browser blocks site data, and the form has to keep working either way. Clearing on submit should happen after you confirm the submission succeeded if the form posts by script, so a network error does not wipe the draft.

Telling the user what happened

Games show a spinning icon in the corner. A form can show a line of small text under the submit button that changes to "Saved on this device until you close this tab" after the first save. That one sentence tells the person their work is safe and tells them how long it stays. Next to it, a "Clear this form" link gives them control on a shared device.

Keep the message honest. Do not say "saved" in a way that suggests the firm has received anything. Only the submit button sends the information.

Making the form shorter matters more

A save point helps people who get interrupted. It does nothing for people who give up because the form asks too much. Before building any of this, look at which fields the firm actually uses at the first call. Some intake forms ask for date of birth, case number and a long narrative that the lawyer will cover by phone anyway. A guide to designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish goes through trimming the form itself.

Track the effect with your existing form analytics. Compare form starts with completed submissions for a few weeks before and after adding the save feature. Small sites will need longer to see a pattern.

Questions about saving intake form progress

Should the form use localStorage so drafts survive closing the browser?

For criminal defense intake, that is risky on shared devices. Session-scoped storage is the safer default unless the firm has a clear reason and tells users plainly.

Does saving in the browser send anything to the firm?

No. Data in sessionStorage stays on the device until the user submits the form.

Does the firm need to mention this in its privacy policy?

Ask the firm to review its privacy policy with whoever maintains it. Describing local draft saving in plain words is good practice.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one firm per city, and helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits. Its notes on UX lessons from video game design cover more ideas from games that apply to law firm sites.

title: What a short-link redirect costs: about 4 microseconds in Go
description:
A short-link redirect looks like the simplest thing a web service can do: take a slug, return a 301 or 302. It is also the one request every click on every link has to pass through, so we built it as its own service with a written latency budget.

This post walks through that service: the choices we made, the reasons recorded in our ADRs, a few trimmed excerpts from the code, and a benchmark of what one request costs in-process. The benchmark is local and narrow, and we will say exactly how narrow. The conclusion is a little anticlimactic.

Split by latency budget, not by domain

The first decision (ADR-0013) was to divide the system by how fast each part has to be, not by business area. A link service that handled both redirects and link CRUD would share one latency budget between two very different workloads.

So there are three tiers:

  • Hot path: edge-redirect only. Target p50 5 ms and p95 15 ms on a cache hit. Nothing synchronous beyond the cache lookup.
  • Warm path: api-core, analytics-api, billing. User-facing CRUD, ClickHouse queries, payments.
  • Cold path: async workers fed by the event bus, such as click-ingester, notifications and the URL scanner.

The 5 ms figure is a design target recorded in the ADR. It is not a measured production number, and we are not presenting it as one.

The rule this buys is easy to enforce in code review: if it is not a cache lookup, it does not belong in the redirect handler.

Why Go, and why fasthttp

ADR-0002 picks Go for the latency-sensitive services. The reasons are unglamorous: static binaries that deploy trivially, goroutines for concurrency, short and tunable GC pauses, and a team that already knew the language. Rust was considered and set aside because the development cost was not justified at our scale. The ADR names a trigger for revisiting it: if p99 on cache hits exceeds 50 ms sustained at 10K RPS, benchmark Rust for this one service.

ADR-0003 goes one level down and picks fasthttp over net/http for the HTTP layer of this single service. fasthttp pools its request and response objects, which cuts allocation and GC pressure at high request rates. The ADR is honest about the cost: it does not work with the net/http middleware ecosystem, and its ownership rules (you must not hold a RequestCtx after the handler returns) are an easy way to introduce bugs. Every other Go service in the repo stays on net/http and chi.

That ownership rule shows up in the code. When a click is recorded, the handler copies what it needs out of the context before handing work to a goroutine:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
// Snapshot fields before the fasthttp ctx is recycled; the goroutine below
// outlives the request cycle.
fullIP, _ := netip.AddrFromSlice(clientIP(ctx))
acceptLang := string(ctx.Request.Header.Peek("Accept-Language"))
...
h.spawn(func() { h.finishClick(ev, fullIP.Unmap(), acceptLang) })

The lookup: L1, then Redis, then origin

ADR-0004 describes the cache. The source of truth is Postgres behind api-core, and a round trip there on every request would eat the whole budget. So the service asks three places in order.

 client
   |
   v
 Caddy (TLS) --> edge-redirect (Go, fasthttp)
                    |
                    |  1. L1: in-process LRU, TTL in seconds
                    |  2. L2: Redis, longer TTL
                    |  3. origin: api-core (gRPC Resolve, else HTTP)
                    |
                    +--> 301/302 back to the client
                    |
                    +--> goroutine: enrich click, Produce() ---> Redpanda
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                           click-ingester
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                              ClickHouse

The resolver that implements this is short enough to read in one go:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/resolver/resolver.go (trimmed)
func (r *Resolver) resolve(ctx context.Context, host, slug string) (*origin.Link, error) {
    key := cacheKey(host, slug)

    if v, ok := r.l1.Get(key); ok {
        return v, nil
    }
    if v, ok := r.l2.Get(ctx, key); ok {
        r.l1.Set(key, v)
        return v, nil
    }

    link, err := r.origin.Resolve(ctx, host, slug)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    r.l1.Set(key, link)
    r.l2.Set(ctx, key, link)
    return link, nil
}

L1 is hashicorp/golang-lru with expiry. A hit is a map lookup in the same process, with no network at all. The ADR's argument against Redis-only is that every request would pay a network round trip (it estimates 0.5 to 1 ms inside a datacenter) while an in-process hit costs about 50 ns. Redis then absorbs the long tail of less popular slugs so they do not all fall through to origin. The ADR also notes the system degrades sensibly: if Redis is down, L1 still serves recent hits.

The trade-off is that you now have two TTLs, and a short L1 TTL means a deleted link cannot be served forever by one node. That is stated in the LRU's doc comment, and it leads to invalidation.

Cache invalidation

TTLs alone would make edits feel slow. ADR-0004 adds explicit invalidation on link update and delete. What the code does today is this: after every link mutation, api-core deletes the Redis key and publishes the cache key on a Redis pub/sub channel. Each edge process subscribes and evicts its own L1 copy.

// services/edge-redirect/internal/cache/invalidate.go (trimmed)
// api-core already DELs the L2 key; this channel only exists to evict the
// per-process L1 copy so an edit is live in about a second instead of after
// the L1 TTL.
const InvalidateChannel = "elido:link:invalidate"

The subscriber runs in a background goroutine and is never on the request path. If Redis is unavailable, the only consequence is that L1 entries live out their TTL. Note that the ADR text mentions Redpanda for these events; the implementation we read uses Redis pub/sub, and the code is what we describe here.

Clicks: fire and forget

Analytics is the reason a redirect service has side effects at all, and side effects are where latency budgets go to die. The rule from ADR-0013 is that the response never waits for them.

The handler builds a click event from cheap header copies, then starts a goroutine. That goroutine does the expensive parts (IP classification, scanner flagging, truncating the IP, hashing the visitor) and publishes the event to Redpanda, which speaks the Kafka protocol, through a franz-go producer. A separate service, click-ingester, consumes the topic and writes to ClickHouse. The redirect service never talks to ClickHouse.

The consequence is the usual one for this design: a click can be lost if the process dies between the response and the produce call, and we accept that trade for a hot path that has no dependency on the analytics store being up.

What one request costs

Now the numbers. These come from Go's go test -bench . -benchmem on an Apple M3 laptop, run on 2026-11-18. They are in-process handler benchmarks. There is no network, no TLS and no real client, so they measure our code and nothing around it.

Benchmark ns/op B/op allocs/op
Redirect, L1 hit, full request including spawning click work 4032 4680 71
Redirect, L1 hit, request path only 3619 3728 52
Click enrichment (runs off the request path) 911 912 19
Redirect through the CTA overlay page 28781 36526 297
Blocklist check 44 0 0
Query-parameter forwarding (mixed case) 379 192 3

Read the first two rows together: The request path itself is about 3.6 microseconds, and starting the click work adds about 0.4 more. The click enrichment, at roughly 0.9 microseconds, happens after the response is already decided. The blocklist check allocates nothing, which is the kind of result you hope for from a check that runs on every request. The CTA overlay page costs about eight times a plain redirect, since it does more work per request.

The allocation profile

Fifty-two allocations for a redirect is more than a pooled HTTP library might lead you to expect. Profiling the request path shows where they come from:

  • fasthttp header and argument handling, which are the largest allocators.
  • A context.WithTimeout for the origin call, created on every request even when L1 answers and the origin is never called.
  • Client IP parsing with net.ParseIP, done more than once per request.

You can see the second one in the handler:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
resolveCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, h.cfg.OriginTimeout)
defer cancel()
link, err := h.resolver.Resolve(resolveCtx, host, slug)

All three are fixable. Creating the timeout only once the resolver misses L1 is a small change, and parsing the client IP once instead of several times is another.

Why we have not fixed them

At about 3.6 microseconds, the request path uses less than 0.1% of the 5 ms target. If we removed every allocation in the list above and saved, say, a third of that, the user would see no difference. A real redirect spends its time on the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, and the distance between the client and the server. Those are measured in milliseconds, and no amount of work on net.ParseIP changes them.

There is also a cost on the other side of the ledger. Hand-tuning a handler to shave allocations tends to make it harder to read, and this handler already has to deal with passwords, previews, agent-readable JSON responses and warning pages.

So the plan is deliberately boring: keep the benchmarks in the repo so a regression shows up, fix the cheap allocations when we are in that code anyway, and put effort where the time is. We run in production today as a single EU VPS behind Caddy, so network distance is the next thing we would look at, long before another microsecond of Go.

The benchmark does not tell us about p99 under load, GC behavior at sustained throughput, or cache hit rate on real traffic. It tells us our own code is not the problem. That is a narrower claim than "fast", and it is the one we can back up.

What we would repeat

Split services around the budget, because "only cache lookups on the hot path" cannot be enforced inside a shared service. Push slow work behind a queue. Measure in-process, then say what you did not measure.

Elido is a hosted URL shortener built EU-first with custom domains, QR codes and click analytics. The docs are at elido.app/docs.

title: Why Your 300ms Cubic-Bezier Feels Dead (And What Springs Do Differently)
description:
Every product has one. transition: all 300ms ease-in-out. It is the reason a lot of interfaces feel like they are made of cardboard.

This is not a taste argument. There is a mechanical reason a fixed-duration curve feels wrong for interaction, and a specific set of cases where it is still exactly right.

A curve is a script; a spring is a physics system

A cubic-bezier transition says: over exactly 300ms, move from A to B following this shape. It is a script with a fixed ending.

The problem appears when the user interrupts it. Click a toggle, then click it back at 150ms. What should happen?

With a fixed transition, the browser usually restarts the curve from wherever it is, with a full 300ms duration again. The object visibly hesitates. If you interrupt repeatedly, you get a stuttering object that is clearly not obeying anything.

A spring has no duration. It has a target and a state — position and velocity. When the target changes mid-flight, the object keeps its current velocity and accelerates toward the new target. Reversing direction feels like reversing a physical object because that is what is being simulated.

That is the whole difference, and it is why springs feel "alive" and fixed tweens feel like slides.

The math, without the ceremony

A damped spring is a second-order system:

m·x'' + c·x' + k·x = 0

where m is mass, c is damping, k is stiffness, and x is displacement from the target. The behaviour is governed by the damping ratio:

ζ = c / (2·√(k·m))
  • ζ < 1 — underdamped, overshoots and settles. This is "bouncy".
  • ζ = 1 — critically damped, fastest approach with no overshoot.
  • ζ > 1 — overdamped, sluggish, no overshoot.

A concrete implementation, if you want to feel the difference in a CodePen:

function stepSpring(
  state: { x: number; v: number },
  target: number,
  { stiffness: k, damping: c, mass: m, dt }: Params
) {
  const force = -k * (state.x - target) - c * state.v;
  const accel = force / m;
  const v = state.v + accel * dt;
  return { x: state.x + v * dt, v };
}

Integrate at a fixed timestep, not per frame, or the motion changes with the refresh rate. That detail is where most hand-rolled springs go wrong.

Tuning it like a human

Numbers that produce good UI, in the units most spring libraries use:

Feel Stiffness Damping Mass
Snappy button / badge 240 22 1.0
Card or modal entrance 120 18 1.2
Playful metric reveal 180 14 1.0
Heavy panel, no bounce 90 26 1.4

These are in the same family as the values in React Spring and Framer Motion, which is a useful sanity check if you are porting a component.

The practical rule: more damping for things that carry information, less for things that celebrate. A price change should not bounce twice; a success checkmark can.

Where curves win

I am not going to pretend springs are universally correct. There are three cases where a curve is better.

1. Choreographed sequences. A 12-step launch animation with precise holds and overlaps needs a timeline. A spring cannot express "hold for 400ms then move". Use curves and keyframes.

2. Exit animations tied to a deadline. If a toast must be gone in 200ms because a modal is opening under it, a fixed duration is a feature, not a limitation.

3. Non-spatial property changes. Opacity, colour and blur do not have momentum. A spring on opacity looks like a bug. Use a short curve — 120–180ms, ease-out — and be done.

There is also the accessibility case: prefers-reduced-motion should replace spatial springs with instant or short fades. Springs make that easy if the runtime supports it, but you have to actually wire it up.

Why design tools struggle with this

Here is the part that connects to tooling.

A spring is not a keyframe. There is no "end time" to place on a timeline, because the end depends on the physics. Tools built around timelines therefore tend to approximate springs — they bake a 500ms curve that looks like a spring for one specific distance, then ship it. Move the object twice as far and the easing is wrong, because a real spring's duration scales with distance.

That is why "we support springs" in a design tool often means "we have a spring-shaped bezier preset". It is fine for playback. It falls apart the moment the object travels a different distance, or gets interrupted.

An environment that stores stiffness/damping/mass as values, and integrates them at runtime, does not have that problem. The design file and the shipped behaviour are the same simulation. That is the argument for a physics-first format, and it is testable: interrupt the animation on the canvas and in the exported component and see whether they behave the same.

A 30-second audit of your own UI

Open your product. Do these three things:

  1. Rapidly toggle a switch five times. Does it keep its momentum, or hesitate?
  2. Open and close a modal before it finishes appearing. Does it reverse smoothly?
  3. Slow your network to 3G and trigger a state change. Does the motion still make sense when it arrives late?

If any of those feel wrong, the issue is almost never the easing curve. It is that the motion was scripted instead of simulated.

The one-line summary

Use springs for anything the user can interrupt. Use curves for anything that is choreographed, non-spatial, or on a deadline. Never use transition: all — that is not a motion decision, it is an accident.

UX Baba writes about interaction design. Exode stores springs as physics parameters rather than baked curves; the free tier at exodeui.com is enough to feel the difference.

title: What is a researcher’s worth?
description:
Why the debate over research isn’t a technology story – and why effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.

We’re no stranger to this question.

For many years, research practitioners have talked with one another about how to “mature” teams so that they understand the value of our work in bringing success to their ventures. Or when we share the results of our research, we are peppered with questions about whether the findings are real, whether the methods are too weak or lack representativeness, or whether our subjects are even telling the truth when they express to us what they need.

But it’s not just research practitioners. Researchers in academia have been stripped of the funding they need to advance science. Academic departments have shuttered, and scholars’ voices have been dismissed as part of major civic scientific efforts, like the Census, the Environmental Protection Agency, or the Department of Education.

Put in this context, contemporary discourse around artificial intelligence replacing our jobs feels less like “the reason” than one reason among many when people question whether researchers (and research, in general) matter.

Over the last ten years, I’ve worked as an industry researcher while keeping a foot in academia, and have had some of the best work experiences of my life. There is a joy and a magic I find in what happens when you bring experts of different disciplines together – research, business, engineering, design, and more – to solve complex puzzles.

So if that cross-disciplinary magic is so real — and so productive — why do researchers in both companies and public life spend so much of their careers on the defensive? Most hot takes right now answer that question with new kinds of work: prompt faster, automate your synthesis, prove your return on investment.

As a social scientist, I think those takes miss what is actually happening. The debate over a researcher’s worth isn’t really a technology story. It’s a story about how institutions handle inconvenient truths.

Why institutions put research on trial.

Back in 2020, I wrote about one of my favorite scenes from the all-too-accurate show, Silicon Valley. In the episode, technologists watch through a one-way mirror as focus group participants give honest feedback about their app. One participant explained that the app made them feel “totally freaked out,” and another explained that it “made me feel stupid.”

Behind the mirror, the exec got angry. “Clearly none of these people get it, maybe this is a bad group…everyone that I showed the beta to loved it.” His colleague explained that this was the fifth focus group and they all shared the same feedback. She then realized he only gave the beta to his engineer friends. “I wanted to give it to people who would understand what I’m trying to do so I could get useful feedback,” he said. “And with all due respect, I gave it to you — the one person without a computing background – and you said it felt engineered.”

Those of us who love the craft of research love talking about research methods. But I find that in many cases, debates about methods in settings like these are not about finding what’s valuable. Methodological nitpicking is a way to avoid disruptions to a preferred plan. In this way, it is a shield against uncertainty – ironically, the very thing that research tries to disambiguate.

Social scientists argue that when under pressure, organizations gravitate toward commensuration – a process by which people working together flatten a messy, pluralistic set of realities into a single spreadsheet metric. The truth is, we do live in a world with a lot of unknowns, and the “winners” of today’s marketplace may not be the same in a few months or years. Under that uncertainty, it is tempting to flatten complex human behavior into click metrics – and flatten researchers into headcount cost compared against a chatbot – mistaking a tidy spreadsheet for certainty.

What AI actually changed: a mirror that rarely talks back.

In 2020, the lead technologist in Silicon Valley had to walk through the door and argue with human beings using their products. In 2026, they don’t have to do that anymore. They can swap the humans behind the glass for a synthetic AI persona trained to give feedback in specific ways.

I’m not here to say that AI is bad for science. I actually love a lot of the applications of artificial intelligence I get to use. I’m more troubled by the discourse around artificial intelligence and research in industry – how people talk about it – and the way it is compared to the human worth of social scientists.

For one, when organizations treat research as theater to rubber-stamp decisions they have already made, synthetic users and LLM summaries offer “good enough” reassurance at a fraction of the cost. Replacing hard-to-reach or marginalized communities with LLM agents doesn’t actually include them, either. It builds statistical caricatures out of dominant internet texts while erasing human consent and real-world inequities – the kind of blind spot that lets an automated camera “touch-up” feature quietly lighten darker skin tones if real people aren’t in the room.

And think about how culture actually moves. A few years ago, if you asked a model trained on historical averages what romance audiences wanted, it would tell you to center a man and a woman falling in love – it never would have bet on a breakout love story about two men playing hockey. Models fed past averages and synthetic data lose the tails of the distribution, the emerging subcultures and edge cases where the future actually starts. Meanwhile, algorithmic platforms mistake digital traces for human intent: a frustrated user clicking three times to fix a broken output looks like “high engagement” in behavioral logs.

Artificial intelligence is an interesting tool, not a good social scientist. But today, AI is giving anxious institutions the frictionless validation they secretly always wanted.

Looking in our own mirror.

Listen, I don’t think researchers are perfect by any means. We’re human after all! I actually think that researchers both in industry and academia accidentally made our worth easy to caricature.

Often professions survive or shrink based on what they claim jurisdiction over – what we diagnose problems to be, to what we attribute their causes, and how we offer treatment. In 2020, I warned that industry research was used too tactically (“go run a focus group”) as a way to drive impact. But over the last decade, much of industry research leaned into method gatekeeping – measuring our worth by how many people we interviewed or surveyed, or how many “insights” we delivered, or how many slide decks were shared.

At the same time, in academia, career incentives rewarded the world’s smartest experts for speaking mainly to peers behind journal paywalls rather than embedding social science into civic and institutional design. For example, a senior professor in my field asked me how I’d like the discipline to advance. I said that we should consider hiring clinical professors to more genuinely bring our findings to the field. He actually laughed at me. “Save it for social work,” he said.

I’m of the opinion that neither of these approaches has really helped anyone. In the former, we have traded using appropriate and defensible methods, asking big questions, and discussing complicated answers for a “study complete” checkbox. In the latter, we have siloed the magic of expert discovery almost entirely to the few people who read a published paper.

Where the magic of research lives.

Why does bringing research, engineering, design, and business together feel like magic? David Stark showed that breakthrough innovation happens in what he calls “heterarchies” – teams that hold competing accounts of worth in creative tension rather than collapsing everything into shipping speed. When AI coding tools let teams spin up twenty working prototypes in a week, velocity is no longer the scarce resource. Knowing which human dream is worth building becomes the scarcest asset in the room. For example, when do you pause a team buried in fifty usability bug fixes to instead ask whether we’re focused on the right value?

Some unfortunate news for my colleagues: humans don’t follow linear product models. They improvise inside their own social groups and cultural ecosystems. They react and adapt to major changes in their lives.

Engineers see systems; product managers see markets and funnels; and social scientists see social structure.

Social scientists can find and explain why youth culture over the last twenty years has shifted from public broadcasting to more intimate pockets of the internet. Or why a certain design aesthetic feels exciting in one region and troubling in another, shaped by the cultural meanings people there share. Or how chaotic-looking livestreams with tens of thousands of people are actually held together by the patterned, organized activities of moderators who keep conversation focused and fun.

In The Tacit Dimension, Hungarian-British polymath Michael Polanyi wrote that “we can know more than we can tell.” A vast amount of human knowledge is nonverbal. It includes how we think about cultural norms that we can’t summarize in a survey, or sometimes even in the context of an interview. My bet is that unguided LLMs can’t uncover that tacit knowledge on their own. But social scientists can. We triangulate methods and hold magnifying glasses up to a social problem in a variety of ways, including by testing our assumptions against an accumulated body of scholarly work in purposefully specific subfields.

Worth is built together.

Whether in a product sprint, a university lab, or a public agency, a researcher’s worth was never the focus group they run, how big or small their sample size is, or the paper they publish. Our worth is how we apply our training and our lens to the messy, plural, inconvenient realities of human life, even when institutions are tempted by easy mirrors that boil experience down to a lone metric.

To my research peers: bring your expertise and critical thinking to the work that you do. Show value to your teams by how you and your work “make the strange familiar, and the familiar strange” in the pursuit of a shared understanding grounded in human experience.

To my academic colleagues: get out of the ivory tower. Meet people who do research and engage in practice for purposes that have nothing to do with publishing. Learn new ways to talk about your work that shed both academic-ese and didactic habits in favor of two-way learning.

To my partners in research: resist the seduction of a mirror that always agrees with you. When AI makes spinning up twenty new ideas effortless, speed stops being your competitive edge – knowing what is actually true about people outside your building is. Invite the friction of someone trained to tell you when your favorite plan doesn’t match how humans really live.

We’ve spent years talking about how to “mature” organizations into valuing research, as if worth were a favor. It isn’t. Worth is built together.

Dr. Matt Rafalow is a senior staff researcher at YouTube, and a visiting scholar at University of Southern California. The views expressed in this article reflects the individual opinions of the author.

What is a researcher’s worth? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Estados de email accesibles en React
description:
Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Crear cuenta”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada: enviar el email, esperar la respuesta, mostrar el resultado y permitir que la persona continúe sin adivinar qué ocurrió.

En proyectos React he encontrado que este flujo se trata aveces como un detalle visual. Un spinner aparece, el botón se desactiva y, si todo va bien, llega un mensaje verde. Ese enfoque falla cuando el correo tarda, cuando el usuario navega con teclado o cuando un lector de pantalla no recibe el cambio. La interfaz necesita un modelo de estados explícito, no solo una animación.

El problema: verificar no es solo mostrar un spinner

Un estado de email tiene al menos cinco momentos útiles:

  1. Inicial: todavía no se ha enviado nada.
  2. Enviando: la petición está en curso y no debe duplicarse.
  3. Esperando: el servidor aceptó la solicitud, pero el mensaje aún no ha sido confirmado.
  4. Verificado: el enlace fue aceptado y el flujo puede continuar.
  5. Error: la persona necesita una explicación y una acción posible.

Separar “enviando” de “esperando” mejora la experiencia. El primer estado responde a la petición HTTP; el segundo describe una espera real del usuario. Mezclarlos en un único loading hace más dificil decidir qué texto anunciar, cuándo habilitar un reenvío y qué parte del formulario debe conservar el foco.

Para probar el flujo sin tocar buzones personales, un generador de correo temporal puede servir como fixture de desarrollo o QA. La regla importante es aislar cada prueba y no usar esos datos para cuentas reales.

Un pequeño modelo de estados para React

Un useState con varios booleanos suele producir combinaciones imposibles: isSending y isVerified activos a la vez, o un error visible después de un reenvío exitoso. Prefiero un único estado discriminado:

type EmailState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "waiting"; address: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

const [emailState, setEmailState] = useState<EmailState>({ kind: "idle" });

El render puede decidir qué mostrar a partir de kind, sin depender de una colección de flags que se contradicen. También facilita las pruebas: cada acción tiene una transición visible y es más facil comprobar que un reintento no aparece antes de tiempo.

Para un reenvío, conservaría un contador local o una marca de tiempo de la última petición. El objetivo no es castigar al usuario, sino evitar que varios clics creen mensajes difíciles de distinguir. Si el servidor responde con un error temporal, el mensaje debe explicar qué puede hacer la persona ahora, por que el siguiente intento está disponible y si el email anterior sigue siendo válido.

Accesibilidad: foco, mensajes y semántica

El texto de estado debe existir en el DOM, no solo cambiar el color del botón. Un contenedor role="status" con aria-live="polite" puede anunciar que el mensaje fue enviado sin interrumpir una tarea actual. Para un fallo que requiere atención inmediata, role="alert" es más apropiado, pero no conviene usarlo para cada cambio pequeño.

Cuando aparece un error debajo del campo, relaciónalo con el input mediante aria-describedby. Si la validación impide avanzar, el foco debe ir al primer control con un problema, no a un banner lejano. La validación y el foco visual debe mantenerse consistente tanto con teclado como con ratón.

El estado de espera necesita una salida clara. Un enlace “Cambiar dirección” o “Reenviar email” debe tener un nombre comprensible fuera de contexto. “Haz clic aquí” no explica nada en una lista de enlaces de un lector de pantalla.

También revisaría el contraste, el indicador de foco y el movimiento. prefers-reduced-motion permite eliminar una animación innecesaria, mientras que un icono no debe ser la única señal de éxito. Un pequeño checklist de calidad antes del email ayuda a revisar estos detalles junto con el resto del onboarding.

CSS y rendimiento sin perder claridad

Los estados visuales no necesitan una biblioteca grande. Una clase por estado, una transición corta y una estructura estable suelen bastar:

.email-status {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
}

.email-status[data-state="error"] {
  color: var(--color-error);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .email-status,
  .email-status * {
    transition: none;
    animation: none;
  }
}

Mantener una altura mínima evita que el formulario salte cuando entra el mensaje. Ese cambio pequeño reduce ruido visual y hace que el foco no parezca moverse. Para medir el resultado, observaría el tiempo hasta el primer mensaje útil, los reintentos duplicados y los errores de validación, no solo el tiempo de carga inicial.

En la práctica, el frontend también debe tolerar respuestas lentas. Una señal como “Estamos esperando el email” es mejor que un spinner infinito. Si el backend finalmente deja de reintentar, la interfaz debe reflejar la misma decisión; este principio de decidir cuándo dejar de reintentar un email evita prometer una recuperación que ya no existe.

Checklist para revisar el flujo

  • ¿Cada transición tiene un texto visible y entendible?
  • ¿El botón evita peticiones duplicadas mientras se envía?
  • ¿El lector de pantalla recibe los cambios mediante una región viva?
  • ¿El foco llega al campo correcto cuando hay un error?
  • ¿El color no es la única diferencia entre éxito, espera y fallo?
  • ¿Existe una acción para corregir la dirección o reenviar el email?
  • ¿La prueba usa un buzón aislado, como tamp mail com, y limpia sus datos después?
  • ¿Los estados funcionan sin animación y con una conexión lenta?

Diseñar esta frontera con cuidado produce una interfaz más tranquila y más fácil de probar. React aporta la estructura, CSS comunica el estado y las reglas de accesibilidad convierten una espera incierta en una secuencia que el usuario puede entender.

title: crdt-sync: محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust، مع CRDT و sqlite و websocket
description:
شخصان يعدّلان الملاحظة نفسها. أحدهما في قطار بلا تغطية، والآخر على مكتبه. وكلاهما يواصل الكتابة. حين يخرج القطار من النفق، كيف يجب أن تكون الملاحظة؟

الجواب الكلاسيكي أن يكون الخادم هو الحَكَم: كل تعديل يذهب إليه، وهو يقرر الترتيب، والعميل الذي بلا اتصال ينتظر. تطبيقات local-first (المحلي أولًا) تقلب هذا. كل جهاز يحمل نسخة كاملة، والتعديلات تُطبَّق فورًا ودون اتصال، والأجهزة تتبادل التغييرات كلما استطاعت الوصول إلى بعضها. والشرط الصعب: بعد تبادل كل شيء، يجب أن تتطابق كل النسخ، مهما كان الترتيب الذي وصلت به التغييرات.

هياكل البيانات التي تضمن ذلك تسمّى CRDT، أي conflict-free replicated data types. و Automerge و Yjs هما المكتبتان المعروفتان المبنيتان عليها. وهما مكتبتان ناضجتان وفيهما تحسينات كثيرة، فقراءتهما طويلة إن كان هدفك أن تفهم كيف تعمل الفكرة.

crdt-sync محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust. المستندات أشجار من CRDT، وراءها سجل عمليات (operation log) و vector clocks. النسخ (replicas) تعدّل دون اتصال، وتخزّن العمليات في sqlite، وتتزامن عبر خادم websocket مبني بـ axum ببروتوكول من رسالتين. ويسمّي الـ README جمهورَيه: المطورون الذين يريدون فهم كيف تعمل تطبيقات local-first من الداخل، ومن يحتاج نقطة انطلاق مدمجة ومقروءة لمزامنة مستندات صغيرة بين أجهزة وخادم يتحكم فيه.

ماذا يقدّم

أربعة أنواع CRDT. المستند شجرة مبنية من هذه:

  • LwwRegister، سجل من نوع last-writer-wins: الختم الأعلى (Lamport، ثم replica) هو الذي يفوز.
  • LwwMap، خريطة فيها سجل LWW لكل مفتاح. الحذف كتابة لـ "لا شيء"، والقيمة قد تكون قيمة بسيطة أو كائنًا متداخلًا.
  • OrSet، مجموعة observed-remove تفوز فيها الإضافة (add-wins): كل إضافة تنشئ وسمًا (tag) فريدًا، والحذف يزيل فقط الوسوم التي رآها.
  • Rga، للنص. كل محرف يُدرج بعد محرف مرجعي، والإدراجات المتزامنة في الموضع نفسه تُرتَّب حسب الختم، والحذف يترك شواهد (tombstones).

سجل العمليات. كل تعديل هو Op له معرّف (replica, seq)، حيث seq يعدّ 1 و2 و3 وهكذا لكل نسخة، ومعه ختم Lamport، والكائن المستهدف، والفعل. ولأن الأرقام التسلسلية بلا ثغرات، فإن vector clock من الشكل replica → highest seq يقول بالضبط أي العمليات تملكها نسخة ما. والسؤال "هل رأيت العملية X" مقارنة واحدة.

التسليم بأي ترتيب. الدالة Doc::apply_remote تقبل العمليات بأي ترتيب وأي عدد من المرات. المعروفة تُهمل. والباقية تنتظر في قائمة حتى تُدمج تبعياتها: العملية السابقة من النسخة نفسها، والكائن المستهدف، والمحرف الذي يأتي الإدراج بعده، والوسوم التي رآها حذف من المجموعة.

بروتوكول مزامنة من رسالتين. الرسالة StateVector(clock) يُجاب عنها بـ Ops(missing)، والرسالة Ops(ops) تُدمج. الطرفان يرسلان الـ state vector عند الاتصال، فجولة واحدة في كل اتجاه تكفي ليصير الاثنان محدَّثين. ثم ينقل الخادم العمليات المدمجة حديثًا إلى كل عميل آخر على المستند نفسه.

ترميز مدمج. أعداد LEB128 varint، وجدول نسخ لكل دفعة حتى يأخذ معرّف العملية بايتًا أو اثنين، وأرقام تسلسلية وأختام Lamport مرمَّزة بالفرق (delta)، واختصارات من بايت واحد لحالتي "الكائن نفسه كالعملية السابقة" و"إدراج بعد العملية السابقة". ويذكر الـ README أن كتابة 1000 محرف تُرمَّز في أقل من 8 KB. والـ decoder يرفض المدخل المبتور أو العدائي دون panic ودون حجز ذاكرة مفرط.

خادم وتخزين. خادم axum يقدّم GET /sync/{doc} كـ websocket بإطارات ثنائية (binary frames)، وGET /docs وGET /docs/{doc} بصيغة JSON. يحتفظ بـ Doc واحد في الذاكرة لكل مستند مفتوح، يُحمَّل من sqlite عند أول استعمال، ويضيف العمليات المدمجة إلى sqlite قبل نقلها. والتخزين جدول واحد، ops(doc, replica, seq, body)، يُكتب بـ INSERT OR IGNORE فيكون الحفظ idempotent.

طريقة الاستعمال

ثبّت الملفين التنفيذيين crdt-server وcrdt-cli من GitHub بواسطة Cargo، أو أضِف المكتبة إلى مشروعك:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

البداية السريعة في الـ README تشغّل خادمًا وعميلين، لكل عميل قاعدة بياناته المحلية، من نسخة محلية للمستودع:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice و Bob كلاهما يكتب status وهو "غير متصل"، و Bob يضيف وسمًا. وبعد المزامنة، يحمل الاثنان المستند نفسه:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

السجل احتفظ بواحدة من الكتابتين المتزامنتين، وهي نفسها على كل نسخة. والمجموعة احتفظت بالوسمين معًا.

أوامر الـ CLI هي: show، info، set KEY VALUE، del KEY، insert KEY INDEX TEXT، erase KEY INDEX COUNT، add KEY VALUE، remove KEY VALUE، sync، watch.

وكمكتبة:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

ما يجب معرفته

قسم الحدود في الـ README طويل وصريح. اقرأه قبل أن تبني على المشروع:

  • لا مصادقة ولا صلاحيات في الخادم. كل من يستطيع الوصول إليه يستطيع قراءة كل مستند والكتابة فيه. شغّله على localhost أو خلف proxy يقوم بالمصادقة.
  • السجلات تكبر بلا نهاية. لا ضغط (compaction)، ولا snapshots، ولا تنظيف للشواهد. والمستند يُعاد بناؤه بإعادة تشغيل سجله كاملًا.
  • النص للملاحظات لا للكتب. البحث في RGA مسح خطي، وهناك عملية لكل محرف.
  • مجموعة صغيرة من الأنواع. لا نص منسَّق، ولا قوائم كائنات، ولا عدّادات، ولا نقل. والإنشاء المتزامن لكائن متداخل تحت المفتاح نفسه يُبقي كائنًا واحدًا (LWW)، والتعديلات على الآخر تُخفى.
  • تحقق محدود من الأطراف. العمليات القادمة من طرف معطوب، والتي تستهدف كائنًا غير موجود أو من نوع خاطئ، تُسجَّل وتُتجاهل. ولا يوجد تحقق ممن يحق له الكتابة بأي replica id.
  • الأمر watch يطبع التغييرات البعيدة فقط. والتعديلات تتم بتشغيلات منفصلة للـ CLI.

ما تم اختباره. الأمر cargo test يشغّل 17 اختبار وحدة، و6 خصائص proptest، و4 اختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية (end-to-end). الخاصية الأساسية هي التقارب (convergence): ثلاث نسخ تقوم بإدراجات وحذوف عشوائية في النص، وإضافات وحذوف في المجموعة، وكتابات في السجل، وتعديلات وحذوف في الخريطة، بينما تُسلَّم مجموعات جزئية عشوائية من سجلات بعضها مخلوطة ومكررة. وفي النهاية يستلم الجميع كل شيء بترتيب مبعثر، مرتين. ويجب ألا تبقى عند أي نسخة عمليات معلّقة، وأن تتساوى الساعات والـ JSON، على 300 حالة. وخصائص أخرى تتحقق من تقارب البروتوكول بمزامنات ثنائية في حلقة، ومن أن النص في نسخة واحدة يطابق نموذج Vec<char>، ومن أن البايتات العشوائية والرسائل المقلوبة بعض بتاتها لا تسبب panic في الـ decoder.

والاختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية تغطي دمج تعديلات عميلين دون اتصال، وخادمًا أُعيد تشغيله يقدّم المستند نفسه من sqlite، وعميلًا متصلًا يستلم التعديلات المنقولة، وعمليتَي crdt-cli تعدّلان دون اتصال ثم تتقاربان. وكفحص إضافي، يذكر الـ README أن كسر قاعدة الترجيح في LWW أو ترتيب الإخوة في RGA يجعل خصائص التقارب تفشل بعد حالات قليلة.

لماذا بنيته

فكرة local-first سهلة القول وصعبة التصديق إلى أن ترى كل قطعة: كيف تُعرَّف العملية، ولماذا يكفي vector clock لمعرفة ما ينقص الطرف الآخر، وماذا يعني "انتظر التبعيات" في الكود، وكيف يُدمج نص يكتب فيه شخصان في الموضع نفسه. المكتبات الناضجة تجيب عن كل هذا، لكن وسط كثير من التحسينات.

أردت المسار كله في كود صغير يُقرأ من أوله إلى آخره: الـ CRDT، والسجل، والترميز الثنائي، والتخزين، والبروتوكول، والخادم. وأردت أن يُتحقق من ادّعاء التقارب باختبارات خصائص لا ببضعة أمثلة مختارة باليد، لأن الأخطاء في هذا النوع من الكود تسكن في التداخلات التي لا تخطر على بال أحد.

الكود

الكود والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. الرخصة MIT. اعتبره نقطة انطلاق مقروءة للمستندات الصغيرة، مع الحدود المذكورة أعلاه.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: crdt-sync: a small local-first sync engine in Rust, with CRDTs, sqlite and websockets
description:
Two people edit the same note. One is on a train with no signal, the other at a desk. Both keep typing. When the train leaves the tunnel, what should the note look like?

The classic answer is to make the server the judge: every edit goes to it, it decides the order, and a client without a connection waits. Local-first apps turn this around. Each device holds a full copy, edits apply immediately and offline, and devices exchange changes whenever they can reach each other. The hard requirement is that after exchanging everything, all copies are identical, no matter in which order the changes arrived.

Data structures with that guarantee are called CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types. Automerge and Yjs are the well-known libraries built on them. They are mature, optimized libraries, which makes them a long read if your goal is to learn how the idea works.

crdt-sync is a small local-first sync engine in Rust. Documents are trees of CRDTs, backed by an operation log and vector clocks. Replicas edit offline, store operations in sqlite, and sync through an axum websocket server with a two-message protocol. The README names its two audiences: developers who want to understand how local-first apps work underneath, and those who need a compact, readable starting point for syncing small documents between devices and a server they control.

What it does

Four CRDT types. A document is a tree built from these:

  • LwwRegister, a last-writer-wins register: the highest (Lamport, replica) stamp wins.
  • LwwMap, a map with an LWW register per key. A delete is a write of "nothing", and a value can be a scalar or a nested object.
  • OrSet, an observed-remove set with add-wins behaviour: each add makes a unique tag, and a remove deletes only the tags it observed.
  • Rga, text. Each character is inserted after a reference character, concurrent inserts at the same spot are ordered by stamp, and deletes leave tombstones.

An operation log. Every edit is an Op with an id (replica, seq), where seq counts 1, 2, 3 and so on per replica, plus a Lamport timestamp, a target object and an action. Because sequence numbers have no gaps, a vector clock replica → highest seq says exactly which operations a replica has. "Have I seen op X" is one comparison.

Delivery in any order. Doc::apply_remote accepts operations in any order, any number of times. Known ones are dropped. The rest wait in a pending list until their dependencies are integrated: the previous op of the same replica, the object they target, the character an insert goes after, and the tags a set-remove observed.

A two-message sync protocol. StateVector(clock) is answered with Ops(missing), and Ops(ops) is integrated. Both ends send their state vector on connect, so one round trip each way brings both up to date. The server then relays newly integrated operations to every other client on the same document.

A compact encoding. LEB128 varints, a per-batch replica table so op ids take one or two bytes, delta-coded sequence numbers and Lamport times, and one-byte shortcuts for "same object as the previous op" and "insert after the previous op". The README states that typing 1000 characters encodes to under 8 KB. The decoder rejects truncated or hostile input without panicking or over-allocating.

A server and storage. The axum server exposes GET /sync/{doc} as a websocket with binary frames, plus GET /docs and GET /docs/{doc} as JSON. It keeps one in-memory Doc per open document, loaded from sqlite on first use, and appends integrated ops to sqlite before relaying them. Storage is one table, ops(doc, replica, seq, body), written with INSERT OR IGNORE so saving is idempotent.

How to use it

Install the two binaries, crdt-server and crdt-cli, from GitHub with Cargo, or add the library to a project:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

The README's quick start runs a server and two clients, each with its own local database, from a clone of the repository:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice and Bob both set status while "offline", and Bob adds a tag. After syncing, both hold the same document:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

The register kept one of the two concurrent writes, the same one on every replica. The set kept both tags.

The CLI commands are show, info, set KEY VALUE, del KEY, insert KEY INDEX TEXT, erase KEY INDEX COUNT, add KEY VALUE, remove KEY VALUE, sync and watch.

As a library:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

Things to know

The README's limitations section is long and plain. Read it before you build on this:

  • No authentication or authorization on the server. Anyone who can reach it can read and write every document. Run it on localhost or behind an authenticating proxy.
  • Logs grow forever. There is no compaction, no snapshots and no tombstone garbage collection. A document is rebuilt by replaying its whole log.
  • Text is for notes, not books. RGA lookups are linear scans, and there is one op per character.
  • A small set of types. No rich text, lists of objects, counters or moves. Concurrent creation of a nested object under the same key keeps one object (LWW), and edits made to the other are hidden.
  • Limited peer validation. Ops from a buggy peer that target a missing object or the wrong kind are logged and ignored. There is no check of who may write which replica id.
  • watch only prints remote changes. Edits are made with separate CLI invocations.

What is tested. cargo test runs 17 unit tests, 6 proptest properties and 4 end-to-end tests. The main property is convergence: three replicas perform random text inserts and deletes, set adds and removes, register writes and map sets and deletes, while random subsets of each other's logs are delivered shuffled and duplicated. In the end everyone receives everything in a scrambled order, twice. All replicas must have no pending ops, equal clocks and equal JSON, over 300 cases. Other properties check protocol convergence over pairwise syncs in a ring, that single-replica text matches a Vec<char> model, and that random bytes and bit-flipped messages never panic the decoder.

The end-to-end tests cover offline edits from two clients merging, a restarted server serving the same document from sqlite, a live client receiving relayed edits, and two crdt-cli processes that edit offline and converge. As a sanity check, the README notes that breaking the LWW tie-break or the RGA sibling ordering makes the convergence properties fail within a few cases.

Why I built it

The idea behind local-first is easy to state and hard to trust until you have seen every piece: how an operation is identified, why a vector clock is enough to know what a peer is missing, what "wait for dependencies" means in code, and how text can merge when two people type at the same position. The mature libraries answer all of this, but inside a lot of optimization.

I wanted the whole path in one small codebase that can be read end to end: the CRDTs, the log, the binary encoding, the storage, the protocol and a server. And I wanted the convergence claim to be checked by property tests and not by a few hand-picked examples, because the bugs in this kind of code live in the interleavings nobody thinks of.

Get the code

The source and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. It is MIT licensed. Treat it as a readable starting point for small documents, with the limits listed above.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available
description:
Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale — you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user.

Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on EC2, this release adds Spark Connect support on multi-primary clusters, along with Secret Agent improvements that cut user-provisioning latency by up to 97% under high concurrency. On EMR Serverless, new scaling profiles for Spark (performance-optimized, balanced, or cost-optimized) let you tune how quickly executors scale, and applications can now run Lake Formation-governed Glue UDFs. On EMR on EKS, the Spark Operator is upgraded to version 2 (based on open-source Spark Operator 2.5.0).

Amazon EMR 8.2 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EMR 8.2 Release Guide for EMR on EC2, the EMR Serverless release notes, and the EMR on EKS release notes, or get started by creating a cluster from the Amazon EMR console.

title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless
description:
Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. Data engineers can also use the agent during development to tune configurations before promoting to production. All access is authenticated with AWS IAM and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge in all Regions where EMR Serverless is available, except GovCloud (US) and China Regions, for EMR release versions 7.6 and later. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless.
