title: AWS Transform now accelerates migration deals for Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) benefits
description:
AWS Partners can now expedite Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) deals, from qualification to incentive payout, with an end-to-end agentic workflow in AWS Transform. Partners can manage the full MAP lifecycle without leaving AWS Transform, including deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, migration planning and execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement.

Previously, Partners had to switch between separate systems for opportunity discovery, assessments, deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. This fragmentation, along with manual handoffs between steps, led to longer qualification cycles.

Now, with the agentic MAP experience in AWS Transform, Partners connect their AWS Partner Central account and invite customers into the same engagement. Partners start by scoping customer environments with the built-in agentic discovery tool, or by importing data from RVTools or AWS-validated ISV tools listed in AWS Marketplace. AWS Transform then combines this discovery data with opportunity details from APN Customer Engagements (ACE) to automatically qualify Partner-initiated opportunities in a guided flow, so Partners get eligibility decisions sooner and close deals faster. As the migration progresses, MAP resource tags are applied automatically, and Partner cash and customer credits are disbursed based on actual usage data. Throughout, customers get shared, real-time visibility into migration projects alongside their Partner.

AWS Transform with integrated MAP is now available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) page. Partners can get started with the AWS Partner Central user guide (login required) or by contacting their Partner Development Manager. Customers can contact their AWS account team or AWS Partner.

title: Amazon EC2 C8gn instances are now available in AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region
description:
Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8gn instances, powered by the latest-generation AWS Graviton4 processors, are available in the AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region. The C8gn instances provide up to 30% better compute performance than Graviton3-based Amazon EC2 C7gn instances. Amazon EC2 C8gn instances feature the latest 6th generation AWS Nitro Cards, and offer up to 600 Gbps network bandwidth, the highest network bandwidth among network optimized EC2 instances. 

Take advantage of the enhanced networking capabilities of C8gn to scale performance and throughput, while optimizing the cost of running network-intensive workloads such as network virtual appliances, data analytics, CPU-based artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) inference. 

For increased scalability, C8gn instances offer instance sizes up to 48xlarge, up to 384 GiB of memory, and up to 120 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS). C8gn instances support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on the 16xlarge, 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes, which enables lower latency and improved cluster performance for workloads deployed on tightly coupled clusters. 

C8gn instances are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon, N.California), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain, Zurich, Milan, Paris), Asia Pacific (Singapore, Malaysia, Sydney, Thailand, Mumbai, Seoul, Melbourne, Jakarta, Hyderabad, Tokyo, Hong Kong), Middle East (UAE), Israel (Tel Aviv), Africa (Cape Town), Canada West (Calgary, Central), South America (Sao Paulo), AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West).

title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition.

Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before.

Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide.

title: Your device rebooted at a customer site. What do you know?
description:
Picture a small device you built, a sensor inside a machine at a customer's site a few hundred kilometres away. One morning the customer tells you it restarted during the night. What do you know about why?

On your desk, a debugger would answer that: a cable to the chip and a tool that stops the program and shows where it is. In the field there is no cable, no screen and nobody watching. The device is the only witness, and as we'll see in a moment, by default it forgets everything when it restarts.

ferrite exists for this situation: a device in the field has crashed, and there is no stack trace, no log and nothing that says what happened.

We'll follow one crash twice. First we ask what it leaves behind with nothing in place. Then we let ferrite, an open-source Rust library for this problem, save a small record of the crash, and we turn that record back into the line of code that crashed. Everything runs in QEMU, a program that emulates a computer, here a board with an Arm Cortex-M3 processor, so you can repeat it without hardware. The crash is planted on purpose: this post shows how a crash gets recorded, not how to find a real bug.

What happens when a microcontroller crashes?

A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip, with a processor, memory and peripherals, running one program, the firmware, with no operating system underneath. When the processor meets something it cannot do, such as an instruction it does not know or a memory access that fails, it stops what it was doing and calls a fault handler: a function the program provides for exactly this case. On Cortex-M chips the catch-all one is called HardFault.

Here is the function that will crash for us:

/// The bug we are going to find. `udf` is an instruction the processor
/// refuses to execute, so this function crashes every time.
#[inline(never)]
fn handle_message() {
    unsafe { core::arch::asm!("udf #0") };
}

udf means "undefined": an instruction reserved to be invalid, so running it always faults. #[inline(never)] keeps handle_message a function of its own, so the crash has a name we can find later.

What does the fault handler do if we don't write one? cortex-m-rt, the startup crate this program is built on, provides a default that loops forever (its source). The device freezes. Many products have a watchdog, a hardware timer that resets the chip unless the program checks in regularly, so a frozen device restarts a moment later. I ran this program without ferrite in QEMU, and it printed its first line and then nothing, until I stopped QEMU.

So after the restart, what is left? Before main runs, the startup code gives every global variable its initial value: it zeroes some memory and copies initial values into the rest. Whatever the crashed run knew is overwritten, and the new run starts exactly like the first one. That is why all the customer can tell you is "it restarted".

What would we want the device to tell us?

Suppose the device could leave us a note. What should it say? Three things get us from "it restarted" to a line of code:

  • That it crashed, and the processor's reason. Cortex-M chips keep this in a fault status register, a few bits that tell an undefined instruction apart from, say, a bad memory access.
  • Where it was: the program counter, the address of the instruction that was running.
  • Which build it was running, because an address only means something in the exact program that produced it.

The note also has to travel from the device to someone who can read it. That part comes in later posts. Here the device prints its note.

A note that survives the reset

ferrite brings its own HardFault handler. It copies the registers that matter into a small region of RAM and then resets the chip itself. What makes this work is where it writes. That region is a small block, at most 256 bytes (192 in this build), in a part of RAM the build sets aside under the name .uninit.ferrite. It lies outside the memory the startup code initialises, so the next run's startup leaves it alone. A reset restarts the program, but it does not erase RAM, so the note is still there afterwards. Post 2 looks at this region more closely, including why it does not survive a power cut.

Here is main. Look for two things: init, which tells ferrite about the device, and last_fault, which returns the note if a previous run left one.

#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    ferrite_sdk::init(SdkConfig {
        device_id: "qemu-demo-01",
        firmware_version: "0.1.0",
        build_id: 0,
        ticks_fn: || 0,
        ram_regions: &[RamRegion { start: 0x2000_0000, end: 0x2000_FC00 }],
    });

    if let Some(fault) = last_fault() {
        hprintln!("boot: the previous run crashed");
        hprintln!("  pc   = {:#010x}", fault.frame.pc);
        hprintln!("  cfsr = {:#010x}", fault.cfsr);
        debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }

    hprintln!("boot: no crash recorded, handling a message");
    handle_message();
    hprintln!("message handled");
    debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    loop {}
}

hprintln! prints to your terminal through a debug channel QEMU provides, and debug::exit ends QEMU. ram_regions tells the fault handler which addresses are safe to read while it collects its note. pc is the program counter, and cfsr is the fault status register.

Before we run it, what should it print? On the first run there is no note, so we should see "no crash recorded", then the crash in handle_message. The handler saves its note and resets, and the program starts again from the top. This time last_fault finds the note, so we should see a second "boot" line from the same QEMU session, and never "message handled".

Running it in QEMU

The project is the program above plus a Cargo.toml and a few build files for this QEMU board, in the ferrite-sdk repository as examples/qemu-fault at commit b51bfed. With QEMU and Rust's thumbv7m-none-eabi target installed, run this in that directory:

cargo build --release
qemu-system-arm -cpu cortex-m3 -machine lm3s6965evb -nographic \
  -semihosting-config enable=on,target=native \
  -kernel target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault

I ran it from a fresh checkout of commit b51bfed, with rustc 1.97.0 and QEMU 7.2.22 (Debian 12's package), and it printed:

Timer with period zero, disabling
boot: no crash recorded, handling a message
boot: the previous run crashed
  pc   = 0x00000158
  cfsr = 0x00010000

The first line is QEMU's own message about a timer on the emulated board, not our program's. The rest matches the prediction. When the handler asked for a reset, QEMU restarted the emulated chip and loaded the program again, and like the real chip it left the rest of RAM as it was, so the note survived.

What about cfsr = 0x00010000? Only bit 16 is set, and in Arm's documentation for this register bit 16 is called UNDEFINSTR: the processor tried to run an undefined instruction. That is our udf. So the note already tells us why. Where is the next question.

From an address to a line of code

0x00000158 is only a number. To turn it into a line, we need the file the compiler produced, the ELF file. Besides the program, it can carry debug information: a table from addresses to source lines. Our Cargo.toml asks for it in release builds with debug = 2. The tool addr2line from GNU binutils (in the arm-none-eabi build) looks an address up in that table:

arm-none-eabi-addr2line -f -C -s -e target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault 0x00000158

-f asks for the function name, -C turns Rust's encoded symbol names back into readable ones, and -s leaves out the directories. It prints:

qemu_fault::handle_message
main.rs:39

Line 39 of main.rs is the udf line.

There is a condition hiding in that step. We looked the address up in the same file that ran. Change one line above handle_message, rebuild, and the code moves to different addresses: the same 0x00000158 would then point somewhere else, and addr2line would print that other line without complaint. That is why the build belongs in the note. ferrite sends the firmware_version from init with every report, so whoever reads a report knows which release's ELF to look it up in. A version string only identifies a build if it changes with every build, though: our example says "0.1.0" whatever we change, so after that one-line edit its note would still claim 0.1.0. The field meant for the exact build is build_id, which the SDK documents as the first 8 bytes of the ELF's build ID. We left it at 0 here; post 4 is about matching reports to builds.

What a real device does differently

Our program stops after printing so that QEMU exits. A device in the field would carry on with its work after the reset. When it next has a connection, ferrite sends the note, together with the device name and firmware version, to ferrite's server. The server stores the ELF files you upload and runs the addr2line step itself. Making sure each report is looked up in the ELF of the build that produced it is the subject of post 4. After a successful upload, the device clears the note, ready for the next crash.

Let's take stock. With a small block of RAM the startup code does not touch, the program counter and the fault status survived the reset, and the ELF of the same build turned the address into main.rs:39. That rests on one claim we haven't examined: that RAM keeps its contents through a reset. Why does it, how does the program tell a real note from leftover noise, and what happens when the power goes? That's the next post.

title: My Dashboard Synced Itself Only While You Watched. Background Tabs Broke That.
description:
VoiceDash is the client portal I build for voice AI agencies: each agency's clients log in and see their own agent's calls, transcripts and analytics. For a long time those calls arrived two ways. Retell pushed them by webhook, and there was a "Sync Calls" button for everything the webhook missed.

The button was the problem. Nobody presses a sync button on a dashboard they opened to read numbers. So I wrote a small React hook that syncs on its own, shipped it, and less than an hour later shipped a fix for a case I had not thought about: a tab you have not looked at yet.

This is that hook, the one-line bug, and the parts I still have not fixed.

What the hook does

Two client pages show calls: the conversation list and the analytics dashboard. Both now call the same hook with the agent's ID and a callback that reloads the page's data.

const SYNC_EVERY_MS = 60_000;
/** Returning to the tab syncs again unless the last sync was this recent. */
const MIN_GAP_ON_RETURN_MS = 15_000;

export function useCallSync(agentId: string | undefined, onSynced: () => void) {
  const onSyncedRef = useRef(onSynced);
  onSyncedRef.current = onSynced;

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!agentId) return;
    let stopped = false;
    let running = false;
    let lastRun = 0;
    // sync(), onVisibilityChange(), the timer and the cleanup go here
  }, [agentId]);
}

Three triggers: when the page opens, when the tab comes back into view (unless it synced in the last 15 seconds), and every minute while the tab is visible. The callback lives in a ref so the effect does not tear down and restart its timer every time the parent re-renders with a new arrow function. The effect depends only on agentId.

The running flag stops a slow sync from overlapping with the next tick. stopped stops a sync that finishes after the user navigated away from calling back into an unmounted page.

Why "only while visible"

The server route behind the hook calls Retell's list-calls API with the agent's key. A dashboard left open in a forgotten tab for a weekend should not call a vendor API 2,880 times for nobody. So the first version guarded every sync the same way:

const sync = async () => {
  if (running || document.visibilityState !== "visible") return;
  // ...
};

sync();
const timer = setInterval(sync, SYNC_EVERY_MS);

That reads fine. It is also wrong for one case that showed up almost immediately.

The background tab

Open a dashboard with a middle click. Or restore a browser session with five portal tabs. The page loads, renders the calls already in the database, and its visibilityState is "hidden". The opening sync returns early.

Nothing is broken yet. The moment you switch to that tab, visibilitychange fires and the hook syncs. But between load and switch, the page shows stale data while looking finished, and the dashboard's whole promise was "you never press Sync".

The fix was to treat the opening sync differently from the repeat:

const sync = async ({ evenIfHidden = false } = {}) => {
  if (running || (!evenIfHidden && document.visibilityState !== "visible")) return;
  running = true;
  lastRun = Date.now();
  try {
    await fetch("/api/retell/sync-calls", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ agentId }),
    });
  } catch {
    // Calls that arrived by webhook still show; the next sync retries.
  } finally {
    running = false;
  }
  if (!stopped) onSyncedRef.current();
};

sync({ evenIfHidden: true });
const timer = setInterval(() => sync(), SYNC_EVERY_MS);

Note the () => sync() in setInterval. Passing sync directly would still work here because setInterval calls it with no arguments, but the wrapper makes it obvious that the repeat never gets evenIfHidden.

The rule I took from it: a page someone opened is a request, even if they are not looking at it yet. A timer someone forgot about is not. Those deserve different guards, and I had written one guard for both.

Refreshing without flicker

Syncing is half of it. After a sync the page has to show the result without becoming a loading skeleton every minute.

On analytics, the fetch takes a quiet flag that skips the loading placeholders, plus a request counter so an old response cannot overwrite a newer date range the user picked meanwhile:

const fetchData = async (quiet = false) => {
  const request = ++latestRequest.current;
  if (!quiet) setLoading(true);
  // ... fetch /api/analytics
  if (res.ok && request === latestRequest.current) setData(await res.json());
};

useCallSync(agentId, () => fetchData(true));

The conversation list was harder because the user might have scrolled through three pages and opened a transcript. Replacing the list would throw that away. So the refresh fetches the newest page and merges: unseen calls go on top, calls already shown get their fields updated (a call stored mid-call gets its final duration and transcript later), and the list is re-sorted by start time. If the search box changed while the request was in flight, the result belongs to a different list and is dropped.

What makes it safe to call this often

The client side is the easy part. The reason a once-a-minute sync is cheap lives on the server, and I covered most of it in A Webhook Tells You Something Happened, Not That You Have Everything. The short version:

  • Each agent stores callsSyncedUntil, how far its Retell history is known to be complete. A routine sync reads oldest first from two hours before that point, so it is usually a single request.
  • The watermark only moves forward. The update is conditional (callsSyncedUntil: null or lt: until), so two syncs of the same agent racing each other cannot move it backward.
  • Inserts use createMany with skipDuplicates against a unique key on (agentId, platformCallId). Two tabs syncing the same agent at the same second store each call once.
  • The route spends at most 25 seconds answering, then hands whatever is left of a long history to Next.js after() with a bigger budget and a resume cursor.

Without those four, a polling hook on the client would be a load generator. With them, the hook is mostly a trigger.

What I have not fixed

Honest list, from reading the code again for this post. None of these have shipped.

The hook ignores the response status. fetch only rejects on network failure. If the route returns 502 because Retell is down, or 400 because the key was removed, the hook treats it as a finished sync, calls onSynced, and tries again in a minute. No backoff, and nothing on screen says the numbers are no longer being refreshed. The page just quietly stops changing. I would rather show a small "last synced 14 minutes ago" line than have someone trust a frozen dashboard.

Every visible tab polls on its own. running is per hook instance. Two tabs on the same agent's analytics, both visible on two monitors, make two sync requests a minute. The server makes that safe, not free. A BroadcastChannel so one tab syncs and the others just refresh would fix it. I have not needed it badly enough yet.

The list merge only looks at the newest page. If a sync backfills calls from last month (a gap left by a broken webhook, say), they land in the database but not in a list you already scrolled, because the merge only fetches the first 50. They appear on the next full load. Rare, but it is exactly the case the backfill exists for.

A first sync can hold the request for 25 seconds. For an agent with no watermark, the opening sync reads Retell history up to the route's budget before answering. The page is usable the whole time, but the "new calls appear" moment can lag on a freshly connected agent.

What I would tell myself before writing it

Polling from the browser is a reasonable choice when the server work is idempotent and incremental. Most of my effort went there, not into the hook, and that was the right split.

The hook itself needed exactly one more distinction than I gave it: who asked for this sync? The page opening, the user coming back, or a timer. Each one deserves its own guard, and collapsing them into a single visibilityState check cost me a release.

If you build portals for voice agents, this is part of what goes into VoiceDash. And if you have solved the "one tab syncs, the rest listen" problem in production, I would like to know whether BroadcastChannel held up or whether you ended up with locks in localStorage.

title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
description: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
